The morning sun rose over the rolling hills of Virginia, casting long shadows across the fields where the Esmond family had lived for generations. It was a day of quiet anticipation, the kind that precedes change. Harry Esmond, a young man whose spirit burned brighter than the summer heat, stood at the edge of the estate, his gaze fixed on the distant road leading toward England. His heart was heavy with a mixture of longing and duty; he had heard whispers of trouble brewing across the Atlantic, whispers that suggested the old order was fracturing under the weight of new ideas.

He turned back to the house, where the familiar sounds of domestic life drifted out—the clatter of dishes, the murmur of conversation. Inside, his mother, Lady Esmond, moved with a grace that belied her age, her eyes often finding Harry as he passed. She saw the restlessness in him, the same restlessness that had driven his father before him to seek fortune and glory. "You cannot stay here forever, Harry," she said softly, meeting his eyes as he entered the hall. "The world is calling you, and though it may be dangerous, it is also where your destiny lies."

Harry nodded, though his mind was already miles away. He thought of the stories his father used to tell, of battles fought and lands won, of the thrill of adventure that seemed so far removed from the quiet routine of their plantation life. Yet, there was a pull, a magnetic force drawing him outward, urging him to see what lay beyond the horizon.

As the day wore on, the family gathered for supper. The table was set with the simple fare of Virginia, but the atmosphere was charged with unspoken tension. Harry's uncle, Mr. Warrington, sat at the head of the table, his presence commanding and his words sharp. He spoke of the growing unrest in the colonies, of the whispers of rebellion that were beginning to circulate among the people. "We must be prepared," he warned, his voice low but firm. "Times are changing, and those who do not adapt will find themselves left behind."

Harry listened intently, his mind racing with the implications of his uncle's words. He felt a surge of excitement mixed with fear. The idea of war, of conflict, was not entirely foreign to him, but the prospect of being caught in its midst was daunting. Yet, there was also a sense of purpose, a feeling that he was meant to play a role in the unfolding drama of history.

After supper, Harry wandered outside, the cool night air refreshing against his skin. He walked along the path that led to the edge of the woods, where the trees stood tall and silent, guarding the secrets of the forest. Here, he found solace in the solitude, allowing his thoughts to drift freely. He imagined himself in England, amidst the bustling streets of London, surrounded by friends and foes alike. He wondered if he would ever return to this peaceful home, or if his journey would take him far beyond the reach of his family's influence.

As he stood there, lost in thought, a figure emerged from the shadows. It was his cousin, George, who had recently returned from a trip to the city. George's face was etched with worry, his eyes reflecting the turmoil of the times. "Harry," he called out, breaking the silence. "Have you heard the news? There are rumors of a gathering in the north, of men preparing for battle. Something big is coming, and we cannot ignore it."

Harry turned to face his cousin, his expression serious. "What do you think we should do, George?" he asked. "Should we stay here and hope for the best, or should we prepare ourselves for whatever comes?"

George hesitated, then shook his head. "We cannot afford to wait," he replied. "If there is going to be trouble, we need to be ready. We need to know our strengths and weaknesses, and we need to work together as a family. Only then can we face whatever challenges lie ahead."

With these words, the two cousins parted ways, each lost in their own thoughts. But the seed of change had been planted, and soon, the quiet days of Virginia would give way to a storm that would shake the foundations of the colony and reshape the course of history.

The following evening, Harry found himself in a small tavern in the nearby town, seeking refuge from the growing unease that permeated the air. The place was dimly lit, the air thick with the smell of ale and roasted meat. Patrons filled the room, their voices rising in animated conversation about the latest news from the capital. Harry sat alone at a corner table, nursing a glass of wine, his mind still preoccupied with the thoughts of England and the uncertain future that awaited him.

A man approached his table, his bearing confident and his smile warm. "Good evening, sir," he said, extending a hand. "I am Mr. Blackwood, a traveler passing through. May I join you?"

Harry accepted the invitation, and the two men engaged in lively conversation. Mr. Blackwood proved to be a man of many stories, his tales ranging from the exotic lands he had visited to the political intrigues of the court. As they talked, Harry learned more about the state of affairs in the colonies and the growing tensions that threatened to tear them apart.

"You speak of England with such passion," Mr. Blackwood observed, leaning forward. "Do you truly believe that your destiny lies there?"

Harry sighed, setting down his glass. "I do not know," he admitted. "All I know is that something is changing, and I feel compelled to be part of it. Whether it leads to greatness or ruin, I cannot say."

Mr. Blackwood nodded sympathetically. "Change is always perilous," he agreed. "But it is also the engine of progress. Perhaps your journey will lead you to discover things you never imagined possible."

As the night wore on, Harry found himself drawn deeper into the conversation, his initial reservations melting away under the warmth of Mr. Blackwood's company. For a moment, he forgot about the troubles that loomed on the horizon and allowed himself to dream of the adventures that lay ahead.

But dreams, like reality, are fleeting. Before long, the clock struck midnight, and Harry was forced to bid farewell to his new acquaintance. As he stepped out into the cool night air, he felt a renewed sense of determination. Whatever challenges lay ahead, he knew he would face them with courage and resolve.

The Esmond family continued to navigate the turbulent waters of the times, each member grappling with their own fears and hopes. Lady Esmond, ever the matriarch, worked tirelessly to maintain the stability of the household, her strength serving as a beacon of hope for her children. Her son, Thomas, a man of quiet dignity, took on the responsibility of managing the estate's affairs, ensuring that the family's resources were preserved for the uncertain future.

Harry, meanwhile, remained restless, his mind constantly wandering to the possibilities of what lay beyond the horizon. He spent his days reading books on history and politics, seeking to understand the forces that shaped the world around him. At night, he would sit by the fire, listening to the stories of his ancestors and dreaming of the legacy he hoped to leave behind.

As the weeks passed, the signs of impending conflict became harder to ignore. Rumors of armed gatherings and secret meetings spread like wildfire, fueling the anxieties of the people. The Esmonds, like many other families in the colony, found themselves caught in the crossfire of a brewing storm.

Yet, amidst the chaos, there were moments of clarity. Harry realized that the true test of character was not in avoiding danger, but in facing it with integrity and courage. He resolved to stand by his family, no matter what challenges lay ahead. And so, the stage was set for a drama that would unfold over the coming months, a drama that would test the limits of human endurance and redefine the course of history.

Upon the library wall of a celebrated American writer hang two crossed swords, relics of the Great War of Independence. One blade was drawn in loyal service to the Crown; the other, wielded by a brave and honored republican soldier. The owner of these harmless trophies has earned a name revered equally in his ancestral land and his own, where genius is always welcomed in peace.

This history mirrors those swords in the historian's study at Boston. During the Revolutionary War, the subjects of this tale—native-born Americans and children of the Old Dominion—found themselves arrayed on opposing sides. Yet, at the conflict's conclusion, they reunited peacefully as brethren should, their enduring love having diminished only slightly despite the anger of their contest. In the wainscoted parlour of the Warringtons in England, the portrait of the colonel in scarlet hangs beside that of the general in blue and buff. A descendant of one brother has shown me these effigies, along with letters and papers belonging to them. Within the Warrington family, distinguished from other members of that respectable race, these figures are known simply as "The Virginians"; by this name, their memoirs are titled.

Both spent considerable time in Europe, living on the very verge of that Old World from which we drift so swiftly. They encountered a vast variety of men and fortunes, mingling with personages known only from books, yet vividly alive in the letters they penned. I read these yellowed pages, scored with the boyish tears of disappointed passion, dutifully dispatched after grand balls and ceremonies of the Old World, scribbled by campfires or from prison cells. One letter bears a bullet hole, its text largely blotted out with the blood of its bearer.

Had it not been for the affectionate thrift of one person, these letters might have perished. Their mother preserved every missive from her sons, beginning with the first, in which Henry, the younger twin, sends his love to his brother, then ill with a sprain at his grandfather's house of Castlewood in Virginia, and thanking his grandpapa for a horse ridden with his tutor. The correspondence ends with the final message, "from my beloved son," reaching her mere hours before her death. The venerable lady, known as Madam Esmond after the burning of Castlewood during the war, rarely visited Europe, taking refuge in Richmond when her home was consumed by flames. She held the name and family of Warrington in slight esteem compared to her own.

As the reader will soon discover, the letters of the Virginians are far from exhaustive. They offer hints rather than full descriptions—indications and outlines chiefly. Perhaps the present writer has mistaken the forms or filled in the colors wrongly; yet, poring over these documents, I have endeavored to imagine the writer's situation, the persons surrounding him, and to draw the figures as I fancied them. I have set down conversations as I believe I might have heard them, striving to revivify the bygone times and people to the best of my ability. Whether this task has been accomplished successfully, and whether it has provided profit or amusement, the kind reader shall determine.

One summer morning in the year 1756, during the reign of King George the Second, the *Young Rachel*, a Virginian ship commanded by Edward Franks, ascended the Avon River on her happy return from her annual voyage to the Potomac. She proceeded to Bristol with the tide, mooring near Trail's Wharf, to which she was consigned. Mr. Trail, a part-owner who could survey his vessel from his counting-house windows, immediately took a boat and approached her side. The owner of the *Young Rachel*, a large, grave man with his own hair and a demure aspect, extended a hand of welcome to Captain Franks, who stood upon the deck. Congratulating the captain on the speedy and fortunate voyage, the owner promptly turned to business, inquiring particulars regarding cargo and passengers.

Franks was a pleasant man who loved a jest. "We have," he said, "but yonder ugly negro boy fetching the trunks, and a passenger who has the state cabin to himself."

Mr. Trail looked as though he would prefer fewer mercies from Heaven. "Confound you, Franks, and your luck! The *Duke William*, which arrived last week, brought fourteen, and she is not half our tonnage."

"And this passenger, who occupies the whole cabin, pays nothing," continued the Captain. "Swear now, it will do you good, Mr. Trail; indeed it will. I have tried the medicine."

"A passenger takes the whole cabin and pays nothing? Gracious mercy, are you a fool, Captain Franks?"

"Ask the passenger himself, for here he comes." As the master spoke, a young man of about nineteen emerged from the hatchway. He wore a cloak and carried a sword under his arm, dressed in deep mourning. "Gumbo, you idiot, why don't you fetch the baggage out of the cabin?" he called out. "Well, shipmate, our journey is ended. You will see all the little folks tonight whom you have been talking about. Give my love to Polly, and Betty, and Little Tommy; not forgetting my duty to Mrs. Franks. I thought yesterday the voyage would never be done, and now I am almost sorry it is over. That little berth in my cabin looks very comfortable now that I am leaving it."

Mr. Trail scowled at the young passenger who had paid no money for his passage. He scarcely nodded to the stranger when Captain Franks introduced him: "This here gentleman is Mr. Trail, sir, whose name you have heard of."

"It's pretty well known in Bristol, sir," said Mr. Trail, majestically.

"And this is Mr. Warrington, Madam Esmond Warrington's son, of Castlewood," continued the Captain.

The British merchant instantly removed his hat, and the owner of the beaver began making a prodigious number of bows as if a crown prince stood before him.

"Gracious powers, Mr. Warrington! This is a delight, indeed! What a crowning mercy that your voyage should have been so prosperous! You must have my boat to go on shore. Let me cordially and respectfully welcome you to England: let me shake your hand as the son of my benefactress and patroness, Mrs. Esmond Warrington, whose name is known and honoured on Bristol 'Change, I warrant you. Isn't it, Franks?"

"There's no sweeter tobacco comes from Virginia, and no better brand than the Three Castles," said Mr. Franks, drawing a great brass tobacco-box from his pocket and thrusting a quid into his jolly mouth. "You don't know what a comfort it is, sir! You'll take to it, bless you, as you grow older. Won't he, Mr. Trail? I wish you had ten shiploads of it instead of one. You might have ten shiploads: I've told Madam Esmond so; I've rode over her plantation; she treats me like a lord when I go to the house; she doesn't grudge me the best of wine, nor keep me cooling my heels in the counting-room as some folks do" (casting a look at Mr. Trail). "She is a real born lady, she is; and might have a thousand hogsheads as easy as her hundreds, if there were but hands enough."

"I have lately engaged in the Guinea trade, and could supply her ladyship with any number of healthy young negroes before next fall," said Mr. Trail, obsequiously.

"We are averse to the purchase of negroes from Africa," said the young gentleman, coldly. "My grandfather and my mother have always objected to it, and I do not like to think of selling or buying the poor wretches."

"It is for their good, my dear young sir! For their temporal and their spiritual good!" cried Mr. Trail. "And we purchase the poor creatures only for their benefit; let me talk this matter over with you at my own house. I can introduce you to a happy home, a Christian family, and a British merchant's honest fare. Can't I, Captain Franks?"

"Can't say," growled the Captain. "Never asked me to take a bite or sup at your table. Asked me to psalm-singing once, and to hear Mr. Ward preach; don't care for them sort of entertainments."

Not choosing to take notice of this remark, Mr. Trail continued in a low tone: "Business is business, my dear young sir, and I know 'tis only my duty, the duty of all of us, to cultivate the fruits of the earth in their season. As the heir of Lady Esmond's estate—for I speak, I believe, to the heir of that great property?—"

The young gentleman made a bow.

"—I would urge upon you, at the very earliest moment, the propriety, the duty of increasing the ample means with which Heaven has blessed you. As an honest factor, I could not do otherwise; as a prudent man, should I scruple to speak of what will tend to your profit and mine? No, my dear Mr. George."

"My name is not George; my name is Henry," said the young man as he turned his head away, his eyes filling with tears.

"Gracious powers! What do you mean, sir? Did you not say you were my lady's heir? And is not George Esmond Warrington, Esq.—"

"Hold your tongue, you fool!" cried Mr. Franks, striking the merchant a tough blow on his sleek sides as the young lad turned away. "Don't you see the young gentleman swabbing his eyes, and note his black clothes?"

"What do you mean, Captain Franks, by laying your hand on your owners? Mr. George is the heir; I know the Colonel's will well enough."

"Mr. George is there," said the Captain, pointing with his thumb to the deck.

"Where?" cries the factor.

"Mr. George is there!" reiterated the Captain, again lifting his finger toward the topmast or the sky beyond. "He is dead a year, sir, come next the 9th of July. He would go out with General Braddock on that dreadful business to the Belle Rivière. He and a thousand more never came back again. Every man of them was murdered as he fell. You know the Indian way, Mr. Trail?" And here the Captain passed his hand rapidly round his head. "Horrible! Ain't it, sir? Horrible! He was a fine young man, the very picture of this one; only his hair was black, which is now hanging in a bloody Indian wigwam. He was often and often on board of the *Young Rachel*, and would have his chests of books broken open on deck before they were landed. He was a shy and silent young gent: not like this one, which was the merriest, wildest young fellow, full of his songs and fun. He took on dreadful at the news; went to his bed, had that fever which lays so many of 'em by the heels along that swampy Potomac, but he's got better on the voyage: the voyage makes everyone better; and, in course, the young gentleman can't be forever a-crying after a brother who dies and leaves him a great fortune. Ever since we sighted Ireland he has been quite gay and happy, only he would go off at times, when he was most merry, saying, 'I wish my dearest Georgy could enjoy this here sight along with me,' and when you mentioned the other's name, you see, he couldn't stand it." And the honest Captain's own eyes filled with tears as he turned and looked toward the object of his compassion.

Mr. Trail assumed a lugubrious countenance befitting the tragic compliment with which he prepared to greet the young Virginian; but the latter answered him very curtly, declined his offers of hospitality, and only stayed in Mr. Trail's house long enough to drink a glass of wine and to take up a sum of money of which he stood in need. But he and Captain Franks parted on the very warmest terms, and all the little crew of the *Young Rachel* cheered from the ship's side as their passenger left it.

Again and again Harry Warrington and his brother had pored over the English map, determining the course they should take upon arriving at home. All Americans who love the old country—and what gently nurtured man or woman of Anglo-Saxon race does not?—have ere this rehearsed their English travels, visiting in fancy the spots with which their hopes, their parents' fond stories, and their friends' descriptions have rendered them familiar. There are few things more affecting in the history of the quarrel which divided the two great nations than the recurrence of that word "home," as used by the younger toward the elder country. Harry Warrington had his chart laid out. Before London, and its glorious temples of St. Paul's and St. Peter's; its grim Tower, where the brave and loyal had shed their blood, from Wallace down to Balmerino and Kilmarnock, pitied by gentle hearts; before the awful window of Whitehall, whence the martyr Charles had issued to kneel once more, and then ascend to Heaven; before Playhouses, Parks, and Palaces, wondrous resorts of wit, pleasure, and splendour; before Shakespeare's resting-place under the tall spire which rises by Avon, amidst the sweet Warwickshire pastures; before Derby, and Falkirk, and Culloden, where the cause of honour and loyalty had fallen, it might be to rise no more: before all these points of their pilgrimage there was one which the young Virginian brothers held even more sacred, and that was the home of their family—that old Castlewood in Hampshire, about which their parents had talked so fondly. From Bristol to Bath, from Bath to Salisbury, to Winchester, to Hexton, to Home; they knew the way, and had mapped the journey many and many a time.

We must fancy our American traveller to be a handsome young fellow, whose suit of sables only made him look the more interesting. The plump landlady from her bar, surrounded by her china and punch-bowls, and stout gilded bottles of strong waters, and glittering rows of silver flagons, looked

The heavy iron knocker of Castlewood rang out a solitary, defiant sound against the silence of the ancestral house, but no soul within seemed inclined to answer. When the servant finally emerged, his face a mask of indifference, he treated the news that the visitor was a relation of the family with the same casual disregard one might offer a stray dog. The household was in disarray; the masters were away, and in their absence, John, the steward, cared little for kinship. His mind was fixed on the card game waiting for him in the window-seat with Thomas. Meanwhile, the housekeeper was already bustling, preparing the grand reception for the arriving lords and ladies.

Only through persistent pleading did Harry manage to glimpse the interior—the sitting-room and the picture-gallery. There, framed in gold, stood the portraits of his lineage: his grandfather in a powdered wig and breastplate, a mirror image of the man he had known in Virginia; and his grandmother, Lady Castlewood, depicted in the garb of Charles II., her neck bare, her golden hair cascading in ringlets that Harry remembered once seeing snow-white. Yet, the sight of these honored ancestors could not warm the chill in his heart. With a scowl, the housekeeper drove him away, citing the imminent arrival of the Countess, the Lord, his brother, the young ladies, and the Baroness, who was to claim the state bedroom. Harry scribbled his name on a scrap from his pocket-book and left it on the hall table: *Henry Esmond Warrington, of Castlewood, Virginia, arrived yesterday—staying at the Three Castles.*

The lackeys, abandoning their cards to collect their tips, opened the door. Gumbo, the gatekeeper, stepped down from his bench to take Harry's guinea, a gesture of charity he barely understood. Walking away from the house of his fathers, Harry felt a profound disappointment settle over him. He had seen little kindness in the entire estate save for the fleeting, unselfish smile of little Polly. Here, in the shadow of his own heritage, he was reduced to asking for bacon and eggs at a roadside alehouse.

Later, after a solitary dinner, Harry sat upon the bridge, watching the sun dip below the old house as the rooks returned to their elm nests. His imagination wandered to the knights and cavaliers of old, the huntsmen of King Charles's reign, and the ghost of his lost brother, George. The memory of his dear companion struck him with such tenderness that he hung his head, grief renewing itself in his chest. Suddenly, the peace was shattered. Two young men on horseback dashed across the bridge, one swearing at Harry to move aside, the other pushing him roughly as if to send him over the parapet. They were followed swiftly by livery servants who glared with a "British welcome" of pure hostility, and then by a heavy coach-and-six.

Three pale, handsome faces peered out at Harry as the carriage crossed the bridge, ignoring his salute to the family arms. The gentleman seated behind the carriage glared haughtily. Harry felt a crushing loneliness. The inn-keepers confirmed his fears: the passengers were the Countess, her stepdaughter Lady Maria, her daughter Lady Fanny, and the young gentlemen, Mr. William and the Lord. It was the Lord who had sworn loudest, and it was Mr. William in the grey frock who had nearly driven Harry into the ditch.

Harry had refused to unpack his trunks, hoping for an invitation to the great house. Hours passed in vain. Just as darkness fell, a second carriage arrived, carrying a stout, high-colored lady with dark eyes—the Baroness Bernstein, the Lord's aunt. Soon, the entire retinue vanished behind the castle gates, leaving Harry alone in the inn, consumed by a cruel sense of neglect. He could not sleep, disturbed by the raucous laughter and shouting from the bar downstairs.

It was only when Gumbo tried to block the door that the chaos truly began. A shrill, drunken voice cursed Gumbo, pushing past him into Harry's room.

"Beg your pardon, Cousin Warrington!" cried the intruder, stumbling over his words. "Are you asleep? I beg your pardon for riding you over on the bridge. Didn't know you... course shouldn't have done it. Thought it was a lawyer with a writ. Gad! Thought it was Nathan come to nab me." It was Mr. William, visibly intoxicated.

"You did me great honor to mistake me for a sheriff's officer, cousin," Harry replied, sitting up in his nightcap with grave dignity.

"Gad! I thought it was Nathan, and was going to send you souse into the river," William laughed incoherently. "But I ask your pardon. You see, I had been drinking at the Bell at Hexton... Hullo! Davis! A bowl of punch!"

"I have had my share for tonight, cousin," Harry said firmly.

"You want me to go, Cousin What's-your-name?" William demanded, his voice rising. "You want me to go, and they want me to come, and I didn't want to come. I said I'd see him hanged first. Why should I trouble myself to look after a fellow I don't care a pin for? Zackly what I said. Zackly what Castlewood said. Why the devil should he go down? Castlewood says, and so said my lady, but the Baroness would have you. It's all the Baroness's doing. So you must just get up and come."

Mr. Esmond spoke with amiable rapidity, tacking about the room, but Harry was in a fury. "I tell you what, cousin," he cried, "I won't move for the Countess, or for the Baroness, or for all the cousins in Castlewood."

When the landlord entered with the punch, William screamed at him to turn the "sot" out, calling him a "Cherokee" and threatening to drive his sword through his body. The scene devolved into a cacophony of oaths until the household staff dragged the drunkard away. Harry closed his tent around himself in sulky wrath, finally succumbing to sleep.

The next morning, the landlord was obsequious, having learned Harry's name and quality. He reported that Mr. William had been returned in a wheelbarrow, claiming the young gentleman was of a "real kind nature" despite beating the servants the night before.

Meanwhile, within the walls of Castlewood, a domestic council had convened. The family found Harry's note and debated his reception. Lord Castlewood reasoned that since they hadn't drowned him on the bridge, they must invite him. Lady Fanny suggested one of the brothers should go personally to apologize for their rude greeting. Lord Castlewood agreed to send his brother William. William, however, declared he would be hanged if he went. Lady Maria, however, found the American "pretty enough," noting that her brothers were dreadfully dull and that Harry might be vulgar, but worth seeing. Lady Castlewood, the matriarch, opted for delay, suggesting they wait for the Baroness's return. Thus, Harry's hospitality remained in abeyance.

When the Baroness Bernstein finally arrived, the atmosphere shifted. The family, usually indifferent, suddenly displayed enthusiasm for their wealthy kinswoman. The dining room was set with old plate, the walls lined with portraits of the Esmond line. The Baroness, full of spirits and humor, recounted wild stories of Europe, causing the demure Countess to smile and the young people to giggle. She drank freely of champagne and punch, pointing out the empty chair where her father once sat, lamenting that the old plate had been melted down to pay gambling debts.

Her conversation turned to the family history. When the Lord laughed at the Virginian's utility, the Baroness struck the table with such force that the glasses danced. "I say he was the best of you all," she declared, pointing to the portrait of Colonel Esmond. "There never was one of the male Esmonds that had more brains than a goose, except him. He was not fit for this wicked, selfish old world of ours, and he was right to go and live out of it."

Excited by the wine, she pressed the topic further. "Who has been here to-day?" she demanded, her face flushed. "Harry Esmond Warrington, of Virginia," the Lord admitted. "A lad whom Will nearly pitched into the river."

"You mean that a grandson of Henry Esmond... has been here, and none of you have offered him hospitality?" the Baroness cried, her indignation mounting.

"Since we didn't know it," Will stammered.

"That he is staying at the Inn, and you are sitting there!" the old lady shrieked. "This is too bad! Call somebody to me. Get me my hood—I'll go to the boy myself."

The young men rose in wrath. "Madame the Baroness of Bernstein," the Lord declared, "your ladyship is welcome to go; but as for me, I don't choose to have such words as 'shameful' applied to my conduct. I won't go and fetch the young gentleman from Virginia."

The Baroness looked at the family, who held their heads down, and then at the Lord. Leaning forward, she whispered rapidly in German, "I had unright when I said the Colonel was the only man of the family. Thou canst, if thou willest, Eugene." The Lord bowed. She then commanded, "If you do not wish an old woman to go out at this hour, let William, at least, go and fetch his cousin."

The daughters cried out in agreement. The Lord relented, ordering William to put on his pattens and get a lantern. William, already drunk, agreed to fetch the Virginian and promised another bowl of punch upon his return.

When the Baroness finally caught sight of Harry by the riverside, she saw a handsome, interesting youth of nineteen. Though she had her own reasons for hesitating to encourage such a match, her generous nature, warmed by the wine, overrode her caution. She had dispatched a note earlier, signed simply "B. Bernstein," inviting him to "Colonel Esmond's house in England."

Harry approached, hat in hand, his fair hair blowing from his flushed cheeks, clad in mourning. He made a low bow that would have done credit to Versailles. The Baroness held out her hand, placing her other hand softly on his ruffle.

"I knew your grandfather very well, Harry," she said gently. "So you came yesterday to see his picture, and they turned you away, though you know the house was his of right?"

Harry blushed crimson. "The servants did not know me. A young gentleman came to me last night," he admitted, "when I was peevish, and he, I fear, was tipsy. I spoke rudely to my cousin, and would ask his pardon. Your ladyship knows that in Virginia our manners towards strangers are different. I own I had expected another kind of welcome."

"I sent him," the Baroness assured him, her eyes kind. "But you will find your cousins most friendly to you to-day. You must stay here. Lord Castlewood would have been with you this morning, only I was so eager to see you. There will be breakfast in an hour; and meantime you must talk to me."

She took his arm, dropping her cane in the process, and jokingly declared, "You shall be my cane."

"My grandfather used to call us his crutches," Harry replied.

"You are like him, though you are fair," she observed.

"You should have seen—you should have seen George," the boy said, his honest eyes welling with tears. The bitterness of yesterday's humiliation, the affection of this present greeting, and the sheer relief of being welcomed softened his heart. He felt tenderly grateful to the lady who had opened her home to him.

In the hour they spent together, Harry poured out his honest heart to this new friend. When breakfast time arrived, she led him to the room, presenting him to his aunt, the Countess, and bidding him embrace his cousins. Lord Castlewood was frank and gracious; honest Will, suffering from a hangover, was utterly unconscious of the night's disgrace. The ladies were pleasant and polite, masking their fury at Harry's presence and their awe of the Baroness's favor.

Harry, a simple truth-teller from a distant colony, unaware of the social currents beneath the surface, believed he had found a home. The Baroness, however, was *folle* of him, talking of no one else, trotting him through the house, showing him the room where his grandfather slept and the cupboard made during the Catholic persecutions. She drove him out into the countryside, pointing out remarkable sites, while he, in return, told her his entire story. It was a brief biography, cast not in his own precise words, but in the form it would take in the chapters to follow.

Colonel Henry Esmond, a veteran who had borne the rank of Colonel through the wars of Queen Anne's reign, found himself, at the close of that turbulent era, entangled in plots to restore the Stuart line to the English throne. Fortunately for the stability of the realm, the nation chose a different dynasty; yet, among the few who opposed the House of Hanover, Colonel Esmond was numbered. Advised by friends to seek safety abroad, he initially felt a deep regret for his political involvement. However, recognizing the pacific nature of the new Prince Regnant, his allies swiftly secured his pardon.

It is recorded that Colonel Esmond hailed from the noble English line of Castlewood in Hants. It was widely whispered that King James II and his son had once offered him and his father the title of Marquis, and that the Irish peerage held by his family might have been assumed had he not chosen to overlook a certain informality. Wearied by the ceaseless political strife and annoyed by family troubles in Europe, he elected to settle in Virginia, where he took possession of a vast estate originally granted by King Charles I to his ancestor. There, his daughter and grandsons were born, and his wife passed away. This lady, upon her marriage, was the widow of the Colonel's kinsman—the unfortunate Viscount Castlewood, who had fallen in a duel with Lord Mohun at the end of King William's reign.

Colonel Esmond named his American residence Castlewood, mirroring the ancestral home across the ocean. Indeed, the entire fabric of Virginia life was lovingly modeled upon English customs. It was a fiercely loyal colony, boasting that King Charles II had ruled in Virginia before he did in England. The English monarch and the Church were honored with equal devotion. The resident gentry, allied with distinguished English families, held their heads high above the Dutch merchants of New York and the mercantile Roundheads of Pennsylvania and New England. Fewer people were truly republican than those of this great province, which was destined to lead the memorable revolt against the British Crown.

The Virginia gentry lived upon their great estates in a manner almost patriarchal. Each property employed a multitude of hands—purchased and assigned servants—who were subject to the master's command. The land provided their food, livestock, and game; the great rivers teemed with fish. From their banks, the journey home was clear. Ships loaded tobacco from private wharves on the Potomac or James River, carrying it to London or Bristol in exchange for English goods and manufactured articles, the sole produce the Virginian gentry deemed worth cultivating. Their hospitality was boundless; no stranger was ever turned away. The gentry received one another and traveled between homes in a state nearly feudal.

The question of slavery was not yet fully formed in the minds of the people at this time. To own black servants did not shock the sensibilities of any Virginian gentleman, nor was the despotism exercised over the negro race generally savage. Food was plentiful, and the poor black people were lazy and not unhappy. One might preach emancipation to Madam Esmond of Castlewood as easily as telling her to let her horses run loose; she possessed no doubt that the whip and corn-bag were beneficial for both.

Her father may have harbored different thoughts, possessing a skeptical turn of mind on many points, but his doubts never broke forth into active denial. Rather, he appeared disaffected than rebellious. Once, he had participated in active life at home and might have been eager to share its rewards, but in later years, he seemed indifferent to them. Something had occurred in his life that cast a melancholy tinge over his entire existence. He was not unhappy—he was kind to those around him, affectionate, and even obsequious to the women of his family, whom he rarely contradicted—but he suffered from a bankruptcy of the heart that his spirit never recovered. He submitted to life rather than enjoying it, and he was never in better spirits than in his final hours as he prepared to lay it down.

Having lost his wife, his daughter assumed the management of the Colonel and his affairs. He handed them over to her charge with entire acquiescence. Provided he had his books and his quiet, he cared for nothing else. When company arrived at Castlewood, he entertained them handsomely, displaying a pleasant, sarcastic turn of wit. He was not in the least sorry when they departed.

"My love, I shall not be sorry to go myself," he told his daughter. "And you, though the most affectionate of daughters, will console yourself after a while. Why should I, who am so old, be romantic? You may, who are still a young creature." He spoke these words without meaning them entirely, for the lady he addressed was a matter-of-fact little person with very little romance in her nature.

After fifteen years of residence upon his great Virginian estate, affairs prospered so well with the worthy proprietor that he acquiesced in his daughter's plans to build a mansion much grander and more durable than the plain wooden edifice in which he had been content to live, ensuring his heirs had a habitation worthy of their noble name. Several of Madam Warrington's neighbors had built handsome houses for themselves; perhaps it was her ambition to take rank in the country that inspired this desire for improved quarters. Colonel Esmond, of Castlewood, cared neither for quarters nor quarterings. But his daughter held a very high opinion of the merit and antiquity of her lineage. Her sire, growing exquisitely calm and good-natured in his serene, declining years, humored his child's peculiarities in an easy, bantering way, nay, even assisted her with his antiquarian learning, which was considerable, and with his skill in painting, in which he was proficient.

A knowledge of heraldry, a hundred years prior, formed part of the education of most noble ladies and gentlemen. During her visit to Europe, Miss Esmond had eagerly studied family histories and pedigrees, returning to Virginia with a store of documents regarding her family, which she relied upon with implicit gravity. Alongside these were the most edifying volumes then published in France and England concerning the noble science. These works satisfied her perfectly that the Esmonds were descended not only from noble Norman warriors who came to England with their victorious chief but also from native English of royal dignity. Two magnificent heraldic trees, cunningly painted by the Colonel's hand, represented the family springing from the Emperor Charlemagne on one side—drawn in plate-armour with his imperial mantle and diadem—and from Queen Boadicea on the other, whom the Colonel insisted upon painting in the light costume of an ancient British queen, wearing a prodigious gilded crown, a trifling mantle of furs, and a lovely symmetrical person tastefully tattooed with figures of a brilliant blue tint. From these two illustrious stocks, the family tree rose until it united in the thirteenth century in the person of the fortunate Esmond who claimed descent from both.

Of the Warrington family into which she married, good Madam Rachel thought but little. She wrote herself Esmond Warrington but was universally called Madam Esmond of Castlewood after her father's death, when she came to rule over that domain. It is even to be feared that quarrels for precedence in colonial society occasionally disturbed her temper. Though her father had possessed a marquis's patent from King James, which he had burned and disowned, she frequently acted as if that document existed and was in full force. She considered the English Esmonds of inferior dignity to her own branch, and regarding the colonial aristocracy, she made no scruple of asserting her superiority over the whole body of them. Hence arose quarrels, angry words, and even a scuffle or two, as we gather from her notes, at the Governor's assemblies in Jamestown. Why recall the memory of these squabbles? Are not the persons who engaged in them beyond the reach of quarrels now, and has not the Republic put an end to these social inequalities? Before the establishment of Independence, there was no more aristocratic country in the world than Virginia; so the Virginians, whose history we have to narrate, were bred to have the fullest respect for the institutions of home, and the rightful king had not two more faithful little subjects than the young twins of Castlewood.

When the boys' grandfather died, their mother, in great state, proclaimed her eldest son, George, her successor and heir to the estate. Harry, George's younger brother by half an hour, was always enjoined to respect his senior. The whole household was equally instructed to pay him honor: the negroes, of whom there was a large and happy family, and the assigned servants from Europe, whose lot was made as bearable as it might be under the government of the lady of Castlewood. In the whole family, there was scarcely a rebel save Mrs. Esmond's faithful friend and companion, Madam Mountain, and Harry's foster-mother, a faithful negro woman who could never understand why her child should not be first, who was handsomer, stronger, and cleverer than his brother, as she vowed. Though in truth there was scarcely any difference in beauty, strength, or stature between the twins, in disposition they were exceedingly unlike. Yet in feature, they resembled each other so closely that but for the color of their hair, it would have been difficult to distinguish them. In their beds, and when their heads were covered with those vast ribboned nightcaps worn by our great and little ancestors, it was scarcely possible for anyone but a nurse or mother to tell one from the other.

However, alike in form, we have said they differed in temper. The elder was peaceful, studious, and silent; the younger was warlike and noisy. He was quick at learning once he began, but very slow to start. No threats of the ferule would provoke Harry to learn in an idle fit, nor would they prevent George from helping his brother with his lessons. Harry possessed a strong military turn; he drilled the little negroes on the estate and caned them like a corporal, having many good boxing matches with them, never bearing malice if he was worsted. George, conversely, was sparing of blows and gentle with all about him.

As was the custom in all families, each boy had a special little servant assigned to him. It was a known fact that George, finding his little wretch of a blackamoor asleep on his master's bed, sat down beside it and brushed the flies off the child with a feather fan. This act filled old Gumbo, the child's father, with horror as he found his young master so engaged, and provoked the indignation of Madam Esmond, who ordered the young negro off to the proper officer for a whipping. In vain George implored and entreated, bursting into passionate tears and beseeching a remission of the sentence. His mother was inflexible regarding the young rebel's punishment, and the little negro went off beseeching his young master not to cry.

A fierce quarrel ensued between mother and son out of this event. Her son would not be pacified. He declared the punishment a shame—a shame—that he was the master of the boy and that no one, not even his mother, had a right to touch him. He acknowledged she might order him to be corrected and that he would suffer the punishment, as he and Harry often had, but no one should lay a hand on his boy. Trembling with passionate rebellion against what he conceived to be injustice, he vowed—actually shrieking out an oath that shocked his fond mother and governor, who had never heard such language from the usually gentle child—that on the day he came of age, he would set young Gumbo free. He went to visit the child in the slaves' quarters and gave him one of his own toys.

The young black martyr was an impudent, lazy, saucy little personage who would be none the worse for a whipping, as the Colonel no doubt thought. He acquiesced in the child's punishment when Madam Esmond insisted upon it, laughing in his good-natured way when his indignant grandson called out, "You let mamma rule you in everything, grandpapa."

"Why, so I do," said grandpapa. "Rachel, my love, the way in which I am petticoat-ridden is so evident that even this baby has found it out."

"Then why don't you stand up like a man?" said little Harry, who was always ready to abet his brother.

Grandpapa looked queerly.

"Because I like sitting down best, my dear," he replied. "I am an old gentleman, and standing fatigues me."

On account of a certain apish drollery and humor which exhibited itself in the lad, and a liking for some of the old man's pursuits, the first of the twins became the grandfather's favorite and companion. He would laugh and talk out all his infantine heart to the old gentleman, to whom the younger had seldom a word to say. George was a demure, studious boy, and his senses seemed to brighten in the library, where his brother was so gloomy. He knew the books before he could well-nigh carry them and read in them long before he could understand them. Harry, on the other hand, was all alive in the stables or in the wood, eager for all parties of hunting and fishing, promising to be a good sportsman from a very early age.

Their grandfather's ship sailed for Europe once when the boys were children, and they were asked what present Captain Franks should bring them back. George was divided between books and a fiddle; Harry instantly declared for a little gun. Madam Warrington (as she then was called) was hurt that her elder boy should have low tastes and applauded the younger's choice as more worthy of his name and lineage. "Books, papa, I can fancy to be a good choice," she replied to her father, who tried to convince her that George had a right to his opinion, "though I am sure you must have pretty nigh all the books in the world already. But I never can desire—I may be wrong, but I never can desire—that my son, and the grandson of the Marquis of Esmond, should be a fiddler."

"Should be a fiddlestick, my dear," the old Colonel answered.

"Remember that Heaven's ways are not ours, and that each creature born has a little kingdom of thought of his own, which it is a sin in us to invade. Suppose George loves music

Is a person truly happy when they possess every earthly comfort? Consider Madam Esmond Warrington: she held an ancient name, a vast estate, and a fortune sufficient for all desires. Her home at Castlewood was stocked with necessities and luxuries alike, attended by a bustling household of eager black and white servants. She enjoyed robust health, affectionate children, and the humble blessings of a good cook, cellar, and library. In her morning and evening prayers, she meticulously cataloged these advantages, convinced that such a life warranted the title of "very decently happy."

Yet, despite this princely existence, the little Princess Pocahontas, as she was known, was far from content. Enthroned in her Westmorland County dominion, she ruled with an iron fist. The local gentry fawned over her; her sons bowed to her will; the poor whites accepted her medicine without question, and the lesser nobility invariably lost at backgammon to her. Her husband, cut off in early life, was perhaps fortunate to be gone; had he lived, the marriage would have ended in fierce quarrels or the humiliation of a henpecked spouse. Madam Esmond never sought companionship, only domination. She was a tyrant who demanded obedience, offering friendship only to those who submitted, and fighting relentlessly against anyone who resisted. While she preached the sins of despotism with a clear voice on Sundays, she rarely acknowledged her own faults, save for the occasional amusement her father derived from watching her haughty streaks. Without her father's restraining influence, her reign became absolute, and one can only imagine the misery of living under her rule in Virginia.

Her management of the estate was rigorous. She had replaced her father's English factor, expanded the tobacco plantations, hired a new overseer, and imported a strict tutor. Though she loved her father, she rejected his wisdom, believing that a dutiful daughter must override parental counsel. She discarded her husband's surname, adopting "Madam Esmond" to assert her seniority over her half-brother, Lord Castlewood. She claimed precedence over all colonial officials except Lord Fairfax, engaging in legendary battles of etiquette with the wives of judges and governors. To her, the Warringtons were nothing; she had married an English baronet's younger son merely to satisfy her parents, a union she viewed as a sacrifice she was bound to make.

Her behavior toward her English kin was equally cold. Annual letters to the Warrington family and the Hampshire Esmonds often went unanswered. Once, a judge's wife returning to London recounted Madam Esmond's disparaging remarks about her relatives to Lady Warrington, who then shared the tale with Lady Castlewood. The correspondence ceased, leaving Madam Esmond in a state of wounded pride.

Strife soon erupted within her own household. The dismissal of Mr. Dempster, the late Colonel's secretary and the boys' tutor, marked the beginning of the end. Madam Esmond distrusted scholars, fearing they instilled dangerous principles. Suspicious that Dempster was a Jesuit in disguise, she forced him to leave the house, where he built a cabin to teach and practice medicine among the sparse settlers. Master George, loyal to his mentor, refused to abandon him, while Harry, preferring fishing and sport to books, had never been close to the Dominie.

A second, more financial rift followed the deaths of an aunt and the Colonel. George Warrington, as heir, was entitled to six thousand pounds held in trust by his mother and a London lawyer. Madam Esmond, however, viewed herself as the sole proprietor. Furious when the lawyer refused to release the funds prematurely, she berated the agent and insulted Mr. Draper, the trustee, calling him an insolent pettifogger. She believed the money should be used immediately to buy Boulter's estate and slaves, thereby securing an annual income for Harry. Neither George nor his friend, Mr. Washington of Mount Vernon, could persuade her that the lawyer was acting correctly.

George sided with the lawyer, stating he did not desire the money and would gladly give it to his mother if he could. But Madam Esmond saw only a betrayal. She lamented that her younger son, Harry, was left with a mere pittance while his brother inherited everything. She poured out her grievances in tears, scorn, and passionate appeals to Heaven, convinced that the London lawyers were mean-spirited wretches denying her child his fortune. This conviction hardened her resolve to save every penny for Harry's future, halting the grand building projects her husband had begun and ordering the cessation of wine shipments. She mourned the cost of a fine carriage she had imported from England, groaning in church that she wished she had saved the three hundred and eighty guineas for Harry instead.

"You will give me plenty while you live, and George will give me plenty when you die," Harry replied cheerfully.

"Not unless he changes in spirit, my dear," the lady retorted, casting a grim look at her elder son. "Not unless Heaven softens his heart and teaches him charity, for which I pray day and night. Does Mountain know?"

Mrs. Mountain, the widow of Ensign Mountain and Madam Esmond's companion, shook her head. "Humph! You are always disturbing yourself over this legacy. I see no need."

"Oh, no need!" the widow cried, rustling her silks. "Because my eldest is a disobedient son and an unkind brother, and my poor Harry, bless him, has nothing but a mess of pottage."

George looked at his mother with despair, tears welling in his eyes. "I wish you would bless me, too, O my mother!" he cried, bursting into weeping.

Instantly, Harry threw his arms around his brother's neck, kissing him repeatedly. "Never mind, George. I know you are a good brother. Don't mind what she says; she doesn't mean it."

"I do mean it, child," the mother wailed. "Would to Heaven..."

"HOLD YOUR TONGUE, I SAY!" Harry roared. "It is a shame to speak so to him, ma'am."

"And so it is, Harry," Mrs. Mountain agreed, shaking his hand. "You never said a truer word in your life."

"Mrs. Mountain, do you dare to set my children against me?" the widow shrieked. "From this very day, madam—"

"Turn me and my child into the street? Do," Mrs. Mountain declared calmly. "That will be a fine revenge because the English lawyer won't give you the boy's money. Find another companion who will tell you black is white and flatter you; it is not my way. When shall I go? I shan't be long packing. I brought little into Castlewood House, and I shall take little out."

"Hush! The bells are ringing for church, Mountain. Let us try to compose ourselves," the widow said, though her eyes softened with affection as she looked at her sons. George kept his head down, while Harry sat close, his arm wrapped protectively around his brother's neck throughout the sermon.

Later, Harry continued his narrative, interspersed with youthful exclamations and answers to his listener's questions. The old lady seemed inexhaustible in her attention, declining rides, walks, tea, or cards in favor of listening to him. When the Castlewood family was present, she redoubled her attentions, insisting Harry speak close to her ear and commanding the others to be silent so she could hear their cousin. They would retreat to the corners of the room, feigning pleasure.

"Are you my cousin, too?" the honest boy asked. "You see kinder than my other cousins."

Their conversation took place in the wainscoted parlour, hung with portraits of the family for two centuries. Above Madam Bernstein's great chair hung a brilliant painting by Kneller, depicting a young lady of Queen Anne's time with auburn hair and a lovely neck.

"That picture is by Sir Godfrey," she explained. "He thought himself the greatest painter in the world, but he was not so good as Lely, who painted your grandmother—my Lady Castlewood, Colonel Esmond's wife; nor as Van Dyck, who painted your great-grandfather yonder. Some of us are painted blacker than we are. Did you recognize your grandmother? She had the loveliest fair hair and shape of any woman of her time."

"I fancied I knew the portrait from instinct, perhaps, and a certain likeness to my mother," Harry replied.

"Did Mrs. Warrington—though I think she calls herself Madam or Lady Esmond now—ever tell you of another daughter her mother had in England before she married your grandfather?"

"She never spoke of one."

"Nor your grandfather?"

"Never. But in his picture-books, which he constantly made for us children, he used to draw a head very like that above your ladyship. That, and Viscount Francis, and King James III., he drew a score of times, I am sure."

"And the picture over me reminds you of no one, Harry?"

"No, indeed."

"Ah! Here is a sermon!" the lady sighed, her face falling. "Harry, that was my face once—yes, it was—and then I was called Beatrix Esmond. And your mother is my half-sister, child, and she has never even mentioned my name!"

Harry Warrington recounted his adventures to his newfound relative, and Madam Bernstein, a woman of sharp wit and worldly experience, formed her judgment upon the tale. Though her opinion was not entirely favorable, she recognized the imperfection of human nature; a city-bred lady like herself would indeed recoil at the thought of such a countrified existence, finding it wearisome. Yet, little Madam Warrington knew no better. She was content with her life and with herself, for she understood that while epicures demand fine dining, the simple man named Hodge finds joy in his homely bread and bacon. Madam Warrington was a brisk woman of business, the unseen architect of every affair at Castlewood. No pie was baked without her little finger in the dough. She directed the maids, supervised the kitchen wenches, rode afield on her pony to oversee the overseers and the negro hands in the tobacco and corn fields, and personally tended to the sick slaves in any weather, armed with a book of old-fashioned receipts and a medicine chest that terrified her neighbors into health.

A century prior, Virginia held few towns; the gentry's estates were little villages where masters and vassals dwelt together. Rachel Esmond ruled Castlewood like a queen, while neighboring potentates governed their lands with varying degrees of neediness. Some lived plentifully but roughly, with ragged liveries and open houses that welcomed all strangers. Madam Warrington was as hospitable as her peers but a sharper economist. Many would have gladly shared her life-interest in the estate to serve as a father to her boys, yet none seemed good enough for a lady of her exalted birth. Gossips joked that she waited for the Duke of Cumberland to be made viceroy or king of America, to which she responded with grave dignity that persons of such high rank had already offered alliance to the Esmond family.

Her household included an officer's widow, a former school companion and the late husband's regimental friend. At the Kensington Academy, while English girls teased the American stranger for her princified airs, Fanny Parker had defended and befriended her. Both married ensigns in Kingsley's and remained tenderly attached, exchanging letters signed "my Fanny" and "my Rachel." Tragically, Fanny's husband died in sad circumstances, leaving her a widow with an infant. Later, Captain Franks brought Mrs. Mountain to Virginia aboard the *Young Rachel*.

Mrs. Mountain enlivened Castlewood House. She played cards with the mistress, assisted the eldest boy with music, greeted guests warmly, and managed the household linens. A kind, brisk, and jolly widow, she declined proposals from unmarried gentlemen, preferring to keep her name Mountain. Her first husband had amiably spent her fortune and his own, and she valued her home at Castlewood over any new suitors. Though the two ladies quarreled frequently, they loved each other deeply, reconciling quickly whenever illness struck the boys. In the Colonel's final days, Mrs. Mountain's cheerfulness was greatly appreciated, and Madam Warrington cherished her memory above all living persons. Consequently, when Captain Franks asked if she would return, she always declined, promising to stay another year.

When suitors approached Madam Warrington, she received them kindly but often asked if they sought Mrs. Mountain. She would graciously accept compliments, grow tired of them, and treat them with her wayward imperial humor, much like Queen Elizabeth. She had favorites, accepted flatteries, and grew bored easily. Rattling Jack Firebrace of Henrico county enjoyed free quarters for months, addressing stolen verses to her, while Tom Humbold of Spotsylvania wagered fifty hogsheads that she would institute an order of knighthood—a bet he won.

The elder boy, George, chafed at these oddities. From an early age, he revolted against the flatteries paid to his mother, exposing them with juvenile satire. His mother noted gravely that the Esmonds were always of a jealous disposition and that her poor boy took after his parents. George hated Jack and Tom, whereas Harry, his younger brother, enjoyed sporting, fowling, fishing, and cock-fighting with them.

One winter, after dismissing their first tutor, Madam Esmond took the boys to Williamsburg for education. There, they heard the famous Mr. Whitfield, whose great voice stirred the colony unlike the harmless Mr. Broadbent. Virginia was a Church of England colony, yet lacking bishops, they imported divines who were often noblemen's hangers-on or insolvent parsons seeking a living. Whitfield's fervor excited the boys; they sang hymns with fervor, dreaming of the sacred "call." Though Whitfield could not stay, he promised to send a tutor capable of teaching profane learning and strengthening them in spiritual science.

Soon, a chosen vessel arrived with Young Mr. Ward. He possessed a voice as loud as Whitfield's and spoke endlessly. The hall echoed with his exhortations night and evening, drawing even the domestic negroes to the doors. He had the most influence over the "black sheep" of the flock, inspiring a negro chorus unheard in the Colonel's time. Ward was handsome, and Madam Esmond, credulous and eager to admire, found his glib voice and voluble commonplaces delightful. She insisted neighbors attend and ordered them to be converted. She was especially anxious to influence her young favorite, Mr. Washington, pressing him repeatedly to stay at Castlewood. But Washington always ordered his horse when the time came for Mr. Ward's exercises.

The twins, however, grew tired and rebellious under their new teacher. They found him a bad scholar, dull, and ill-bred. George knew more Latin and Greek than his master, catching him in perpetual blunders. Harry, taking greater liberties, mimicked Ward's manner of eating and talking until Mrs. Mountain and Madam Esmond were forced to laugh. Madam Esmond, defending Ward against her sons' opposition, argued that profane learning mattered less than spiritual truth. "What matters whether he has more or less of profane learning?" she asked. "In that which is most precious, Mr. W. is able to be a teacher to all of us... It is your wicked pride—the pride of all the Esmonds—which prevents you from listening to him." Ward's discourse that evening concerned Naaman the Syrian and his pride in his native rivers, with the moral that Ward was the keeper of the healing waters of Jordan and the boys must submit or perish.

George adopted a wicked sarcastic method, perhaps inherited from his grandfather. He mocked Ward's pompous remarks, causing the young divine to choke over his meals. He made Madam Esmond angry, doubly so when he sent Harry into fits of laughter. Her authority was defied, her officer scorned, and her youngest child perverted by the obstinate elder brother. She made a desperate attempt to maintain her power.

The boys were fourteen, Harry taller and more advanced, while George was delicate and childlike. The "baculine method"—the use of the cane—was common among sergeants and schoolmasters. Harry was accustomed to it, but since the Colonel's death, the cane had been laid aside, and the youths were allowed their own way. With authority spurned, the mother considered coercion. Consulting Mr. Ward, she found biblical justification for the practice, which was deemed wholesome in those days.

But the boys laughed at his flattery, scorned his bad manners, and yawned at his sermons. The more their mother favored him, the more they disliked him; tutor and pupils cordially hated each other. Mrs. Mountain, the boys' friend and George's confidante, warned them of a conspiracy. "Ward is more obsequious than ever to your mamma," she warned. "It turns my stomach to hear him flatter... You must be on your guard... A mischief will come." She mentioned Major Washington, whom she disliked, noting that Washington had advised the mother that "Discipline is discipline, and must be preserved. There can be but one command in a house." Harry confirmed that Washington had urged him to press George to obey. George replied haughtily, "Let him manage his own house, not mine," becoming only more supercilious.

The next day, the storm broke. During morning study, George was insubordinate. Even Harry admitted his brother was in the wrong. Mr. Ward kept his temper, promising to speak to Madam Esmond. At dinner, Ward laid the subject before her. He asked Harry to confirm his statements, which Harry did. George, standing under his grandfather's portrait, agreed haughtily that Ward was correct.

"To be a tutor to such a pupil is absurd," Ward declared, interspersing Scripture phrases that George mocked with scornful smiles. Ward asked to retire.

"Not before you have punished this wicked and disobedient child," Madam Esmond commanded, her anger gathering.

"Punish!" cried George.

"Yes, sir, punish! If means of love and entreaty fail... other means must be found... I punish you now, rebellious boy, to guard you from greater punishment hereafter. The discipline of this family must be maintained. There can be but one command in a house, and I must be the mistress of mine." She demanded Ward punish the boy, threatening that her servants would aid him if there was resistance.

In her harangue, filled with vehement Scriptural allusions, Madam Esmond revealed her schooling from her impetuous spiritual guide. George suddenly felt he had been wrong. "There can be but one command in the house, and you must be mistress—I know who said those words before you," George said slowly, looking very white. "And—and I know, mother, that I have acted wrongly to Mr. Ward."

"He owns it! He asks pardon!" cried Harry. "That's right, George! That's enough: isn't it?"

"No, it is not enough!" cried the little woman. "The disobedient boy must pay the penalty... I desire you will do your duty, Mr. Ward."

"Stop, mother—you don't quite know what you are doing," George said, agitated.

"I know that he who spares the rod spoils the child, ungrateful boy!" Madam Esmond retorted with more references. George looked pale and desperate.

Upon the mantelpiece stood a china cup, cherished by the widow as her father had used it. George suddenly took it, a strange smile passing over his pale face. "Stay one minute. Don't go away yet," he cried to his departing mother. "You—you are very fond of this cup, mother?" Harry looked on, wondering. "If I broke it, it could never be mended, could it? All the tinkers' rivets would not make it a whole cup again. My dear old grandpapa's cup! I have been wrong. Mr. Ward, I ask pardon. I will try and amend."

The widow looked at her son indignantly. "I thought," she said, "I thought an Esmond had been more of a man than to be afraid, and—" She screamed as Harry exclaimed and dashed forward.

George raised the cup, opened his hand, and let it fall on the marble slab. Harry tried in vain to catch it.

"It is too late, Hal," George said. "You will never mend that again—never. Now, mother, I am ready, as it is your wish. Will you come and see whether I am afraid? Mr. Ward, I am your servant. Your servant? Your slave! And the next time I meet Mr. Washington, madam, I will thank him for the advice which he gave you."

"I say, do your duty, sir!" cried Mrs. Esmond, stamping her foot. George bowed to Mr. Ward and asked him to lead the way to the study.

"Stop! For God's sake, mother, stop!" cried poor Hal. But passion boiled in the little woman's heart. "You only abet him, sir!" she cried. "If I had to do it myself, it should be done!" Harry, with sadness and wrath, left the room.

The widow sank onto a great chair, staring vacantly at the broken cup fragments. Silence held for a moment, then a loud outcry made her start. Mr. Ward emerged bleeding from a great wound on his head, followed by Harry, eyes flaring, brandishing a little couteau-de-chasse from the library wall.

"I don't care. I did it," Harry shouted. "I couldn't see this fellow strike my brother; and, as he lifted his hand, I flung the great ruler at him. I couldn't help it. I won't bear it; and, if one lifts a hand to me or my brother, I'll have his life."

The widow gasped, then sighed. She suffered terribly during the boys' absence, imagining the stripes inflicted on the elder had smitten her own heart. She was not angry now; perhaps she was delighted with the younger's prowess. "You are a very naughty disobedient child," she said in a peaceable voice. "My poor Mr. Ward! What a rebel, to strike you! Papa's great ebony ruler, was it? Lay down that hanger, child. 'Twas General Webb gave it to my papa after the siege of Lille. Let me bathe your wound, my good Mr. Ward, and thank Heaven it was no worse." She called for Mrs. Mountain to fetch court-plaster. "Put on your coat and waistcoat, child! You were going to take your punishment, sir, and that is sufficient. Ask pardon, Harry, of good Mr. Ward... And guard against your passionate nature, child—and pray to be forgiven. My son, O my son!" With a burst of tears, she threw herself on her eldest-born's neck. Harry laid down the hanger and apologized feebly.

The widow looked up at George's pale face. In reply to her eager caresses, he coldly kissed her on the forehead and separated from her. "You meant for the best, mother," he said. "and I was in the wrong. But the cup is broken; and all the king's horses and all the king's men cannot mend it. There—put the fair side outwards on the mantelpiece, and the wound will not show."

Following the departure of her disgraced chaplain, Madam Esmond and her son appeared reconciled, though the shadow of their estrangement lingered heavily. George fell ill with a fever shortly thereafter, his mind wandering in delirium until he shrieked, "Broken! Broken! It never, never can be mended!" His mother watched him toss upon the midnight bed, helpless against a malady that defied her remedies. Desperate, she rode through the snow on her pony to implore Mr. Dempster for aid. "I shall bury my resentment, madam," he promised, "as your ladyship buried your pride." He returned to Castlewood with his medical kit and a loyal servant, saving George from death and restoring him to health.

Though a voyage to England was suggested, the widow's quarrel with her kin there prevented it. Instead, the two young gentlemen, accompanied by Mr. Dempster as tutor and two servants, sailed to New York and ascended the Hudson to Albany. There, they entered the French provinces, welcomed by the local gentry. Harry, eager for adventure, camped with the Indians, hunting bears and trading furs. George, however, found his true calling among the French ladies. With a delicate constitution, he perfected his French accent until he could pass for a native, dancing the minuet with elegance and playing the violin with such mastery that he even engaged in an affair of honor with a young ensign of the Auvergne regiment, the Chevalier de la Jabotiere. Madame de Mouchy wrote to Madam Esmond praising her son's refinement, a letter that would have brought little joy to Mr. Whitfield.

Upon their return after ten delightful months, the boys had grown indistinguishable in stature, George's raven hair contrasting with Harry's light locks tied in ribbons. Yet, the journey had not softened George's nature. He returned with no goodwill toward George Washington, whom he viewed with the same suspicion he held for his grandfather's friend. Washington, though barely of age, carried an air of grave maturity, managing family affairs with a trustworthiness that surpassed men twice his senior.

At Castlewood, Mrs. Mountain, Madam Esmond's droll and match-making companion, spun webs of suspicion regarding the Major. She convinced herself that Washington coveted the widow, noting his constant presence and the widow's reliance on his counsel for everything from estate management to selling tobacco. "Great tall men always marry little chits of women," she reasoned, dismissing the fifteen-year age gap as trivial. When George sternly begged her to silence these absurdities, she merely shrugged, unable to keep her eyes shut on the evidence of his affection. George responded with frigid courtesy and biting sarcasm, retreating to his bookroom to study mathematics and Latin in lonely solitude, while Harry rode out with sporting friends.

The tension nearly erupted when Washington visited Castlewood, receiving the widow's cordiality with such tenderness that George's jealousy threatened to boil over. However, the visit was a farewell; Washington was departing for a perilous mission to the western frontier. The French, having claimed the Ohio River valley, were encroaching on British settlements. In 1753, amidst the uneasy peace of Europe, the colonial dispute ignited on the Ohio. Young Washington volunteered to carry Governor Dinwiddie's demand for the French to withdraw. Accompanied by a guide and attendants, he braved the frozen forests and rivers to reach Fort Le Boeuf, only to be told bluntly that the French intended to hold the land and drive the English out.

Harry, returning from a cockfight, lamented his absence from such noble sport, while the widow hailed Washington's return as proof of his superiority over her sons' idle pursuits. When George expressed his desire to serve under the Major, the widow refused, insisting an Esmond could only serve with a royal commission. Undeterred, Washington raised a regiment of provincials to confront the French. At the forks of the Ohio, near the site of future Pittsburgh, a small force under Colonel Trent faced overwhelming numbers. The French seized the fort, renaming it Fort Duquesne. No shots had been fired yet, but the stage was set for a war that would span sixty years and reshape the continent.

In the following year, Washington took command of the provincial troops. He engaged the French advance guard, killing their leader, but was ultimately forced to capitulate due to superior enemy forces. On July 4, 1754, he marched out from Fort Necessity, surrendering the post and returning home. Defeated and humbled, he presented himself at Castlewood, admitting his earlier boasts had been born of anger at George's perceived scorn. "I thought you laughed at us," he confessed.

George, moved by his comrade's sorrow, reached out to comfort him, forgetting his jealousy in the face of shared misfortune. He defended Washington's honor, noting that starvation and lack of ammunition had doomed the fight. But the widow interrupted, declaring that English regiments would have routed the French, and offering a fine curtsey to the defeated Colonel. This gesture of pity only inflamed George's jealousy anew, leaving the young soldier to hang his head while the widow praised her sex's kindness to the unhappy.

No man possesses a claim to sympathy quite as potent as the combination of bravery, youth, beauty, and misfortune. Madam Esmond might have borne twenty sons, yet she possessed every right to admire her young soldier. Her devotion to Mr. Washington intensified; she raved of him and praised him in every assembly, pointing out his sterling virtues to her own children with fervor. She contrasted these qualities sharply with Harry's love of pleasure—whom she dismissed as "the wild boy!"—and George's listless musings over his books. George, however, was not disposed to warm to Mr. Washington any more readily because of his mother's extravagant eulogies. Instead, he coaxed the jealous demon within him until he became a pest to himself and all around him. He uttered jokes so profound that his simple mother remained bewildered, unable to grasp their meaning, while his moody, saturnine humor left her powerless to respond.

Meanwhile, public events were unfolding that would alter the fortunes of their humble family. The quarrel between the French and English North Americans had ceased to be merely provincial, swelling into a national conflict. Reinforcements from France had already arrived in Canada, and English troops were expected in Virginia. "Alas! my dear friend!" wrote Madame la Presidente de Mouchy from Quebec to her young correspondent, George Warrington. "How contrary is destiny to us! I see you quitting the embrace of an adored mother to precipitate yourself into the arms of Bellona. I see you pass wounded from combats. I hesitate almost to wish victory to our lilies when I behold you ranged under the banners of the Leopard. There are enmities which the heart does not recognize—ours assuredly remain at peace amidst the tumults. All here love and salute you, as well as Monsieur the Bear-hunter, your brother (that cold Hippolyte who preferred the chase to the soft conversation of our ladies!) Your friend, your enemy, the Chevalier de la Jabotiere, burns to meet on the field of Mars his generous rival. M. Du Quesne spoke of you last night at supper. M. Du Quesne, my husband, sends affectionate remembrances to their young friend, joined ever by those of your sincere Presidente de Mouchy."

Indeed, the banner of the Leopard was flung out to the winds, rallying a number of the King's soldiers. It was resolved to wrest from the French all conquests made upon British dominion. Two regiments were raised and paid by the King in America, and a fleet accompanied by two additional ships was dispatched from home under an experienced commander. In February, 1755, Commodore Keppel, aboard the famous ship *Centurion*—in which Anson had made his voyage round the world—anchored in Hampton Roads with two ships of war under his command, carrying on board General Braddock, his staff, and a portion of his troops. Mr. Braddock had been appointed by the Duke. A century prior, the Duke of Cumberland had been hailed as "The Duke par excellence" in England; though not so great a warrior as his party esteemed him, nor so villainous as his enemies painted him, he commanded respect. A fleet of transports swiftly followed, bringing stores, men, and money in abundance.

The General landed his troops at Alexandria on the Potomac River and repaired to Annapolis in Maryland, where he ordered the governors of the various colonies to meet him in council, urging each to call upon their respective provinces to aid the common cause in this strait.

The arrival of the General and his small army caused a mighty excitement throughout the provinces, nowhere greater than at Castlewood. Harry departed forthwith to see the troops under canvas at Alexandria. The sight of their lines delighted him, as did the inspiring music of their fifes and drums. He quickly made acquaintance with the officers of both regiments, longing to join the expedition upon which they were bound, and became a welcome guest at their mess.

Madam Esmond was pleased that her sons should have the opportunity of enjoying the society of gentlemen of good fashion from England.
