"But he tended me most kindly in my fever," Harry interjected. "He was yet ill when he gave up his bed to me, thinking only of his friend, when any other man would have thought only of himself."

"A friend! A pretty friend!" she sneered. "Of all his Excellency's aides-de-camp, my gentleman is the only one who comes back unwounded. The brave and noble fall, but he, to be sure, is unhurt. I confide my boy to him, the pride of my life, whom he will defend with his, forsooth! And he leaves my George in the forest, and brings me back himself! Oh, a pretty welcome I must give him!"

"No gentleman," Harry cried warmly, "was ever refused shelter under my grandfather's roof."

"Oh no—no gentleman!" the little widow exclaimed. "Let us go down, if you like, son, and pay our respects to this one. Will you please to give me your arm?" Taking an arm that could barely support her, she walked down the broad stairs into the apartment where the Colonel sat.

She made a ceremonious curtsey, extending a small hand that rested briefly in his. "I wish that our meeting had been happier, Colonel Washington," she said.

"You do not grieve more than I do that it is otherwise, madam," the Colonel replied.

"I might have wished that the meeting had been spared, that I might not have kept you from friends whom you are naturally anxious to see—that my boy's indisposition had not detained you. Home and his good nurse Mountain, and his mother and our good Doctor Dempster, will soon restore him. 'Twas scarce necessary, Colonel, that you, who have so many affairs on your hands, military and domestic, should turn doctor too."

"Harry was ill and weak, and I thought it was my duty to ride by him," the Colonel faltered.

"You yourself, sir, have gone through the fatigues and dangers of the campaign in the most wonderful manner," the widow said, curtseying again, her black eyes impenetrable.

"I wish to Heaven, madam, some one else had come back in my place!"

"Nay, sir, you have ties which must render your life more than ever valuable and dear to you, and duties to which, I know, you must be anxious to betake yourself. In our present deplorable state of doubt and distress, Castlewood can be a welcome place to no stranger, much less to you, and so I know, sir, you will be for leaving us ere long. And you will pardon me if the state of my own spirits obliges me for the most part to keep my chamber. But my friends here will bear you company as long as you favour us, whilst I nurse my poor Harry upstairs. Mountain, you will have the cedar-room on the ground-floor ready for Mr. Washington, and anything in the house is at his command. Farewell, sir. Will you be pleased to present my compliments to your mother, who will be thankful to have her son safe and sound out of the war—as also to my young friend Martha Custis, to whom and to whose children I wish every happiness. Come, my son!" With these words and another freezing curtsey, the pale little woman retreated, staring steadily at the Colonel, who stood dumb on the floor.

Though Madam Esmond's belief in her son's safety seemed absolute, the house of Castlewood remained sad and gloomy. She forbade mourning for herself and family, yet her heart was in black, whatever resolute face she wore before the world. To look for her son was to hope against hope. No authentic account of his death had arrived, and no one had seen him fall; hundreds more had been struck down that day with no eyes to behold their last pangs. A fortnight after the defeat, when Harry was absent on his quest, George's servant, Sady, reappeared wounded and maimed at Castlewood. He could give no coherent account of the battle, only of his flight from the center where he was with the baggage. He had no news of his master since the morning of the action. For many days, Sady lurked in the negro quarters, away from the sight of Madam Esmond, whose anger he dared not face. Her neighbors spoke of her as laboring under a delusion. So strong was it that there were times when Harry and the other members of the little Castlewood family were almost brought to share in it. It seemed nothing strange to her that her father, from another world, should promise her her son's life. In this world or the next, that family must be of consequence, she thought. Nothing had ever happened to her sons—no accident, no fever, no important illness—but she had a prevision of it. She could enumerate half a dozen instances, which her household was obliged to confirm, of how, when anything had happened to the boys at ever so great a distance, she had known of their mishap and its consequences. No, George was not dead; George was a prisoner among the Indians; George would come back and rule over Castlewood; as sure as sure as his Majesty would send a great force from home to recover the tarnished glory of the British arms and drive the French out of the Americas.

As for Mr. Washington, she would never behold him again with her own goodwill. He had promised to protect George with his life. Why was her son gone and the Colonel alive? How dared he to face her after that promise, and appear before a mother without her son? She trusted she knew her duty. She bore illwill to no one, but as an Esmond, she had a sense of honor, and Mr. Washington had forfeited hers in letting her son out of his sight. He had to obey superior orders? Psha! A promise was a promise. He had promised to guard George's life with his own, and where was her boy? And was not the Colonel sound and safe? Do not tell me that his coat and hat had shots through them! This was her answer to another humble plea in Mr. Washington's behalf. Could she not go into the study instantly and fire two shots with her papa's pistols through her paduasoy skirt—and should she be killed? She laughed at the notion of death resulting from any such operation, nor was her laugh very pleasant to hear. The satire of people who have little natural humor is seldom good sport for bystanders. I think dull men's facetiae are mostly cruel.

So, if Harry wanted to meet his friend, he had to do so in secret, at court-houses, taverns, or various places of resort; or in their little towns, where the provincial gentry assembled. No man of spirit, she vowed, could meet Mr. Washington after his base desertion of her family. She was exceedingly excited when she heard that the Colonel and her son had absolutely met. What a heart must Harry have to give his hand to one whom she considered little better than George's murderer! For shame to say so! For shame upon you, ungrateful boy, forgetting the dearest, noblest, most perfect of brothers, for that tall, gawky, fox-hunting Colonel, with his horrid oaths! How can he be George's murderer, when I say my boy is not dead? He is not dead, because my instinct never deceived me; because, as sure as I see his picture now before me—only 'tis not near so noble or so good as he

When the wandering hero of Troy recounted his trials to Queen Dido, the monarch listened with rapt attention, captivated by the eloquent danger of his tale. A history was born from that moment, more poignant than any prior chapter of Aeneas's life, leaving the princess to regret the day she yielded to such a persuasive speaker. Harry Warrington possessed none of Pius Aeneas's rhetorical fire, nor was his elderly aunt, we may presume, as soft-hearted as the sentimental queen; yet, the lad's narrative struck a chord. Delivered with an artless sincerity and a warm, cordial voice, his story moved Madam Bernstein to a tenderness she rarely permitted herself. In the vast desert of her existence, there were few oases, few moments of sweet respite. Her life had been a long solitude until this friendly voice broke the silence, causing her heart to flutter with unfamiliar pangs of love and sympathy. She doted on the boy, intoxicated by this sudden capacity for compassion. Save for a fleeting, faint sensation in her earliest youth, she had known no tender affection for another soul. Such a woman would surely watch her own pulse with suspicion, marveling at how it quickened when the boy approached. Her cheeks flushed with joy at his arrival; her eyes welcomed him with a fondness that lingered long after he had turned away. "Ah, if she could have borne a son like that, how she would have cherished him!"

"Wait," whispered Conscience, the dark mocker within her breast. "Wait, Beatrix Esmond. You know you will tire of this infatuation, as you have of all others. You know that when the passing fancy fades, the boy may perish, and you will shed no tear; or worse, you will grow bored with his stories, and your destiny remains one of loneliness." Well? Suppose life is indeed a desert? Then there are halting places, shades, and refreshing waters; let us drink deeply of them for today. We know we must march on when tomorrow arrives, trudging toward our inevitable fate.

She smiled inwardly, following the lad's narrative, recognizing in his simple tales of his mother the traits of family resemblance. Madam Esmond was very jealous? Yes, Harry admitted. She was fond of Colonel Washington? He liked him, but only as a friend, Harry declared, though he confessed a hundred times having heard his mother vow otherwise. He was ashamed to admit that he himself had once been absurdly jealous of the Colonel. "Well, you will see that my half-sister will never forgive him," Madam Beatrix remarked. "And you need not be surprised, sir, that women take a fancy to men younger than themselves; for do I not dote upon you? And do not all these people of Castlewood fret with jealousy?"

Despite the fierce jealousy the family harbored for Madame de Bernstein's new favorite, the House of Castlewood showed no ill will in their words or actions toward their young guest and kinsman. After a couple of days in the ancestral home, Mr. Harry Warrington had become simply "Cousin Harry" to the young and the middle-aged. Especially in the presence of the Baroness, the Countess of Castlewood was most gracious to her kinsman. She seized every private opportunity to inform the Baroness how charming the young Huron was, boasting of the elegance of his manners and appearance, and wondering how, in his distant province, the child could have learned such politeness.

These notes of admiration and interrogation, the Baroness accepted with equal complacency. Speaking parenthetically, the present chronicler cannot help but offer a respectful remark on the conduct of ladies toward one another, and the things they say, which they forbear to say, and which they whisper behind each other's backs. With what smiles and curtseys they stab each other! With what compliments they hate each other! With what determined long-suffering they refuse to be offended! With what innocent dexterity they can drop a drop of poison into the cup of conversation, handing the goblet round to the whole family to drink, making the dear domestic circle miserable! I burst out of my parenthesis. I fancy my Baroness and Countess smiling at each other a hundred years ago, exchanging hands and cheeks, calling each other "My dear," "My dear creature," "My dear Countess," "My dear Baroness," "My dear sister"—even when they were most ready to fight.

"You wonder, my dear Maria, that the boy should be so polite?" cried Madame de Bernstein. "His mother was bred up by two very perfect gentlefolks. Colonel Esmond had a certain grave courteousness and a grand manner, which I do not see among gentlemen nowadays."

"Eh, my dear, we all praise our own time! My grandmamma used to declare there was nothing like Whitehall and Charles the Second."

"My mother saw King James the Second's court for a short while, and though not a court-educated person, as you know—her father was a country clergyman—yet was exquisitely well-bred. The Colonel, her second husband, was a person of great travel and experience, as well as of learning, and had frequented the finest company of Europe. They could not go into their retreat and leave their good manners behind them, and our boy has had them as his natural inheritance."

"Nay, excuse me, my dear, for thinking you too partial about your mother. She could not have been that perfection which your filial fondness imagines. She left off liking her daughter—you have owned that she did—and I cannot fancy a complete woman who has a cold heart. No, no, my dear sister-in-law! Manners are very requisite, no doubt, and, for a country parson's daughter, your mamma was very well—I have seen many of the cloth who are very well. Mr. Sampson, our chaplain, is very well. Dr. Young is very well. Mr. Dodd is very well; but they have not the true air—as how should they? I protest, I beg pardon! I forgot my lord bishop, your ladyship's first choice. But, as I said before, to be a complete woman, one must have, what you have, what I may say and bless Heaven for, I think I have—a good heart. Without the affections, all the world is vanity, my love! I protest I only live, exist, eat, drink, rest, for my sweet, sweet children!—for my wicked Willy, for my self-willed Fanny, dear naughty loves!" (She rapturously kissed a bracelet on each arm which contained the miniature representations of those two young persons.) "Yes, Mimi! Yes, Fanchon! You know I do, you dear, dear little things! And if they were to die, or you were to die, your poor mistress would die too!" Mimi and Fanchon, two quivering Italian greyhounds, jumped into their lady's arms and kissed her hands, but respected her cheeks, which were covered with rouge. "No, my dear! For nothing do I bless Heaven so much (though it puts me to excruciating torture very often) as for having endowed me with sensibility and a feeling heart!"

"You are full of feeling, dear Anna," said the Baroness. "You are celebrated for your sensibility. You must give a little of it to our American nephew—cousin—I scarce know his relationship."

"Nay, I am here but as a guest in Castlewood now. The house is my Lord Castlewood's, not mine, or his lordship's whenever he shall choose to claim it. What can I do for the young Virginian that has not been done? He is charming. Are we even jealous of him for being so, my dear? And though we see what a fancy the Baroness de Bernstein has taken for him, do your ladyship's nephews and nieces—your real nephews and nieces—cry out? My poor children might be mortified, for indeed, in a few hours, the charming young man has made as much way as my poor things have been able to do in all their lives: but are they angry? Willy hath taken him out to ride. This morning, was not Maria playing the harpsichord whilst my Fanny taught him the minuet? 'Twas a charming young group, I assure you, and it brought tears into my eyes to look at the young creatures. Poor lad! We are as fond of him as you are, dear Baroness!"

Now, Madame de Bernstein had happened, through her own ears or her maid's, to overhear what really took place in consequence of this harmless little scene. Lady Castlewood had come into the room where the young people were thus engaged in amusing and instructing themselves, accompanied by her son William, who arrived in his boots from the kennel.

"Bravi, bravi! Oh, charming!" cried the Countess, clapping her hands, nodding with one of her best smiles to Harry Warrington, and darting a look at his partner which Lady Fanny perfectly understood; and so, perhaps, did Lady Maria at her harpsichord, for she played with redoubled energy and nodded her waving curls over the chords.

"Infernal young Choctaw! Is he teaching Fanny the war-dance? And is Fan going to try her tricks upon him now?" asked Mr. William, whose temper was not of the best.

And that was what Lady Castlewood's look said to Fanny. "Are you going to try your tricks upon him now?"

She made Harry a very low curtsey, and he blushed, and they both stopped dancing, somewhat disconcerted. Lady Maria rose from the harpsichord and walked away.

"Nay, go on dancing, young people! Don't let me spoil sport, and let me play for you," said the Countess; and she sat down to the instrument and played.

"I don't know how to dance," said Harry, hanging his head down, with a blush that the Countess's finest carmine could not equal.

"And Fanny was teaching you? Go on teaching him, dearest Fanny!"

"Go on, do!" said William, with a sidelong growl.

"I—I had rather not show off my awkwardness in company," added Harry, recovering himself. "When I know how to dance a minuet, be sure I will ask my cousin to walk one with me."

"That will be very soon, dear Cousin Warrington, I am certain," remarked the Countess, with her most gracious air.

"What game is she hunting now?" thought Mr. William to himself, who could not penetrate his mother's ways; and that lady, fondly calling her daughter to her elbow, left the room.

They were no sooner in the tapestried passage leading away to their own apartment than Lady Castlewood's bland tone entirely changed. "You booby!" she began to her adored Fanny. "You double idiot! What are you going to do with the Huron? You don't want to marry a creature like that, and be a squaw in a wigwam?"

"Don't, mamma!" gasped Lady Fanny. Mamma was pinching her ladyship's arm black-and-blue. "I am sure our cousin is very well," Fanny whimpered, "and you said so yourself."

"Very well! Yes; and heir to a swamp, a negro, a log-cabin and a barrel of tobacco! My Lady Frances Esmond, do you remember what your ladyship's rank is, and what your name is, and who was your ladyship's mother, when, at three days' acquaintance, you commence dancing—a pretty dance, indeed—with this brat out of Virginia?"

"Mr. Warrington is our cousin," pleaded Lady Fanny.

"A creature come from nobody knows where is not your cousin! How do we know he is your cousin? He may be a valet who has taken his master's portmanteau, and run away in his postchaise."

"But Madame de Bernstein says he is our cousin," interposed Fanny; "and he is the image of the Esmonds."

"Madame de Bernstein has her likes and dislikes, takes up people and forgets people; and she chooses to profess a mighty fancy for this young man. Because she likes him to-day, is that any reason why she should like him to-morrow? Before company, and in your aunt's presence, your ladyship will please to be as civil to him as necessary; but, in private, I forbid you to see him or encourage him."

"I don't care, madam, whether your ladyship forbids me or not!" cried out Lady Fanny, wrought up to a pitch of revolt.

"Very good, Fanny! Then I speak to my lord, and we return to Kensington. If I can't bring you to reason, your brother will."

At this juncture, the conversation between mother and daughter stopped, or Madame de Bernstein's informer had no further means of hearing or reporting it.

It was only in after days that she told Harry Warrington a part of what she knew. At present, he but saw that his kinsfolk received him not unkindly. Lady Castlewood was perfectly civil to him; the young ladies pleasant and pleased; my Lord Castlewood, a man of cold and haughty demeanor, was not more reserved towards Harry than to any of the rest of the family; Mr. William was ready to drink with him, to ride with him, to go to races with him, and to play cards with him. When he proposed to go away, they one and all pressed him to stay. Madame de Bernstein did not tell him how it arose that he was the object of such eager hospitality. He did not know what schemes he was serving or disarranging, whose or what anger he was creating. He fancied he was welcome because those around him were his kinsmen, and never thought that those could be his enemies out of whose cup he was drinking, and whose hand he was pressing every night and morning.

The second day following Harry's arrival at Castlewood fell upon a Sunday. The chapel attached to the great house served as the parish church for the village. A private door from the mansion opened directly into a magnificent state pew reserved for the family, and at the appointed hour, they all took their places in strict order, while a respectable congregation from the village filled the benches below. High upon the church roof hung several ancient, dusty banners; Harry indulged himself in imagining that these had been carried by retainers of his own lineage during the Commonwealth wars, in which his ancestors had fought with such loyal distinction. Within the altar rails knelt the effigy of the Esmond of the time of King James the First, the common forefather of the assembly. Beside him, Madame de Bernstein, in her capacity as Bishop's widow, never failed her attendance. She conducted her devotions with a gravity almost as exemplary as that of the ancestor in his square beard and red gown, forever kneeling on his stone hassock before his marble desk and book, beneath his emblazoned shield of arms.

The clergyman, a tall, high-colored, and handsome young man, read the service in a lively, agreeable voice, imparting a dramatic flair to the chapters of Scripture. The music was excellent, performed by one of the young ladies of the family at the organ, though it was marred by an interruption—a burst of laughter rising from the servants' pew. This was occasioned by Mr. Warrington's lacquey, Gumbo. Knowing the air assigned for the psalm, the man began to sing it in a voice so exceedingly loud and sweet that the entire congregation turned toward the African warbler. The parson himself covered his mouth with his handkerchief, and the liveried gentlemen from London were thrown into a state of astonishment. Perhaps pleased with the sensation he had created, Mr. Gumbo continued his performance until it became almost a solo, silencing the voice of the clerk entirely. For the truth was, though Gumbo held onto the book alongside pretty Molly, the porter's daughter who had first welcomed the strangers to Castlewood, he sang and recited entirely by ear, unable to read a single syllable of the verses before him.

Once this choral performance concluded, a brief sermon followed, which Harry found rather too short. In a lively, familiar, and striking discourse, the clergyman described a scene he had witnessed the previous week: the execution of a horse-stealer after the Assizes. He painted the man's former good character, his loving family, and his agony at parting from them. He depicted the execution in a manner that was startling, terrible, and picturesque. Rather than employing the heavy Scripture phraseology Harry was accustomed to hearing from the somewhat Calvinistic preachers his mother favored, the divine spoke as one man of the world addressing other sinful souls who might profit from good advice. The unfortunate man had begun as a farmer of good prospects but had succumbed to the vices of the age—drinking, card-playing, horse-racing, and cock-fighting. Against these, the young clergyman was generously indignant. Then came poaching and horse-stealing, for which the man suffered. The divine rapidly drew striking and fearful pictures of these rustic crimes, startling his hearers by showing that the Eye of the Law watched the poacher at midnight and set traps to catch the criminal. He galloped the stolen horse over highway and common, from one county to another, yet showed Retribution ever galloping after, seizing the malefactor at the country fair, carrying him before the justice, and never unlocking his manacles until he dropped them at the foot of the gallows. "Heaven be pitiful to the sinner!" the clergyman cried, acting out the scene. He whispered in the criminal's ear at the cart; he dropped his handkerchief on the clerk's head. Harry started back as that handkerchief fell. The clergyman had been speaking for more than twenty minutes. Harry could have listened for an hour more and would not have felt it had been five. The gentlefolk in the great pew were thoroughly enlivened by the discourse. Once or twice, Harry, observing the pew where the house servants sat, noted their intense attention; especially Gumbo, his own man, who sat in an attitude of profound consternation. Yet the smockfrocks seemed to heed nothing, clamping out of church quite unconcerned. Gaffer Brown and Gammer Jones took the matter as it came, and the rosy-cheeked, red-cloaked village lasses sat under their broad hats entirely unmoved. My lord, from his pew, nodded slightly to the clergyman in the pulpit as the divine's head and wig surged up from the cushion.

"Sampson has been strong to-day," said his lordship. "He has assaulted the Philistines in great force."

"Beautiful, beautiful!" exclaimed Harry.

"Bet five to four it was his Assize sermon. He has been over to Winton to preach, and to see those dogs," cried William.

The organist had played the little congregation out into the sunshine. Only Sir Francis Esmond, temp. Jac. I., still knelt on his marble hassock before his prayer-book of stone. Mr. Sampson emerged from his vestry in his cassock and nodded to the gentlemen still lingering in the great pew.

"Come up, and tell us about those dogs," said Mr. William, and the divine nodded a laughing assent.

The gentlemen passed out of the church into the gallery of their house, which connected them with the sacred building. Mr. Sampson made his way through the court and presently joined them. He was introduced by my lord to the Virginian cousin of the family, Mr. Warrington. The chaplain bowed very profoundly and hoped Mr. Warrington would benefit by the virtuous example of his European kinsmen. Was he related to Sir Miles Warrington of Norfolk? Sir Miles was Mr. Warrington's father's elder brother. What a pity he had a son! 'Twas a pretty estate, and Mr. Warrington looked as if he would become a baronetcy, and a fine estate in Norfolk.

"Tell me about my uncle," cried Virginian Harry.

"Tell us about those dogs!" said English Will, in a breath.

"Two more jolly dogs, two more drunken dogs, saving your presence, Mr. Warrington, than Sir Miles and his son, I never saw. Sir Miles was a staunch friend and neighbor of Sir Robert's. He can drink down any man in the county, except his son and a few more. The other dogs about which Mr. William is anxious, for Heaven hath made him a prey to dogs and all kinds of birds, like the Greeks in the Iliad—"

"I know that line in the Iliad," said Harry, blushing. "I only know five more, but I know that one." And his head fell. He was thinking, "Ah, my dear brother George knew all the Iliad and all the Odyssey, and almost every book that was ever written besides!"

"What on earth" (only he mentioned a place under the earth) "are you talking about now?" asked Will of his reverence.

The chaplain reverted to the dogs and their performance. He thought Mr. William's dogs were more than a match for them. From dogs they went off to horses. Mr. William was very eager about the Six Year Old Plate at Huntingdon. "Have you brought any news of it, Parson?"

"The odds are five to four on Brilliant against the field," said the parson, gravely, "but, mind you, Jason is a good horse."

"Whose horse?" asked my lord.

"Duke of Ancaster's. By Cartouche out of Miss Langley," said the divine. "Have you horse-races in Virginia, Mr. Warrington?"

"Haven't we!" cried Harry; "but oh! I long to see a good English race!"

"Do you—do you—bet a little?" continued his reverence.

"I have done such a thing," replied Harry with a smile.

"I'll take Brilliant even against the field, for ponies with you, cousin!" shouted out Mr. William.

"I'll give or take three to one against Jason!" said the clergyman.

"I don't bet on horses I don't know," said Harry, wondering to hear the chaplain now, and remembering his sermon half an hour before.

"Hadn't you better write home, and ask your mother?" said Mr. William, with a sneer.

"Will, Will!" called out my lord, "our cousin Warrington is free to bet, or not, as he likes. Have a care how you venture on either of them, Harry Warrington. Will is an old file, in spite of his smooth face, and as for Parson Sampson, I defy our ghostly enemy to get the better of him."

"Him and all his works, my lord!" said Mr. Sampson, with a bow.

Harry was highly indignant at this allusion to his mother. "I'll tell you what, cousin Will," he said, "I am in the habit of managing my own affairs in my own way, without asking any lady to arrange them for me. And I'm used to make my own bets upon my own judgment, and don't need any relations to select them for me, thank you. But as I am your guest, and, no doubt, you want to show me hospitality, I'll take your bet—there. And so Done and Done."

"Done," said Will, looking askance.

"Of course it is the regular odds that's in the paper which you give me, cousin?"

"Well, no, it isn't," growled Will. "The odds are five to four, that's the fact, and you may have 'em, if you like."

"Nay, cousin, a bet is a bet; and I take you, too, Mr. Sampson."

"Three to one against Jason. I lay it. Very good," said Mr. Sampson.

"Is it to be ponies too, Mr. Chaplain?" asked Harry with a superb air, as if he had Lombard Street in his pocket.

"No, no. Thirty to ten. It is enough for a poor priest to win."

"Here goes a great slice out of my quarter's hundred," thought Harry. "Well, I shan't let these Englishmen fancy that I am afraid of them. I didn't begin, but for the honour of Old Virginia I won't go back."

These pecuniary transactions arranged, William Esmond went away scowling towards the stables, where he loved to take his pipe with the grooms; the brisk parson went off to pay his court to the ladies and partake of the Sunday dinner which would presently be served. Lord Castlewood and Harry remained for a while together. Since the Virginian's arrival, my lord had scarcely spoken with him. In his manners he was perfectly friendly, but so silent that he would often sit at the head of his table and leave it without uttering a word.

"I suppose yonder property of yours is a fine one by this time?" said my lord to Harry.

"I reckon it's almost as big as an English county," answered Harry, "and the land's as good, too, for many things." Harry would not have the Old Dominion, nor his share in it, underrated.

"Indeed!" said my lord, with a look of surprise. "When it belonged to my father it did not yield much."

"Pardon me, my lord. You know how it belonged to your father," cried the youth, with some spirit. "It was because my grandfather did not choose to claim his right." [This matter is discussed in the Author's previous work, *The Memoirs of Colonel Esmond*.]

"Of course, of course," said my lord, hastily.

"I mean, cousin, that we of the Virginian house owe you nothing but our own," continued Harry Warrington; "but our own, and the hospitality which you are now showing me."

"You are heartily welcome to both. You were hurt by the betting just now?"

"Well," replied the lad, "I am sort o' hurt. Your welcome, you see, is different to our welcome, and that's the fact. At home we are glad to see a man, hold out a hand to him, and give him of our best. Here you take us in, give us beef and claret enough, to be sure, and don't seem to care when we come, or when we go. That's the remark which I have been making since I have been in your lordship's house; I can't help telling it out, you see, now 'tis on my mind; and I think I am a little easier now I have said it." And with this, the excited young fellow knocked a billiard-ball across the table, and then laughed, and looked at his elder kinsman.

"A la bonne heure! We are cold to the stranger within and without our gates. We don't take Mr. Harry Warrington into our arms, and cry when we see our cousin. We don't cry when he goes away—but do we pretend?"

"No, you don't. But you try to get the better of him in a bet," said Harry, indignantly.

"Is there no such practice in Virginia, and don't sporting men there try to overreach one another? What was that story I heard you telling our aunt, of the British officers and Tom somebody of Spotsylvania!"

"That's fair!" cried Harry. "That is, it's usual practice, and a stranger must look out. I don't mind the parson; if he wins, he may have, and welcome. But a relation! To think that my own blood cousin wants money out of me!"

"A Newmarket man would get the better of his father. My brother has been on the turf since he rode over to it from Cambridge. If you play at cards with him—and he will if you will let him—he will beat you if he can."

"Well, I'm ready!" cried Harry. "I'll play any game with him that I know, or I'll jump with him, or I'll ride with him, or I'll row with him, or I'll wrestle with him, or

Having extracted considerable sums from his cousin and the chaplain, our young Virginian felt a moral imperative to allow them a chance at recovery, though I suspect his mother and other upright moralists would have disapproved of his chosen method. He indulges in card games with excessive frequency. Beyond the daily whist or quadrille with the ladies, which commences shortly after dinner at three o'clock and concludes only at supper, there exist high-stakes contests involving fortunes, in which all the gentlemen, including my lord, participate. Following their Sunday conversations, his lordship had become notably more open and confiding with his kinsman, betting with him affably and engaging him in backgammon and piquet. Both Mr. William and the pious chaplain relished a touch of hazard; however, this diversion was pursued clandestinely, unknown to the ladies of the house, who had repeatedly extracted promises from Cousin Will that he would not lead the Virginian into mischief, nor would he himself partake. Thus, Will pledged as much as his aunt or mother demanded, swearing on his honor that he would never play—nay, never; and when the family retired, Mr. Will would stroll over with a dice-box and a bottle of rum to Cousin Harry's quarters, where he, Hal, and the reverend gentleman would gamble until dawn.

When Harry bestowed upon Lord Castlewood those glowing descriptions of the maternal estate in America, he harbored no intent to deceive, boast, or lie, for the lad possessed a nature of profound honesty; yet, in his domestic life, it must be acknowledged that the young fellow had associated with all manner of peculiar company—horse-jockeys, tavern loafers, gamblers, and sportsmen, of whom the colonies were replete. A landed aristocracy, supported by a population of negroes to till their fields and cultivate tobacco and corn, found little amusement other than the hunt or the card table and the punch-bowl. The hospitality of the province was boundless: every man's house was his neighbor's; and idle gentlemen rode from mansion to mansion, finding in each similar sport, welcome, and rough plenty. The Virginian squire often possessed a barefooted valet and a cobbled saddle; yet within the crumbling fences and behind the broken windows of the hall, there was ample corn for the horses and abundant drink and venison for the master. Harry had slept on countless straw mattresses and engaged in endless jovial nocturnal bouts over claret and punch in cracked bowls until morning broke and the hounds were followed. His poor brother was of a far more sober disposition, as the lad admitted with contrition. Thus does Nature fashion her folk; some cherish books and tea, while others prefer Burgundy and a gallop across the countryside. Harry's tastes were quickly evident to his friends in England. None favored the Puritan discipline, nor did they dislike Harry for lacking the demeanor of a milksop. Manners, you see, were far looser a century prior; tongues were vastly more free and easy; names were spoken, and deeds performed, which we would now shriek to hear mentioned. Yes, madam, we are not as our ancestors were. Should we not thank the Fates for improving our morals so prodigiously, rendering us so eminently virtuous?

Keeping a shrewd eye upon those around him, and correctly surmising that his cousins sought to probe him, Harry Warrington deemed it prudent to keep his own counsel regarding his affairs, proving himself quite a match for the three gentlemen into whose company he had fallen in all games of chance or sport. Even in the noble game of billiards, he could hold his own after a few days of play with his cousins and their revered pastor. His grandfather, who had imported one of the very few tables existing in His Majesty's province of Virginia from Europe, loved the game. Though Mr. William could defeat him initially, he could not secure undue odds from the young gambler. After their first wager, Harry was on his guard against Mr. William, and Cousin William admitted, with respect, that the American was his equal in most things and superior in many. Yet, though Harry played so well that he could best the parson and soon equal William—who, of course, could best both the girls—how came it that in contests with these, especially with one of them, Mr. Warrington frequently came second? He was profoundly courteous to every being who wore a petticoat; nor has that traditional politeness yet departed from his country. All the women of the Castlewood establishment adored the young gentleman. The grim housekeeper was mollified by him; the fat cook greeted him with boisterous smiles; the ladies' maids, whether French or English, smirked and giggled in his favor; the pretty porter's daughter at the lodge always replied kindly. Madame de Bernstein noted all these things, saying nothing, yet watching carefully the boy's disposition and behavior.

Who can say how old Lady Maria Esmond was? Books of the Peerage were scarce in those days compared to our blessed times, and I cannot tell to a few years, or even a lustre or two. When Will used to claim she was thirty-five, he was abusive and prone to exaggeration. Maria was Will's half-sister, daughter of the late Lord Castlewood's first wife, a German lady whom my lord married during Queen Anne's wars. Baron Bernstein, who married Maria's Aunt Beatrix, Bishop Tusher's widow, was also a German, a Hanoverian nobleman and relative of the first Lady Castlewood. If Lady Maria was born under George I., and His Majesty George II. had reigned for thirty years, how could she be twenty-seven, as she told Harry Warrington? "I am old, child," she would say. She used to call Harry "child" when they were alone. "I am a hundred years old. I am twenty-seven. I might be your mother almost." To which Harry would reply, "Your ladyship might be the mother of all the cupids, I am sure. You don't look twenty, on my word you do not!"

Lady Maria appeared any age one wished. She was a fair beauty with a dazzling white and red complexion, an abundance of fair hair flowing over her shoulders, and beautiful round arms which showed to uncommon advantage when she played billiards with Cousin Harry. When she had to stretch across the table to make a stroke, that youth caught glimpses of a little ankle, a little clocked stocking, and a little black satin slipper with a little red heel, which filled him with unutterable rapture, making him swear that there never was such a foot, ankle, clocked stocking, satin slipper in the world. And yet, oh, foolish Harry! your mother's foot was ever so much more slender, and half an inch shorter, than Lady Maria's. But somehow, boys do not gaze with rapture upon their mothers' slippers and ankles.

No doubt Lady Maria was very kind to Harry when they were alone. Before her sister, aunt, stepmother, she made light of him, calling him a simpleton, a chit, and various trivial names. Behind his back, and even before his face, she mimicked his accent, which smacked somewhat of his province. Harry blushed and corrected the faulty intonation under the guidance of his English monitresses. His aunt pronounced that they would soon make him a pretty fellow.

Lord Castlewood, we have said, became daily more familiar and friendly with his guest and relative. Until the crops were gathered, there was no sporting except an occasional cock-match at Winchester and bull-baiting at Hexton Fair. Harry and Will rode to many jolly fairs and races around the county, where the young Virginian was introduced to some of the county families—the Henleys of the Grange, the Crawleys of Queen's Crawley, the Redmaynes of Lionsden, and so forth. Neighbors arrived in their great heavy coaches, passing two or three days in country fashion. More would have come, but for the fear the entire Castlewood family held of offending Madame de Bernstein. She disliked country company; the rustic society and conversation annoyed her. "We shall be merrier when my aunt leaves us," the young folks admitted. "We have cause, as you may imagine, for being very civil to her. You know what a favorite she was with our papa? And with reason. She secured him his earldom, being very well indeed at Court at that time with the King and Queen. She commands here naturally, perhaps a little too much. We are all afraid of her: even my elder brother stands in awe of her, and my stepmother is much more obedient to her than she ever was to my papa, whom she ruled with a rod of iron. But Castlewood is merrier when our aunt is not here. At least we have much more company. You will come to us in our gay days, Harry, won't you? Of course you will: this is your home, sir. I was so pleased—oh, so pleased—when my brother said he considered it was your home!"

A soft hand was held out after this pretty speech, a pair of very well-preserved blue eyes looking exceedingly friendly. Harry grasped his cousin's hand with ardor. I do not know what privilege of cousinship he would not like to claim, only he was so timid. They call the English selfish and cold. He at first thought his relatives were so; but how mistaken he was! How kind and affectionate they were, especially the Earl—and dear, dear Maria! How he wished he could recall the letter he had written to Mrs. Mountain and his mother, in which he hinted that his welcome had been cold! The Earl, his cousin, was everything that was kind, promising to introduce him to London society, present him at Court, and at White's. He was to consider Castlewood his English home. He had been most hasty in his judgment regarding his relatives in Hampshire. All this, with many contrite expressions, he wrote in his second despatch to Virginia. And he added, for it hath been hinted that the young gentleman did not spell with especial accuracy at this early time, "My cousin, the Lady Maria, is a perfect Angle."

"Ille praeter omnes angulus ridet," muttered little Mr. Dempster, at home in Virginia.

"The child can't be falling in love with his angle, as he calls her!" cried out Mountain.

"Pooh, pooh! my niece Maria is forty!" said Madam Esmond. "I perfectly well recollect her when I was at home—a great, gawky, carroty creature, with a foot like a pair of bellows." Where is truth, forsooth, and who knoweth it? Is Beauty beautiful, or is it only our eyes that make it so? Does Venus squint? Has she got a splay-foot, red hair, and a crooked back? Anoint my eyes, good Fairy Puck, so that I may ever consider the Beloved Object a paragon! Above all, keep on anointing my mistress's dainty peepers with the very strongest ointment, so that my noddle may ever appear lovely to her, and that she may continue to crown my honest ears with fresh roses!

Now, not only was Harry Warrington a favorite in the drawing-room and among all the ladies of the servants' hall, but, like master, like man, his valet Gumbo was very much admired and respected by many of the domestic circle. Gumbo possessed a hundred accomplishments. He was famous as a fisherman, huntsman, and blacksmith. He could dress hair beautifully, improving himself in the art under my lord's own Swiss gentleman. He excelled at cooking many of his Virginian dishes, learning new culinary secrets from my lord's Frenchman. We have heard how exquisitely and melodiously he sang at church; he sang not only sacred but secular music, often inventing airs and composing rude words after the habit of his people. He played the fiddle so charmingly that he set all the girls dancing in Castlewood Hall, and was ever welcome to a gratis mug of ale at the Three Castles in the village, if he would but bring his fiddle. He was good-natured and loved to play for the village children; so that Mr. Warrington's negro was a universal favorite in all the Castlewood domain.

It was not difficult for the servants' hall folks to perceive that Mr. Gumbo was a liar, a fact undoubted in spite of all his good qualities. For instance, that day at church, when he pretended to read from Molly's psalm-book, he sang quite other words than those written in the book, of which he could not decipher a syllable. He pretended to understand music, whereupon the Swiss valet brought him some, and Master Gumbo turned the page upside down. These instances of long-bow practice occurred daily and were patent to all the Castlewood household. They knew Gumbo was a liar, perhaps not thinking the worse of him for this weakness; but they did not know how great a liar he was, and believed him much more than they had reason to do, and because, I suppose, they liked to believe him.

Whatever might be his feelings of wonder and envy upon first viewing the splendor and comforts of Castlewood, Mr. Gumbo kept his sentiments to himself, examining the place, park, appointments, and stables very coolly. "The horses," he said, "are very well, what there are of them; but at Castlewood in Virginia we have six times as many, and let me see, fourteen eighteen grooms to look after them." Madam Esmond's carriages were much finer than my lord's—great deal more gold on the panels. As for her gardens, they covered acres, growing every kind of flower and fruit under the sun. "Pineapples and peaches?" he remarked. "Pineapples and peaches were so common in my country, they were given to pigs." They had twenty forty gardeners, not white gardeners, all black gentlemen, like himself. In the house were twenty forty gentlemen in livery, besides women-servants—he could never remember how many women-servants, there were so many—"dere were fifty women-servants"—all Madam Esmond's property, worth ever so many hundred pieces of eight apiece. Young Harry Warrington's sudden revolt caught Madame de Bernstein completely off guard. Her only defense was the immediate flare of anger that had ended the previous scene. As she stormed out, she cast two piercing glares at Lady Fanny and her mother before disappearing. Meanwhile, Lady Maria remained oblivious to the storm, her attention fixed entirely on her tambour-frame. She barely lifted her head from her embroidery to watch her aunt retreat or to register the silent, venomous exchange of looks between the mother-in-law and her daughter.

"So, despite all our efforts, you have succeeded, madam?" the maternal gaze seemed to demand.

"Have what?" Lady Fanny's eyes queried, feigning confusion. Yet, innocence was not her forte. She looked puzzled rather than pure. Had she truly been guilty, she would have mastered the art of appearing innocent with far greater cunning, carefully composing a face ready to meet any accusation. Whatever expression she wore, her mother stared at her with such intensity that it felt as though she might tear the eyes from her head.

Lady Castlewood, however, lacked the immediate brutality of the stage monsters in *King Lear*. When her ladyship intended to destroy her daughter, she would instead retire with a smile, her arm affectionately around the child's waist, only to inflict her punishment in private.

"So you do not wish to accompany the old lady to Tunbridge Wells?" she asked Cousin Warrington, masking her displeasure with a perfectly practiced, well-bred smile.

"And small blame to our cousin!" Lord Castlewood interjected. "A young man cannot spend his entire existence idling and taking holidays. He must blend something useful with his pleasures. He can visit the fiddles and pump-rooms of Tunbridge or Bath later. Mr. Warrington is destined to manage a vast estate in America; let him observe how our estates here in England are run. Will has already shown him the kennels and stables, and the fashionable games, which I believe, cousin, you play as well as your tutors. After the harvest, we will introduce him to English fowling and shooting; in winter, we will take him hunting. Although there has been a cooling of relations between us and our kinswoman in Virginia, we share the same blood. Before sending our cousin back to his mother, let us demonstrate what the life of an English gentleman entails at home. I have been urging him to stay and keep me company, partly for sport, but also to read with him."

Lord Castlewood spoke with such unfeigned frankness that his mother-in-law, half-brother, and sister were left bewildered, unable to decipher his true intent. These three often engaged in quiet conspiracies, plotting against the head of the household. When he adopted this open tone, his meaning remained opaque, often taking months to unravel. He did not simply state a fact; he commanded that his statement be accepted as truth within the family. Consequently, it became the prevailing notion that Lord Castlewood possessed a noble desire to cultivate domestic affections and to educate, amuse, and improve his young relative, having developed a genuine fondness for the lad and wishing for Harry to remain near him for some time.

"What is Castlewood's game now?" William whispered to his mother and sister as they slipped away into the corridors. "Wait! By George, I have it!"

"What, William?"

"He intends to get him involved in gambling and win the Virginia estate back from him. That is his plan!"

"But the lad has no Virginia estate to lose if he fails," his mother remarked.

"If my brother has no scheme in mind, may I be damned."

"Hush! Of course he has a scheme. But what is it?"

"He can't mean Maria—Maria is as old as Harry's mother," Mr. William mused.

"Pooh! With her aged face, sandy hair, and freckled skin! Impossible!" Lady Fanny cried, letting out a small sigh.

"Of course, your ladyship fancied the Iroquois, too!" his mother retorted.

"I trust I know my station and duty better, madam! If I had liked him, that is no reason to marry him. Your ladyship has taught me that much."

"My Lady Fanny!"

"I am sure you married our father without loving him. You have told me so a thousand times!"

"And if you did not love our father before marriage, you certainly did not fall in love with him afterwards," Mr. William laughed. "Fan and I remember how our honored parents used to fight. Don't we, Fan? And our brother Esmond kept the peace."

"Do not recall those dreadful, low scenes, William!" his mother cried. "When your father drank too much, he was like a madman; his conduct should be a warning to you, sir, who are fond of the same horrid practice."

"I am sure, madam, you were not much happier for marrying the man you did not like, and your ladyship's title has brought very little along with it," Lady Fanny whimpered. "What is the use of a coronet with the jointure of a tradesman's wife? How many of them are richer than we are? Recently, a grocer's widow from London Bridge moved into our square at Kensington. Her daughters have three gowns where I have one; and though they are served by only a man and two maids, I know they eat and drink a thousand times better than we do with our scraps of cold meat and our great, flaunting, impudent, lazy lackeys!"

"He! He! Glad I dine at the palace and not at home!" Mr. Will remarked. Through his aunt's influence with Count Puffendorff, Groom of the Royal Powder-Closet, he held one of the many minor court positions as Deputy Powder.

"Why should I not be happy without any title except my own?" Lady Frances continued. "Many people are. I dare say they are even happy in America."

"Yes—with a mother-in-law who is a perfect Turk and Tartar, for all I hear, with Indian war-whoops howling all around you, and with the constant danger of losing your scalp or being eaten by a wild beast every time you go to church."

"I wouldn't go to church," Lady Fanny declared.

"You'd go with anyone who asked you, Fan!" Mr. Will roared. "And so would old Maria, and so would any woman, that's the fact." He laughed at his own wit.

"Pray, good folks, what is all your merriment about?" Madame Bernstein asked, peering in from the tapestried door leading to the gallery where they conversed.

Will explained that his mother and sister had been fighting—a novelty only in appearance, as Madame Bernstein knew well—because Fanny desired to marry their cousin, the wild Indian, and my lady Countess would not allow it. Fanny immediately protested this fabrication. Since the day her mother forbade her to speak to the young gentleman, she had scarcely exchanged two words with him. She knew her station better. She did not wish to be scalped by wild Indians or eaten by bears.

Madame de Bernstein looked puzzled. "If he is not staying for you, for whom is he staying?" she asked. "At the houses to which he has been taken, you have ensured no woman is shown to him who is not either a fright or confined to the nursery; and I think the boy is too proud to fall in love with a dairymaid, Will."

"Humph! That is a matter of taste, ma'am," Mr. William shrugged.

"Of Mr. William Esmond's taste, as you say; but not of yonder boy's. The Esmonds of his grandfather's nurture would not go courting in the kitchen."

"Well, ma'am, every man to his taste, I say again. A fellow might go farther and fare worse than my brother's servants' hall, and besides Fan, there's only the maids or old Maria to choose from."

"Maria! Impossible!" Yet, as she spoke the words, a sudden thought crossed Madame Bernstein's mind. This elderly Calypso might have captivated her young Telemachus. She recalled half a dozen instances in her own experience of young men infatuated by older women. She remembered how frequent Harry Warrington's absences had become lately—absences she had attributed to his love for field sports. She recalled how often, when Harry was away, Maria Esmond was also absent. Walks in cool avenues, whispers in garden temples, behind clipped hedges, casual squeezes of the hand in twilight corridors, or sweet glances and ogles in meetings on the stairs—all these possibilities and chances suggested themselves to Madame de Bernstein just as she was dismissing them as impossible.

"Impossible, ma'am! I don't know," Will continued. "My mother warned Fan off him."

"Oh, your mother did warn Fanny off?"

"Certainly, my dear Baroness!"

"Didn't she? Didn't she pinch Fanny's arm black-and-blue? Didn't they fight about it?"

"Nonsense, William! For shame, William!" both implicated ladies cried in unison.

"And now, since we have heard how rich he is, perhaps it is sour grapes, that is all. And now, since he is warned off the young bird, perhaps he is hunting the old one, that's all. Impossible? Why impossible? You know old Lady Suffolk, ma'am?"

"William, how can you speak about Lady Suffolk to your aunt?"

A grin spread across the young gentleman's face. "Because Lady Suffolk was a special favorite at Court? Well, other folks have succeeded her."

"Sir!" Madame Bernstein cried, perhaps having reasons to take offense.

"So they have, I say; or who, pray, is my Lady Yarmouth now? And didn't old Lady Suffolk go and fall in love with George Berkeley, and marry him when she was ever so old? Nay, ma'am, if I remember right—and we hear a deal of town-talk at our table—Harry Estridge went mad about your ladyship when you were somewhat rising twenty; and would have changed your name a third time if you would but have let him."

This allusion to an adventure of her own later days, which was indeed notorious to all the world, did not anger Madame de Bernstein like Will's earlier hint about his aunt's favor at George II's Court. Instead, it put her in good humor.

"Au fait," she said, musing as she played a pretty little hand on the table, no doubt thinking about mad young Harry Estridge; "'tis not impossible, William, that old folks, and young folks, too, should play the fool."

"But I can't understand a young fellow being in love with Maria," Mr. William continued, "however he might be with you, ma'am. That's *oter shose*, as our French tutor used to say. You remember the Count, ma'am? He! He!--and so does Maria!"

"William!"

"And I dare say the Count remembers the bastinado Castlewood gave him. A confounded French dancing-master calling himself a count, and daring to fall in love in our family! Whenever I want to make myself uncommonly agreeable to old Maria, I just say a few words of *parly voo* to her. She knows what I mean."

"Have you abused her to your cousin, Harry Warrington?" Madame Bernstein asked.

"Well—I know she is always abusing me—and I have said my mind about her," Will admitted.

"Oh, you idiot!" the old lady cried. "Who but a gaby ever spoke ill of a woman to her sweetheart? He will tell her everything, and they both will hate you."

"The very thing, ma'am!" Will burst out laughing. "I had a sort of a suspicion, you see, and two days ago, as we were riding together, I told Harry Warrington a bit of my mind about Maria;—why shouldn't I, I say? She is always abusing me, ain't she, Fan? And your favorite turned as red as my plush waistcoat, wondering how a gentleman could malign his own flesh and blood, and, trembling all over with rage, said I was no true Esmond."

"Why didn't you chastise him, sir, as my lord did the dancing-master?" Lady Castlewood cried.

"Well, mother—you see that at quarter-staff there are two sticks used," Mr. William replied. "My opinion is, that Harry Warrington can guard his own head uncommonly well. Perhaps that is one of the reasons why I did not offer to treat my cousin to a caning. And now you say so, ma'am, I know he has told Maria. She has been looking battle, murder, and sudden death at me ever since. All which shows—" and here he turned to his aunt.

"All which shows what?"

"That I think we are on the right scent; and that we've found Maria—the old fox!" The ingenuous youth clapped his hand to his mouth and gave a loud halloo.

How far had this pretty intrigue gone? That was the question. Mr. Will said that at her age, Maria would conduct matters as rapidly as possible, having little time to lose. There was not much love lost between Will and his half-sister.

"Who would sift the matter to the bottom? Scolding one party or the other was of no avail. Threats only serve to aggravate people in such cases. I never was in danger but once, young people," Madame de Bernstein said, "and I think that was because my poor mother contradicted me. If this boy is like others of his family, the more we oppose him, the more *entêté* he will be; and we shall never get him out of his scrape."

"Faith, ma'am, suppose we leave him in it?" Will grumbled. "Old Maria and I don't love each other too much, I grant you; but an English earl's daughter is good enough for an American tobacco-planter, when all is said and done."

Here his mother and sister broke out in protest. They would not hear of such a union. To which Will answered, "You are like the dog in the manger. You don't want the man yourself, Fanny."

"I want him, indeed!" Lady Fanny cried, tossing her head.

As Lady Castlewood, her son, and her daughter withdrew through one door of the saloon, leaving the space where they had all been seated, my Lord Castlewood departed by another. The demure eyes of the young woman, previously fixed upon the tambour-frame where she had been diligently stitching innocent violets and jonquils, lifted to meet Harry Warrington. He stood beneath an ancestral portrait near the great fireplace, his countenance adorned with a great heap of blushes—those rare blooms that appear only in the springtime of gentlefolk. The color flushed his cheeks, his forehead, and even his youthful ears.

"Why did you refuse to go with our aunt, cousin?" asked the lady of the tambour frame.

"Because your ladyship bade me stay," answered the lad.

"I bid you stay! La! child! What one says in fun, you take in earnest! Are all you Virginian gentlemen so obsequious as to fancy every idle word a lady says is a command? Virginia must be a pleasant country for our sex if it be so!"

"You said—when—we walked in the terrace two nights since—O heaven!" cried Harry, his voice trembling with emotion.

"Ah, that sweet night, cousin!" cried the Tambour-frame.

"When you gave me this rose from your own neck," roared out Harry, suddenly producing a crumpled and decayed vegetable from his waistcoat—"which I will never part with! By heavens, whilst this heart continues to beat! You said, 'Harry, if your aunt asks you to go away, you will go, and if you go, you will forget me.' Didn't you say so?"

"All men forget!" said the Virgin, with a sigh.

"In this cold, selfish country they may, cousin, but not in ours," continued Harry, still in a state of exaltation. "I had rather have lost an arm almost than refused the old lady. It went to my heart to say no to her, and she was so kind to me, and who had been the means of introducing me to—O heaven!"

(Here a kick was delivered to an intervening spaniel, which flew yelping from before the fire, followed by a rapid advance toward the tambour-frame.) "Look here, cousin! If you were to bid me jump out of yonder window, I should do it; or murder, I should do it."

"La! but you need not squeeze one's hand so, you silly child!" remarked Maria.

"I can't help it—we are so in the south. Where my heart is, I can't help speaking my mind out, cousin—and you know where that heart is! Ever since that evening—that—O heaven! I tell you I have hardly slept since. I want to do something—to distinguish myself—to be ever so great. I wish there were giants, Maria, as I have read of in books, that I could go and fight them. I wish you were in distress, that I might help you, somehow. I wish you wanted my blood, that I might spend every drop of it for you. And when you told me not to go with Madame Bernstein..."

"I tell thee, child? never."

"I thought you told me. You said you knew I preferred my aunt to my cousin, and I said then what I say now, 'Incomparable Maria! I prefer thee to all the women in the world and all the angels in Paradise—and I would go anywhere, were it to dungeons, if you ordered me!' And do you think I would not stay anywhere, when you only desired that I should be near you?" he added, after a moment's pause.

"Men always talk in that way—that is, that is, I have heard so," said the spinster, correcting herself; "for what should a country-bred woman know about you creatures? When you are near us, they say you are all raptures and flames and promises and I don't know what; when you are away, you forget all about us."

"But I think I never want to go away as long as I live," groaned out the young man. "I have tired of many things; not books and that, I never cared for study much, but games and sports which I used to be fond of when I was a boy. Before I saw you, it was to be a soldier I most desired; I tore my hair with rage when my poor dear brother went away instead of me on that expedition in which we lost him. But now, I only care for one thing in the world, and you know what that is."

"You silly child! don't you know I am almost old enough to be...?"

"I know—I know! but what is that to me? Hasn't your br—well, never mind who, some of 'em told me stories against you, and didn't they show me the Family Bible, where all your names are down, and the dates of your birth?"

"The cowards! Who did that?" cried out Lady Maria. "Dear Harry, tell me who did that? Was it my mother-in-law, the grasping, odious, abandoned, brazen harpy? Do you know all about her? How she married my father in his cups—the horrid hussey!--and..."

"Indeed it wasn't Lady Castlewood," interposed the wondering Harry.

"Then it was my aunt," continued the infuriate lady. "A pretty moralist, indeed! A bishop's widow, forsooth, and I should like to know whose widow before and afterwards. Why, Harry, she intrigued with the Pretender, and with the Court of Hanover, and, I dare say, would with the Court of Rome and the Sultan of Turkey if she had had the means. Do you know who her second husband was? A creature who..."

"But our aunt never spoke a word against you," broke in Harry, more and more amazed at the nymph's vehemence.

She checked her anger. In the inquisitive countenance opposite to her, she thought she read some alarm as to the temper which she was exhibiting.

"Well, well! I am a fool," she said. "I want thee to think well of me, Harry!"

A hand was somehow put out and seized, and no doubt, kissed by the rapturous youth. "Angel!" he cried, looking into her face with his eager, honest eyes.

Two fish-pools irradiated by a pair of stars would not kindle to greater warmth than did those elderly orbs into which Harry poured his gaze. Nevertheless, he plunged into their blue depths and fancied he saw heaven in their calm brightness. So that silly dog (of whom Aesop or the Spelling-book used to tell us in youth) beheld a beef-bone in the pond, and snapped at it, and lost the beef-bone he was carrying. O absurd cur! He saw the beef-bone in his own mouth reflected in the treacherous pool, which dimpled, I dare say, with ever so many smiles, coolly sucked up the meat, and returned to its usual placidity. Ah! what a heap of wreck lies beneath some of those quiet surfaces! What treasures we have dropped into them! What chased golden dishes, what precious jewels of love, what bones after bones, and sweetest heart's flesh! Do not some very faithful and unlucky dogs jump in bodily, when they are swallowed up heads and tails entirely? When some women come to be dragged, it is a marvel what will be found in the depths of them. *Cavete, canes!* Have a care how ye lap that water. What do they want with us, the mischievous siren sluts? A green-eyed Naiad never rests until she has inveigled a fellow under the water; she sings after him, she dances after him; she winds round him, glittering tortuously; she warbles and whispers dainty secrets at his cheek, she kisses his feet, she leers at him from out of her rushes: all her beds sigh out, "Come, sweet youth! Hither, hither, rosy Hylas!" Pop goes Hylas. (Surely the fable is renewed for ever and ever?) Has his captivator any pleasure? Doth she take any account of him? No more than a fisherman landing at Brighton does of one out of a hundred thousand herrings.... The last time. Ulysses rowed by the Sirens' bank, he and his men did not care though a whole shoal of them were singing and combing their longest locks. Young Telemachus was for jumping overboard: but the tough old crew held the silly, bawling lad. They were deaf, and could not hear his bawling nor the sea-nymphs' singing. They were dim of sight, and did not see how lovely the witches were. The stale, old, leering witches! Away with ye! I dare say you have painted your cheeks by this time; your wretched old songs are as out of fashion as Mozart, and it is all false hair you are combing!

In the last sentence you see Lector Benevolus and Scriptor Doctissimus figure as tough old Ulysses and his tough old Boatswain, who do not care a quid of tobacco for any Siren at Sirens' Point; but Harry Warrington is green Telemachus, who, be sure, was very unlike the soft youth in the good Bishop of Cambray's twaddling story. He does not see that the siren paints the lashes from under which she ogles him; will put by into a box when she has done the ringlets into which she would inveigle him; and if she eats him, as she proposes to do, will crunch his bones with a new set of grinders just from the dentist's, and warranted for mastication. The song is not stale to Harry Warrington, nor the voice cracked or out of tune that sings it. But—but—oh, dear me, Brother Boatswain! Don't you remember how pleasant the opera was when we first heard it? *Cosi fan tutti* was its name—Mozart's music. Now, I dare say, they have other words, and other music, and other singers and fiddlers, and another great crowd in the pit. Well, well, *Cosi fan tutti* is still upon the bills, and they are going on singing it over and over and over.

Any man or woman with a pennyworth of brains, or the like precious amount of personal experience, or who has read a novel before, must, when Harry pulled out those faded vegetables just now, have gone off into a digression of his own, as the writer confesses for himself he was diverging whilst he has been writing the last brace of paragraphs. If he sees a pair of lovers whispering in a garden alley or the embrasure of a window, or a pair of glances shot across the room from Jenny to the artless Jessamy, he falls to musing on former days when, etc. etc. These things follow each other by a general law, which is not as old as the hills, to be sure, but as old as the people who walk up and down them. When, I say, a lad pulls a bunch of amputated and now decomposing greens from his breast and falls to kissing it, what is the use of saying much more? As well tell the market-gardener's name from whom the slip-rose was bought—the waterings, clippings, trimmings, manurings, the plant has undergone—as tell how Harry Warrington came by it. Rose, elle a vecu la vie des roses, has been trimmed, has been watered, has been potted, has been sticked, has been cut, worn, given away, transferred to yonder boy's pocket-book and bosom, according to the laws and fate appertaining to roses.

And how came Maria to give it to Harry? And how did he come to want it and to prize it so passionately when he got the bit of rubbish? Is not one story as stale as the other? Are not they all alike? What is the use, I say, of telling them over and over? Harry values that rose because Maria has ogled him in the old way; because she has happened to meet him in the garden in the old way; because he has taken her hand in the old way; because they have whispered to one another behind the old curtain (the gaping old rag, as if everybody could not peep through it!); because, in this delicious weather, they have happened to be early risers and go into the park; because dear Goody Jenkins in the village happened to have a bad knee, and my lady Maria went to read to her, and gave her calves'-foot jelly, and because somebody, of course, must carry the basket. Whole chapters might have been written to chronicle all these circumstances, but *A quoi bon?* The incidents of life, and love-making especially, I believe to resemble each other so much, that I am surprised, gentlemen and ladies, you read novels any more. *Psha!* Of course that rose in young Harry's pocket-book had grown, and had budded, and had bloomed, and was now rotting, like other roses. I suppose you will want me to say that the young fool kissed it next? Of course he kissed it. What were lips made for, pray, but for smiling and simpering, and (possibly) humbugging, and kissing, and opening to receive mutton-chops, cigars, and so forth? I cannot write this part of the story of our Virginians, because Harry did not dare to write it himself to anybody at home, because, if he wrote any letters to Maria (which, of course, he did, as they were in the same house, and might meet each other as much as they liked), they were destroyed; because he afterwards chose to be very silent about the story, and we can't have it from her ladyship, who never told the truth about anything. But *cui bono?* I say again. What is the good of telling the story? My gentle reader, take your story: take mine.
