The next morning, when the household gathered for breakfast, the air was thick with a sudden, inexplicable warmth. Madame de Bernstein's face, usually a map of sharp grievances, was smooth and serene. Her manner toward the entire company, Harry included, was nothing short of radiant. She praised the cook effusively, declaring the fricassee superior to anything found in the Castlewood moats, and dismissed any suggestion that the wine was corked as an absurdity fit only for a useless old woman like herself. When the new vintage was poured, she raised her glass to toast Madam Esmond Warrington of Virginia, hoping earnestly that Harry had secured his mother's permission to bring an English bride home. Harry, caught off guard, forgot to recall his grandmother; instead, he found himself listening to the Baroness's tales of her own mother—a woman of such striking beauty and goodness, whose happiness with her second husband, despite the age gap, was celebrated throughout the countryside. To see them together was, she claimed, a delight that silenced all talk of marital disparity. My Lady Castlewood and her two children sat in respectful silence while Madame Bernstein prattled, but Harry felt his heart swell with enchantment, while Maria watched with a mixture of surprise and apprehension. Lord Castlewood, puzzled by his aunt's sudden transformation, maintained a mask of perfect satisfaction, hiding any trace of doubt.

The Baroness's good humor was infectious, sweeping across the table like a gentle tide. When Mr. Will, an artless youth, expressed his astonishment at her behavior, she turned to him with frank sincerity. "Complimentary, my dear!" she exclaimed. "Of course I am. I wish to make amends for my excessive rudeness this morning. When I was a child, living in this very house, I adopted exactly the same conduct. If I had been naughty in the morning, I would coax my parents at night. I remember doing so right here, at this very table—oh, centuries ago!—coaxing my father, my mother, and your grandfather, Harry Warrington. There were eels for supper then, just as there are tonight, and that dish of collared eels brought the memory rushing back. I was as wayward at seven as I am today at seventy, so I confess my sins and ask forgiveness, like a good girl."

"I absolve your ladyship!" cried the chaplain, joining the party.

"But your reverence knows not how cross and ill-tempered I truly was," she continued, her eyes glistening. "I scolded my sister, Castlewood; I scolded her children; I boxed Harry Warrington's ears—all because he refused to ride with me to Tunbridge Wells."

"But I will go, madam! I will ride with you with all the pleasure in life," Mr. Warrington promised eagerly.

"You see, Mr. Chaplain, what dutiful children they all are. It was I alone who was peevish. Oh, it was cruel of me to treat them so! Maria, I ask your pardon, my dear."

"Sure, madam, you have done me no wrong," Maria replied humbly.

"Indeed I have, a very great wrong, child! Because I was weary of myself, I told you your company would be wearisome. You offered to come to Tunbridge, and I rudely refused you."

"Nay, ma'am, if you were sick and my presence annoyed you..."

"But it will not annoy me! You were most kind to say you would come. I beg, pray, entreat, implore, command that you will come."

Lord Castlewood filled his glass and sipped it, his expression utterly unconscious of the comedy unfolding. This, then, was the meaning of the previous farce.

"Anything which can give my aunt pleasure will surely delight me," Maria said, striving to appear as happy as possible.

"You must come and stay with me, my dear, and I promise to be good and good-humoured. My dear lord, you will spare your sister to me?"

"Lady Maria Esmond is of age to judge for herself," Lord Castlewood replied with a bow, though the sentence, interpreted charitably, likely meant, "Plague take the old woman! She is taking Maria away to separate her from this young Virginian."

"Oh, Tunbridge will be delightful!" sighed Lady Maria.

"Mr. Sampson will go and see Goody Jones for you," the lord continued.

Harry traced patterns on the tablecloth with his finger, lost in a whirlwind of speculation. What delights awaited him? What walks, rides, interminable conversations, delicious shrubberies, and sequestered summer-houses? What poring over music-books, moonlight, and billing and cooing? Yes, the day was coming. They were all departing—My Lady Castlewood to her friends, Madame Bernstein to the waters—and he was to be left alone with his divine charmer. Alone with her and unutterable rapture! The thought was maddening. These people were leaving, and he was to enjoy that heaven, to sit at the feet of that angel and kiss the hem of her white robe. O Gods! 'Twas too great bliss to be real! "I knew it couldn't be," thought poor Harry. "I knew something would happen to take her from me."

"But you will ride with us to Tunbridge, nephew Warrington, and keep us from the highwaymen?" Madame Bernstein asked.

Harry Warrington hoped the company did not see how red his cheeks had grown. He forced his voice to remain calm and steady. Yes, he would ride with their ladyships, and he was certain they need fear no danger. Danger! Harry felt he would rather embrace danger than deny it. He would slay ten thousand highwaymen if they approached his mistress's coach. At least, he would ride alongside that coach, catching glimpses of her eyes at the window. He might not speak to her, but he should be near her. He should press the blessed hand at the inn at night and feel it reposing on his as he led her to the carriage at dawn. They would spend two whole days traveling to Tunbridge, and perhaps he could stay there a day or two. Was not the condemned man at Newgate thankful for even two or three days of respite?

We have only indicated, not described at length, the condition of Mr. Harry Warrington, or that utter depth of imbecility into which the poor young wretch had now plunged. Some boys suffer from love favorably and gently; others, when struck by the fever, are sick unto death, carrying the marks of the malady to their graves or to remotest old age. I say, it is not fair to record a young fellow's words when he is raging in that delirium. Suppose he is in love with a woman twice his age; have we not all read of the young gentleman who committed suicide in consequence of his fatal passion for Mademoiselle Ninon de l'Enclos, who turned out to be his grandmother? Suppose thou art making an ass of thyself, young Harry Warrington of Virginia! Are there not people in England who heehaw too? Kick and abuse him, you who have never brayed; but bear with him, all honest fellow-cardophagi, long-eared messmates, recognize a brother-donkey!

"You will stay with us for a day or two at the Wells," Madame Bernstein continued. "You will see us put into our lodgings. Then you can return to Castlewood and the partridge-shooting, and all the fine things which you and my lord are to study together."

Harry bowed an acquiescence. A whole week of heaven! Life was not altogether a blank, then.

"And as there is sure to be plenty of company at the Wells, I shall be able to present you," the lady graciously added.

"Company! ah! I shan't need company," sighed out Harry. "I mean that I shall be quite contented in the company of you two ladies," he added eagerly; and no doubt Mr. Will wondered at his cousin's peculiar taste.

Since this was to be the last night of cousin Harry's visit to Castlewood, cousin Will suggested that he, the chaplain, and Warrington meet at the latter's quarters to settle accounts. To this proposal, Harry, being a considerable winner in his recent play transactions with the two gentlemen, had no objection. Accordingly, when the ladies retired for the night and Lord Castlewood withdrew, as was his custom, to his own apartments, the three gentlemen found themselves assembled in Mr. Harry's small room before the punch-bowl, Will's usual midnight companion.

But Will's method of settling accounts involved producing a couple of fresh packs of cards and offering to submit Harry's debt to the process of being doubled or acquitted. The poor chaplain possessed no more ready cash than Lord Castlewood's younger brother. Harry Warrington did not wish to win the money of either. Would he give pain to the brother of his adored Maria, or allow any of her near kinsfolk to tax him with a lack of generosity or forbearance? He was ready to give them their revenge, as the gentlemen proposed. Until midnight, he would play with them for whatever stakes they chose to name. So they set to work, the dice-box rattled, and the cards were shuffled and dealt.

Very likely, he did not think about the cards at all. Very likely, he was thinking: "At this moment, my beloved one is sitting with her beauteous golden locks outspread under the fingers of her maid. Happy maid! Now she is on her knees, the sainted creature, addressing prayers to that Heaven which is the abode of angels like her. Now she has sunk to rest behind her damask curtains. Oh, bless, bless her!" "You double us all round? I will take a card upon each of my two. Thank you, that will do—a ten—now, upon the other, a queen—two natural vingt-et-uns, and as you doubled us, you owe me so-and-so."

I imagine volleys of oaths from Mr. William and brisk pattering of imprecations from the chaplain at the young Virginian's luck. He won because he did not want to win. Fortune, that notoriously coquettish jade, came to him because he was thinking of another nymph, who possibly was as fickle. Will and the chaplain may have played against him, constantly soliciting increased stakes and supposing that the wealthy Virginian wished to let them recover their losses. But this was by no means Harry Warrington's notion. When at home, he had taken part in scores of such games, keeping many little circumstances of his life mum from his lady mother, and had learned to play and pay. As he practiced fair play toward his friends, he expected it in return.

"The luck does seem to be with me, cousin," he said, replying to further oaths and growls from Will, "and I am sure I do not want to press it; but you don't suppose I'm going to be such a fool as to fling it away altogether? I have quite a heap of your promises on paper by this time. If we are to go on playing, let us have the dollars on the table, please; or, if not the money, the worth of it."

"Always the way with you rich men," grumbled Will. "Never lend except on security—always win because you are rich."

"Faith, cousin, you have been of late forever flinging my riches into my face. I have enough for my wants and for my creditors."

"Oh, that we could all say as much!" groaned the chaplain. "How happy we, and how happy the duns would be! What have we got to play against our conqueror? There is my new gown, Mr. Warrington. Will you set me five pieces against it? I have but to preach in stuff if I lose. Stop! I have a Chrysostom, a Foxe's Martyrs, a Baker's Chronicle, and a cow and her calf. What shall we set against these?"

"I will bet one of cousin Will's notes for twenty pounds," cried Mr. Warrington, producing one of those documents.

"Or I have my brown mare, and will back her red against your honour's notes of hand, but against ready money."

"I have my horse. I will back my horse against you for fifty," bawled out Will.

Harry accepted the offers of both gentlemen. Within ten minutes, the horse and the bay mare had both changed owners. Cousin William swore more fiercely than ever. The parson dashed his wig to the ground, emulating his pupil in the loudness of his objurgations. Mr. Harry Warrington remained quite calm, not the least elated by his triumph. They had asked him to play, and he had played. He knew he should win. O beloved slumbering angel! he thought, am I not sure of victory when you are kind to me? He looked out from his window toward the casement on the opposite side of the court, which he knew to be hers. He had forgotten about his victims and their groans, and ill-luck, as they crossed the court. Under yonder brilliant flickering star, behind yonder casement where the lamp burned faintly, was his joy, his heart, and his treasure.

While the Bishop of Cambray, in his romantic chronicle, dwelt upon the desolation of Calypso at Ulysses' departure, he omitted to mention the sorrow of Calypso's maid as she parted from Odysseus's own gentleman. The servants must have wept in unison within the kitchen precincts while their masters embraced wildly in the drawing-room; they must have clung to one another in the fore-cabin as their principals shattered their hearts in the grand saloon. When the final bell rang and the mate bawled, "Now! any one for shore!" Calypso and her attendant must have traversed the same plank, hearts pounding and eyes streaming, waving handkerchiefs of vastly different textures to their friends on the departing vessel, while the shore crowd and the crew in the bows shouted their equivalent of *hip, hip, huzzay*. Yet the essential truth remains: if Calypso could not console herself, neither could her maid. They walked the same plank of grief, feeling the identical pang of separation. Upon returning home, they might not use handkerchiefs of equal value, but the tears shed in marble halls were as salt and plentiful as those poured forth in the servants' quarters.

Not only did Harry Warrington leave Castlewood a victim to love, but Gumbo departed the same premises prey to the same delightful passion. His wit, accomplishments, good humour, and skills in dancing, cookery, and music had endeared him to the entire female domestic circle. While some men might have been jealous, the ladies were entirely his. In that era, there was no such objection to black men in England as exists today among white-skinned people. Their condition was not one of equality, yet they possessed a sufferance and a certain grotesque sympathy from all, and from women, a kindness far more generous. When Ledyard and Parke in Blackmansland were persecuted by men, did they not find black women pitiful and kind? Women are always kind toward our sex. What mental negroes do they not cherish? What moral hunchbacks do they not adore? What lepers, idiots, dull drivellers, misshapen monsters (speaking figuratively) do they not fondle and cuddle? Gumbo was treated by the women as kindly as many people no better than himself; it was only the men in the servants' hall who rejoiced at the Virginian lad's departure. I should like to witness his farewell: Molly the housemaid stealing to the terrace gardens in the grey dawn to cull a wistful posy; Betty the kitchenmaid cutting off a thick lock of her chestnut ringlets to exchange for a woolly token from young Gumbo's pate. Of course, he claimed to be *regum progenies*, a descendant of Ashantee kings. In Caffraria, Connaught, and other places now inhabited by hereditary bondsmen, there must have been vast numbers of these potent sovereigns in former times, judging by their descendants now extant.

At the morning announced for Madame de Bernstein's departure, the numerous domestics of Castlewood crowded the doors and passages. Some sought a last glimpse of her ladyship's men and the fascinating Gumbo; others wished to take leave of her ladyship's maid; all aimed to waylay the Baroness and her nephew for parting fees, a custom of that day to distribute liberally among household servants. Both gave generous gratuities to the liveried society, the gentlemen in black and ruffles, and the swarm of female attendants. Castlewood was the home of the Baroness's youth. As for her honest Harry, who had not only lived at free charges but had won horses and money—or promises thereof—from his cousin and the unlucky chaplain—he was naturally generous and felt he ought not to stint his benevolent disposition. "My mother, I know," he thought, "will wish me to be liberal to all the retainers of the Esmond family." Thus, he scattered his gold pieces right and left, acting as if he were as rich as Gumbo announced him to be. No one approached him without a share in his bounty. From the major-domo to the shoeblack, Mr. Harry offered a peace-offering to them all. To the grim housekeeper in her still-room, to the feeble old porter in his lodge, he distributed tokens of remembrance. When a man loves one woman in a family, it is astonishing how fond he becomes of every person connected with it. He ingratiates himself with the maids; he is bland with the butler; he interests himself about the footman; he runs errands for the daughters; he lends money to the young son at college; he pats little dogs he would otherwise kick; he smiles at old stories that would make him yawn if uttered by anyone but papa; he drinks sweet port wine he would otherwise curse the steward for serving; he bears with the cantankerous old maiden aunt; he beats time when darling little Fanny performs on the piano; and he smiles when wicked, lively little Bobby upsets coffee over his shirt.

Harry Warrington, in his way and according to the customs of that age, had for a brief time past—concluding that his love had been declared and accepted only briefly—given the Castlewood family these artless testimonies of affection for one of them. Cousin Will should have won back his money and welcome, or as much of Harry's own as the lad could spare. Nevertheless, the lad, though a lover, was shrewd, keen, fond of sport and fair play, and a judge of a good horse. Having played for and won all the money Will had, besides a great number of Mr. Esmond's valuable autographs, Harry was very well pleased to win Will's brown horse—that very quadruped which had nearly pushed him into the water on the first evening of his arrival at Castlewood. He had seen the horse's performance often, and amidst all his passion and romance, was not sorry to possess such a sound, swift, well-bred hunter and roadster. After gazing at the stars shining over his mistress's window and putting her candle to bed, he repaired to his own dormitory. There, no doubt, he thought of his Maria and his horse with youthful satisfaction, imagining how sweet it would be to have one pillioned on the other, touring the island with such an animal and such a pair of white arms round his waist. He fell asleep ruminating on these things, meditating a million blessings on his Maria, in whose company he was to luxuriate for at least a week more.

In the early morning, poor Chaplain Sampson sent over his little black mare by the hands of his groom, footman, and gardener, who wept and bestowed countless kisses on the beast's white nose as they handed it over to Gumbo. Gumbo and his master were both affected by the fellow's sensibility; the negro servant showed his sympathy by weeping, and Harry produced a couple of guineas, astonishing and swiftly comforting the chaplain's boy. Then Gumbo and the late groom led the beast away to the stable, having commands to bring him round with Mr. William's horse after breakfast, at the hour when Madam Bernstein's carriages were ordered.

So courteous was he to his aunt, or so grateful for her departure, that the master of the house even appeared at the morning meal to take leave of his guests. The ladies and the chaplain were present—the only family member absent was Will, who left a note for his cousin stating, in exceedingly bad spelling, that he was obliged to go to Salisbury Races that morning but had left the horse his cousin won the previous night, which Tom, Mr. Will's groom, would hand over to Mr. Warrington's servant. Will's absence did not prevent the rest of the party from drinking tea amicably. In due time, the carriages rolled into the courtyard, servants packed them with the Baroness's multiplied luggage, and the moment of departure arrived.

A large open landau contained the stout Baroness and her niece; a couple of men-servants mounted on the box before them with pistols and blunderbusses ready in case of highwaymen. In another carriage were their ladyships' maids, and another servant guarded the trunks, vast and numerous as they were, which were as nothing compared to the enormous baggage-train accompanying a lady of the present time. Mr. Warrington's modest valises were placed in this second carriage under the maid's guardianship, and Mr. Gumbo proposed to ride by the window for the chief part of the journey.

My lord, with his stepmother and Lady Fanny, accompanied their kinswoman to the carriage steps, bidding her farewell with many dutiful embraces. Her Lady Maria followed in a riding-dress, which Harry Warrington thought the most becoming costume in the world. A host of servants stood around, begging Heaven bless her ladyship. The Baroness's departure was known in the village, and scores of folks stood waiting under the trees outside the gates, huzzaying and waving their hats as the ponderous vehicles rolled away.

Gumbo was gone for Mr. Warrington's horses while my lord, with his arm under his young guest's, paced up and down the court. "I hear you carry away some of our horses out of Castlewood?" my lord said.

Harry blushed. "A gentleman cannot refuse a fair game at the cards," he said. "I never wanted to play, nor would have played for money had not my cousin William forced me. As for the chaplain, it went to my heart to win from him, but he was as eager as my cousin."

"I know—I know! There is no blame to you, my boy. At Rome you can't help doing as Rome does; and I am very glad that you have been able to give Will a lesson. He is mad about play—would gamble his coat off his back—and I and the family have had to pay his debts ever so many times. May I ask how much you have won of him?"

"Well, some eighteen pieces the first day or two, and his note for a hundred and twenty more, and the brown horse, sixty—that makes nigh upon two hundred. But, you know, cousin, all was fair, and it was even against my will that we played at all. Will ain't a match for me, my lord—that is the fact. Indeed he is not."

"He is a match for most people, though," said my lord. "His brown horse, I think you said?"

"Yes. His brown horse—Prince William, out of Constitution. You don't suppose I would set him sixty against his bay, my lord?"

"Oh, I didn't know. I saw Will riding out this morning; most likely I did not remark what horse he was on. And you won the black mare from the parson?"

"For fourteen. He will mount Gumbo very well. Why does not the rascal come round with the horses?" Harry's mind was away to lovely Maria. He longed to be trotting by her side.

"When you get to Tunbridge, cousin Harry, you must be on the look-out against sharper players than the chaplain and Will. There is all sorts of queer company at the Wells."

"A Virginian learns pretty well to take care of himself, my lord," said Harry, with a knowing nod.

"So it seems! I recommend my sister to thee, Harry. Although she is not a baby in years, she is as innocent as one. Thou wilt see that she comes to no mischief?"

"I will guard her with my life, my lord!" cried Harry.

"Thou art a brave fellow. By the way, cousin, unless you are very fond of Castlewood, I would in your case not be in a great hurry to return to this lonely, tumble-down old house. I want myself to go to another place I have, and shall scarce be back here till the partridge-shooting. Go you and take charge of the women, of my sister and the Baroness, will you?"

"Indeed I will," said Harry, his heart beating with happiness at the thought.

"And I will write thee word when you shall bring my sister back to me. Here come the horses. Have you bid adieu to the Countess and Lady Fanny? They are kissing their hands to you from the music-room balcony."

Harry ran up to bid these ladies farewell. He made that ceremony very brief, for he was anxious to be off to the charmer of his heart, and came downstairs to mount his newly-gotten steed, which Gumbo, himself astride on the parson's black mare, held by the rein.

There was Gumbo on the black mare, indeed, and holding another horse. But it was a bay horse, not a brown—a bay horse with broken knees—an aged, worn-out quadruped.

"What is this?" cries Harry.

"Your honour's new horse," says the groom, touching his cap.

"This brute?" exclaims the young gentleman, with one or more of those expressions then in use in England and Virginia. "Go and bring me round Prince William, Mr. William's horse, the brown horse."

"Mr. William have rode Prince William this morning away to Salisbury Races. His last words was, 'Sam, saddle my bay horse, Cato, for Mr. Warrington this morning. He is Mr. Warrington's horse now. I sold him to him last night.' And I know your honour is bountiful: you will consider the groom."

My lord could not help breaking into a laugh at these words of Sam the groom, whilst Harry, for his part, indulged in a number more of those remarks which politeness does not admit of our inserting here.

"Mr. William said he never could think of parting with the Prince under a hundred and twenty," said the groom, looking at the young man.

Lord Castlewood only laughed the more. "Will has been too much for thee, Harry Warrington."

"Too much for me, my lord! So may a fellow with loaded dice throw sixes, and be too much for me. I do not call this betting, I call it ch—"

"Mr. Warrington! Spare me bad words about my brother, if you please. Depend on it, I will take care that you are righted. Farewell. Ride quickly, or your coaches will be at Farnham before you;" and waving him an adieu, my

Let no tender-hearted reader tremble for Mr. Harry Warrington's safety, nor imagine that his tumble from a broken-kneed steed has spirited him away entirely from this tale. We assure you, at the outset, that no tragedy of consequence has befallen him. How could we possibly dispatch our heroes while they are still mere adolescents, before the story has even matured into manhood? We are already mourning one Virginian lost to the perils of America; surely we need not extinguish the other in England? Heroes do not meet such abrupt ends without compelling cause. Were a gentleman to perish every time his horse stumbled, the hero would indeed be lost, but so too would the chronicler of this chronicle, who currently sprawls safely outside the grave, ready to rise again once Harry is carried into the house where Madame de Bernstein's servants have rung the bell.

To prove that this youngest of the Virginians still breathes, consider this authentic correspondence from the lady who took him in after his fall, a woman in whom he found a kindred spirit:

"At her House at Richmond, in Virginia

"If Mrs. Esmond Warrington of Virginia can recall twenty-three years past, when Miss Rachel Esmond attended Kensington Boarding School, she may perhaps remember Miss Molly Benson, her classmate. Miss Molly has long since forgotten the petty squabbles they once shared—squabbles in which Miss Molly was frequently at fault—and retains only the memory of the generous, high-spirited, and vivacious Miss Esmond, the Princess Pocahontas, to whom so many of our schoolfellows paid court.

'Dear madam! I cannot forget that you were dear Rachel once, as I was your dearest Molly. Though we parted not on the most amicable terms when you returned to Virginia, you know how fond we once were. I still possess the gold etui your father gifted me during his visit to our speech-day at Kensington, when we two enacted the quarrel of Brutus and Cassius from Shakespeare. It was only yesterday morning I dreamed we were summoned to recite our lessons before the formidable Miss Hardwood, unaware of the summons, and as usual, Miss Rachel Esmond rose above me. How vividly those days remain! How youthful we appear in memory! I recall our walks and exercises, our beloved King and Queen strolling through Kensington Gardens with their court trailing behind, while the pupils of Miss Hardwood's school curtseyed in a row. I can still recount our dinners for each day of the week and point to the spot where your garden stood, always more meticulously tended than mine. Miss Esmond's chest of drawers was a model of neatness, whereas mine were in a state of disarray. Do you remember our storytelling in the dormitory, interrupted by Madame Hibou, the French governess, rising from bed with her characteristic hoot? Have you forgotten the poor dancing-master who claimed to have been ambushed by assassins, only to be beaten, it seems, by your brother's footmen? My dear, your cousin, Lady Maria Esmond (whose father was, I believe, Viscount Castlewood at the time), recently visited this house. I spared her mention of those sorrowful times, about which I am now chatting to Mrs. Esmond.

'Her ladyship has been staying here, along with another relative of yours, the Baroness of Bernstein. Both ladies have departed for Tunbridge Wells; yet another and dearer relative remains in my house, sound asleep, I trust, in the very next room. His name is Mr. Henry Esmond Warrington. Now, do you understand how you receive this news? Do not be alarmed, dear madam! I know you are thinking, "My boy is ill; that is why Miss Molly Benson writes." No, my dear; Mr. Warrington was ill yesterday, but today he is quite comfortable. Our physician, no less a person than my dear husband, Colonel Lambert, has bled him, set his dislocated shoulder, and declares that in two days Mr. Warrington will be fit to travel.

'I fear my household and I shall be saddened that he recovers so swiftly. Yesterday evening, a great ringing at our gate disturbed us all, for the bell rarely sounds in this quiet place unless a passing beggar pulls it for charity. The servants rushed out and returned with news that a young gentleman, having fallen from his horse, lay lifeless on the road, surrounded by his traveling companions. At this, my Colonel—who is surely the most Samaritan of men!—hurried forth to assist the fallen traveler. Presently, aided by the servants and followed by two ladies, he brought into the house such a pale, seemingly lifeless, yet beautiful young man! Ah, my dear, how I rejoice to think your child has found shelter and succour under my roof! That my husband has spared him from pain and fever, and restored him to you and health! We shall be friends again, shall we not? I was gravely ill last year, and it was even thought I should die. Do you know, I often thought of you then, and how we had parted in anger so many years ago? I began a foolish note to you, which sickness prevented me from finishing, to tell you that if I were to depart this life, I wished to leave the world in charity with every soul I had ever known.

'Your cousin, the Right Honourable Lady Maria Esmond, displayed great maternal tenderness and concern for her young kinsman after his accident. I am sure she possesses a kind heart. The Baroness de Bernstein, being of advanced age, could not be expected to feel as keenly as we young people; nevertheless, she was deeply moved until Mr. Warrington regained consciousness, whereupon she expressed anxiety to proceed to Tunbridge, fearing to linger where no doctor was available. My Aesculapius laughed, stating he would not attend a lady of quality, though he would certainly care for his young patient. Indeed, the Colonel, during his campaigns, has ample experience with such accidents, and I am certain that were we to summon every practitioner within twenty miles, Mr. Warrington could receive no better treatment. Leaving the young gentleman to my care and my daughters, the Baroness and her ladyship took their leave, the latter reluctant to depart. When he is well enough, my Colonel will ride with him as far as Westerham, on his own horses, to an old army-comrade of Mr. Lambert's residence. Since this letter will not reach Falmouth until, by God's blessing, your son is well and fully restored, you need harbor no alarm for him while he rests under the roof of, madam, your affectionate and humble servant, MARY LAMBERT.

'P.S. Thursday.

'I am glad to hear (Mr. Warrington's colored gentleman informed our staff of this gratifying development) that Providence has blessed Mrs. Esmond with such vast wealth and an heir likely to honor it. Our current means are sufficient, but will be diminished when divided among our survivors. Ah, dear madam! I have heard of your calamity last year. Though the Colonel and I have raised many children (five), we have lost two, and a mother's heart feels for yours! I confess, mine yearned toward your boy today when, in a manner inexpressibly affecting to me and Mr. Lambert, he mentioned his dear brother. 'Tis impossible to see your son and not to love and regard him. I am thankful it has been our lot to succor him in his trouble, and that in receiving a stranger within our gates, we offered hospitality to the son of an old friend.'"

Nature has inscribed a letter of credit upon the faces of certain men, honored almost wherever presented. Harry Warrington's countenance bore such a stamp in his youth. His eyes were bright, his cheek red and healthy, his gaze so frank and open that almost everyone who beheld him, nay, even those who sought to deceive him, chose to trust him. Nevertheless, as hinted, the lad was by no means the artless stripling he appeared. He was knowing enough with all his blushing cheeks; perhaps more wily and wary than he would become in later years. Surely, a shrewd and generous man, who has lived honestly and bears no secret blushes for his conscience, grows simpler with age; arrives at the sum of right through more rapid calculations; learns to discard false arguments more readily, and strikes the mark of truth with less prior trouble and mental disturbance. Or is it merely a senile delusion that our vanities are cured with growing years, and that we become more just in our perceptions of our own and our neighbor's shortcomings? ... I would humbly suggest that young people, though prettier, with larger eyes and fewer wrinkles around their eyelids, are often as artful as some of their elders. What little monsters of cunning your frank schoolboys are! How they cheat mamma! How they hoodwink papa! How they humbug the housekeeper! How they cringe to the big boy for whom they toil at school! What a long lie and five years of hypocrisy and flattery constitute their conduct toward Dr. Birch! And the little boys' sisters? Are they any better, and is it only after they enter the world that the little darlings learn a trick or two?

You may see, by the letter above from Mrs. Lambert, that she, like all good women (and indeed, almost all bad women), was a sentimental person. As she gazed at Harry Warrington lying in her best bed, after the Colonel had bled him and secured his shoulder, holding her husband's hand as she beheld the lad in a sweet slumber, murmuring faint, inarticulate words, a faint blush quivering on his cheek, she owned he was a pretty lad indeed. She confessed with a sort of compunction that neither of her two boys—Jack, at Oxford, and Charles, who had just returned to school after the Bartlemytide holidays—was half so handsome as the Virginian. What a good figure the boy had! And when papa bled him, his arm was as white as any lady's!

"Yes, as you say, Jack might have been as handsome but for the small-pox: and as for Charley----" "Always took after his papa, my dear Molly," said the Colonel, gazing at his own honest face in a small looking-glass with a cut border and a japanned frame, by which the chief guests of the worthy gentleman and lady had surveyed their patches and powder, or shaved their hospitable beards.

"Did I say so, my love?" whispered Mrs. Lambert, looking rather startled.

"No; but you thought so, Mrs. Lambert."

"How can you tell one's thoughts so, Martin?" asked the lady.

"Because I am a conjurer, and because you tell them yourself, my dear," answered her husband. "Don't be frightened: he won't wake after that draught I gave him. Because you never see a young fellow but you compare him with your own. Because you never hear of one but you think which of our girls he shall fall in love with and marry."

"Don't be foolish, sir," said the lady, placing a hand upon the Colonel's lips. They had softly trodden out of their guest's bedchamber by this time, entering the adjoining dressing-closet, a snug little wainscoted room overlooking gardens, adorned with India curtains, numerous Japan chests and cabinets, a treasure of china, and a most refreshing odor of fresh lavender.

"You can't deny it, Mrs. Lambert," the Colonel resumed. "As you were looking at the young gentleman just now, you were thinking to yourself which of my girls will he marry? Shall it be Theo, or shall it be Hester? And then you thought of Lucy who was at boarding-school."

"There is no keeping anything from you, Martin Lambert," sighed the wife.

"There is no keeping it out of your eyes, my dear. What is this burning desire all you women have for selling and marrying your daughters? We men don't wish to part with 'em. I am sure, for my part, I should not like yonder young fellow half as well if I thought he intended to carry one of my darlings away with him."

"Sure, Martin, I have been so happy myself," said the fond wife and mother, looking at her husband with her very best eyes, "that I must wish my girls to do as I have done, and be happy, too!"

"Then you think good husbands are common, Mrs. Lambert, and that you may walk any day into the road before the house and find one shot out at the gate like a sack of coals?"

"Wasn't it providential, sir, that this young gentleman should be thrown over his horse's head at our very gate, and that he should turn out to be the son of my old schoolfellow and friend?" asked the wife. "There is something more than accident in such cases, depend upon that, Mr. Lambert!"

"And this was the stranger you saw in the candle three nights running, I suppose?"

"And in the fire, too, sir; twice a coal jumped out close by Theo. You may sneer, sir, but these things are not to be despised. Did I not see you distinctly coming back from Minorca, and dream of you at the very day and hour when you were wounded in Scotland?"

"How many times have you seen me wounded, when I had not a scratch, my dear? How many times have you seen me ill when I had no sort of hurt? You are always prophesying, and 'twere very hard on you if you were not sometimes right. Come! Let us leave our guest asleep comfortably, and go down and give the girls their French lesson."

So saying, the honest gentleman put his wife's arm under his, and they descended together the broad oak staircase of the comfortable old hall, round which hung the effigies of many foregone Lamberts, worthy magistrates, soldiers, country gentlemen, as was the Colonel whose acquaintance we have just made. The Colonel was a gentleman of pleasant, waggish humour. The French lesson which he and his daughters recited together was a scene from Monsieur Moliere's comedy of "Tartuffe," and papa was pleased to be very facetious with Miss Theo, addressing her as Madam and treating her with great mock respect and ceremony. The harmonious sounds of the night had lulled the young patient into a sweet, unconscious slumber. When he awoke, the morning sun streamed warmly through the window, illuminating the bed-curtains where his kind host and hostess smiled upon him. Hunger gnawed at him, but his doctor, seeing him fit, immediately permitted him to partake of a hearty mess of chicken, which the doctor's wife proudly attributed to the hands of one of her daughters.

A fleeting image rose in Harry Warrington's mind—a vision of two young persons with flushed cheeks and dark, waving hair, smiling around his couch before vanishing as he regained full consciousness. This was followed by a sharp pang of memory regarding a different woman: lovely, yet considerably older, and with... horrors and remorse surged through him as a specific recollection crossed his mind. An immense gulf of time yawned between him and that past. How long had it been since he learned those pearls were artificial and those golden locks merely pinchbeck? It was a long time ago, when he was an innocent boy. Now he was a man, and felt quite an old one. He had been bled copiously, suffered a fever, gone without food for hours, and endured a sleeping draught that had dragged him into a deep, restorative slumber.

"What is it, my dear child?" cried kind Mrs. Lambert as he started.

"Nothing, madam; a twinge in my shoulder," said the lad. "I speak to my host and hostess? You have been very kind to me."

"We are old friends, Mr. Warrington," replied Mrs. Lambert. "My husband, Colonel Lambert, knew your father, and I and your mother were schoolgirls together at Kensington. You were no stranger to us when your aunt and cousin told us who you were."

"Are they here?" asked Harry, looking somewhat blank.

"They must have lain at Tunbridge Wells last night. They sent a horseman from Reigate yesterday for news of you."

"Ah! I remember," Harry said, glancing at his bandaged arm.

"I have made a good cure of you, Mr. Warrington. Now Mrs. Lambert and the cook must take charge of you."

"Nay; Theo prepared the chicken and rice, Mr. Lambert," the lady corrected gently. "Will Mr. Warrington rise after breakfast? We will send your valet."

"If howling proves fidelity, your man must be a most fond creature," Mr. Lambert observed with a chuckle.

"He let your baggage travel off after all in your aunt's carriage," Mrs. Lambert added. "You must wear my husband's linen, which, I dare say, is not so fine as yours."

"Pish, my dear! my shirts are good enough for any Christian," cried the Colonel.

"They are Theo's and Hester's work," said the mother, arching her eyebrows at her husband. "And Theo has ripped and sewed your sleeve to make it comfortable for your shoulder," she added.

"What beautiful roses!" exclaimed Harry, admiring a fine china vase full of them on the toilet-table beneath a Japan-framed glass.

"My daughter Theo cut them this morning. Well, Mr. Lambert? She did cut them!"

The Colonel likely thought his wife had introduced Theo too prominently into the conversation, nudging her into a sense of propriety with a subtle gesture.

"And I fancied I heard someone singing the Evening Hymn very sweetly last night—or was it only a dream?" asked the young patient.

"Theo again, Mr. Warrington!" laughed the Colonel. "My servants said your negro man began to sing it in the kitchen as if he were a church organ."

"Our people sing it at home, sir. My grandpapa loved it very much. His wife's father was a great friend of good Bishop Ken, who wrote it; and—and my dear brother used to love it too," said the boy, his voice dropping.

It was then that Mrs. Lambert felt inclined to give the boy a kiss. His accident, illness, and recovery, along with the kindness of those around him, had softened Harry Warrington's heart, opening it to better influences than those that had plagued him for the past six weeks. He breathed a purer air than the tainted atmosphere of selfishness, worldliness, and corruption into which he had been plunged since arriving in England. Often, fate or weakness leads a young man into the fellowship of the giddy and vain; happy is he whose lot introduces him to wiser company, whose lamps are trimmed, and whose pure hearts keep modest watch.

The pleased matron left her young patient devouring Miss Theo's meal of rice and chicken, while the Colonel sat by the bedside. Gratitude for his hospitable entertainers and contentment after a comfortable meal placed Mr. Warrington in a pleasant state of mind and body. He was ready to talk more freely than usual; for unless excited by strong interest or emotion, the young man was commonly taciturn and cautious, lacking an imaginative turn. He had been a remiss student of books, and his remarks on literature were neither profound nor valuable; yet regarding dogs, horses, and the ordinary business of life, he was a far better critic, conversing freely with anyone interested in such subjects.

Harry's host, possessing considerable shrewdness and experience with books, cattle, and men, quickly took the measure of his young guest during their conversation. It was the first time the Virginian learned that Mrs. Lambert had been an early friend of his mother, and that the Colonel's own father had served with Harry's grandfather, Colonel Esmond, in the famous wars of Queen Anne. He found himself in a friend's country, soon at ease with his honest host, whose manners were simple and cordial, and who appeared perfectly a gentleman despite wearing a plain fustian coat and a waistcoat devoid of lace.

"My boys are both away," said the host, "or they would have shown you the country when you rose, Mr. Warrington. Now you can only have the company of my wife and her daughters. Mrs. Lambert has already told you about one of them, Theo, our eldest, who made your broth, cut your roses, and mended your coat. She is not such a wonder as her mother imagines; but little Theo is a smart little housekeeper and a very good, cheerful lass, though her father says so."

"It is very kind of Miss Lambert to take so much care for me," said the young patient.

"She is no kinder to you than to any other mortal, and does but her duty." The Colonel smiled. "I laugh at their mother for praising our children, and I think I am as foolish about them myself. The truth is, God has given us very good and dutiful children, and I see no reason to disguise my thankfulness for such a blessing. You have never a sister, I think?"

"No, sir, I am alone now," Mr. Warrington replied.

"Ay, truly, I ask your pardon for my thoughtlessness. Your man has told our people what befell last year. I served with Braddock in Scotland; and hope he mended before he died. A wild fellow, sir, but there was a fund of truth about the man, and no little kindness under his rough swaggering manner. Your black fellow talks very freely about his master and his affairs. I suppose you permit him these freedoms as he rescued you—"

"Rescued me?" cried Mr. Warrington.

"From ever so many Indians on that very expedition. My Molly and I did not know we were going to entertain so prodigiously wealthy a gentleman. He says that half Virginia belongs to you; but if the whole of North America were yours, we could but give you our best."

"Those negro boys, sir, lie like the father of all lies. They think it is for our honor to represent us as ten times as rich as we are. My mother has what would be a vast estate in England, and is a very good one at home. We are as well off as most of our neighbors, sir, but no better; and all our splendor is in Mr. Gumbo's foolish imagination. He never rescued me from an Indian in his life, and would run away at the sight of one, as my poor brother's boy did on that fatal day when he fell."

"The bravest man will do so at unlucky times," said the Colonel. "I myself saw the best troops in the world run at Preston, before a ragged mob of Highland savages."

"That was because the Highlanders fought for a good cause, sir."

"Do you think," asked Harry's host, "that the French Indians had the good cause in the fight of last year?"

"The scoundrels! I would have the scalp of every murderous redskin among them!" cried Harry, clenching his fist. "They were robbing and invading British territories, too. But the Highlanders were fighting for their king."

"We, on our side, were fighting for our king; and we ended by winning the battle," said the Colonel, laughing.

"Ah!" cried Harry; "if his Royal Highness the Prince had not turned back at Derby, your king and mine, now, would be his Majesty King James the Third!"

"Who made such a Tory of you, Mr. Warrington?" asked Lambert.

"Nay, sir, the Esmonds were always loyal!" answered the youth. "Had we lived at home, and twenty years sooner, brother and I often agreed that our heads would have been in danger. We certainly would have staked them for the king's cause."

"Yours is better on your shoulders than on a pole at Temple Bar. I have seen them there, and they don't look very pleasant, Mr. Warrington."

"I shall take off my hat, and salute them, whenever I pass the gate," cried the young man, "if the king and the whole court are standing by!"

"I doubt whether your relative, my Lord Castlewood, is as staunch a supporter of the king over the water," said Colonel Lambert, smiling. "Or your aunt, the Baroness of Bernstein, who left you in our charge. Whatever her old partialities may have been, she has repented of them; she has rallied to our side, landed her nephews in the Household, and looks to find a suitable match for her nieces. If you have Tory opinions, Mr. Warrington, take an old soldier's advice, and keep them to yourself."

"Why, sir, I do not think that you will betray me!" said the boy.

"Not I, but others might. You did not talk in this way at Castlewood? I mean the old Castlewood which you have just come from."

"I might be safe amongst my own kinsmen, surely, sir!" cried Harry.

"Doubtless. I would not say no. But a man's own kinsmen can play him slippery tricks at times, and he finds himself none the better for trusting them. I mean no offense to you or any of your family; but lacqueys have ears as well as their masters, and they carry about all sorts of stories. For instance, your black fellow is ready to tell all he knows about you, and a great deal more besides, as it would appear."

"Hath he told about the broken-kneed horse?" cried out Harry, turning very red.

"To say truth, my groom seemed to know something of the story, and said it was a shame a gentleman should sell another such a brute; let alone a cousin. I am not here to play the Mentor to you, or to carry about servants' tittle-tattle. When you have seen more of your cousins, you will form your own opinion of them; meanwhile, take an old soldier's advice, I say again, and be cautious with whom you deal, and what you say."

Very soon after this colloquy, Mr. Lambert's guest rose, with the assistance of Gumbo, his valet, to whom he, for the hundredth time at least, promised a sound caning if ever he should hear that Gumbo had ventured to talk about his affairs again in the servants'-hall—a prohibition Gumbo solemnly vowed and declared he would forever obey; but I dare say he was chattering the whole of the Castlewood secrets to his new friends in Colonel Lambert's kitchen, for Harry's hostess certainly heard a number of stories concerning him which she could not prevent her housekeeper from repeating. Though I would not accuse that worthy lady, or any of her sex or ours, of undue curiosity regarding their neighbors' affairs, how can you prevent servants talking, or listening when the faithful, attached creatures talk to you?

Mr. Lambert's house stood on the outskirts of the little town of Oakhurst, which, if the patient reader travels in the right direction, will be found on the road between Farnham and Reigate—where Madame Bernstein's servants naturally pulled at the first bell at hand when the young Virginian met with his mishap. A few hundred yards farther lay the long street of the little old town, where hospitality might have been found under the great swinging ensigns of a couple of tuns, and medical relief was to be had, as a blazing gilt pestle and mortar indicated. But what surgeon could have ministered more cleverly to a patient than Harry's host, who tended him without a fee, or what Boniface could make him more comfortably welcome?

Two tall gates, each surmounted by a couple of heraldic monsters, led from the highroad up to a neat, broad stone terrace whereon stood Oakhurst House: a square brick building with windows faced with stone, many high chimneys, and a tall roof surmounted by a fair balustrade. Behind the house stretched a large garden, where there was plenty of room for cabbages as well as roses to grow; and before the mansion, separated from it by the highroad, was a field of many acres where the Colonel's cows and horses were at grass. Over the center window was a carved shield supported by the same monsters who pranced or ramped upon the entrance-gates, with a coronet above. The fact is, that the house had originally been the jointure-house of Oakhurst Castle, which stood hard by—its chimneys and turrets appearing over the surrounding woods, now bronzed with the darkest foliage of summer.
