The spell of Mrs. Lambert's reverie broke as swiftly as it had formed. Miss Theo and her mother were forced to admit, in the quiet corners of their hearts, that their hero was merely a man. They spoke little of it, yet the silence between them was thick with understanding; the mother, sensing her daughter's deflated spirit, offered a tenderness that bordered on adoration. "Never mind, my dear," she whispered, pressing a kiss to Theo's cheek. "Our hero has proven to be but an ordinary mortal, and no such man is worthy of my Theo. You shall find a true husband soon, if Providence has one waiting in England. I was scarcely fifteen when your father first saw me at the Bury Assembly, and I vowed then that no other man would suffice. Yet, if Heaven grants me a spouse—the finest man in the entire kingdom—surely He will bless my child equally, for she deserves a king if she dreams of one!" It was possible, Mrs. Lambert mused, that she harbored a secret fantasy: perhaps the Prince of Wales himself would ride past her gate, tumble from his steed, be ushered inside, be healed, and win the favor of her grandfather, securing a regiment for Martin Lambert and, inevitably, falling in love with Theo.

Colonel Lambert and his second daughter, Miss Hetty, stood firmly on the opposite shore of this emotional river, laughing and scoffing at the sentimentality. Mrs. Lambert was a woman perpetually engaged in matchmaking, addicted to novels that caused her to weep with excessive fervor. Not a carriage passed the gate without her expecting a suitor to alight and ring the bell. Miss Hetty, however, wielded her tongue with a saucy precision rarely seen. She peppered their conversations with references to Prussia and Persia, delivered with a pertness that bordered on the offensive. She queried whether the current King of Prussia was known as the Shaw or the Sophy, and calculated the distance from Ispahan to Saxony—a campaign her father was currently studying with maps and newspapers. She produced *The Persian Tales* from her mother's closet and slid them onto the parlor table where the family sat. "I would not marry a Persian prince," Hetty declared, "for I prefer a gentleman who does not require multiple wives simultaneously." She dubbed the young Virginian, Theo's companion, "Theo's prince," and jokingly asked her mother if she intended to claim the other visitor, the "black prince," for herself. She relentlessly teased her sister and mother on their sentimental inclinations, driving them to the brink of anger before retreating into tears, only to be coaxed back with violent kisses and affectionate coaxing.

Simple Harry Warrington remained oblivious to the whirlwind of jokes, tears, reconciliations, and matrimonial schemes that revolved around him. He was the innocent catalyst for a hundred allusions to Prussian kings and Persian sultans, yet these Parthian arrows failed to pierce his simple nature. Was a "Shaw" a title? Was a "Sophy" a lady? He likely found the notion of a man with a great black beard bearing such a name to be the height of absurdity. Like a stone dropped into a still pool, Harry entered this quiet domestic sphere, unaware of the flutter and excitement he generated among the fish and ducks of their social world. He possessed a sound opinion of himself but lacked confidence regarding women, being of an age that requires encouragement and having been raised in a modest, primitive environment concerning the opposite sex. Thus, Hetty's jests circled him like summer gnats, unnoticed and unheeded. He was not stupid, as Hetty assumed; he was simply consumed by his own honest concerns, too absorbed in his immediate reality to perceive the dramas unfolding in the drawing rooms of his hosts.

While the sisters combed their ringlets or conversed intimately in the great bed—a custom of the era where they lay side by side—Harry remained ignorant of the profound role he played in their thoughts. Three days after his arrival, the Colonel and his daughters walked with him through the magnificent park of Lord Wrotham, a space where they were free to roam. Upon reaching a sheet of water, they encountered swans, birds the young ladies were accustomed to feeding with bread. As the majestic creatures approached, Hetty cast a peculiar glance at her mother and sister, followed by a look at her father, who stood nearby, content and happy in his red waistcoat. "Mamma's swans are something like these, papa," Hetty remarked.

"What swans, my dear?" her mother asked.

"Something like, but not quite. They have shorter necks than these, and there are scores of them on our common," Hetty continued, her voice dropping slightly. "I saw Betty plucking one in the kitchen this morning. We shall have it for dinner, with apple-sauce and—"

"Don't be a little goose!" Theo interrupted.

"And sage and onions. Do you love swan, Mr. Warrington?"

"I shot three last winter on our river," the Virginian replied. "Ours are not such white birds as these—they eat very well, though."

The simple youth had no inkling that he was the allegory at that very moment, nor that Miss Hetty was weaving a fable about him. In some obscure Latin text, I have read that long before Virginia was discovered, other peoples were equally slow to comprehend the obvious.

It was a premature sentiment on Miss Theo's part—that tender flutter of the bosom she felt upon first beholding the handsome, pale, and bleeding Virginian. This was not the great passion her heart was capable of feeling. Like the birds, it had awakened and begun to sing at a false dawn. *Hop back to thy perch, and cover thy head with thy wing, thou tremulous little creature!* It was not yet light; roosting was preferable to singing. Soon, however, the morning would break, the sky would redden, and she would soar to salute the sun with her music.

A phrase from earlier in the narrative may have caught the eye of the fair and suspicious reader: "Three days after his arrival, Harry was walking with..." If he could walk, as he clearly could, what business did he have strolling with anyone but Lady Maria Esmond on the Pantiles at Tunbridge Wells? His shoulder was set, his health fully restored, and he lacked even a change of coats, owing his raiment to the Colonel. Surely, a young man in such a state had no right to linger at Oakhurst. He was bound by every tie of duty, convenience, love, and relationship—and by a washerwoman finally—to return to Tunbridge. Why did he stay, unless he was in love with one of the young ladies? Could it be that he did not wish to go? Had the reader grasped the meaning of the mystic 'S' that commenced the previous chapter, depicting Sinbad the Sailor surmounted by that odious old man of the sea? What if Harry Warrington was that sailor, and his fate that choking, deadening, inevitable old man? What if, for the past two days, he had felt those knees throttling him round the neck? If his aunt's purpose was answered, and if his former love was killed as dead by her poisonous communications as fair Rosamond was by her royal rival, then perhaps Hero was lighting the lamp and preparing supper while Leander sat comfortably with another party, never thinking of taking to the water. Since that coward's blow struck in Lady Maria's back by her own relative, surely kind hearts must pity her. I know she has faults—yes, and she wears false hair—but a woman in distress deserves pity, not laughter. Between her old aunt and her unhappy delusion, Lady Maria Esmond was having a most unpleasant time at Tunbridge Wells. No one protected her; Madam Beatrix held her entirely in thrall. Lady Maria was poor, hoping for money from her aunt, yet possessing secrets the old woman knew and brandished over her. I am quite melted thinking of her. Imagine her alone, a victim to that old woman! Picture that antique Andromeda, with her rich, flowing hair falling over her shoulders, chained to a rock on Mount Ephraim and surrendered to that dragon of a Baroness! Where is Perseus? He is not in the least hurry. The dragon has her will for day after day.

Harry Warrington, who would not have allowed his dislocated and mended shoulder to prevent him from hunting, remained day after day contentedly at Oakhurst, finding each passing day increased his affection for the kindly folk who welcomed him. Perhaps he had never, since his grandfather's death, been in such good company. His lot had previously fallen among fox-hunting Virginian squires, whose society he had endured contentedly, riding their horses, living their lives, and sharing their punch-bowls. The ladies of his home and mother's acquaintance were well-bred, decorous, and pious, yet somewhat narrow-minded. His home was a small place, defined by pompous ways, minute etiquettes, small flatteries, trivial conversations, and petty scandals. Only after leaving did he realize how confined his existence had been. He was personally free; he had dogs and horses, and could shoot and hunt for miles around. But the little lady-mother domineered at home, and within those walls, he had to submit to her influence and breathe her air.

Here, he found himself amidst a circle where everything was incomparably gayer, brighter, and freer. He lived with a man and woman who had seen the world, though they now lived retired from it, both enjoying from their earliest times not only good books but good company—those living books that are such pleasant and often profitable reading. Society possesses this great benefit: it lessens our conceit by teaching us our insignificance and introducing us to our betters. If you are a young person reading this, depend upon it, there is nothing more wholesome than to acknowledge and associate with your superiors. If I could, I would not have my son Thomas be the first Greek and Latin prize boy, the first oar, and the cock of the school. Better for his soul and body that he occupy a good place, not the first, surrounded by a fair set of competitors, receiving a good thrashing now and then, followed by a hearty shake of the hand that administered the beating. What honest man would choose to be a prince, with all society walking backwards before him, attended only by obsequious household gentlemen, and with all mankind silent except when your High Mightiness asks a question? One of the greatest benefits Harry Warrington received from this family, before whose gate Fate had shot him, was learning that he was a profoundly ignorant young fellow, and that there were many people in the world far superior to himself. Arrogant with some, in the company of his superiors, he became magnanimously docile. He had seen how faithfully he admired his brother at home and his friend, the gallant young Colonel of Mount Vernon; of the gentlemen, his kinsmen at Castlewood, he had felt himself at least their equal. But in his new acquaintances at Oakhurst, he found a man who had read far more books than Harry could judge, who had seen the world and emerged unwounded from its dangers and battles, possessing goodness and honesty written on his face and breathing from his lips—qualities for which our brave lad had always an instinctive sympathy.

As for the women, they were the kindest, merriest, and most agreeable he had yet known. They were pleasanter than Parson Broadbent's black-eyed daughter at home, whose laugh carried as far as a gunshot. They were as well-bred as the ladies of Castlewood, with the exception of Madam Beatrix, who was indeed as grand as an empress on certain occasions. Yet, after a talk with Madam Beatrix and vast amusement at her stories, the lad would depart with a bitter taste in his mouth, fancying all the world wicked. They were not squeamish; they laughed over pages of Mr. Fielding and cried over volumes of Mr. Richardson, containing jokes and incidents that would make Mrs. Grundy's hair stand on end, yet their merry prattle left no bitterness behind. Their tales of neighbors were droll, not malicious; their descriptions of the courteous salutations and cordial bounties received from the folks of the neighboring town were delightful. Truly, it is good to be with good people. How good Harry Warrington did not know at the time, perhaps, until subsequent experience revealed contrasts or caused him to feel remorse. Here was a tranquil, sunshiny day in a life destined to be agitated and stormy—a happy hour or two to remember. Little happened during these hours; it was only sweet sleep, pleasant waking, friendly welcome, and serene pastime. The gates of the old house seemed to shut the wicked world out, making the inhabitants within appear better, purer, and kinder than others. He was not in love—not the least, either with saucy Hetty or generous Theodosia. But when the time came for him to depart, he fastened on both their hands and felt an immense regard for them. He thought he should like to know their brothers, believing them to be fine fellows. As for Mrs. Lambert, I believe she was as sentimental at his departure as if he had been the last volume of *Clarissa Harlowe*.

"He is very kind and honest," Theo said gravely, looking from the terrace as they saw him, their father, and the servants riding away on the road to Westerham.

"I don't think him stupid at all now," little Hetty replied. "And, mamma, I think he is very like a swan indeed."

"It felt just like one of the boys going to school," their mother said.

"Just like it," Theo answered, sadly.

"I am glad he has got papa to ride with him to Westerham," Miss Hetty resumed. "And that he bought Farmer Briggs's horse. I don't like his going to those Castlewood people. I am sure that Madame Bernstein is a wicked old woman. I expected to see her ride away on her crooked stick."

"Hush, Hetty!"

"Do you think she would float if they tried her in the pond, as poor old mother Hely did at Elmhurst? The other old woman seemed fond of him—I mean the one with the fair tour. She looked very melancholy when she went

Mrs. Lambert stood by the roadside, her lily-white handkerchief pressed to her lips as a final token of farewell to the departing travelers. Beside her, her daughters watched the two gentlemen pace leisurely along the first few hundred yards of the road, their figures growing smaller until a clump of lime trees obscured them from view. Behind that green screen, the good matron had watched countless departures: husbands marching to battle, sons bound for school, each vanishing into the distance to return only when Heaven's will decreed. The leisure of home life fostered a tender fidelity in women; with the men gone, the house fell silent, filled only with the ache of absence. There was the vacant room where the boy had slept, the faint impression of his carpet bag still lingering on the bed, his whip hanging in the hall, his fishing rod and basket—mute memorials of brief pleasures. At dinner, the cherry tart remained untouched, for the boy had eaten his share hours ago, sandwiched between his choking sisters. Evening prayers were said without his voice joining the responses, and midnight silence descended, leaving the mother wakeful, counting the hours until the next letter might arrive. Those rustling limes formed a protective barrier between the domestic sphere and the wider world. Mrs. Lambert often became silent and contemplative when walking near these trees, wishing to carve the names of her loved ones into the grey, silvered trunks amidst the knots of true love, a custom of the time. Her daughter, Miss Theo, possessed an elegant turn for verse and composed a poem for the trees, which her delighted mother later submitted to a periodical.

"Now we are out of sight of the ladies," Colonel Lambert said, tipping his hat as the gentlemen trotted past the lime trees. "I know my wife watches from her window until we round this corner. I hope we shall see the trees and the house again, Mr. Warrington; and with the boys at home, there may be better sport for you."

"I never wish to be happier than I have been, sir," replied Mr. Warrington warmly. "I feel as if I am leaving behind old friends."

"The friend at whose house we shall sup tonight has a son who is also an old friend of our family," the Colonel continued. "My wife, an inveterate marriage-monger, would have arranged a match between him and one of my girls, but the Colonel has chosen to fall in love with someone else."

"Ah!" sighed Mr. Warrington.

"Others have done the same before Agamemnon," the Colonel added with a laugh.

"Is the gentleman's name Aga...?" the young traveler inquired meekly, having missed the name.

"No, his name is James Wolfe," the Colonel corrected, smiling. "He is still young, or what we call so, being scarce thirty. He is the youngest lieutenant-colonel in the army, barring a few scores of our nobility who take rank before us common folk."

"Of course, of course!" the Colonel's young companion remarked with true colonial notions of aristocratic precedence.

"I have seen him commanding captains who were thirty years his senior, men with neither his merit nor his good fortune. Yet, lucky as he is, no one envies his superiority, for most acknowledge him as our superior. He is beloved by every man in our old regiment, knows them all, and is a good scholar as well as a consummate soldier, a master of many languages."

"Ah, sir!" Harry Warrington sighed with great humility. "I feel I have neglected my youth sadly. I have come to England but an ignoramus. Had my dear brother been alive, he would have represented our name and our colony far better than I can. George was a scholar, a musician, capable of conversing with the most learned men in our country. Do you know, sir, I am glad to have come home, and to you especially, if only to learn how ignorant I am."

"If you know that well, 'tis a great gain already," the Colonel smiled.

"At home, especially since we lost my brother, I used to think myself a mighty fine fellow, and no doubt the folks around flattered me. I am wiser now—or I hope I am, though perhaps I am only bragging again. You see, sir, the gentry in our colony know very little, except about dogs, horses, betting, and games. I wish I knew more about books and less about them."

"Nay. Dogs and horses are very good books in their way; we can read much truth from them. Some men are not made to be scholars, yet may be worthy citizens and gentlemen in spite of their ignorance. What call have all of us to be especially learned or wise, or to take a first place in the world? His Royal Highness commands, Martin Lambert is colonel, and Jack Hunt, who rides behind yonder, was a private soldier and is now a very honest, worthy groom. If we all do our best in our station, it matters not whether that be high or low. Nay, how do we know what is high and what is low? Perhaps Jack's currycomb, my epaulets, or His Royal Highness's baton may prove equally significant. When I began life, I dreamed of success and honor; now I think of duty, and those folks we parted with just hours ago. Let us trot on, else we shall not reach Westerham before nightfall."

At Westerham, the two friends were welcomed by their hosts: a stately matron, an old soldier whose memories and services dated back fifty-four years, and his son, the Lieutenant-Colonel of Kingsley's regiment, currently stationed at Maidstone. Harry looked with curiosity at this officer, who, though young, had seen extensive service and earned a high character. There was little beauty in his face; he was very lean and pale, with red hair and high cheekbones. Yet, he possessed a fine courtesy toward elders, a cordial greeting to friends, and an animation in conversation that caused listeners to forget, and even admire, his homely features.

"Mr. Warrington is going to Tunbridge?" the hostess asked. "Their James will bear him company." She whispered something to Colonel Lambert at supper, eliciting smiles and knowing winks from the officer. He called for wine and toasted "Miss Lowther." "With all my heart," cried the enthusiastic Colonel James, draining his glass to the very last drop. His mother whispered to her friend how James and the lady were planning a match, noting that she came from the famous Lowther family of the North.

"If she were the daughter of King Charlemagne," Lambert declared, "she is not too good for James Wolfe, or for his mother's son."

"Mr. Lambert would not say so if he knew her," the young Colonel declared.

"Oh, of course, she is the priceless pearl, and you are nothing," the mother cried. "No, I am of Colonel Lambert's opinion. If she brought all of Cumberland as a jointure, I should say it was my James's due. That is the way with them, Mr. Warrington. We tend our children through fevers, measles, whooping-cough, and smallpox; we send them to the army and cannot sleep for worry; we break our hearts parting with them, having them home only for a week or two a year, or maybe ten years. And after all our care, there comes a lass with bright eyes, and away goes our boy, caring not a fig for us afterwards."

"And pray, my dear, how did you come to marry James's father?" the elder Colonel Wolfe asked. "And why didn't you stay at home with your parents?"

"Because James's father was gouty and needed someone to care for him, I suppose; not because I liked him a bit," the lady answered. Thus, with easy talk and kindness, the evening passed.

On the morrow, Colonel Lambert, expressing much kindness and friendship for his late guest, handed the young Virginian over to Mr. Wolfe's charge and turned his horse's head homeward, while the two gentlemen sped toward Tunbridge Wells. Wolfe was eager to reach the destination; Harry Warrington was perhaps less so. Indeed, as Lambert rode toward his home, Harry's thoughts followed him with longing desire for the parlor at Oakhurst, where he had spent three days in happy calm. Mr. Wolfe agreed with all of Harry's enthusiastic praise of the Lambert family. "To have such a good name and to live such a life as Colonel Lambert's," Wolfe said, "seems to me now the height of human ambition."

"And glory and honor?" Warrington asked. "Are those nothing? Would you give up the winning of them?"

"They were my dreams once," the Colonel answered, his ideas of happiness now different. "Now my desires are much more tranquil. I have followed arms since I was fourteen. I have seen almost every kind of duty connected with my calling. I know all the garrison towns in this country and have served wherever there was work to be done during the last ten years. I have done nearly the whole of a soldier's duty, except the command of an army, which can hardly be hoped for by one of my years. Now, methinks, I would like quiet, books to read, a wife to love me, and some children to dandle on my knee. I have imagined such an Elysium for myself, Mr. Warrington. True love is better than glory; and a tranquil fireside, with the woman of your heart seated by it, is the greatest good the gods can send us."

Harry imagined the picture his comrade described. He said "Yes" to the remark, but his assent was not cheerful, for his companion noted the expression on his face.

"You say 'Yes' as if a fireside and a sweetheart were not particularly to your taste," Wolfe observed.

"Why, look you, Colonel, there are other things a young fellow might like to enjoy. You have had sixteen years of the world; I am but a few months away from my mother's apron-strings. When I have seen a campaign or two, or six, as you have; when I have distinguished myself like Mr. Wolfe and made the world talk of me, then I may think of retiring from it."

To these remarks, Mr. Wolfe, whose heart was full of a very different matter, replied with a further encomium of the joys of marriage and a special rhapsody on the beauties and merits of his mistress—a theme intensely interesting to himself, though perhaps not so to his hearer, whose views on married life, if he entertained any, were somewhat melancholy and despondent. A pleasant afternoon brought them to the end of their ride, unaccompanied by accident or incident, save perhaps for a mistake Harry made a few miles from Tunbridge Wells, where two horsemen stopped them. Harry, pistol in hand, was about to charge, supposing them to be highwaymen. Colonel Wolfe, laughing, bade him reserve his fire, explaining that these were merely innkeepers' agents, not robbers (except in their calling). Gumbo, whose horse ran away at that critical moment, was brought back after much bawling from his master, and the two gentlemen rode into the little town, alighted at their inn, and then separated, each seeking the ladies he had come to visit.

Mr. Warrington found his aunt installed in handsome lodgings, attended by a guard of London lacqueys in her anteroom and following her chair when she went abroad. She received him with the utmost kindness. His cousin, Lady Maria, was absent upon his arrival; it is unknown whether the young gentleman was unhappy at not seeing her, whether he disguised his feelings, or whether Madame de Bernstein took note of them.

A beau in a richly figured suit—the first of his kind Harry had seen—and two dowagers with voluminous hoops and plenty of rouge were visiting the Baroness when her nephew made his bow. She introduced the young man to these personages as her nephew, the young Croesus from Virginia, of whom they had heard. She spoke of the immensity of his estate, as large as Kent and infinitely more fruitful. She mentioned how her half-sister, Madam Esmond, was called Princess Pocahontas in her own country. She never tired of praising mother and son, their riches, and their good qualities. The beau shook the young man's hand, delighted to make his acquaintance. The ladies praised him so loudly to his aunt that the modest youth was fain to blush at their compliments. They departed to inform the Tunbridge society of his arrival, and the little place soon buzzed with accounts of the wealth, good breeding, and good looks of the Virginian.

"You could not have come at a better moment, my dear," the Baroness said to her nephew as her visitors departed with many curtseys and congees. "Those three individuals have the most active tongues in the Wells. They will trumpet your good qualities in every company they go. I have introduced you to a hundred people already, and Heaven help me! have told all sorts of fibs about the geography of Virginia to describe your estate. It is a prodigiously large one, but I am afraid I have magnified it. I have filled it with all sorts of wonderful animals, gold mines, spices; I am not sure I have not said diamonds. As for your negroes, I have given your mother armies of them, and in fact represented her as a sovereign princess reigning over a magnificent dominion. So she has a magnificent dominion: I cannot tell to a few hundred thousand pounds how much her yearly income is, but I have no doubt it is very great. And you must prepare, sir, to be treated here as the heir-apparent of this royal lady. Do not let your head be turned. From this day forth, you are going to be flattered as you have never been flattered in your life."

"And to what end, ma'am?" the young gentleman asked. "I see no reason why I should be reputed so rich or get so much flattery."

"In the first place, sir, you must not contradict your old aunt, who has no desire to be made a fool of before her company. And as for your reputation, you must know we found it here almost ready-made upon our arrival. A London newspaper somehow heard of you and came out with a story of the immense wealth of a young gentleman from Virginia lately landed

Cousin Maria made her entrance, flanked by two gardener's boys carrying baskets brimming with blooms intended to transform Madame de Bernstein's drawing-room for the arrival of her guests. Three footmen, their livery gorgeously laced with worsted, arranged double the number of card tables. A major-domo, dressed in black with fine ruffled cuffs and a bag slung over his shoulder—looking as though a sword belonged by his side—followed the lacqueys bearing fasces of wax candles. He placed a pair upon each table and set others in the silver sconces mounted on the wainscoting. Sunlight streamed through the windows, gilding the walls and illuminating the view of the green common beyond, where rocks, tree clumps, and distant houses twinkled in the afternoon light. Groups of figures in hoops, powder, and brocade sauntered across the lawn, casting dappled shadows upon the plain. Across the way lay the Pantiles, a perpetual fair where the clatter and buzz of society never ceased. A band played for the benefit of the visitors to the Wells. Madame Bernstein's chief sitting-room might not suit a recluse or a scholar, but for those who preferred bustle, gaiety, bright cross-light, and a panoramic view of the cheery, busy place, no lodging could be more pleasant. As the windows were lit, passersby below knew her ladyship was at home holding a card assembly, accessible to any with an introduction.

Reflecting on the past, one realizes that the night-life of society a century prior was far darker than today. There was not one wax candle for ten that we now see in a lady's drawing-room, let alone gas or the wondrous new illuminations of clubs. Horrible, guttering tallow smoked and stank in the passages. The candle-snuffer was a notorious officer in the theatre. Consider Hogarth's pictures: how dark they are, how his feasts seem begrimed with tallow! In "Marriage à la Mode," in Lord Viscount Squanderfield's grand saloons, where he and his wife sit yawning before the horror-stricken steward after their party, there are but eight candles—one on each card-table, half a dozen in a brass chandelier. If Jack Briefless had convoked his friends to oysters and beer in his chambers at Pump Court, he would have had twice as many. Let us comfort ourselves by thinking that Louis Quatorze, in all his glory, held his revels in the dark, and bless Mr. Price and other Luciferous benefactors of mankind for banishing the abominable gloom of our youth.

Maria, the fairest flower herself, popped her roses, sweet-williams, and other blossoms into vases here and there, adorning the apartment to the best of her art. She lingered fondly over this bowl and that dragon jar, casting only sly, timid glances at young cousin Harry. His own blush would have become any young woman, and one might have thought she intended to outstay her aunt. But the Baroness, seated in her armchair with her crooked tortoiseshell stick in hand, pointed the servants imperiously to their duties. She rated them soundly: Tom for a darn in his stocking, John for having greased his locks too profusely from the candle-box, and so forth, maintaining a stern domination over them. Another remark concerning poor James of a hundred years ago: James slept two to a bed, four to a room, and that room was likely a cellar; he washed in a trough such as one would hardly see anywhere in London now outside the barracks of Her Majesty's Foot Guards.

If Maria hoped for a present interview, her fond heart was disappointed. "Where are you going to dine, Harry?" asked Madame de Bernstein. "My niece Maria and I shall have a chicken in the little parlour—I think you should go to the best ordinary. There is one at the White Horse at three; we shall hear his bell in a minute or two. And you will understand, sir, that you ought not to spare expense, but behave like Princess Pocahontas's son. Your trunks have been taken over to the lodging I have engaged for you. It is not good for a lad to be always hanging about the aprons of two old women. Is it, Maria?"

"No," said her ladyship, dropping her meek eyes, whilst the other lady glared in triumph. I think Andromeda had been exposed to the Dragon considerably during the last five or six days; and if Perseus had cut the latter's cruel head off, he would have committed not unjustifiable monstricide. But he did not bare sword or shield; he only looked mechanically at the lacqueys in tawny and blue as they creaked about the room.

"And there are good mercers and tailors from London always here to wait on the company at the Wells. You had better see them, my dear, for your suit is not of the very last fashion—a little lace—"

"I can't go out of mourning, ma'am," said the young man, looking down at his sables.

"Ho, sir!" cried the lady, rustling up from her chair and rising on her cane. "Wear black for your brother till you are as old as Methuselah, if you like. I am sure I don't want to prevent you. I only want you to dress, and to do like other people, and make a figure worthy of your name."

"Madam," said Mr. Warrington with great state, "I have not done anything to disgrace it that I know."

Why did the old woman stop and give a little start as if she had been struck? Let bygones be bygones. She and the boy had a score of little passages of this kind in which swords were crossed and thrusts rapidly dealt or parried. She liked Harry none the worse for his courage in facing her. "Sure a little finer linen than that shirt you wear will not be a disgrace to you, sir," she said, with rather a forced laugh.

Harry bowed and blushed. It was one of the homely gifts of his Oakhurst friends. He felt pleased somehow to think he wore it; thought of the new friends, so good, so pure, so simple, so kindly, with immense tenderness, and felt, while invested in this garment, as if evil could not touch him. He said he would go to his lodging and make a point of returning arrayed in the best linen he had.

"Come back here, sir," said Madame Bernstein, "and if our company has not arrived, Maria and I will find some ruffles for you!" And under a footman's guidance, the young fellow walked off to his new lodgings.

Harry found not only handsome and spacious apartments provided for him, but a groom in attendance waiting to be engaged by his honour, and a second valet, if he was inclined to hire one to wait upon Mr. Gumbo. Ere he had been many minutes in his rooms, emissaries from a London tailor and bootmaker waited him with the cards and compliments of their employers, Messrs. Regnier and Tull; the best articles in his modest wardrobe were laid out by Gumbo, and the finest linen with which his thrifty Virginian mother had provided him. Visions of the snow-surrounded home in his own country, of the crackling logs and the trim quiet ladies working by the fire, rose up before him. For the first time, a little thought crossed the young man's mind that the homely clothes were not quite smart enough, the home-worked linen not so fine as it might be. That he should be ashamed of anything belonging to him or to Castlewood! That was strange. The simple folks there were only too well satisfied with all things that were done, or said, or produced at Castlewood; and Madam Esmond, when she sent her son forth on his travels, thought no young nobleman need be better provided. The clothes might have fitted better and been of a later fashion, to be sure—but still the young fellow presented a comely figure enough when he issued from his apartments, his toilet over; and Gumbo calling a chair, marched beside it, until they reached the ordinary where the young gentleman was to dine.

Here he expected to find the beau whose acquaintance he had made a few hours before at his aunt's lodging, and who had indicated to Harry that the White Horse was the most modish place for dining at the Wells. He mentioned his friend's name to the host: but the landlord and waiters, leading him into the room with many smiles and bows, assured his honour that his honour did not need any other introduction than his own. They helped him hang up his coat and sword on a peg, asked him whether he would drink Burgundy, Pontac, or champagne to his dinner, and led him to a table.

Though the most fashionable ordinary in the village, the White Horse did not happen to be crowded on this day. Monsieur Barbeau, the landlord, informed Harry that there was a great entertainment at Summer Hill, which had taken away most of the company. Indeed, when Harry entered the room, there were but four other gentlemen in it. Two of these guests were drinking wine and had finished their dinner; the other two were young men in the midst of their meal. As the landlord passed, he must have whispered the name of the newcomer to them, for they looked at him with some appearance of interest and made him a slight bow across the table as the smiling host bustled away for Harry's dinner.

Mr. Warrington returned the salute of the two gentlemen, who bade him welcome to Tunbridge and hoped he would like the place upon better acquaintance. Then they smiled and exchanged waggish looks with each other, of which Harry did not understand the meaning, nor why they cast knowing glances at the two other guests over their wine.

One of these persons was in a somewhat tarnished velvet coat with a huge queue and bag, voluminous ruffles, and embroidery. The other was a little beetle-browed, hook-nosed, high-shouldered gentleman, whom his opposite companion addressed as "milord" or "my lord" in a very high voice. My lord, who was sipping the wine before him, barely glanced at the newcomer and then addressed himself to his own companion.

"And so you know the nephew of the old woman—the Croesus who comes to arrive?"

"You're thrown out there, Jack!" said one young gentleman to the other.

"Never could manage the lingo," said Jack. The two elders had begun to speak in the French language.

"But assuredly, my dear lord!" said the gentleman with the long queue.

"You have shown energy, my dear Baron! He has been here but two hours. My people told me of him only as I came to dinner."

"I knew him before! I have met him often in London with the Baroness and my lord, his cousin," said the Baron.

A smoking soup for Harry came in, borne by the smiling host. "Behold, sir! Behold a potage of my fashion!" said my lord, laying down the dish and whispering to Harry the celebrated name of the nobleman opposite. Harry thanked Monsieur Barbeau in his own language, upon which the foreign gentleman, turning round, grinned most graciously at Harry and said, "Fous bossedez notre langue barfaidement, monsieur." Mr. Warrington had never heard the French language pronounced in that manner in Canada. He bowed in return to the foreign gentleman.

"Tell me more about the Croesus, my good Baron," continued his lordship, speaking rather superciliously to his companion and taking no notice of Harry, which perhaps somewhat nettled the young man.

"What will you, that I tell you, my dear lord? Croesus is a youth like other youths; he is tall, like other youths; he is awkward, like other youths; he has black hair, as they all have who come from the Indies. Lodgings have been taken for him at Mrs. Rose's toy-shop."

"I have lodgings there too," thought Mr. Warrington. "Who is Croesus they are talking of? How good the soup is!"

"He travels with a large retinue," the Baron continued, "four servants, two postchaises, and a pair of outriders. His chief attendant is a black man who saved his life from the savages in America, and who will not hear, on any account, of being made free. He persists in wearing mourning for his elder brother from whom he inherits his principality."

"Could anything console you for the death of yours, Chevalier?" cried out the elder gentleman.

"Milor! his property might," said the Chevalier, "which you know is not small."

"Your brother lives on his patrimony—which you have told me is immense—you by your industry, my dear Chevalier."

"Milor!" cries the individual addressed as Chevalier.

"By your industry or your esprit—how much more noble! Shall you be at the Baroness's to-night? She ought to be a little of your parents, Chevalier?"

"Again I fail to comprehend your lordship," said the other gentleman, rather sulkily.

"Why, she is a woman of great wit—she is of noble birth—she has undergone strange adventures—she has but little principle (there you happily have the advantage of her). But what care we men of the world? You intend to go and play with the young Creole, no doubt, and get as much money from him as you can. By the way, Baron, suppose he should be a guet-apens, that young Creole? Suppose our excellent friend has invented him up in London and brings him down with his character for wealth to prey upon the innocent folks here?"

"J'y ai souvent pensé, milor," said the little Baron, placing his finger to his nose very knowingly, "that Baroness is capable of anything."

"A Baron—a Baroness, que voulez-vous, my friend? I mean the late lamented husband. Do you know who he was?"

"Intimately. A more notorious villain never dealt a card. At Venice, at Brussels, at Spa, at Vienna—the gaols of every one of which places he knew. I knew the man, my lord."

"I thought you would. I saw him at the Hague, where I first had the honour of meeting you, and a more dis

Within the precinct of the White Horse Tavern, approaching the windows of the eating-room, lay a bowling-green dotted with tables where guests might sip punch or tea. Having concluded their dinner simultaneously, Mr. Morris proposed they adjourn to the Green for a cool bottle. "Jack Morris would adjourn to the Dust Hole as a pretext for a fresh drink," observed my Lord Chesterfield. Upon this, Jack retorted that each gentleman possessed his own favored method of descending to the deuce, admitting frankly that his own weakness was a bottle.

"My Lord Chesterfield's deuce is deuce-ace," remarked my Lord March. "His lordship cannot keep away from cards or dice."

"My Lord March possesses not one devil, but several," Jack countered. "He loves gambling, horse-racing, betting, drinking, eating, money, and women. You have fallen into bad company, Mr. Warrington, when you lighted upon his lordship. He will play you for every acre you hold in Virginia."

"With the greatest pleasure in life, Mr. Warrington!" interjected my Lord.

"And for all your tobacco, spices, slaves, oxen, and asses, and everything that is yours."

"Shall we begin now? Jack, you are never without a dice-box or bottle-screw. I will set Mr. Warrington for what he likes."

"Unfortunately, my lord, the tobacco, slaves, asses, and oxen are not yet mine," replied Harry. "I am just of age, and my mother, scarce twenty years older, has quite as good a chance of long life as I have."

"I will bet you that you survive her," my Lord March declared. "I will pay you a sum now against four times the sum payable at her death. I will set you a fair sum over this table against the reversion of your estate in Virginia upon her departure. What do you call your place?"

"Castlewood."

"A principality, I hear it is. I will bet that its value has been exaggerated tenfold amongst the quidnuncs here. How came you by the name of Castlewood? Are you related to my lord? Oh, stay: I know—my lady, your mother, descends from the real head of the house. He took the losing side in '15. I have heard the story a dozen times from my old Duchess. She knew your grandfather. He was a friend of Addison, Steele, Pope, and Milton, I dare say, and the bigwigs. It is a pity he did not stay at home and transport the other branch of the family to the plantations."

"I have just been staying at Castlewood with my cousin there," remarked Harry.

"Hm! Did you play with him? He's fond of pasteboard and bones."

"Never, but for sixpences and a pool of commerce with the ladies."

"So much the better for both of you. But you played with Will Esmond if he was at home? I will lay ten to one you played with Will Esmond."

Harry blushed and admitted that, in the evenings, he and his cousin had played a few games of cards.

"And Tom Sampson, the chaplain," cried Jack Morris. "Was he of the party? I wager that Tom made a third, and the Lord deliver you from Tom and Will Esmond together!"

"Nay; the truth is, I won of both of them," said Harry.

"And they paid you? Well, miracles will never cease!"

"I did not say anything about miracles," Harry smiled over his wine.

"And you don't tell tales out of school—the *volto sciolto*—hey, Mr. Warrington?" asked my Lord.

"I beg your pardon," said straightforward Harry. "French is the only language besides my own of which I know a little."

"My Lord March has learned Italian at the Opera, and a pretty penny his lessons have cost him," noted Jack Morris. "We must show him the Opera—mustn't we, March?"

"Must we, Morris?" my lord asked, as if he only half relished the familiarity.

Both gentlemen were dressed alike in small scratch-wigs without powder, blue frocks with plate buttons, buckskins, riding-boots, and little hats with narrow cords of lace, showing no outward mark of fashion.

"I don't care about the Opera much, my lord," Harry said, warming with his wine. "But I should like to go to Newmarket and long to see a good English hunting-field."

"We will show you Newmarket and the hunting-field, sir. Can you ride pretty well?"

"I think I can," Harry replied. "And I can shoot pretty well, and jump some."

"What's your weight? I bet we weigh even, or I weigh most. I bet you Jack Morris beats you at birds or a mark at fifty paces. I bet I jump farther than you on flat ground, here on this green."

"I don't know Mr. Morris's shooting—I never saw either gentleman before—but I take your bets, my lord, at what you please," cried Harry, now more than warm with Burgundy.

"Ponies on each!" cried my lord.

"Done and done!" cried my lord and Harry together. The young man thought it was for the honor of his country not to be ashamed of any bet made to him.

"We can try the last bet now, if your feet are pretty steady," my lord said, springing up, stretching his arms and limbs, and looking at the crisp, dry grass. He drew his boots off, then his coat and waistcoat, buckling his belt round his waist and flinging his clothes to the ground.

Harry had more respect for his garments. It was his best suit. He removed the velvet coat and waistcoat, folded them daintily, and, seeing the tables around were slopped with drink, placed them on a table in the eating-room, where the windows stood open.

Here a new guest had entered; this was no other than Mr. Wolfe, who was soberly eating a chicken and salad with a modest pint of wine. Harry was in high spirits. He told the Colonel he had a bet with my Lord March and asked if the Colonel would stand him halves. The Colonel said he was too poor to bet. Would he come out and see fair play? That he would with all his heart. Colonel Wolfe set down his glass and stalked through the open window after his young friend.

"Who is that tallow-faced Put with the carroty hair?" asked Jack Morris, on whom the Burgundy had had its due effect.

Mr. Warrington explained that this was Lieutenant-Colonel Wolfe of the 20th Regiment.

"Your humble servant, gentlemen!" the Colonel said, making a rigid military bow.

"Never saw such a figure in my life!" cried Jack Morris. "Did you—March?"

"I beg your pardon, I think you said March?" the Colonel said, looking very much surprised.

"I am the Earl of March, sir, at Colonel Wolfe's service," the nobleman bowed. "My friend, Mr. Morris, is so intimate with me that, after dinner, we are quite like brothers."

Why is not all Tunbridge Wells by to hear this? thought Morris. And he was so delighted he shouted, "Two to one on my lord!"

"Done!" called out Mr. Warrington; and the enthusiastic Jack was obliged to cry "Done!" too.

"Take him, Colonel," Harry whispered to his friend.

But the Colonel said he could not afford to lose, and therefore could not hope to win.

"I see you have won one of our bets already, Mr. Warrington," my Lord March remarked. "I am taller than you by an inch or two, but you are broader round the shoulders."

"Pooh, my dear Will! I bet you you weigh twice as much as he does!" cried Jack Morris.

"Done, Jack!" said my lord, laughing. "The bets are all ponies. Will you take him, Mr. Warrington?"

"No, my dear fellow—one's enough," said Jack.

"Very good, my dear fellow," said my lord. "And now we will settle the other wager."

Having already arrayed himself in his best silk stockings, black satin-net breeches, and neatest pumps, Harry did not care to take off his shoes as his antagonist had done, whose heavy riding-boots and spurs were little calculated for leaping. Before them lay a fine even green turf of some thirty yards in length, enough for a run and enough for a jump. A gravel walk ran around this green, beyond which was a wall and gate-sign—a field azure bearing the Hanoverian White Horse rampant between two skittles proper, and for motto the name of the landlord and of the animal depicted.

My lord's friend laid a handkerchief on the ground as the mark whence the leapers were to take their jump, and Mr. Wolfe stood at the other end of the grass-plat to note the spot where each came down. "My lord went first," writes Mr. Warrington in a letter to Mrs. Mountain at Castlewood, Virginia, still extant. "He was for having me take the lead; but, remembering the story about the Battle of Fontenoy which my dearest George used to tell, I said, 'Monseigneur le Comte, tirez le premier, s'il vous plaît.' So he took his run in his stocken feet, and for the honor of Old Virginia, I had the gratification of beating his lordship by more than two feet—viz., two feet nine inches—I jumping twenty-one feet three inches, by the drawer's measured tape, and his lordship only eighteen six. I had won from him about my weight before (which I knew the moment I set my eye upon him). So he and Mr. Jack paid me these two bets. And with my best duty to my mother—she will not be displeased with me, for I bet for the honor of the Old Dominion, and my opponent was a nobleman of the first quality, himself holding two Earldoms, and heir to a Duke. Betting is all the rage here, and the bloods and young fellows of fashion are betting away from morning till night."

"I told them—and that was my mischief perhaps—that there was a gentleman at home who could beat me by a good foot; and when they asked who it was, and I said Col. G. Washington of Mount Vernon—as you know he can, and he's the only man in his county or mine that can do it—Mr. Wolfe asked me ever so many questions about Col. G. W., and showed that he had heard of him, and talked over last year's unhappy campaign as if he knew every inch of the ground, and he knew the names of all our rivers, only he called the Potomac Pottamac, at which we had a good laugh at him. My Lord of March and Ruglen was not in the least ill-humor about losing, and he and his friend handed me notes out of their pocket-books, which filled mine that was getting very empty, for the values to the servants at my cousin Castlewood's house and buying a horse at Oakhurst have very nearly put me on the necessity of making another draft upon my honored mother or her London or Bristol agent."

These feats of activity over, the four gentlemen strolled out of the tavern garden into the public walk, where, by this time, a great deal of company was assembled. Upon whom Mr. Jack, who was of a frank and free nature with a loud voice, chose to make remarks that were not always agreeable. And here, if my Lord March made a joke, of which his lordship was not sparing, Jack roared, "Oh, ho, ho! Oh, good Gad! Oh, my dear earl! Oh, my dear lord, you'll be the death of me!" "It seemed as if he wished everybody to know," writes Harry sagaciously to Mrs. Mountain, "that his friend and companion was an Earl!"

There was indeed a great variety of characters who passed. M. Poellnitz, no finer dressed than he had been at dinner, grinned and saluted with his great laced hat and tarnished feathers. Then came by my Lord Chesterfield, in a pearl-colored suit, with his blue ribbon and star, and saluted the young men in his turn.

"I will back the old boy for taking his hat off against the whole kingdom, and France either," said my Lord March. "He has never changed the shape of that hat of his for twenty years. Look at it. There it goes again! Do you see that great, big, awkward, pock-marked, snuff-colored man who hardly touches his clumsy beaver in reply? D---- his confounded impudence—do you know who that is?"

"No, curse him! Who is it, March?" asked Jack, with an oath.

"It's one Johnson, a Dictionary-maker, about whom my Lord Chesterfield wrote some most capital papers, when his dictionary was coming out, to patronize the fellow. I know they were capital. I've heard Horace Walpole say so, and he knows all about that kind of thing. Confound the impudent schoolmaster!"

"Hang him, he ought to stand in the pillory!" roared Jack.

"That fat man he's walking with is another of your writing fellows—a printer—his name is Richardson; he wrote *Clarissa*, you know."

"Great heavens! my lord, is that the great Richardson? Is that the man who wrote *Clarissa*?" called out Colonel Wolfe and Mr. Warrington in a breath.

Harry ran forward to look at the old gentleman toddling along the walk with a train of admiring ladies surrounding him.

"Indeed, my very dear sir," one was saying, "you are too great and good to live in such a world; but sure you were sent to teach it virtue!"

"Ah, my Miss Mulso! Who shall teach the teacher?" said the good, fat old man, raising a kind, round face skywards. "Even he has his faults and errors! Even his age and experience does not prevent him from stumbling... Heaven bless my soul, Mr. Johnson! I ask your pardon if I have trodden on your corn."

"Tell me about those children, Harry," Lady Maria said, her voice light as they strolled along the common. "The ones I saw darting about the house where you were taken in after your terrible fall? Oh, that accident! I nearly fainted when I saw you lying there. Please, do not squeeze my arm so tightly; it makes me feel you do not care for me."

"The people are the finest I have ever known in the world," Mr. Warrington replied, his eyes bright with gratitude. "Mrs. Lambert was a close friend of my mother's during her time in Europe. Colonel Lambert is a distinguished gentleman, a veteran of Scotland, Flanders, and Minorca. No natural parents could have shown me greater kindness. I must reward them. I simply must make them a gift." He reached into his pocket, his fingers brushing against the crisp banknotes won from Morris and March.

"We could visit the toy shop," Lady Maria suggested gently. "Buy a couple of dolls for the children. It would be an insult to offer anything else in return for their charity."

"Dolls for Hester and Theo? Do you really believe a woman ceases to be a woman at forty?" Harry teased, though a faint wince betrayed his companion's discomfort beneath his arm. "Miss Hester is hardly a child, and Miss Theo is older still. They speak several languages fluently. They have read countless volumes, play the harpsichord with mastery, and sing beautifully. Theo even composes her own songs."

"I barely noticed them," Maria admitted, her tone shifting. "I assumed they were mere children. I had no idea they possessed such talents."

"That is the nature of women," Harry declared, striding forward with renewed vigor. "If George or I praise a woman, Mrs. Esmond or Mrs. Mountain will inevitably find fault with her!"

"I would never fault anyone who has been kind to you, Mr. Warrington," Maria sighed, her voice dropping. "Though I cannot blame you for envying them. They cared for you when you were wounded and ill, while I... while I had to leave you."

"You dear, good Maria!"

"No, Harry! Do not call me that. Stop pressing your attentions on me. Look!" She pointed down the street. "There is your black servant walking among a dozen others in livery. They are heading to the tea-garden to get drunk, just like their masters. That dreadful Mr. Morris was already tipsy when I found you, frightening you half to death."

"I had just secured large bets from both of them," Harry said, his mood instantly lifting. "What shall I buy for you, my dear cousin?" He recounted his recent triumphs with a laugh that rang with youthful arrogance. "For the honor of Virginia, I decided to show them what true jumping is. With a bit of practice, I believe I could leap two feet farther."

Lady Maria smiled, pleased by the victories of her young champion, though a shadow crossed her face. "But you must be careful with gambling, child. It has ruined our family. My brother Castlewood, Will, our poor father, and even Lady Castlewood herself fell victim to it. And my Lord March? He is the most terrible gambler and the most successful nobleman in the land."

"I have no intention of fearing him or his friend Jack Morris," Harry dismissed, running his fingers over the gold coins in his pocket. "What games do you play at Aunt Bernstein's? Cribbage, all-fours, brag, whist, commerce, piquet, quadrille? I am ready for any of them. What time is that clock striking? Surely it is seven!"

"And you wish to begin now?" Maria asked, her voice plaintive. "You do not care to walk with your poor cousin anymore. You used to."

"Hey! Youth is youth, cousin!" Harry cried, tossing his head back. "A young man must have his fling!" He strutted beside her, confident, happy, and eager for the night ahead. Only yesterday he had preferred the company of Theo and Hester and Mrs. Lambert; now, the allure of pleasure, life, and the desire to conquer had seized him. He accepted the cup of fortune without calculating the headache that might follow.

As they spoke, the fiddles from the open orchestra on the Parade began their usual evening tuning, a raucous squeaking that signaled the start of the concert. Maria knew her aunt was already awake and waiting; she would soon be dragged back to her duties. Harry never asked about this slavery, though he must have known it existed if he had bothered to think. He felt no pity for his cousin. He was not thinking of her at all. Yet, when his own misfortune had struck, she had been wounded far more cruelly. She had carried his thoughts, burying them under a mask of smiling hypocrisy, as women of her station were expected to do. Perhaps Mrs. Grundy thought her an old fool? Did fools' caps not cover gray hair as well as jet or auburn? One must bear gently with elderly *fredaines*. There are late crops of wild oats as well as early harvests; the *avena fatua* grows right to the end of the year.

Madame Bernstein and her attendants, like worldly parents eager to escape a troublesome child, had already put the sun to bed while it was still light. They drew the curtains, lit their candles, and prepared their tea and negus. One by one, ladies arrived at the Baroness's door—some painted, some patched, all brocaded. Gentlemen in gala attire followed. Mr. Poellnitz arrived with the largest star and the most embroidered coat. My Lord March and Ruglen appeared transformed from the rough individual Harry had met at the White Horse. His tight brown wig was replaced by a neatly curled feather top with a bag and grey powder; his jockey's dress and leather breeches were swapped for a rich, elegant French suit. Mr. Jack Morris wore a similar wig and a suit of fine cloth. Mr. Wolfe attended his beautiful mistress, Miss Lowther, and her aunt, who loved cards as the world did.

When Lady Maria Esmond entered, her appearance belied Madame Bernstein's earlier descriptions. Her figure was exquisite, her dress revealing much of it. Her complexion was naturally fair, enhanced by a dark frilled ribbon clasped with a jewel around her neck, which made her skin look snow-white. Her cheeks held a healthy bloom, purchased openly at the perfumery shops, perhaps aided by an artful patch or two. Her hoops were modest compared to modern iron contrivances. The costume, absurd in some points, was pleasing in its entirety. One might wonder if ladies today wore bangles and nose-rings; surely we would laugh at the ornaments but not dislike them, and lovers would not hesitate to lift a ring to reach the rosy lips beneath.

As for the Baroness de Bernstein, when she took the trouble to make a grand toilette, she appeared handsome and magnificent, yet melancholy and somewhat terrifying. One reads the past in such old faces. The fires go out of some eyes as crow's-feet pucker around them; they flash no longer with scorn, anger, or love. They gaze, unmelted by sapphire glances; they look, undazzled. My fair young reader, if you are not as perfect as the peerless Lindamira, Queen of the Ball, and if, at the end of the night, you meekly admit you had only two or three partners while Lindamira danced with a crowd—console yourself. Think that at fifty, you will look as kind and pleasant as she appears now at eighteen. You will not have to lay down your coach-and-six of beauty and walk yourself through the rest of life. You will not witness the depreciation of your smiles or see fashion forsake your quarter. You may not have known grandeur, but you will not feel desertion. You may not have enjoyed millions, but you will have escaped bankruptcy.

"Our hostess," whispered My Lord Chesterfield to a friend, "reminds me of Covent Garden in my youth. Then it was the court end of the town, inhabited by the highest fashion. Now, a nobleman's house is merely a gaming-house, or you may enter with a friend to call for a bottle."

"A bottle and a tavern are good things in their way," My Lord March shrugged. "I was not born before the Georges came in, though I intend to live to a hundred. I never knew the Bernstein but as an old woman; if she ever had beauty, hang me if I know how she spent it."

"No, hang me, how did she spend it?" Jack Morris laughed.

"Here is a table! Shall we sit down and play? Do not let the Frenchman come in. He will not pay. Mr. Warrington, will you take a card?" Mr. Warrington and My Lord Chesterfield found themselves partners against Mr. Morris and the Earl of March. "You have come too late, Baron," the elder nobleman said to the other as he approached. "We have made our game. What, have you forgotten Mr. Warrington of Virginia—the young gentleman you met in London?"

"The young gentleman I met at Arthur's Chocolate House had black hair, a little cocked nose, and was by no means so fortunate in his personal appearance as Mr. Warrington," the Baron replied with much presence of mind. "Warrington, Dorrington, Harrington? We of the continent cannot retain your insular names. I certify that this gentleman is not the individual of whom I spoke at dinner." Glancing kindly at him, the old beau sidled away to a distant corner where Mr. Wolfe and Miss Lowther were engaged in deep conversation. Here, the Baron chose to engage the Lieutenant-Colonel on the Prussian manual exercise, recently introduced into King George II's army—a subject with which Mr. Wolfe was thoroughly familiar. The old gentleman uttered his criticisms and opinions, believing he had perfectly charmed his audience.

At the start of the evening, the Baroness received her guests personally, engaging them in talk and courtesies. But as the rooms and tables filled, Madame de Bernstein grew increasingly restless. Finally, she retreated with three friends to her own corner, where a table reserved for her was occupied by her major-domo. There, the old lady sat resolutely, never changing her place or quitting her game until cock-crow. The duty of receiving the company fell to Lady Maria, who, though she cared little for cards, dutifully did the honors of the house to her aunt's guests. She often rustled past the table where her young cousin was engaged with his three friends.

"Come and cut the cards for us," My Lord March called out as she passed on one of her wistful visits. "Cut the cards and bring us luck, Lady Maria! We have had none tonight, and Mr. Warrington is winning everything."

"I hope you are not playing high, Harry?" the lady asked timidly.

"Oh, no, only sixpences," cried My Lord March, dealing.

"Only sixpences," echoed Mr. Morris, Lord March's partner. Yet Mr. Morris must have been keenly alive to the value of a sixpence, for the loss of a few such coins made his round face look dismal. My Lord Chesterfield sat opposite Mr. Warrington, sorting his cards. No one could tell by inspecting that calm physiognomy whether good or ill fortune attended his lordship.

Some word, not altogether indicative of delight, slipped from Mr. Morris's lips, causing his partner to cry out, "Hang it, Morris, play your cards and hold your tongue!" Considering they were only playing for sixpences, My Lord March was strangely affected.

Lady Maria, still fondly lingering by Harry's chair with her hand resting behind it, could see his cards. A whole covey of trumps was ranged in one corner. She had not taken away his luck. She was pleased to think she had cut that pack which had dealt him all those pretty trumps. As Lord March dealt, he said in a quiet voice to Mr. Warrington, "The bet as before, Mr. Warrington, or shall we double it?"

"Anything you like, my lord," Mr. Warrington replied very quietly.

"We will say, then—shillings."

"Yes, shillings," said Mr. Warrington, and the game proceeded.

The end of the day's sport, and the days that followed, may be gathered from the following letter, which was never delivered to its intended recipient but found its way to America in the papers of Mr. Henry Warrington:

"DEAR GEORGE—As White's two bottles of Burgundy and a pack of cards constitute all the joys of your life, I take for granted that you are in London at this moment, preferring smoke and faro to fresh air and fresh haystacks. This will be delivered to you by a young gentleman with whom I have lately made acquaintance, and whom you will be charmed to know. He will play with you at any game for any stake, up to any hour of the night, and drink any reasonable number of bottles during the play. Mr. Warrington is no other than the Fortunate Youth about whom so many stories have been told in the Public Advertiser and other prints. He has an estate in Virginia as big as Yorkshire, with the incumbrance of a mother, the reigning Sovereign; but, as the country is unwholesome and fevers plentiful, let us hope that Mrs. Esmond will die soon and leave this virtuous lad in undisturbed possession. She is aunt of that polisson of a Castlewood, who never pays his play-debts, unless he is more honorable in his dealings with you than he has been with me. Mr. W. is de bonne race. We must have him of our society, if it be only that I may win my money back from him.

"He has had the devil's luck here and has been winning everything, whilst his old card-playing beldam of an aunt has been losing.
