After a few days at Tunbridge Wells, our young Virginian had ascended to the pinnacle of local celebrity. In that bustling watering-place, no figure commanded such scrutiny as Harry Warrington. Even the Bishop of Salisbury received less deference than the lad, whose every step drew the gaze of the populace. Market-goers paused to stare; matrons at the assembly rooms subtly maneuvered to isolate him with their daughters, whose smiles were plentiful. The town possessed an uncanny, microscopic knowledge of his affairs: they knew the exact acreage of his Virginia estate, the precise sum of his income, and the nightly tally of his gambling winnings. This collective curiosity extended even to his servant, Gumbo, who was treated to ale and cold meats by strangers eager to glean news of their master. Gumbo, fattened by this sudden demand for information, rose to prominence within the Society of Valets, spinning tales of such grandeur that they bordered on the mythical.

Harry found this adulation somewhat bewildering yet bearable. Born in the colonies with a healthy dose of self-regard, he accepted his newfound status without arrogance. He adhered strictly to a personal code of honor; when challenged by the gentlemen of the town to races, drinking bouts, or card games in the name of Old Virginia, he felt compelled to accept. He possessed a sharp mind, a steady hand, a secure seat, and nerves of steel. Thus, in his friendly rivalry with the mother country, the representative of Virginia acquitted himself with distinction.

Madame de Bernstein, who had previously suffered a string of bad luck at the tables, found solace and delight in her nephew's triumphs. He had bested Jack Morris at shooting, outpaced Mr. Scamper in a riding match, and held his own remarkably well against Captain Batts at tennis, despite having never touched a racket before. Even the celebrated gamblers, the Lords of Chesterfield and March, testified to his coolness and breeding. While Harry was not a literary genius, his handwriting was competent enough to satisfy the fashionable set, and his innocent ignorance served as a source of amusement for the Baroness. She, a woman who preferred the lively world to the quiet library, took a maternal pride in curating his appearance, selecting fine laces for his ruffles and presenting him with a diamond brooch. Consequently, Harry became the favorite of all her kin. Lady Maria, though perhaps secretly pleased to see her brothers overshadowed by her nephew's success, watched with a mixture of envy and fear as Harry's reputation soared in her wealthy aunt's favor.

Two weeks into his stay, Harry had become a central figure in the social sphere. He had mastered the art of navigating good company, though he admitted it was difficult to avoid the bad as well. Was it his fault that he drank from the sparkling cup of pleasure offered to him? His aunt, far from being a rigid moralist, encouraged his enjoyment of life. Yet, Harry retained a reserve from his colonial upbringing. Though the vices of London were rampant, the rough towns of America had kept him largely untouched by libertinism. He blushed at the bold talk of his European peers and was often baffled by his aunt's worldly jests, earning her affectionate nickname of "Joseph" or "simpleton."

However, innocence is rarely credited where suspicion abounds. The world assumed Harry was as depraved as his surroundings suggested. He had seen Lord March driving Madame Cattarina in her carriage and, believing there was no harm, had escorted her through the public walks. When she desired a trinket from the toy shop, Harry, flush with cash, had happily purchased it for her. He repeated this generosity with lace and other small gifts, until finally, he laughed off a further request, refusing to buy diamond drops for her ears. He was generous but not reckless.

Yet, who was to believe his modesty? Baroness Bernstein, particularly in the presence of her niece Maria, insisted that Harry was playing the role of Don Juan, supplanting Lord March. She reveled in Maria's silent distress, enjoying the sting of her words: "Boys will be boys, and I don't want Harry to be the first milksop in his family!" The bread Maria ate at her aunt's expense seemed suddenly indigestible.

Meanwhile, Colonel Wolfe, the object of Maria's affection, visited her constantly. Knowing the Colonel was fully occupied with his courtship, Harry expected little interaction, despite valuing the officer's company. Wolfe's conversation stood in stark contrast to the ribald chatter surrounding Harry; he spoke of nothing but duty and avoided the scandals of the age. Indeed, the era was one of open dissoluteness, with kings keeping mistresses and nobles chasing pleasure recklessly. Harry had unwittingly stepped into this whirlpool, finding himself surrounded by wild characters and living with an aunt who thrived in the midst of the rout.

Harry failed to notice the shift in Colonel Wolfe's demeanor. When they met after a tennis match, the Colonel's greeting was icy. While Wolfe bowed politely to Captain Batts, he barely acknowledged Harry with a mere touch of his forefinger. Harry, confused by the coldness, approached the Colonel as they walked.

"I have not seen you these many days," Harry remarked.

"You have had other companions," Wolfe replied curtly.

"But I would rather be with you than any of them," Harry insisted.

"Indeed, I might be better company for you than some of them," Wolfe said grimly.

"Is it Captain Batts you mean?" Harry asked.

"He bears a rascally reputation from the army, and I doubt he has improved since his dismissal. You could find better friends," Wolfe stated bluntly.

"Friend? He is no friend; he merely teaches me tennis. He is hand-in-glove with my lord and the fashionable set."

"I am not a man of fashion," Wolfe corrected.

"My dear Colonel, what is the matter? Have I angered you?" Harry asked, genuinely concerned.

"I will be frank," Wolfe said gravely. "I dislike some of your friends."

"They are men of the highest rank in England," Harry protested, unwilling to take offense.

"Exactly. They are of too high a rank and too great a fashion for a hard-working soldier like me. If you continue to live with such, you will find that humdrum people cannot afford such company. I am here paying my addresses to an honorable lady. Yesterday, I saw you walking openly with a French ballet-dancer and removing your hat. I must tell you, I would prefer you did not remove your hat in such company."

Harry flushed crimson. "Do you mean I am to forgo the honor of your acquaintance altogether?"

"Certainly, when you are in the company of that person," Wolfe said angrily, using a word too vulgar for print, reminiscent of Othello's rage.

"Great heavens! What a shame to speak so of any woman!" Harry cried. "How dare anyone say she is not honest?"

"You ought to know best, sir," Wolfe said, looking at him with surprise, "or the world belies you very much."

"What ought I to know best?" Harry demanded. "I see a poor little French dancer ordered by doctors to drink the waters. I know a gentleman of my rank does not usually keep such company, but are you so squeamish? I can speak a little French, and she is welcome to it. If Colonel Wolfe does not choose to touch his hat to me, he may leave it alone."

"Do you not know the woman's character?" Wolfe pressed.

"Of course, she is a dancer, and no better or worse than her neighbors. But had she been a duchess or your grandmother, I could not have respected her more."

"Were you not to win her at dice from Lord March?" Wolfe countered.

"At what?"

"At dice. Everyone at the Wells knows the story. I heard it just now from Mr. Richardson; the ladies are calling you a colonial Lovelace."

Harry asked what else they had said, and the Colonel laid before him the most alarming accounts of his own wickedness: a corrupter of virtue, an habitual drunkard, a notorious blasphemer, and a fitting companion for the debauched. Wolfe explained that he shared these rumors because Harry's reaction suggested innocence, and he felt a debt to clear the air.

Harry readily accepted the apology, shaking hands with renewed cordiality. He easily refuted most charges, admitting only to the gambling. He believed a gentleman should accept a fair challenge if he could afford it, and since he was playing with other people's money, he felt no guilt. Play was fair, he reasoned, and pleasant; why should England, save for the Methodists, abstain?

Wolfe, however, did not comment on Harry's assessment of the "best company" at the Wells. Instead, he warned the young man that while his life was pleasant, it was not profitable. "Every man was made to do some work," Wolfe urged. "A gentleman, if he has no profession, must make one. Do you know the laws of your country? You will one day be a magistrate. Should you not study the trades and manufactures of the nation? Is there not honor in our profession? Honor is the aim of life. Idle bread is the most dangerous of all foods. Cards and pleasure may be pastimes after work, but never instead of work."

Wolfe concluded with a poignant observation: "Instead of being the Fortunate Youth, as the world calls you, I think you are Warrington the Unlucky, followed by daily idleness, flattery, and temptation. May the Lord grant you deliverance from your good fortune."

Harry returned to the house, unable to explain to his aunt why he looked so grave. He resolved not to drink, yet jolly fellows at the ordinary passed the bottle around, and he could not resist. He refused to play in the evening, but a fourth was needed at his aunt's table, and how could he decline? He became her partner several times that night, relying on his own luck, and once more saw the dawn, feasting on chickens and champagne, blissfully unaware of the storm brewing in the minds of those who loved him.

Madame de Bernstein found her contentment at the Wells, remaining there to scold her niece and play her rubber, while the rest of the ton scattered to the assembly rooms and card tables. For a man of Harry's age, almost any setting becomes a paradise if it offers lively company, fresh air, and a share of sport. Even pleasure itself seems delightful at twenty; we rush to meet it with alacrity, speculate on its arrival, and count the days until our reunion. Yet how gently and coolly we view it in the twilight of life! Do you not recall your first ball, Madam? Does your memory not wander to that golden past as you sit adorning the walls while your daughters dance? I, too, remember when I found joy in walking three miles to dine with old Captain Jones. Can you imagine liking such a trek now, merely to drink his half-pay port? Perhaps it was purchased from a small-town merchant for a modest sum, but it was served with a warm welcome, seasoned by youth in a way that no vintage or matured man can replicate today. *Viximus nuper.* I find no fault in young Harry's conduct or his idleness, unlike his stern friend, the Colonel of the Twentieth Regiment. Oh, blessed idleness! Divine lazy nymph! Fetch me a novel as I lie in my dressing gown at three in the afternoon; mix a sherry-cobbler, and bring a cigar! Dear, slatternly, smiling enchantress! They may assail you with vile names, swear away your character, and brand you the Mother of Evil; yet, for all that, you remain the finest company in the world.

Lord March departed for the North, and Lord Chesterfield, finding the Tunbridge waters ineffective for his deafness, returned to his solitude at Blackheath. However, other gentlemen remained to sport and revel, and Mr. Warrington soon found himself surrounded by companions at the White Horse. He quickly mastered the art of ordering a French dinner with the flair of a St. James's dandy, conversed with Monsieur Barbeau in his native tongue with greater fluency than most, and developed an exquisite palate for wine, distinguishing between Clos Vougeot and Romande with remarkable precision. He became the young king of the Wells, where the frequenters—easygoing men of the world—were far from shocked by the reputation for gallantry and extravagance that Harry had acquired, a reputation that had previously terrified Mr. Wolfe.

Though our Virginian lived amidst the revellers, swimming in the same waters as the loose fish, the boy possessed a natural shrewdness and honesty that kept him clear of the snares commonly set for the unwary. He made very few foolish bets with the jolly idle fellows around him, and the oldest hands found it difficult to take him in. He engaged in games, both indoors and out, due to a natural skill and aptitude, holding his own against almost any fair competitor. He was scrupulous to play only with gentlemen he knew and always settled his debts on the spot. Though he might have fared poorly at a college examination, he possessed prudence, fidelity, keen perception, great generosity, and dauntless personal courage.

He soon had occasion to demonstrate his mettle. When the unfortunate little Cattarina, who had brought him so much trouble, pushed her importunities beyond the limit Harry deemed generous, he withdrew from the advances of the Opera-House Siren with perfect coolness and skill, leaving her to exercise her blandishments upon a more susceptible victim. In vain did the mermaid's hysterical mother wait upon Harry, vowing that a cruel bailiff had seized all her daughter's goods for debt and that her venerable father was languishing in a London gaol. Harry declared that between himself and the bailiff there could be no dealings, stating that because he had the good fortune to be known to Mademoiselle Cattarina and had gratified her caprices with various trinkets, he was not bound to pay the past debts of her family. He refused to act as bail for her father in London or settle her outstanding accounts at Tunbridge. The Cattarina's mother first called him a monster and an ingrate, then asked, with a veteran smirk, why he did not accept payment for the services he had rendered to the young person. Initially, Mr. Warrington could not comprehend the nature of such payment; but when the old woman explained it, the honest lad rose in horror at the thought of a woman trafficking in her child's dishonor. He told her he came from a country where even the savages would recoil from such a bargain. Having bowed the old lady ceremoniously to the door, he ordered Gumbo to mark her well and never admit her to his lodgings again. No doubt she retired breathing vengeance against the Iroquois; she declared that no Turk or Persian would treat a lady so, and she and her daughter retreated to London as soon as their anxious landlord permitted.

Then came Harry's perils of gaming, alongside his perils of gallantry. A man who plays at bowls must expect to meet with rubbers. After dinner at the ordinary, having declined to play piquet further with Captain Batts, and being roughly asked his reason, Harry frankly told the Captain that he only played with gentlemen who paid, like himself. Yet he expressed such readiness to settle Mr. Batts's outstanding account that the Captain declared himself satisfied *d'avance* and straightway left the Wells without paying Harry or any other creditor. On another occasion, he displayed his spirit by beating a chairman who had been rude to old Miss Whiffler as she headed to the assembly. Furthermore, when the calumny regarding himself and the unlucky opera-dancer was repeated by Mr. Hector Buckler, one of the fiercest frequenters of the Wells, Mr. Warrington stepped up to Buckler in the pump-room, where the latter was regaling water-drinkers with the very slander. He publicly informed Buckler that the story was false and warned him to hold anyone accountable who uttered it again. Thus, though our friend, being at Rome, certainly did as Rome did, he proved himself a valorous and worthy Roman; hurling himself among the wolves, he was acknowledged by Mr. Wolfe himself to be as brave as the best of them.

Had that officer told Colonel Lambert the stories that had caused the latter so much pain, we may be sure that when Mr. Wolfe found his young friend innocent, he took the first opportunity to withdraw the odious charges. Joy rippled through the Lamberts at the lad's acquittal—a pleasure felt by higher natures at the recovery of sinners. Never had the little family been happier, not even when they received news of Brother Tom winning his scholarship, as when Colonel Wolfe rode over with the account of his conversation with Harry Warrington. "Hadst thou brought me a regiment, James, I think I should not have been better pleased," said Mr. Lambert. Mrs. Lambert called to her daughters in the garden, kissed them both upon their return, and cried out the good news. Hetty jumped for joy, and Theo performed some uncommonly brilliant operations upon the harpsichord that night. When Dr. Boyle came in for his backgammon, he could not initially account for the illumination in all their faces until the three ladies, in a happy chorus, told him how right he had been in his sermon and how dreadfully they had wronged that poor, dear, good young Mr. Warrington.

"What shall we do, my dear?" the Colonel asked his wife. "The hay is in, the corn won't be cut for a fortnight—the horses have nothing to do. Suppose we..." Here he leaned over the table and whispered in her ear.

"My dearest Martin! The very thing!" cried Mrs. Lambert, taking her husband's hand and pressing it.

"What's the very thing, mother?" cried young Charley, who was home for his Bartholomewtide holidays.

"The very thing is to go to supper. Come, Doctor! We will have a bottle of wine tonight and drink repentance to all who think evil."

"Amen," said the Doctor, "with all my heart!" And with this, the worthy family went to their supper.

Mr. Warrington repaired one day to his customary dinner at the White Horse ordinary, finding the scene exactly as he had anticipated: a raucous assembly of country gentlemen surrounding the table, dominated by the jolly, good-humored countenance of Parson Sampson. The clergyman was regaling the company with a rapid-fire succession of stories and *bons-mots*, keeping the air thick with roars of laughter. Though Harry had not been in London for several months, the parson possessed the latest intelligence—or what passed for such among the folk of the ordinary. He detailed the intrigues at the King's house in Kensington and the Duke's in Pall Mall; he recounted Mr. Byng's behavior in prison and the shifting odds at Newmarket; he named the reigning toasts of Covent Garden.

Parson Sampson was a man of the world, a figure not uncommon in English society a century prior. He was the Abbe Parson, the clergyman who frequented the theater, the tavern, the racecourse, and the height of fashion. His voice was the loudest in the hunting field, his songs the jolliest at the Rose or the Bedford Head, and his ability to call a main at the gaming table was unmatched. The accuracy of his news mattered little to the country gentlemen who listened; whether My Lord Viscount Squanderfield was ruining himself for Mrs. Polly or Mrs. Lucy, whether Lady Jane loved the actor instead of Lady Mary, or whether Harry Hilton of the Horse Grenadiers had the quarrel with Chevalier Solingen rather than Tommy Ruffler of the Foot Guards—these details were secondary. What mattered was that the stories were lively and wicked. Mr. Sampson laughed and chattered, charming his audience with spirits and talk, draining bottle after bottle of claret, which his delighted listeners insisted he finish.

When Mr. Warrington entered, the parson's rosy face reddened further, whether from modesty or the effects of the vintage. He whispered *Maxima debetur* to the laughing squire seated beside him—a man in a drab coat and gold-laced red waistcoat—and rose abruptly, stumbling forward in his haste to greet the Virginian. "My dear sir, my very dear sir, my conqueror of spades, clubs, and hearts!" cried the chaplain. "I am delighted to see your honour looking so fresh and well."

Harry returned the greeting with evident pleasure, equally glad to see Mr. Sampson and quick to compliment the reverend's cheerful complexion and rosy gills. The squire in the drab coat, recognizing Mr. Warrington, immediately made space beside himself and called out for the parson to resume his seat on the other side to continue his tale of Lord Ogle and the grocer's wife. His sentence was cut short, however, by a shout and an oath directed at the parson for having stepped on his gouty toe.

The chaplain apologized profusely, turned quickly to Mr. Warrington, and proceeded to deliver a comprehensive report on the state of Castlewood and its neighborhood. He announced that My Lord Castlewood sent his affectionate remembrances to his cousin and had given special orders for him to come to Tunbridge Wells to oversee the young gentleman's morals. He noted that My Lady Viscountess and My Lady Fanny had departed for Harrogate for the waters, that Mr. Will had won his money at Newmarket and was visiting the Duke, and that Molly, the housemaid, was weeping over Gumbo, Mr. Warrington's valet. In short, he delivered all the news of the region, managing to weave names of the highest rank into his discourse. "All Hampshire has heard of his successes at Tunbridge," Mr. Sampson declared with an arch smile, "successes of every kind." He suggested that the lords and ladies hoped Harry would not be spoiled for his quiet Hampshire home.

As the guests drifted away one by one, leaving the young Virginian to his bottle and the chaplain, the atmosphere shifted. "Though I have had plenty," said the jolly chaplain, "that is no reason why I should not have plenty more." He drank toast after toast and bumper after bumper to Harry's amusement. By the time Sampson had satisfied his appetite, Harry had become equally generous, warm-hearted, and friendly.

"Why should Mr. Sampson incur the expense of an inn when there is a room at Harry's quarters?" The chaplain's trunk was ordered to the lodgings, and Gumbo was commanded to make him as comfortable as possible. Nothing satisfied Mr. Warrington more than seeing Sampson descend to the stables to inspect his horses. Harry now possessed several mounts, and when Sampson recognized his own horse—the one Harry had won from him—the beast whinnied with delight, rubbing his nose against his old master's coat. Harry rapped out a few brisk, energetic expressions and vowed by Jupiter that Sampson should have his old horse back. It was a gift the chaplain accepted with fervor, seizing Harry's hand to bless him, then flinging his arms around the horse's neck and weeping tears of Bordeaux and gratitude. Arm-in-arm, the friends walked to Madame Bernstein's, carrying the scents of the stables into her ladyship's apartment. Their flushed cheeks and brightened eyes testified to the day's amusement.

Madame Bernstein received her nephew's chaplain with kindness. The old lady relished Sampson's broad jokes and rattling talk, much as she enjoyed a highly-spiced dish or a novel entree from her cook, provided it appeared only a few times. Her only enduring amusement, she confessed, was cards. "The cards don't cheat," she would say. "A bad hand tells you the truth to your face, and there is nothing so flattering in the world as a good suite of trumps." When in a good humor, she would laughingly bid the chaplain say grace before the meal. Honest Sampson initially hesitated to join the game at Tunbridge Wells, citing that the stakes were too high for his pocket, which had already been emptied for the fortunate youth at Castlewood. Like most of her age and sex, Madame Bernstein was not prodigal with money. It was likely from Harry Warrington, whose heart overflowed with generosity as his purse with guineas, that the chaplain procured a small stock of ready coin, enabling him to sit at the card table.

Our young gentleman welcomed Mr. Sampson to his coin as readily as he did all the other good things he had gathered about him. It was remarkable how quickly the young Virginian adapted to the habits of the life he now led. His suits remained black, yet of the finest cut and quality. "With a star and ribbon, his stocking down, and his hair over his shoulder, he would make a pretty Hamlet," observed the gay old Duchess Queensberry. "And I make no doubt he has been the death of a dozen Ophelias already, here and amongst the Indians," she added, thinking no less of Harry for his supposed successes with the fair. His lace and linen were as fine as his aunt could desire. He purchased fine shaving plates from toy-shop women and magnificent brocade bedgowns in which he lolled at ease, sipping his chocolate in the mornings. He owned swords, walking canes, French watches with painted backs and diamond settings, and snuff boxes enamelled by artists of that cunning nation. A levee of grooms, jockeys, and tradesmen waited daily in his anteroom, admitted one by one to him and Parson Sampson over their chocolate by Gumbo, the groom of the chambers. No single negro could have managed all the fine things Mr. Warrington now possessed, let alone the horses and the postchaise his honor had bought.

Furthermore, Harry instructed himself in the arts befitting a gentleman of the era. A French fencing-master and a dancing-master of the same nation resided at Tunbridge during that season. The young Virginian frequented these men of science assiduously, acquiring considerable skill and grace in both peaceful and warlike accomplishments. Ere many weeks were over, he could handle foils against his master or any frequenter of the fencing school. With a sigh, Lady Maria—who danced very elegantly herself—owned that there was no gentleman at court who could walk a minuet more gracefully than Mr. Warrington. As for riding, though he took a few lessons on the great horse from a master who came to Tunbridge, he declared that their own Virginian manner was sufficient. He saw no one among the fine folks and jockeys who could ride better than his friend, Colonel George Washington of Mount Vernon.

The obsequious Sampson found himself in better quarters than he had enjoyed for a long time. He knew much of the world and told even more, and Harry was delighted with his stories, whether real or fancied. The man of twenty looked up to the man of thirty, admiring the latter's old jokes, stale puns, and tarnished anecdotes, all slopped with the wine of a hundred dinner tables. Sampson's town and college pleasantries were all new and charming to the young Virginian. A hundred years ago, there used to be grown men in London who loved to consort with fashionable youths entering life, to tickle their young fancies with merry stories, to act as mentors at the Round-house, to accompany lads to the gaming table, and to stagger into the streets with cool heads when young lords reeled out to beat the watch. Of this extinct race, Mr. Sampson was a specimen. It is a comfort to think that in Queen Victoria's reign there are no such flatterers left, no parasites pandering to the follies of young men; that all the toads have been eaten off the face of the island, and the toad-eaters have perished for lack of nourishment.

With some sauces, as I read, the above-mentioned animals are said to be exceedingly fragrant, wholesome, and savoury eating. Indeed, no man could look more rosy and healthy, or flourish more cheerfully, than friend Sampson upon the diet. He became the young friend's confidential leader. From the following letter, preserved in the Warrington correspondence, it will be seen that Mr. Harry not only had dancing and fencing masters but likewise a tutor, chaplain, and secretary:

***

"HONOURED MADAM—Your honoured letter of 20 June, per Mr. Trail of Bristol, has been forwarded to me duly, and I have to thank your goodness and kindness for the good advice which you are pleased to give me, as also for the remembrances of dear home, which I shall love never the worse for having been to the home of our ancestors in England.

"I writ you a letter by the last monthly packet, informing my honoured mother of the little accident I had on the road hither, and of the kind friends who I found and whom took me in. Since then I have been profiting of the fine weather and the good company here, and have made many friends among our nobility, whose acquaintance I am sure you will not be sorry that I should make. Among their lordships I may mention the famous Earl of Chesterfield, late Ambassador to Holland, and Viceroy of the Kingdom of Ireland; the Earl of March and Ruglen, who will be Duke of Queensberry at the death of his Grace; and her Grace the Duchess, a celebrated beauty of the Queen's time, when she remembers my grandpapa at Court. These and many more persons of the first fashion attend my aunt's assemblies, which are the most crowded at this crowded place. Also on my way hither I stayed at Westerham, at the house of an officer, Lieut.-Gen. Wolfe, who served with my grandfather and General Webb in the famous wars of the Duke of Marlborough. Mr. Wolfe has a son, Lieut.-Col. James Wolfe, engaged to be married to a beautiful lady now in this place, Miss Lowther of the North—and though but 30 years old he is looked up to as much as any officer in the whole army, and has served with honour under his Royal Highness the Duke wherever our arms have been employed.

"I thank my honoured mother for announcing to me that a quarter's allowance of 52l. 10s. will be paid me by Mr. Trail. I am in no present want of cash, and by practising a rigid economy, which will be necessary (as I do not disguise) for the maintenance of horses, Gumbo, and the equipage and apparel requisite for a young gentleman of good family, hope to be able to maintain my credit without unduly trespassing upon yours. The linnen and clothes which I brought with me will with due care last for some years—as you say. 'Tis not quite so fine as worn here by persons of fashion, and I may have to purchase a few very fine shirts for great days: but those I have are excellent for daily wear.

"I am thankful that I have been quite without occasion to use your excellent family pills. Gumbo hath taken them with great benefit, who grows fat and saucy upon English beef, ale, and air. He sends his humble duty to his mistress, and prays Mrs. Mountain to remember him to all his fellow-servants, especially Dinah and Lily, for whom he has bought posey-rings at Tunbridge Fair.

"Besides partaking of all the pleasures of the place, I hope my honoured mother will believe that I have not been unmindful of my education. I have had masters in fencing and dancing, and my Lord Castlewood's chaplain, the Reverend Mr. Sampson, having come hither to drink the waters, has been so good as to take a vacant room at my lodging. Mr. S. breakfasts with me, and we read together of a morning—he saying that I am not quite such a dunce as I used to appear at home. We have read in Mr. Rapin's History, Dr. Barrow's Sermons, and, for amusement, Shakspeare, Mr. Pope's Homer, and (in French) the translation of an Arabian Work of Tales, very diverting. To the discerning eye, the truth regarding Harry Warrington and the unfortunate Cattarina was clear; yet, to the gossips of Tunbridge Wells, the Virginian appeared a dissipated nobleman of the highest caliber. Madame de Bernstein, in particular, remained steadfast in her disbelief of his innocence. To the old Baroness, a woman of Roman lineage, it was preferable that her nephew emulate the licentiousness of Rome itself. She eagerly accepted every scandal concerning Mr. Warrington's alleged "Lovelace" adventures. Having witnessed him host tea and music at the Wells, and noting his gallantry toward ladies of superior station and character compared to Cattarina, she had grown complacent. The suspicion that once plagued her regarding the affair begun at Castlewood had faded, replaced by a careless vigilance over Lady Maria. Perhaps she believed the danger had passed, or perhaps she had simply ceased to care, lulled by Maria's artful cajoling. At Maria's age, maidens learn to be cunning; at Madame Bernstein's age, dragons lose their ferocity. Their scales soften, their claws weaken to a feeble pat, and their venom becomes merely disagreeable rather than deadly. They trail their languid tails back to their caverns, their maleficence diminished by the softening influence of years.

If the virtuous folk of Oakhurst could not withstand the testimony of Harry's ill-doings, why should Madame Bernstein, with her vast experience of evil, be more credulous? Every woman in her circle believed the stories of his dissipation. When the little dancer returned to London, it was because heartless Harry had deserted her for another—whose name, or rather whose half-dozen whispered aliases, the society at Tunbridge Wells delighted to circulate. In an age where ancestors of all stripes met at Epsom, Bath, and Tunbridge to dance, game, and drink, Harry's bad reputation served to comfort his aunt, easing her mind regarding his passion for Lady Maria. So secure was she that when the chaplain arrived to escort her niece home, she refused to part, preferring to keep Maria under her watchful eye while whispering tales of her cousin's wild extravagances and promising to secure him a suitable wife of age and fortune.

During the last century, a certain French Duke and Marquis distinguished himself across Europe and America, leaving behind a volume of memoirs that posterity is wisely warned against consulting. Having played the part of Don Juan everywhere, he cataloged the court-beauties who fell to his fascination. It is curious to contrast the elegant refinements of European society, where a siege was all it took to vanquish a woman, with the simple, modest lives of the colonial folks. This European enslaver of hearts, it appears, made not a single conquest in America. While travelers loudly criticized the rudeness of transatlantic manners, the truth remains that American gentlemen conversed modestly and the lives of their women were pure. Harry Warrington brought this colonial modesty to England. Though surrounded by men of pleasure, he remained silent, never indulging in double entendres, boasting no victories over the sex, and appearing shy and awkward when others recounted such tales.

Mr. Sampson had noted this youthfulness at Castlewood, where Harry grew uneasy while his cousin Will told choice stories. My Lord had curtly rebuked his brother, advising him to keep his jokes for the usher's table at Kensington. Thus, the chaplain addressed his neighbor with the exclamation, "Reverentia pueris." Mr. Sampson, lacking the strength to do right himself, possessed at least the grace not to offend innocent young gentlemen with his cynicism.

The chaplain was touched by Harry's gift of the horse and felt a genuine friendliness toward the lad. "You see, sir," he said, "I am of the world and must do as the rest do. I have led a rough life and cannot afford to be more particular than my neighbors. *Video meliora, deteriora sequor*, as we said at college. I have a little sister at boarding school, and since I keep a decent tongue in my head when talking with her, I expect others to do the same, and surely I may try to do as much by you."

The chaplain praised Harry loudly to the old Baroness, who delighted in hearing him commended. She was fond of his good looks, manly bearing, ready blushes, bright eyes, and deep youthful voice. His shrewdness and simplicity constantly amused her. "We must find a good wife for him, Chaplain," she told Mr. Sampson. "I have one or two in my eye who will suit him. We must set him up here; he will never bear returning to his savages or living with his little Methodist mother."

On this point, Mr. Sampson was equally anxious and had a wife in his eye for Harry. He hoped that conversations with the Earl of Castlewood regarding a provision for the chaplain might facilitate a match for the anxious lady. If his good offices could help, Sampson was ready to employ them, waiting to see how effectively he could bring his influence to bear.

Sampson's society was agreeable, and within hours, he and his young friend became intimate. The parson rejoiced in high spirits, good appetite, and good humor. He pretended to no squeamishness and indulged in no sanctimonious hypocrisy, yet he took care not to shock his young friend with needless outbreaks of levity. He initiated his pupil only into the minor mysteries of the trade, withholding the secrets with which the unlucky adept himself was only too familiar. With Harry, Sampson was a brisk, lively companion, ready for drinking bouts, cock-fights, shooting matches, card games, or gallops across the common. Yet his conversation remained decent, aiming more to amuse than to lead astray. The chaplain was successful; possessing immense animal spirits, natural wit, and experience in the business of the "toad-eater"—a calling that had been his livelihood since entering college as a servitor—he navigated the social landscape with ease.

"What a reputation, sir, they have made for you in this place!" cried Mr. Sampson, returning from the coffee-house to his patron. "Monsieur de Richelieu was nothing to you!"

"How do you mean, Monsieur de Richelieu? Never was at Minorca in my life," said straightforward Harry, unaware of the French duke's famous victories at home.

Mr. Sampson explained. The pretty widow Patcham, who had just arrived, was desperate about Mr. Warrington; her behavior at the rooms the night before proved it. As for Mrs. Hooper, that was a known case, and the Alderman had fetched his wife back to London for no other reason. It was the talk of the whole Wells.

"Who says so?" cried Harry, indignantly. "I should like to meet the man who dares say so, and confound the villain!"

"I should not like to show him to you," said Mr. Sampson, laughing. "It might be the worse for him."

"It's a shame to speak with such levity about the character of ladies or gentlemen," continued Mr. Warrington, pacing the room in a fume.

"So I told them," said the chaplain, wagging his head and looking grave, though the truth was he had never considered being angry at such charges.

"It's a shame, I say, to talk away the reputation of any man or woman as people do here. Do you know, in our country, a fellow's ears would not be safe; a little before I left home, three brothers shot down a man for having spoken ill of their sister."

"Serve the villain right!" cried Sampson.

"Already they have had that calumny about me set a-going here, Sampson—about me and the poor little French dancing-girl."

"I have heard," said Mr. Sampson, shaking powder from his wig.

"Wicked, wasn't it?"

"Abominable."

"They said the very same thing about my Lord March. Isn't it shameful?"

"Indeed it is," said Mr. Sampson, preserving a face of wonderful gravity.

"I don't know what I should do if these stories came to my mother's ears. It would break her heart. Why, only a few days before you came, a military friend of mine, Mr. Wolfe, told me how the most horrible lies were circulated about me. Good heavens! What do they think a gentleman of my name and country can be capable of—I a seducer of women? They might as well say I was a horse-stealer or a housebreaker. I vow if I hear any man say so, I'll have his ears!"

"I have read, sir, that the Grand Seignior of Turkey has bushels of ears sometimes sent in to him," said Mr. Sampson, laughing. "If you took all those that had heard scandal against you or others, what basketsful you would fill!"

"And so I would, Sampson, as soon as look at 'em: any fellow who said a word against a lady or a gentleman of honor!" cried the Virginian.

"If you'll go down to the Well, you'll find a harvest of 'em. I just came from there. It was the high tide of Scandal. Detraction was at its height. And you may see the *nymphas discentes* and the *aures satyrorum acutas*," cried the chaplain, shrugging his shoulders.

"That may be as you say, Sampson," replied Mr. Warrington, "but if ever I hear any man speak against my character, I'll punish him. Mark that."

"I shall be very sorry for his sake, sir; for you'll mark him in a way he won't like, and I know you are a man of your word."

"You may be sure of that, Sampson. And now shall we go to dinner, and afterwards to my Lady Trumpington's tea?"

"You know, sir, I can't resist a card or a bottle," said Mr. Sampson. "Let us have the last first and then the first shall come last." And with this, the two gentlemen departed for their accustomed place of refectory.

That was an age in which wine-bibbing was more common than in our politer times. Since the arrival of General Braddock's army in his native country, the young Virginian had acquired a liking for filling bumpers and calling toasts, having heard it was a point of honor among officers never to decline a toast or a challenge. So Harry and his chaplain drank their claret in peace and plenty, naming some favorite lady with each glass.

The chaplain had reasons of his own for desiring to know the extent of the affair between Harry and Lady Maria. He and his young friend were warm enough with the claret to speak with that great eloquence and candor that good wine, taken in rather injudicious quantity, inspires. O kindly harvests of the Aquitanian grape! O sunny banks of Garonne! O friendly caves of Gledstane and Morol! May we not say a word of thanks for all the pleasure we owe you? Are the Temperance men to be allowed to shout in public places? Are the Vegetarians to bellow "Cabbage for ever?" and may we modest Enophilists not sing the praises of our favorite plant? After drinking good Bordeaux, there is a point at which men arrive when all the generous faculties of the soul are awakened; when wit brightens in sudden flashes, intellects are keenest, and pent-up thoughts rush abroad. The kindliest affection shakes hands with mankind, and the timid Truth jumps up naked to proclaim himself to all the world. How, by the kind influence of the wine-cup, we succor the poor and humble! How bravely we rush to the rescue of the oppressed! I say, in the face of all the pumps which ever spouted, that there is a moment in a bout of good wine at which, if a man could but remain, wit, wisdom, courage, generosity, eloquence, and happiness were his; but the moment passes, and that other glass somehow spoils the state of beatitude. There is a headache in the morning; we are not going into Parliament for our native town; we are not going to shoot those French officers who have been speaking disrespectfully of our country; and poor Jeremy Diddler calls about eleven o'clock for another half-sovereign, and we are unwell in bed, sending him away empty-handed.

Well, then, as they sat over their generous cups, the company having departed and the bottle of claret brought in by Monsieur Barbeau, the chaplain found himself in an eloquent state, with a strong desire to inculcate sublime moral precepts while Harry was moved by an extreme longing to explain his private history and impart all his present feelings to his new friend.

"I am glad to hear what your conduct has really been with regard to the Cattarina, Mr. Warrington; I am glad from my soul," said the impetuous chaplain. "The wine is with you. You have shown that you can bear down calumny and resist temptation. Ah! my dear sir, men are not all so fortunate. What famous good wine this is!" and he sucked up a glass with, "A toast from you, my dear sir, if you please?"

"I give you 'Miss Fanny Mountain, of Virginia,'" said Mr. Warrington, filling a bumper as his thoughts flew straightway, thousands of miles, to home.

"One of your American conquests, I suppose?" said the chaplain.

"Nay, she is but ten years old, and I have never made any conquests at all in Virginia, Mr. Sampson," said the young gentleman.

"You are like a true gentleman, and don't kiss and tell, sir."

"I neither kiss nor tell. It isn't the custom of our country, Sampson, to ruin girls, or frequent the society of low women. We Virginian gentlemen honor women; we don't wish to bring them to shame," cried the young toper, looking very proud and handsome. "The young lady whose name I mentioned hath lived in our family since her infancy, and I would shoot the man who did her a wrong;—by Heaven, I would!"
