The secret Mr. Lambert whispered to his wife at the close of the previous chapter was finally unveiled, bringing a wave of delight through the entire Oakhurst household. With the hay harvested and the corn still green, the farm horses were free. "Why," asked Colonel Lambert, "should we not harness them to the coach and pay a visit to Tunbridge Wells, perhaps picking up friend Wolfe at Westerham along the way?"

Mamma embraced the proposal with evident joy, and the honest gentleman who suggested it was rewarded with equal enthusiasm. The children leaped for happiness. The girls immediately scattered to gather their finest attire—calamancoes, paduasoys, falbalas, furbelows, capes, cardinals, sacks, negligees, solitaires, caps, ribbons, mantuas, clocked stockings, and high-heeled shoes, alongside countless other articles of toilet. Mamma's best robes were summoned from the presses, reserved for rare and solemn occasions, retreating afterward to lavender and seclusion. The brave Colonel produced his laced hat, waistcoat, and silver-hilted hanger. Charley rejoiced in a *rasee* holiday suit belonging to his father, in which the Colonel had been married—a garment Mrs. Lambert cut up, not without a pang. Even the dogs, Ball and Dumpling, had their tails and manes tied with ribbon. Chump, the old white cart-horse, was appointed unicorn leader to assist the carriage-horses up the first five hilly miles from Oakhurst to Westerham.

The carriage itself was an ancient vehicle, rumored to have served in the procession that brought George I. from Greenwich to London upon his first assumption of sovereignty. It had belonged to Mr. Lambert's father and was regarded by the family as one of the most splendid coaches in the three kingdoms. Brian, coachman and ploughman of the Oakhurst family, took his place on the box beside Mr. Charley. The precious clothes were packed in imperials on the roof. The Colonel's pistols were secured in the carriage pockets, and a blunderbuss hung behind the box within reach of Brian, an old soldier. Fortunately, no highwayman molested the convoy, nor did any innkeeper levy contributions on Colonel Lambert, whose slender purse and large family rendered him immune to depredators on the king's highway. A reasonable, modest lodging had been engaged by young Colonel Wolfe at his usual haunt, and he accompanied them on horseback.

These lodgings stood opposite Madame Bernstein's. As the Oakhurst family reached their quarters on a Saturday evening, they observed chair after chair discharging powdered beaux and patched, brocaded beauties at the Baroness's door, where she was hosting one of her many card parties. The sun had not yet set, for their ancestors began their dissipations at early hours, indulging in meat, drink, or cards anytime after three in the afternoon until the night or morning. From their window, the young country ladies and their mother watched the various personages entering the Bernstein rout. Colonel Wolfe identified the guests for the ladies. It was almost as delightful as attending the party themselves; Hetty and Theo not only saw the arrivals but peered into the Baroness's open casements to watch the guests inside.

Among the few personages they had glimpsed before, the Duchess of Queensberry passed. When Mr. Wolfe explained her identity, Martin Lambert was ready with a score of lines from his favorite Mat Prior about "Kitty, beautiful and young."

"Think that that old lady was once like you, girls!" cried the Colonel.

"Like us, papa? Well, certainly we never set up for being beauties!" said Miss Hetty, tossing up her little head.

"Yes, like you, you little baggage; like you at this moment, who want to go to that drum yonder:"

*"Inflamed with rage at sad restraint / Which wise mamma ordained, / And sorely vexed to play the saint / Whilst wit and beauty reigned."*

"We were never invited, papa; and I am sure if there's no beauty more worth seeing than that, the wit can't be much worth the hearing," remarked the satirist of the family.

"Oh, but he's a rare poet, Mat Prior!" continued the Colonel. "Though, mind you, girls, you'll skip over all the poems I have marked with a cross. A rare poet! And to think you should see one of his heroines! 'Fondness prevailed, mamma gave way' (she always will, Mrs. Lambert!)"

*"Fondness prevailed, mamma gave way, / Kitty at heart's desire / Obtained the chariot for a day, / And set the world on fire!"*

"I am sure it must have been very inflammable," said Mamma.

"So it was, my dear, twenty years ago, much more inflammable than it is now," remarked the Colonel.

"Nonsense, Mr. Lambert," answered Mamma.

"Look, look!" cried Hetty, running forward to point to the little square and the covered gallery where the door to Madame Bernstein's apartments stood, surrounded by a crowd of street urchins, idlers, and yokels watching the company.

"It's Harry Warrington!" exclaimed Theo, waving a handkerchief to the young Virginian. But Warrington did not see Miss Lambert. The Virginian walked arm-in-arm with a portly clergyman in a crisp, rustling silk gown, and the two entered Madame de Bernstein's door.

"I heard him preach a most admirable sermon here last Sunday," said Mr. Wolfe. "A little theatrical, but most striking and eloquent."

"You seem to be here most Sundays, James," said Mrs. Lambert.

"And Monday, and soon till Saturday," added the Colonel. "See, Harry has beautified himself already; hath his hair in buckle, and I have no doubt he is going to the drum too."

"I had rather sit quiet generally of a Saturday evening," said sober Mr. Wolfe. "At any rate, away from card-playing and scandal; but I own, dear Mrs. Lambert, I am under orders. Shall I go across the way and send Mr. Warrington to you?"

"No, let him have his sport. We shall see him tomorrow. He won't care to be disturbed amidst his fine folks by us country-people," said meek Mrs. Lambert.

"I am glad he is with a clergyman who preaches so well," said Theo softly; her eyes seemed to say, *You see, good people, he is not so bad as you thought him, and as I, for my part, never believed him to be.* "The clergyman has a very kind, handsome face."

"Here comes a greater clergyman," cried Mr. Wolfe. "It is my Lord of Salisbury, with his blue ribbon, and a chaplain behind him."

"And whom a mercy's name have we here?" broke in Mrs. Lambert as a sedan-chair, covered with gilding and topped with no less than five earl's coronets, carried by bearers in richly laced clothes and preceded by three footmen in splendid livery, approached Madame de Bernstein's door. The Bishop, who had been about to enter, stopped and ran back with the most respectful bows and curtseys to the sedan-chair, giving his hand to the lady who stepped forth.

"Who on earth is this?" asked Mrs. Lambert.

"Sprechen sie Deutsch? Ja, meinherr. Nichts verstand," said the waggish Colonel.

"Pooh, Martin."

"Well, if you can't understand High Dutch, my love, how can I help it? Your education was neglected at school. Can you understand heraldry?—I know you can."

"I make," cried Charley, reciting the shield, "three merions on a field or, with an earl's coronet."

"A countess's coronet, my son. The Countess of Yarmouth, my son."

"And pray who is she?"

"It hath ever been the custom of our sovereigns to advance persons of distinction to honour," continued the Colonel, gravely. "And this eminent lady hath been so promoted by our gracious monarch to the rank of Countess of this kingdom."

"But why, papa?" asked the daughters together.

"Never mind, girls!" said Mamma.

But that incorrigible Colonel would go on.

"Y, my children, is one of the last and most awkward letters of the whole alphabet. When I tell you stories, you are always saying Why. Why should my Lord Bishop be cringing to that lady? Look at him rubbing his fat hands together and smiling into her face! It's not a handsome face any longer. It is all painted red and white like Scaramouch's in the pantomime. See, there comes another blue-ribbon, as I live. My Lord Bamborough. The descendant of the Hotspurs. The proudest man in England. He stops, he bows, he smiles; he is hat in hand, too. See, she taps him with her fan. Get away, you crowd of little blackguard boys, and don't tread on the robe of the lady whom the King delights to honour."

"But why does the King honour her?" asked the girls once more.

"There goes that odious last letter but one! Did you ever hear of her Grace the Duchess of Kendal? No. Of the Duchess of Portsmouth? Non plus. Of the Duchess of La Valliore? Of Fair Rosamond, then?"

"Hush, papa! There is no need to bring blushes on the cheeks of my dear ones, Martin Lambert!" said the mother, putting her finger to her husband's lips.

"'Tis not I; it is their sacred Majesties who are the cause of the shame," cried the son of the old republican. "Think of the bishops of the Church and the proudest nobility of the world cringing and bowing before that painted High Dutch Jezebel. Oh, it's a shame! a shame!"

"Confusion!" broke out Colonel Wolfe, making a dash at his hat and running from the room. He had seen the young lady he admired and her guardian walking across the Pantiles on foot to the Baroness's party. They arrived just as the Countess of Yarmouth-Walmoden was engaged in conversation with the two lords spiritual and temporal, who made the lowest reverences and bows to the Countess, waiting until she had passed in at the door on the Bishop's arm.

Theo turned away from the window with a sad, almost awestruck face. Hetty remained there, looking from it with indignation in her eyes and a little red spot on each cheek.

"A penny for little Hetty's thoughts," said Mamma, coming to the window to lead the child away.

"I am thinking what I should do if I saw papa bowing to that woman," said Hetty.

Tea and a hissing kettle appeared, and the family sat down to their evening meal, leaving Miss Hetty, from her place, in command of the window, which she begged her brother not to close. That young gentleman had gone down among the crowd to inspect the armorial bearings of the Countess's and other sedans, and also to invest sixpence in a cheese-cake by Mamma's order and his own desire. He returned presently with the delicacy wrapped in paper.

"Look, mother," he said, coming back. "Do you see that big man in brown beating all the pillars with a stick? That is the learned Mr. Johnson. He comes to the Friars sometimes to see our master. He was sitting with some friends just now at the tea-table before Mrs. Brown's tart-shop. They have tea there, twopence a cup; I heard Mr. Johnson say he had had seventeen cups—that makes two-and-twenty pence. What a sight of money for tea!"

"What would you have, Charley?" asked Theo.

"I think I would have cheese-cakes," said Charley, sighing as his teeth closed on a large slice. "And the gentleman whom Mr. Johnson was with," continued Charley, with his mouth quite full, "was Mr. Richardson who wrote—"

"Clarissa!" cried all the women in a breath, running to the window to see their favorite writer. By this time the sun had sunk, the stars were twinkling overhead, and the footman came to light the candles in the Baroness's room opposite their spies.

Theo and her mother stood together looking from their vantage point. There was a small illumination at Mrs. Brown's tart-and-tea shop by which they could see one lady getting Mr. Richardson's hat and stick, and another tying a shawl round his neck, after which he walked home.

"Oh dear me! he does not look like Grandison!" cried Theo.

"I rather think I wish we had not seen him, my dear," said Mamma, who had been described as a most sentimental woman and eager novel-reader. Here again they were interrupted by Miss Hetty, who cried:

"Never mind that little fat man, but look yonder, mamma."

And they looked yonder. First, they saw Mr. Warrington undergoing the honor of a presentation to the Countess of Yarmouth, who was still followed by the obsequious peer and prelate with blue ribands. Now the Countess graciously sat down to a card-table, the Bishop and the Earl and a fourth person being her partners. Then Mr. Warrington came into the embrasure of the window with a lady they recognized as the one they had seen for a few minutes at Oakhurst.

"How much finer he is!" remarked Mamma.

"How he is improved in his looks! What has he done to himself?" asked Theo.

"Look at his grand lace frills and rules! My dear, he has not got on our shirts any more," cried the matron.

"What are you talking about, girls?" asked Papa, reclining on his sofa, where perhaps he was dozing after the fashion of honest house-fathers.

The girls explained how Harry Warrington was in the window, talking with his cousin Lady Maria Esmond.

"Come away!" cried Papa. "You have no right to be spying the young fellow. Down with the curtains, I say!"

And down the curtains went, so that the girls saw no more of Madame Bernstein's guests or doings for

The first spark in Martin Lambert's chest upon learning the secret his youngest daughter had inadvertently spilled was not love, but a hot, prickling fury directed at the thief who had stolen it. "A plague on all such reckless spirits, whether English or Indian!" the Colonel bellowed to his wife, his face flushing with indignation. "I wish this young rascal had broken his nose against every doorpost in the parish but ours!"

"Perhaps, my dear, we are destined to cure him of his recklessness," Mrs. Lambert interposed, her voice a soothing balm against his storm. "That fall at our gate holds a providential weight. You mocked me when I suggested it before, Mr. Lambert, but if Heaven did not send this young gentleman to us, who would? And it may well be for the blessing of us all that he arrived."

"It is hard, Molly!" the Colonel groaned, the weight of his grievance pressing down on him. "We cherish and dote upon them; we nurse them through sickness and health; we toil and scheme, hoarding pennies in stockings and mending our own worn coats. If they ache, we cannot sleep; if they desire, we labor day and night to grant it. We are their darling daddy and dearest pappy. Yet, on Tuesday morning, I am king of my house. On Tuesday evening, Prince Whippersnapper appears, and my reign is ended. A whole life is forgotten for a pair of blue eyes, a pair of lean legs, and a head of yellow hair."

"'Tis written that we women must leave all to follow our husbands," the matron said gently, laying her hand upon his arm. "I believe our courtship was not very long, dear Martin."

"'Tis human nature, and what can you expect of the jade?" the Colonel sighed.

"And I believe I fulfilled my duty to my husband, though I admit I left my father for him," Mrs. Lambert added softly.

"Excellent wench! Perdition catch my soul, but I do love thee, Molly!" the good Colonel declared. "But mind you, your father never loved me; and if I am ever to have sons-in-law—"

"Ever, indeed! Of course my girls must have husbands, Mr. Lambert!" cried the mother.

"Well, when they come, I shall hate them, madam, just as your father hated me; and quite rightly, for taking his treasure away."

"Do not be irreligious and unnatural, Martin Lambert! I say you are unnatural, sir!" the matron retorted.

"Nay, my dear, I have an old tooth in my left jaw here," the Colonel explained, tapping his chin. "It is natural for the tooth to loosen, but when the tooth-drawer pulls it, it is natural that I should feel pain. Do you suppose, madam, that I do not love Hetty better than any tooth in my head?"

Yet no woman is ever truly averse to the idea of her daughter finding a husband, however violently a father may revolt at the intrusion of the son-in-law. Mothers and grandmothers, in fact, are married anew in the unions of their young ones; their souls don the laces and muslins of their youth, the white ribbons of the postilion bloom once more, and they flutter into the carriage, driving away into the past. What woman, regardless of age, has not stowed away the bridal favors and raiment in the lavender-lined cupboards of her heart?

"It will be a sad thing, parting with her," Mrs. Lambert sighed.

"You have settled that point already, Molly," the Colonel laughed. "Had I not best go out and order raisins and currants for the wedding cake?"

"And then I shall have to leave the house in their charge when I go to her in Virginia. How many miles is it, Martin? Thousands?"

"A hundred and seventy-three thousand, three hundred and ninety-one and three-quarters, my dear, by the near way—that through Prester John's country. By the other route, through Persia—"

"Oh, give me the path with the least sea and your horrid ships, which I cannot bear!" cried the Colonel's spouse. "I hope Rachel Esmond and I shall become better friends. She had a very high spirit when we were girls at school."

"Shall we not attend to the baby linen, Mrs. Martin Lambert?" her husband interjected, sensing a shift in the atmosphere. Now, Mrs. Lambert, who had surely noticed the pretty lace caps and bibs in Mrs. Bobbinit's shop, found herself wondering. On that Sunday afternoon, when the discovery was made and little Hetty lay upon her pillow with feverish cheeks, closed eyes, and a piteous expression, her mother looked at the child with perfect ease of mind, seeming almost pleased by Hetty's distress.

The girl was not merely unhappy; she was enraged with herself for having published her secret. Perhaps she had not known her own state until the sudden emotion revealed it to her, and now the little maid chose to be as ashamed as if she had committed a crime and been caught. She was indignant at her own weakness, breaking into transports of wrath against herself. She vowed she would never forgive herself for submitting to such humiliation. Thus, the young pard, wounded by the hunter's dart, chafes with rage in the forest, angry at the surprise of the rankling steel in his side, snarling and biting at his sister-cubs and the leopardess, his spotted mother.

Little Hetty tore and gnawed and growled so ferociously that one would not wish to be her fraternal cub, nor her spotted dam or sire. "What business has any young woman," she cried out, "to indulge in such nonsense? Mamma, I ought to be whipped and sent to bed. I know perfectly well that Mr. Warrington does not care a fig about me. I dare say he prefers French actresses and the commonest little milliner-girl in the toy-shop to me. And so he ought, and so they are better than me. Why, what a fool I am to burst out crying like a ninny about nothing, simply because Mr. Wolfe said Harry played cards on a Sunday! I know he is not clever like Papa. I believe he is stupid—I am certain he is stupid—but he is not so stupid as I am. Why, of course, I cannot marry him. How could I go to America and leave you and Theo? Of course, he likes somebody else, in America or at Tunbridge or Jericho. He is a prince in his own country and cannot think of marrying a poor half-pay officer's daughter with twopence to her fortune. Did you not tell me, when I was a baby, how I cried and wanted the moon? I am a baby now, a most absurd, silly, little baby—do not talk to me, Mrs. Lambert, I am one. Only there is this to be said: he knows nothing about it, and I would rather cut my tongue out than tell him."

Dire were the threats Hetty leveled at Theo, should her sister betray her. As for the infantile Charley, whose mind was entirely set on cheese-cakes, he had neither remarked nor been moved by Miss Hester's emotion; and the parents and the kind sister, of course, all promised to keep the little maid's secret safe.

"I begin to think it had been best for us to stay at home," sighed Mrs. Lambert to her husband.

"Nay, my dear," replied the other. "Human nature will be human nature; surely Hetty's mother told me herself that she had the beginning of a liking for a certain young curate before she fell head over heels in love with a certain young officer of Kingsley's. And as for me, my heart was wounded in a dozen places ere Miss Molly Benson took entire possession of it. Our sons and daughters must follow in the way of their parents, I suppose. Why, but yesterday, you were scolding me for grumbling at Miss Het's precocious fancies. To do the child justice, she disguises her feelings entirely, and I defy Mr. Warrington to know from her behavior how she is disposed towards him."

"A daughter of mine and yours, Martin," cried the mother with great dignity, "is not going to fling herself at a gentleman's head!"

"Neither herself nor the teacup, my dear," answered the Colonel. "Little Miss Het treats Mr. Warrington like a vixen. He never comes to us, but she boxes his ears in one fashion or another. I protest she is barely civil to him; but, knowing what is going on in the young hypocrite's mind, I am not going to be angry at her rudeness."

"She hath no need to be rude at all, Martin; and our girl is good enough for any gentleman in England or America. Why, if their ages suit, shouldn't they marry after all, sir?"

"Why, if he wants her, shouldn't he ask her, my dear? I am sorry we came. I am for putting the horses into the carriage and turning their heads towards home again."

But mamma fondly said, "Depend on it, my dear, that these matters are wisely ordained for us. Depend upon it, Martin, it was not for nothing that Harry Warrington was brought to our gate in that way; and that he and our children are thus brought together again. If that marriage has been decreed in Heaven, a marriage it will be."

"At what age, Molly, I wonder, do women begin and leave off match-making? If our little chit falls in love and falls out again, she will not be the first of her sex, Mrs. Lambert. I wish we were on our way home again, and, if I had my will, would trot off this very night."

"He has promised to drink his tea here tonight. You would not take away our child's pleasure, Martin?" asked the mother, softly.

In his fashion, the father was not less good-natured. "You know, my dear," said Lambert, "that if either of them had a fancy to our ears, we would cut them off and serve them in a fricassee."

Mary Lambert laughed at the idea of her pretty little delicate ears being so served. When her husband was most tender-hearted, his habit was to be most grotesque. When he pulled the pretty little delicate ear behind which the matron's fine hair was combed back, wherein twinkled a shining line or two of silver, I dare say he did not hurt her much. I dare say she was thinking of the soft, well-remembered times of her own modest youth and sweet courtship. Hallowed remembrances of sacred times! If the sight of youthful love is pleasant to behold, how much more charming the aspect of the affection that has survived years, sorrows, faded beauty perhaps, and life's doubts, differences, and trouble!

Regarding her promise to disguise her feelings for Mr. Warrington in that gentleman's presence, Miss Hester was better, or worse if you will, than her word. Harry not only came to take tea with his friends but invited them for the next day to an entertainment at the Rooms, to be given in their special honor.

"A dance, and given for us!" cried Theo. "Oh, Harry, how delightful! I wish we could begin this very minute!"

"Why, for a savage Virginian, I declare, Harry Warrington, thou art the most civilized young man possible!" said the Colonel. "My dear, shall we dance a minuet together?"

"We have done such a thing before, Martin Lambert!" said the soldier's fond wife. Her husband hummed a minuet tune, whipped a plate from the tea-table, and made a preparatory bow and flourish with it as if it were a hat, whilst madam performed her best curtsey.

Only Hetty, of the party, persisted in looking glum and displeased. "Why, child, have you not a word of thanks to throw to Mr. Warrington?" asked Theo of her sister.

"I never did care for dancing much," said Hetty. "What is the use of standing up opposite a stupid man and dancing down a room with him?"

"Merci du compliment!" said Mr. Warrington.

"I don't say that you are stupid—that is—that is, I—I only meant country dances," said Hetty, biting her lips as she caught her sister's eye. She remembered she had called Harry stupid, and Theo's droll, humorous glance was her only reminder.

But with this, Miss Hetty chose to be as angry as if it had been quite a cruel rebuke. "I hate dancing—there—I own it," she said, with a toss of her head.

"Nay, you used to like it well enough, child!" interposed her mother.

"That was when she was a child: don't you see she is grown up to be an old woman?" remarked Hetty's father. "Or perhaps Miss Hester has got the gout?"

"Fiddle!" said Hester, snappishly, drubbing with her little feet.

"What's a dance without a fiddle?" said the imperturbed papa.

Darkness came over Harry Warrington's face. "I come to try my best and give them pleasure and a dance," he thought, "and the little thing tells me she hates dancing. We do not practice kindness, or acknowledge hospitality, so in our country. No—nor speak to our parents so, neither." He feared that in this particular, usages had changed in the United States during the last hundred years, and that the young folks there were considerably "Hettified."

Not content with this, Miss Hester proceeded to make such fun of all the company at the Wells, and especially of Harry's own immediate pursuits and companions, that the honest lad was still further pained by her behavior. When he saw Mrs. Lambert alone, he asked how or in what he had again offended, that Hester was so angry with him? The kind matron felt more than ever well disposed towards the boy after her daughter's conduct to him. She would have liked to tell the secret which Hester hid so fiercely. Theo, too, remonstrated with her sister in private; but Hester would not listen to the subject, and was as angry in her bedroom,

Generous with his easily acquired wealth, hospitable to a fault, and cordial to all, our young Virginian felt compelled, in his capacity as a man of fashion, to treat his country friends to an entertainment at the Assembly Rooms. According to the custom of the day, he invited nearly every remaining guest from the Wells. Card tables were arranged in one apartment for those who could not endure an evening without the pastime common to all European society; a supper with champagne and bowls of negus was prepared in another chamber; and the large assembly room was set aside for the dance, which Harry Warrington's guests enjoyed in our ancestors' homely fashion. Yet, I cannot fancy the amusement was particularly lively.

Minuets were called first, two or three of which were performed by as many couples. The spinsters of the highest rank withdrew for the minuet, and Lady Maria Esmond, being an earl's daughter and the person of the highest rank present (with the sole exception of Lady Augusta Crutchley, who was lame), Mr. Warrington danced the first minuet with his cousin. He acquitted himself to the satisfaction of the whole room, performing much more elegantly than Mr. Wolfe, who stood up with Miss Lowther. Having completed the dance with Lady Maria, Mr. Warrington begged Miss Theo to do him the honor of walking the next minuet. Accordingly, Miss Theo, blushing and looking very happy, went through her exercise to the great delight of her parents and the rage of Miss Humpleby, Sir John Humpleby's daughter of Liphook, who expected, at least, to have stood up next after Lady Maria.

Then, after the minuets, came country dances. The music was performed by a harp, fiddle, and flageolet perched in a little balcony, thrumming through the evening rather feeble and melancholy tunes. Take up an old book of music and play a few of those airs now, and one wonders how people at any time could have found them otherwise than sad. And yet they loved, frisked, laughed, and courted to that somber accompaniment. There is scarce one of the airs that does not possess an *amari aliquid*, a tang of sadness. Perhaps it is because they are old and defunct, and their plaintive echoes call out to us from the limbo of the past, whither they have been consigned for this century. Perhaps they were gay when they were alive; and our descendants, when they hear—well, never mind names—when they hear the works of certain maestri now popular, will say: *Bon Dieu*, is this the music which amused our forefathers?

Mr. Warrington had the honor of a duchess's company at his tea-drinking—Colonel Lambert's and Mr. Prior's heroine, the Duchess of Queensberry. And though the duchess carefully turned her back upon a countess who was present, laughed loudly, glanced at the latter over her shoulder, and pointed at her with her fan, yet almost all the company pushed, bowed, cringed, smiled, and backed before this countess, scarcely taking any notice of Her Grace of Queensberry and her jokes, her fan, and her airs. Now this countess was no other than the Countess of Yarmouth-Walmoden, the lady whom His Majesty George the Second, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, King and Defender of the Faith, delighted to honor. She had met Harry Warrington in the walks that morning and had been mighty gracious to the young Virginian. She had told him they would have a game at cards that night; and purblind old Colonel Blinkinsop, who fancied the invitation had been addressed to him, had made the profoundest of bows. "Pooh! pooh!" said the Countess of England and Hanover, "I don't mean you. I mean the young Firshinian!" And everybody congratulated the youth on his good fortune. At night, all the world, in order to show their loyalty, doubtless, thronged round Lady Yarmouth; My Lord Bamborough was eager to make her party at quadrille. Lady Blanche Pendragon, that model of virtue; Sir Lancelot Quintain, that pattern of knighthood and valour; Mr. Dean of Ealing, that exemplary divine and preacher; numerous gentlemen, noblemen, generals, colonels, matrons, and spinsters of the highest rank, were on the watch for a smile from her, or eager to jump up and join her card table. Lady Maria waited upon her with meek respect, and Madame de Bernstein treated the Hanoverian lady with profound gravity and courtesy.

Harry's bow had been no lower than hospitality required; but, such as it was, Miss Hester chose to be indignant with it. She scarce spoke a word to her partner during their dance together, and when he took her to the supper-room for refreshment, she was little more communicative. To enter that room, they had to pass by Madame Walmoden's card table, who good-naturedly called out to her host as he was passing and asked him if his "breddy liddle bardner liked tanzing?"

"I thank your ladyship, I don't like tanzing, and I don't like cards," says Miss Hester, tossing up her head; and, dropping a curtsey like a "cheese," she strutted away from the Countess's table.

Mr. Warrington was very much offended. Sarcasm from the young to the old pained him; flippant behavior towards himself hurt him. Courteous in his simple way to all persons whom he met, he expected a like politeness from them. Hetty perfectly well knew what offense she was giving; she could mark the displeasure reddening on her partner's honest face with a sidelong glance of her eye; nevertheless, she tried to wear her most ingenuous smile. As she came up to the sideboard where the refreshments were set, she artlessly said:

"What a horrid, vulgar old woman that is; don't you think so?"

"What woman?" asked the young man.

"That German woman—my Lady Yarmouth—to whom all the men are bowing and cringing."

"Her ladyship has been very kind to me," says Harry, grimly. "Won't you have some of this custard?"

"And you have been bowing to her, too! You look as if your negus was not nice," harmlessly continues Miss Hetty.

"It is not very good negus," says Harry, with a gulp.

"And the custard is bad too! I declare 'tis made with bad eggs!" cries Miss Lambert.

"I wish, Hester, that the entertainment and the company had been better to your liking," says poor Harry.

"'Tis very unfortunate; but I dare say you could not help it," cries the young woman, tossing her little curly head.

Mr. Warrington groaned in spirit, perhaps in body, and clenched his fists and his teeth. The little torturer artlessly continued, "You seem disturbed: shall we go to my mamma?"

"Yes, let us go to your mamma," cries Mr. Warrington, with glaring eyes and a "Curse you, why are you always standing in the way?" to an unlucky waiter.

"La! Is that the way you speak in Virginia?" asks Miss Pertness.

"We are rough there sometimes, madam, and can't help being disturbed," he says slowly, and with a quiver in his whole frame, looking down upon her with fire flashing out of his eyes. Hetty saw nothing distinctly afterwards, and until she came to her mother. Never had she seen Harry look so handsome or so noble.

"You look pale, child!" cries mamma, anxious, like all *pavidæ matres*.

"'Tis the cold--no, I mean the heat. Thank you, Mr. Warrington." And she makes him a faint curtsey, as Harry bows a tremendous bow and walks elsewhere amongst his guests. He hardly knows what is happening at first, so angry is he.

He is aroused by another altercation, between his aunt and the Duchess of Queensberry. When the royal favorite passed the Duchess, Her Grace gave her Ladyship an awful stare out of eyes that were not so bright now as they had been in the young days when they "set the world on fire;" turned round with an affected laugh to her neighbor, and shot at the jolly Hanoverian lady a ceaseless fire of giggles and sneers. The Countess pursued her game at cards, not knowing, or not choosing, perhaps, to know how her enemy was gibing at her. There had been a feud of many years' date between their Graces of Queensberry and the family on the throne.

"How you all bow down to the idol! Don't tell me! You are as bad as the rest, my good Madame Bernstein!" the Duchess says. "Ah, what a true Christian country this is! and how your dear first husband, the Bishop, would have liked to see such a sight!"

"Forgive me, if I fail quite to understand your Grace."

"We are both of us growing old, my good Bernstein, or, perhaps, we won't understand when we don't choose to understand. That is the way with us women, my good young Iroquois."

"Your Grace remarked, that it was a Christian country," said Madame de Bernstein, "and I failed to perceive the point of the remark."

"Indeed, my good creature, there is very little point in it! I meant we were such good Christians, because we were so forgiving. Don't you remember reading, when you were young, or your husband the Bishop reading, when he was in the pulpit, how when a woman amongst the Jews was caught doing wrong, the Pharisees were for stoning her out of hand? Far from stoning such a woman now, look, how fond we are of her! Any man in this room would go round it on his knees if yonder woman bade him. Yes, Madame Walmoden, you may look up from your cards with your great painted face, and frown with your great painted eyebrows at me. You know I am talking about you; and intend to go on talking about you, too. I say any man here would go round the room on his knees, if you bade him!"

"I think, madam, I know two or three who wouldn't!" says Mr. Warrington, with some spirit.

"Quick, let me hug them to my heart of hearts!" cries the old Duchess. "Which are they? Bring 'em to me, my dear Iroquois! Let us have a game of four--of honest men and women; that is to say, if we can find a couple more partners, Mr. Warrington!"

"Here are we three," says the Baroness Bernstein, with a forced laugh; "let us play a dummy."

"Pray, madam, where is the third?" asks the old Duchess, looking round.

"Madam!" cries out the other elderly lady, "I leave your Grace to boast of your honesty, which I have no doubt is spotless: but I will thank you not to doubt mine before my own relatives and children!"

"See how she fires up at a word! I am sure, my dear creature, you are quite as honest as most of the company," says the Duchess.

"Which may not be good enough for her Grace the Duchess of Queensberry and Dover, who, to be sure, might have stayed away in such a case, but it is the best my nephew could get, madam, and his best he has given you. You look astonished, Harry, my dear--and well you may. He is not used to our ways, madam."

"Madam, he has found an aunt who can teach him our ways, and a great deal more!" cries the Duchess, rapping her fan.

"She will teach him to try and make all his guests welcome, old or young, rich or poor. That is the Virginian way, isn't it, Harry? She will tell him, when Catherine Hyde is angry with his old aunt, that they were friends as girls, and ought not to quarrel now they are old women. And she will not be wrong, will she, Duchess?" And herewith the one dowager made a superb curtsey to the other, and the battle just impending between them passed away.

"Egad, it was like Byng and Galissoniere!" cried Chaplain Sampson, as Harry talked over the night's transactions with his tutor next morning. "No power on earth, I thought, could have prevented those two from going into action!"

"Seventy-fours at least--both of 'em!" laughs Harry.

"But the Baroness declined the battle, and sailed out of fire with inimitable skill."

"Why should she be afraid? I have heard you say my aunt is as witty as any woman alive, and need fear the tongue of no dowager in England."

"Hem! Perhaps she had good reasons for being peaceable!" Sampson knew very well what they were, and that poor Bernstein's reputation was so hopelessly flawed and cracked, that any sarcasms levelled at Madame Walmoden were equally applicable to her.

"Sir," cried Harry, in great amazement, "you don't mean to say there is anything against the character of my aunt, the Baroness de Bernstein!"

The chaplain looked at the young Virginian with such an air of utter wonderment, that the latter saw there must be some history against his aunt, and some charge which Sampson did not choose to reveal. "Good heavens!" Harry groaned out, "are there two then in the family, who are----?"

"Which two?" asked the chaplain.

But here Harry stopped, blushing very red. He remembered, and we shall presently have to state, whence he had got his information regarding the other family culprit, and bit his lip, and was silent.

The Colonel and his wife, having conferred in private, resolved to remove their little Hetty from the reach of the charmer with all possible speed. While absence often cures the infatuation of men, it is a remedy rarely effective for women; some will travel ever so far and stay away forever, yet the obstinate disease remains, defying distance and climate. One may whip, abuse, or insult them, and still the deluded creature persists in her fidelity. Indeed, after profound study, I find few better ways to secure the faithfulness of a partner than judicious ill-treatment, a brisk dose of occasional violence as an alterative, and a diet of constant, cooling neglect. Love and kindness should be administered only at sparing intervals; for those who are most indifferent to their husbands are often those cloyed by too much sugar-plum. I have seen a young woman, with every wish gratified, yawn in her adoring husband's face, preferring the conversation of a mere booby. Conversely, I have seen Chloe, whom Strephon has cursed before the servants, creep fondling to his knee at tea-time, playing his favorite tunes and looking round proudly at the butler to say, "Now, John, look how good my dearest Henry is!" Make your game, gentlemen! There is the coaxing line for the henpecked, and the manly, selfish system where she answers to the whistle and knows her master, licking the hand raised to do her good. As the late lamented O'Connell remarked, "Hereditary bondsmen, know ye not, who would be free, themselves must strike the blow?" So up with your cudgels, my enslaved boys!

Women will appreciate this humor, understanding the irony, though young Grubstreet might claim I advocate thrashing women and lack a noble soul. I assure you, ladies, I am only joking; I consider your sex a hundred times more loving and faithful than ours.

But what use is Hetty's removal if she intends to be just as fond of Harry absent as present? Why not let her see him before the Ball and Dobbin are put to, saying, "Good-bye, Harry! I was wilful last night, but you were kind"? She would show no special emotion, too ashamed of her secret to betray it. Harry, too preoccupied to discover it, would part calmly, assuming she is happy to return to her music and flowers. He did not ride partway home by his friend's carriage, having other engagements. When he returned, the Lamberts were gone from Tunbridge Wells; their windows stood open, a card indicating the apartments were to let. A passing sorrow at the blank aspect of rooms once enlivened by such frank countenances may have crossed the young gentleman's mind, but he dined at the White Horse and called fiercely for his bottle. Meanwhile, poor little Hester choked over her tea as the Lamberts arrived at Westerham. The young roses would be wan in her cheeks, black circles around her eyes. It was the thunder, the heat; she could not sleep. Home they came. There was the gate where he fell, the bed he lay in, the chair he used to sit in—what ages seemed to pass! What a gulf between today and yesterday! Who was that little child calling chickens or watering roses yonder? Was she and that girl the same Hester Lambert? She seemed older than Theo, who had always been so composed and clever. But in a night or two, Hester had lived long, long years. Poppy and mandragora would never medicine them to the sweet sleep they tasted yesterday.

Maria Esmond watched the Lambert cavalcade drive away, feeling a grim relief. When Harry entered his aunt's card-room, flushed with Barbeau's wine, she looked at him with hot eyes. He laughed, rattling in reply to his aunt's question about which girl was his sweetheart, gaily declaring he loved them both like sisters. He praised the Lamberts highly, wondering why Lambert was not a general, noting his Royal Highness the Duke's fondness for him. Madame Bernstein, delighted with her boy's success, mimicked the Countess's German accent, saying, "Elle ravvole de fous, cher bedid anche!" She sneered at her niece, asking if Harry carried off the hearts of all the old women.

"You were quite right not to perceive that she cheated at cards," Madame de Bernstein continued, praising Harry's play as that of a grand seigneur.

"Did she cheat?" cried Harry, astonished. "I am sure, ma'am, I saw no unfair play."

"No more did I, my dear, but I am sure she cheated. Bah! Every woman cheats, I and Maria included, when we can get a chance. But when you play with the Walmoden, you don't do wrong to lose in moderation. Cultivate her. She has taken a fancy to your beaux yeux. Why should your Excellency not be Governor of Virginia? You must pay your respects to the Duke and his Majesty at Kensington. The Countess of Yarmouth will be your best friend."

"Why should you not introduce me, aunt?" asked Harry.

The old lady's rouged cheek grew redder. "I am not in favor at Kensington," she said. "Faces so unwelcome to kings are those they wish to forget. All of us want to forget something or somebody. I dare say our ingenu here would like to wipe a sum or two off the slate. Wouldst thou not, Harry?"

Harry turned red, as did Maria, and his aunt laughed a wicked laugh unpleasant to hear. What guilty signals passed on their cheeks? What account was scored upon their memories, which they desired to efface? I fear Madame Bernstein was right; most folks have ugly reckonings on their consciences they are glad to be quit of.

Had Maria known one cause of Harry's disquiet, the spinster would have been more unquiet. For some days he had missed a pocket-book. He remembered possessing it the day he drank claret at the White Horse and Gumbo carried him to bed. He sought it in vain; no servant had seen it, and there were no traces at the inn. He dared not cry the book, making only cautious inquiries. If Lady Maria Esmond knew the outpourings of her heart were in the hands of the public, she would be in a pretty condition of mind. The letters contained disclosures of family secrets, satire, abuse of persons she and Mr. Warrington knew, expostulations about his attentions to other ladies, and scornful jokes. There were appeals of eternal fidelity, the usual farrago written to Edward before becoming Mrs. Jones. Would she like those letters read by anyone else? Did she recall her unfavorable opinions of the Miss Browns or Mrs. Thompson? Would Mr. J. like to see her remarks regarding Jones himself? She wouldn't. Then be pleased to withdraw that imputation already cast in her mind upon Lady Maria Esmond. No doubt her letters were foolish, as most love-letters are, but it does not follow there was anything wrong in them. They are foolish when written by young folks, and how much more foolish when written by an old man to a young lass! No wonder Lady Maria should not like her letters read. Why, the very spelling didn't matter so much in her ladyship's days. It is not the spelling that matters; it is the writing at all. I for one am determined never to speak or write my mind out regarding anything or anybody. I intend to say of every woman that she is chaste and handsome; of every man that he is handsome, clever, and rich; of every book that it is delightfully interesting; of Snobmore's manners that they are gentlemanlike; of Screwby's dinners that they are luxurious; of Jawkins's conversation that it is lively; of Xantippe that she has a sweet temper; of Jezebel that her color is natural; of Bluebeard that he was most indulgent to his wives, and that very likely they died of bronchitis. What? A word against the spotless Messalina? What an unfavorable view of human nature! What? King Cheops was not a perfect monarch? Oh, you railer at royalty and slanderer of all that is noble and good! When this book is concluded, I shall change the jaundiced livery my books have worn since I began to lisp in numbers, give them rose-colored coats with cherubs on the cover, and all characters within shall be perfect angels.

Meanwhile, we are in a society of men and women from whose shoulders no wings have sprouted, who undoubtedly have their little failings. There is Madame Bernstein, fallen asleep after dinner, eating and drinking too much. Mr. Harry Warrington has gone to play billiards with Count Caramboli; I suspect idleness is his failing. This is what Mr. Chaplain Sampson remarks to Lady Maria as they talk in a low tone to avoid interrupting Aunt Bernstein's doze.

"A gentleman of Mr. Warrington's means can afford to be idle," says Lady Maria. "Why, sure you love cards and billiards yourself, my good Mr. Sampson?"

"I don't say, madam, my practice is good, only my doctrine is sound," says the Chaplain with a sigh. "This young gentleman should have some employment. He should appear at court, enter the service of his country, settle down, and choose a woman of suitable rank as his wife." Sampson looks in her ladyship's face.

"Indeed, my cousin is wasting his time," says Lady Maria, blushing slightly.

Here my Lady Maria gave three remarkably shrill screams and tumbled off her chair.

"I will see the Prince. I have a right to see him. What's this?—Where am I?—What's the matter?" cries Madame Bernstein, waking from her sleep, dreaming of old days. The old lady shook in all her limbs, her face very flushed. She stared wildly, then tottered forward on her tortoiseshell cane. "What—what's the matter?" she asked again. "Have you killed her, sir?"

"Some sudden qualm must have come over her ladyship. Shall I cut her laces, madam? or send for a doctor?" cries the Chaplain, with every look of innocence and alarm.

"What has passed between you, sir?" asked the old lady, fiercely.

"I give you my honour, madam, I have done I don't know what. I but mentioned that Mr. Warrington had lost a pocket-book containing letters, and my lady swooned, as you see."

Madame Bernstein dashed water on her niece's face. A feeble moan told presently that the lady was coming to herself.

The Baroness looked sternly after Mr. Sampson as she sent him away on his errand for the doctor. Her aunt's grim countenance offered little comfort to poor Maria when she saw it on waking.

The Baroness Bernstein, though she had clearly suffered the worst of the skirmish described in the previous chapter, met her niece with a composure that belied any lingering rancor. When they next encountered one another, the elder lady offered no reproach. "And you intend to go home in the chaise and coax the letters from him! Delilah! Well, they can be of no use to me, and I trust you may succeed in retrieving them. When will you depart? The sooner the better, you say? We are women of the world, Maria. We only exchange names when we are in a passion. We do not require each other's company; and we part on good terms. Shall we proceed to Lady Yarmouth's? 'Tis her evening. There is nothing like a change of scene after one of those nervous attacks you have suffered, and cards dispel unpleasant thoughts better than any physician."

Lady Maria agreed to attend Lady Yarmouth's card party and was dressed and ready first, awaiting her aunt in the drawing-room. As Madame Bernstein descended, she remarked that Maria's door stood ajar. "She has the letters upon her," the old lady thought. The pair departed for their respective entertainments in separate chairs, displaying that charming cordiality and mutual respect which women can exhibit even after, and sometimes during, the bitterest quarrels.

That night, upon their return from the Countess's assembly, Mrs. Brett, Madame Bernstein's maid, presented herself to Lady Maria's summons, which the lady rang as she retired to her chamber. Betty, Mrs. Brett was ashamed to admit, was not in a fit state to attend her mistress. Betty had been carousing and merrymaking with Mr. Warrington's black servant, Mr. Lord Bamborough's valet, and several other gentlemen and ladies of that station, and the liquor—Mrs. Brett was shocked to acknowledge it—had proved too much for Mrs. Betty. Should Mrs. Brett undress my lady? My lady said she would undress without a maid and granted Mrs. Brett leave to withdraw. "She has the letters in her stays," Madame Bernstein thought. They had bid each other an amicable good-night on the stairs.

The following morning, Betty received a severe scolding when she came to wait upon her mistress from the closet adjoining Lady Maria's apartment, where she lay. She owned, with contrition, her partiality for rum-punch, which Mr. Gumbo possessed the knack of brewing most delicately. She accepted her rebuke with meekness, performed her usual duties regarding her lady's person, and retired.

Now, Betty was one of the Castlewood girls who had been so fascinated by Gumbo, and she was a very good-looking, blue-eyed lass upon whom Mr. Case, Madame Bernstein's confidential man, had also cast the eyes of affection. Consequently, between Messrs. Gumbo and Case, there had been jealousies and even quarrels; which had caused Gumbo, who was of a peaceful disposition, to be rather shy of the Baroness's gentlemen, the chief of whom vowed they would break his bones or take his life if he persisted in his attentions to Mrs. Betty.

But on the night of the rum-punch, though Mr. Case found Gumbo and Mrs. Betty whispering in the doorway in the cool breeze, and Gumbo would have turned pale with fear had he been capable of such a thing, no one could be more gracious than Mr. Case. It was he who proposed the bowl of punch, which was brewed and consumed in Mrs. Betty's room, and which Gumbo concocted with exquisite skill. He complimented Gumbo on his music. Though ordinarily a sober man, he insisted upon more and more drinking, until poor Mrs. Betty was reduced to the state that occasioned her ladyship's just censure.

As for Mr. Case himself, who lay out of the house, he was so ill with the punch that he kept his bed the whole of the next day and did not regain the strength to appear and wait upon his ladies until supper-time; when his mistress good-naturedly rebuked him, saying that it was not often he sinned in that manner.

"Why, Case, I could have sworn it was you I saw on horseback this morning galloping on the London road," said Mr. Warrington, who was supping with his relatives.

"Me! law bless you, sir! I was in bed, and I thought my head would come off with the aching. I ate a bit at six o'clock and drank a deal of small beer, and I am almost my own man again now. But that Gumbo, saving your honour's presence, I won't taste none of his punch again." And the honest major-domo went on with his duties among the bottles and glasses.

As they sat after their meal, Madame Bernstein was friendly enough. She prescribed strong fortifying drinks for Maria against the recurrence of her fainting fits. The lady had such attacks not infrequently. She urged her to consult her London physician and to send up an account of her case by Harry. "By Harry!" asked the lady. "Yes. Harry is going for two days on an errand for his aunt to London." "I do not care to tell you, my dear, that it is on business which will do him good. I wish Mr. Draper to put him into my will, and as I am going traveling upon a round of visits when you and I part, I think, for security, I shall ask Mr. Warrington to take my trinket-box in his postchaise to London with him, for there have been robberies of late, and I have no fancy for being stopped by highwaymen."

Maria looked blank at the notion of the young gentleman's departure but hoped that she might have his escort back to Castlewood, whither her elder brother had now returned. "Nay," says his aunt, "the lad hath been tied to our apron-strings long enough. A day in London will do him no harm. He can perform my errand for me and be back with you by Saturday."

"I would offer to accompany Mr. Warrington, but I preach on Friday before her ladyship," said Mr. Sampson. He was anxious that my Lady Yarmouth should judge of his powers as a preacher; and Madame Bernstein had exerted her influence with the king's favorite to induce her to hear the chaplain.

Harry relished the notion of a rattling journey to London and a day or two of sport there. He promised that his pistols were good and that he would hand the diamonds over in safety to the banker's strong-room. Would he occupy his aunt's London house? No, that would be a dreary lodging with only a housemaid and a groom in charge of it. He would go to the Star and Garter in Pall Mall, or to an inn in Covent Garden. "Ah! I have often talked over that journey," said Harry, his countenance saddening.

"And with whom, sir?" asked Lady Maria.

"With one who promised to make it with me," said the young man, thinking, as he always did, with an extreme tenderness of the lost brother. "He has more heart, my good Maria, than some of us!" says Harry's aunt, witnessing his emotion. Uncontrollable gusts of grief would, not unfrequently, still pass over our young man. The parting from his brother; the scene and circumstances of George's fall last year; the recollection of his words, or of some excursion at home which they had planned together; would recur to him and overcome him. "I doubt, madam," whispered the chaplain, demurely, to Madame Bernstein, after one of these bursts of sorrow, "whether some folks in England would suffer quite so much at the death of their elder brother."

But, of course, this sorrow was not to be perpetual; and we can fancy Mr. Warrington setting out on his London journey eagerly enough, and very gay and happy, if it must be owned, to be rid of his elderly attachment. Yes. There was no help for it. At Castlewood, on one unlucky evening, he had made an offer of his heart and himself to his mature cousin, and she had accepted the foolish lad's offer. But the marriage was now out of the question. He must consult his mother. She was the mistress for life of the Virginian property. Of course she would refuse her consent to such a union. The thought of it was deferred to a late period. Meanwhile, it hung like a weight round the young man's neck and caused him no small remorse and disquiet.

No wonder that his spirits rose more gaily as he came near London, and that he looked with delight from his postchaise windows upon the city as he advanced towards it. No highwayman stopped our traveler on Blackheath. Yonder were the gleaming domes of Greenwich, canopied with woods. There was the famous Thames, with its countless shipping; there actually was the Tower of London. "Look, Gumbo! There is the Tower!" "Yes, master," says Gumbo, who has never heard of the Tower; but Harry has, and remembers how he has read about it in Howell's *Medulla*, and how he and his brother used to play at the Tower, and he thinks with delight now, how he is actually going to see the armor and the jewels and the lions. They pass through Southwark and over that famous London Bridge, which was all covered with houses like a street two years ago. Now there is only a single gate left, and that is coming down. Then the chaise rolls through the city; and, "Look, Gumbo, that is Saint Paul's!" "Yes, master; Saint Paul's," says Gumbo, obsequiously, but little struck by the beauties of the architecture. And so by the well-known course we reach the Temple, and Gumbo and his master look up with awe at the rebel heads on Temple Bar.

The chaise drives to Mr. Draper's chambers in Middle Temple Lane, where Harry handed the precious box over to Mr. Draper, and a letter from his aunt, which the gentleman read with some interest seemingly, and carefully put away. He then consigned the trinket-box to his strong closet, went into the adjoining room, taking his clerk with him, and then was at Mr. Warrington's service to take him to an hotel. An hotel in Covent Garden was fixed upon as the best place for his residence. "I shall have to keep you for two or three days, Mr. Warrington," the lawyer said. The morning light filtered through the window of Mr. Warrington's chamber, illuminating the London Advertiser that lay upon his breakfast table. His eyes scanned the columns until they rested upon a bold announcement: an invitation to all lovers of manly British sport to witness a trial of skill between the great champions Sutton and Figg. The news struck a chord deep within Harry; he resolved immediately to attend the performances. With determination in his step, he mounted the pair of horses he had purchased the day before and set off for the Wooden House in Marybone Fields.

The young charioteer was not yet familiar with the winding roads of the city. His phaeton veered and tacked with unnecessary frequency as he navigated from Covent Garden, momentarily losing his way through the verdant lanes behind Mr. Whitfield's Round Tabernacle and the grounds surrounding Middlesex Hospital. Yet, he eventually reached his destination, finding the area teeming with life. A motley crowd had gathered around the doors of this temple of British valour—a mix of rough London blackguards and the polished equipages of fashionable patrons like himself, all drawn to witness the spectacle.

Beggars and cripples pressed close to the young gentleman, whining for charity, while shoeblack boys scrambled over one another to polish his boots. Nosegay-women and flying fruiterers vied for his attention, and a chaotic throng of piemen, pads, and tramps surrounded the impending battlefield. A flag fluttered atop the building, and from the stage below, accompanied by the rhythmic beat of a drum and the shrill blast of a horn, a manager repeatedly announced that the noble English sports were about to commence.

Mr. Warrington paid his entry fee and secured a seat in a gallery offering a commanding view of the platform. Below him, his servant Gumbo settled into the amphitheatre, ready to retreat whenever the heat of the crowd demanded a pint of beer or a game of cards with the coachmen waiting outside. The scene was a microcosm of old society, encumbered by a prodigious number of liveried servants. Footmen swarmed like ants around every chapel door, theatre, and carriage box, a race that the narrator lamented was doomed to extinction, much like the noble Red Indians of America. Only a few thousand remained, grand and melancholy, clinging to their plush coats and powdered wigs in a world that was rapidly changing.

Before the principal combatants appeared, the arena filled with minor exhibitions. A boxing match took place, but the fighters lacked true spirit, receiving little punishment and offering scant entertainment. This was followed by cudgel-play, where the injuries inflicted were so trivial and the participants so insignificant that the crowd began to hiss and grumble in evident discontent. "The masters! The masters!" the people shouted, demanding the arrival of the famous champions.

Soon, the intrepid Sutton ascended the steps, sword in hand. He saluted the company with martial grace, making a special bow to a private box occupied by a stout gentleman of apparent importance. He was swiftly followed by the renowned Figg, to whom the stout gentleman waved a hand of approval. Both men stood shirtless, their heads shaved clean but marked by the cracks and scars of countless past battles. Each wore an "armiger," a ribbon denoting his color, upon his burly sword arm. The gladiators shook hands, sealing their pact as a contemporary poet noted: "The word it was bilboe."

The combat began with a ferocity that silenced the crowd. Great Figg delivered a blow so tremendous that, had it struck Sutton's head, it would have severed it cleanly. Instead, Sutton deflected the strike with his own sword. However, the force of Figg's blow was so mighty that it shattered the weapon in Sutton's hands, proving the blade less constant than the heart of its wielder. New swords were issued, and the fight continued. The first blood spilled from Figg's panting side, eliciting a roar of delight from Sutton's supporters. Yet, the veteran champion appealed to his audience, particularly the stout gentleman in the gallery, revealing that the wound was a result of his own broken sword.

During the brief pause caused by this incident, Mr. Warrington observed a gentleman in a riding-frock and plain wig entering the stout man's box. It was his friend from Tunbridge Wells, Lord March and Ruglen. The nobleman, usually sparing with his politeness, displayed singular deference to the stout gentleman, accepting bank-bills with a profound bow. Spotting Harry in the gallery, Lord March crossed over and warmly greeted his young friend.

They watched the combat unfold with immense skill and valour on both sides. After the swordplay, the warriors engaged with quarter-staves, and ultimately, victory remained with the ancient champion, Figg. As the warriors fought, a thunderstorm broke over the building. Mr. Warrington gladly accepted a seat in Lord March's chariot, leaving his own phaeton to be driven home by his groom.

Harry was in high spirits, declaring this to be the finest sport he had witnessed since arriving in England. Yet, as was his custom, he associated his pleasure with a longing for his boyhood companion to share it. He sighed, "I wish..." and then stopped himself.

"What do you wish and what don't you wish?" Lord March asked.

"I was thinking, my lord, of my elder brother," Harry replied. "We promised to have our sport together at home. Many times we talked of it. But he wouldn't have liked this rough sort of sport, nor did he care for fighting, though he was the bravest lad alive."

"Oh! He was the bravest lad alive, was he?" Lord March queried, lolling on his cushion with curiosity.

"You should have seen him in a quarrel with a very gallant officer," Harry continued, his voice animated. "It was absurd, but hard to keep George off him. I never saw a fellow so cool, nor more savage and determined. Ah! For the honour of the country, I wish he could have come here instead of me, to show you a real Virginian gentleman."

"Nay, sir, you'll do very well," the amused nobleman countered. "What is this I hear of Lady Yarmouth taking you into favour?"

"I will do as well as another," Harry insisted. "I can ride, and I think I can shoot better than George. But then my brother had the head, sir, the head!" He tapped his own skull. "He had read almost every book ever written; could play the fiddle and harpsichord; could compose poetry and sermons most elegant. What can I do? I am only good to ride, play at cards, and drink Burgundy." He hung his head in penitence. "But them I can do as well as most fellows. In fact, my lord, I'll back myself."

Lord March relished the young man's naivete, much like a jaded voluptuary enjoys a wholesome chop of meat. "By Gad, Mr. Warrington," he said, "you ought to be taken to Exeter Change and put in a show. A gentleman from Virginia who has lost his elder brother and absolutely regrets him. The breed isn't known in this country. Upon my honour, I believe you would like to have him back again."

"Believe!" cried the Virginian, flushing red.

"That is, you believe you believe you would like him back again. But depend on it you wouldn't. 'Tis not in human nature, sir. Here are some fine houses we are coming to. That corner is Sir Richard Littleton's; that great one was my Lord Bingley's. 'Tis a pity they do nothing better with this great empty space of Cavendish Square than fence it with unsightly boards. By George! I don't know where the town's running. Montagu House has been turned into a confounded Don Saltero's museum, stuffed with books, birds, and rhinoceroses. They've even run a cursed cut—the New Road—at the back of Bedford House Gardens, spoiling the Duke's comfort, though I guess they'll console him in the pocket. I don't know where the town will stop. Shall we go down Tyburn Road and the Park, or through Swallow Street into the habitable quarter? We can dine at Pall Mall, or, if you like, with you; and spend the evening as you like—with the Queen of Spades, or..."

"With the Queen of Spades, if your lordship pleases," Mr. Warrington blushed, saying.

The equipage drove to his hotel in Covent Garden, where the landlord, recognizing Lord March, bowed his wig onto the nobleman's shoes in humble welcome. A rich young English peer in the reign of George the Second; a wealthy patrician in the reign of Augustus; which would you rather have been? A question worthy of any modern debating club.

The best English dinner possible was served to the young Virginian and his noble friend. After dinner, wine flowed in plenty, of quality good enough for the epicurean earl. Over the wine, they discussed seeing fireworks at Vauxhall or playing cards. Harry, having never seen fireworks beyond a dozen squibs at Williamsburg on the fifth of November (which he considered a sublime display), would have preferred Vauxhall, but yielded to his guest's preference for piquet. Soon, they were absorbed in the game.

Harry began by winning, as usual. However, within half an hour, luck turned in favor of Lord March. The arrival of Mr. Draper, Harry's man of business, caused a brief interruption. Mr. Warrington always invited everyone to sit and drink, sharing his crust, haunch, or bottle of Burgundy with a kindly spirit. Such hospitality was rare in their selfish world; often brought from the country in youth, these virtues withered under the stifling London air. Draper, though not fond of wine, delighted in witnessing piquet played by men of fashion. Undismayed by Lord March's sidelong scowls, he surveyed the game. Harry was no match for the experienced London club player, especially with Lord March holding superior cards.

Their stakes were no concern of Mr. Draper's. The gentlemen played for shillings, counting gains and losses in a low tone with grave politeness. But a second interruption was destined to occur, bringing execrations from Lord March's lips. First came a scuffle outside, then whispers, then the outcry of a woman in tears. Finally, a female rushed into the room, triggering an explosion of naughty language from the lord.

"I wish your women would take some other time for coming, confound 'em," Lord March said, laying his cards down in a pet.

"What, Mrs. Betty!" cried Harry.

Indeed, it was no other than Mrs. Betty, Lady Maria's maid, with Gumbo standing behind her, his fine countenance beslobbered with tears.

"What has happened?" Mr. Warrington asked, perturbed. "Is the Baroness well?"

"Help! Help, sir, your honour!" Mrs. Betty ejaculated, falling to her knees.

"Help whom?"

A howl erupted from Gumbo.

"Gumbo! You scoundrel! Has anything happened between Mrs. Betty and you?" asked the black's master.

Mr. Gumbo stepped back with great dignity, placing a hand on his heart. "No, sir; nothing hab happened 'twix' this lady and me."

"It's my mistress, sir," Betty cried. "Help! Help! Here's the letter she have wrote, sir! They have gone and took her, sir!"

"Is it only that old Molly Esmond? She's known to be over head and heels in debt!" Lord March dismissed her, taking up his cards. "Dry your eyes in the next room, Mrs. Betty, and let me and Mr. Warrington go on with our game."

"Help! Help her!" Betty cried again. "Oh, Mr. Harry! You won't be a-going on with your cards when my lady calls out to you to come and help her! Your honour used to come quick enough when my lady used to send me to fetch you at Castlewood!"

"Confound you! Can't you hold your tongue?" Lord March snapped, using choice words and oaths.

But Betty would not cease weeping, and it was decreed that Lord March must cease winning for that night. Mr. Warrington rose and rang the bell.

"My dear lord, the game must be over for to-night. My relative writes to me in great distress, and I am bound to go to her."

"Curse her! Why couldn't she wait till to-morrow?" Lord March testily exclaimed.

Mr. Warrington ordered a postchaise instantly. His own horses would take him to Bromley.

"Bet you, you don't do it within the hour!" Lord March challenged. "Bet you, you don't do it within five quarters of an hour! Bet you four to one—or I'll take your bet, which you please—that you're not robbed on Blackheath! Bet you, you are not at Tunbridge Wells before midnight!"

"Done!" said Mr. Warrington. Lord March carefully noted the terms of the four wagers in his pocket-book.

Lady Maria's letter read as follows:

"MY DEAR COUSIN—I am fell into a trapp, which I perceive the machinations of villians. I am a prisner. Betty will tell you all. Ah, my Henrico! Come to the resque of your MOLLY."

Within half an hour of receiving this missive, Mr. Warrington was in his postchaise, galloping over Westminster Bridge on the road to succour his kinswoman.

My early fortune threw me in the path of a gentleman of standing, born upon an island often hailed by impartial critics as the ocean's premier jewel. The tales this man recounted of his kin—stories that once made my youthful blood curdle with sheer dread—depicted a lineage where every commandment was shattered, every moral boundary dissolved. He spoke of crimes so brazen, so devoid of conscience, that even the notorious Thurtell or Turpin would seem tame by comparison. Yet, amidst this catalogue of parricide, forgery, and theft, the family somehow managed to survive, avoiding the hulks entirely. My brother Tim had brought his father's grey hairs to the grave with sorrow; my brother Mick had repeatedly robbed the parish church; and my sister Annamaroia had jilted a Captain, eloped with an Ensign, forged her grandmother's will, and stolen the silver spoons—a felony for which Larry the knife-boy ultimately paid with his life. The family of Atreus was but a whisper compared to this race of O'What-d'ye-call-'em, yet I shall never name the country of their origin.

What struck me with naive astonishment was the sheer contradiction of their existence. These murderers, habitual forgers, and blood-stained rogues corresponded with one another as "my dearest brother" and "my dearest sister," maintaining months-long periods of amicable coexistence. Tim, whose hands reeked of patricide, would mix a screeching tumbler for Maria; Mick, whose lips were black with perjury regarding his grandmother's will and the murder of Thady's orphans, would kiss Julia's cheek. They would share jolly nights, weeping and laughing over memories of the old Castle, the quarterming of the Onetyoneth, and the Major's proposal to Cyaroloine. Their embraces were so profuse, their reconciliations so touching, that one momentarily forgot the stories of how they could hang each other all round if they chose to speak the truth.

What is finer than forgiveness? What more rational than to apologize after hurling every bad name under the sun, to withdraw the decanter flung at an enemy's head, and resume friendship? Some possess this angelic gift. It was beautiful to witness our two ladies at Tunbridge Wells forgiving one another, smiling and fondling despite yesterday's harsh words, seemingly forgetting the past even as they remembered it perfectly. I wonder if you and I can achieve such heights? We must strive for this pacable, Christian spirit. Perhaps you can learn to forgive bad language; it requires practice, but eventually, bad words lose their sting.

Thus, Aunt Bernstein and her niece played cards amicably, toasted each other's health, shared wings of chicken, and pulled bones from the merry-thought pie, scratching their neighbors' eyes out in conversation rather than each other's. History tells us how Peninsular warriors fraternized during truces, exchanging tobacco and wine before resuming battle; similarly, our old soldiers laid down their weapons to hob-nob gaily. Of course, while drinking with Jack Frenchman, one keeps a pistol handy, ready to blow his brains out should he make a hostile move. But for the moment, it is *À votre santé*, mon camarade! Here's to you, mounseer! Everything is pleasant. Regarding Aunt Bernstein's threatened gout? The twinges had vanished. Maria's fainting fits? None returned, save for a slight recurrence the night before. The Baroness was sorry; her niece must see the best doctors, take steel, and continue the regimen even after leaving Tunbridge. How kind of Aunt Bernstein to offer bottled waters! Yet, suppose Madame Bernstein whispers to her maid, "Fainting fits? Pooh! Epilepsy! Inherited from that scrofulous German mother!" What means do we have to know such private confidences? Or suppose Lady Maria orders her maid, Mrs. Betty, to taste every medicinal glass, declaring her aunt capable of poisoning her? Likely, such conversations occur. These are merely precautions—the firelocks our old soldiers keep loaded and cocked at their sides, lying quiet on the grass for now.

Possessing Harry's bond in her pocket, the veteran Maria saw no need to press for immediate payment. She knew the world too well. He was bound to her, but she granted him ample day-rule and parole. It was not her aim to chafe her young slave unnecessarily. She understood the disparity of ages and that Harry required pleasures and diversions. "Take your ease and amusement, cousin," Lady Maria said. "Frisk about, pretty little mousekin," purring grey Grimalkin, watching with green eyes. The ladies, knowing perfectly what constituted a young gentleman's amusements in those days, spoke of them with the frankness characteristic of the era.

Our wily Calypso consoled herself during Harry's absence with whatever diversion presented itself. Mr. Jack Morris, the gentleman associated with Lord March and Mr. Warrington, proved one such diversion. Living with titled personages was Jack Morris's delight, and losing money at cards to an earl's daughter was almost a pleasure. Lady Maria Esmond, an earl's daughter eager to win, obtained permission to take Morris to the Countess of Yarmouth's assembly. They played cards, and everyone was pleased.

Thus, the first eighty-eight hours after Mr. Warrington's departure passed cheerily at Tunbridge Wells until Friday arrived, bringing the sermon Mr. Sampson had been preparing. The company at the Wells was ready to listen. Sampson possessed a reputation for being both amusing and eloquent; if there were no breakfast, conjurers, dancing bears, or concerts, the good folk of the Wells would endure a sermon. He knew Lady Yarmouth was coming, aware of her immense power in granting livings and dispensing bishoprics, and confident that the Defender of the Faith held her opinion in high regard. Consequently, Mr. Sampson prepared his finest discourse for her hearing. When the Great Man is at home at the Castle, walking to the small country church in the park accompanied by the Duke, the Marquis, and Cabinet Ministers, have you ever sat among the congregation to watch Mr. Trotter the curate? He looks anxiously at the Great Pew, faltering over his text, thinking, "Ah! Perhaps his lordship will grant me a living!" Mrs. Trotter and the girls watch the Great Pew with equal anxiety, observing the effect of papa's discourse upon the assembled big-wigs. Once his nervousness passes, his noble voice clears, warms, and kindles. He takes out his pocket-handkerchief, approaching that exquisite passage that always moves them to tears at the parsonage. He has begun it! Then, what is that humming noise filling the edifice, causing hob-nailed Melibaeus to grin at smock-frocked Tityrus? It is the Right Honourable Lord Naseby snoring in the pew by the fire! Poor Trotter's visionary mitre vanishes with the sound.

Sampson was the domestic chaplain of Madame Bernstein's nephew, and the two ladies of the Esmond family patronized him. On the day of the sermon, the Baroness hosted a breakfast in his honor. Sampson appeared rosy and handsome, sporting a fresh-flowered wig and a smart, rustling new cassock bought on credit from a church-admiring mercer at the Wells. Flanked by his patronesses and their lacqueys carrying great gilt prayer-books, Mr. Sampson marched from breakfast to church. Everyone remarked on the Baroness's fine appearance; she laughed, was particularly friendly with her niece, and offered stately smiles to all as she moved along with her tortoiseshell cane. At the door, a dazzling conflux of rank and fashion gathered—all the fine company of the Wells trooping in, including Lady Yarmouth, conspicuous with vermilion cheeks and a robe of flame-coloured taffeta. Shabby people were present as well, though far fewer. What an odd-looking pair were those in ragged coats, one with carroty hair peeking from a scratch-wig, entering just as the organ stopped! He could not have been a Protestant, for he mechanically crossed himself, saying to his comrade, "Bedad, Tim, I forgawt!" I conclude this individual hailed from the island mentioned at the chapter's start. Wherever they go, a rich fragrance of whisky spreads. A man may be a heretic but possess genius; these Catholic gentlemen had come to pay homage to Mr. Sampson.

Not only were members of the old religion present, but disciples of a creed still older. Who were those two individuals with hooked noses and sallow countenances who worked into the church despite the beadle's opposition? Seeing their greasy appearance, Mr. Beadle attempted to deny them entry. But one whispered, "We wants to be conwerted, gov'nor!" while another slipped money into his hand. Mr. Beadle lifted the mace barring the doorway, and the Hebrew gentlemen entered. The organ began; the doors closed. Should we go in to hear Mr. Sampson's sermon, or lie on the grass without?

Preceded by the beadle in gold lace, Sampson walked to the pulpit, appearing as rosy and jolly a man as one could wish.
