Then, when he surged up from his plump cushion, why did his Reverence turn as pale as death? He looked to the western church-door; there, on each side, stood those horrible Hebrew caryatides. He glanced toward the vestry-door near the rector's pew, where he had sat alongside his patronesses. Suddenly, two perfumed Hibernian gentlemen slipped from an adjacent seat, placing themselves on a bench close to the vestry-door and rector's pew, sitting there with eyes meekly cast down until the sermon's conclusion. How can we describe that sermon if the preacher himself never knew how it ended?

Nevertheless, it was considered an excellent sermon. Afterward, the fine ladies buzzed in their pews, offering praise. Madame Walmoden, seated next to our friends, declared it bewdiful, making her dremble all over. Madame Bernstein called it excellent. Lady Maria was pleased that the family chaplain distinguished himself, looking up to catch his eye as he remained in the pulpit. She greeted him with a wave and a flutter of her handkerchief. He scarcely seemed to note the compliment; his face was pale, his eyes fixed yonder toward the font where the Hebrews still remained. The stream of people rushed past them—in a throng, in a march of twos and threes, in a dribble of one at a time—until everyone was gone. The two Hebrews remained by the door.

The Baroness de Bernstein and her niece lingered in the rector's pew, where the old lady was deep in conversation with a gentleman.

"Who are those horrible men at the door? And what a smell of spirits there is!" cried Lady Maria to Mrs. Brett, her aunt's woman.

"Farewell, doctor; you have a darling little boy: is he to be a clergyman, too?" asked Madame de Bernstein. "Are you ready, my dear?" The pew was thrown open, and the Baroness, whose father was only a viscount, insisted that her niece, Lady Maria, an earl's daughter, exit first.

As she stepped forward, the individuals her ladyship designated as two horrible men advanced. One pulled a long strip of paper from his pocket, and her ladyship started, turning pale. She made for the vestry, hoping to clear the door and shut it behind her. However, the two whiskified gentlemen were upon her; one actually laid his hand on her shoulder and said:

"At the suit of Mistress Pincott, of Kensington, mercer, I have the honour of arresting your leedyship. Me neem is Costigan, madam, a poor gentleman of Oireland, binding to circumstances and forced to follow a disagreeable profession. Will your leedyship walk, or shall me man go fetch a cheer?"

In reply, Lady Maria Esmond gave three shrieks and fell swooning to the ground. "Keep the door, Mick!" shouted Mr. Costigan. "Best let in no one else, madam," he said politely to Madame de Bernstein. "Her ladyship has fallen in a feenting fit and will recover here, at her aise."

"Unlace her, Brett!" cried the old lady, whose eyes twinkled oddly. As soon as the operation was performed, Madame Bernstein seized a little bag suspended by a hair chain around Lady Maria's neck and snipped the necklace in twain. "Dash some cold water over her face; it always recovers her!" said the Baroness. "You stay with her, Brett. How much is your suit, gentlemen?"

Mr. Costigan replied, "The deem we have against her leedyship for one hundred and thirty-two pounds, in which she is indebted to Misthress Eliza Pincott."

Meanwhile, where was the Reverend Mr. Sampson? Like the fabled opossum who, spotting the unerring gunner from his gum-tree, declared, "It's no use Major, I will come down," so Sampson surrendered to his pursuers. "At whose suit, Simons?" he asked sadly. Sampson knew Simons; they had met many times before.

"Buckleby Cordwainer," said Mr. Simons.

"Forty-eight pound and charges, I know," said Mr. Sampson with a sigh. "I haven't got the money. What officer is there here?" Mr. Simons's companion, Mr. Lyons, stepped forward, stating his house was most convenient and often used by gentlemen, and that he would be most happy and proud to accommodate his Reverence.

Two chairs happened to be waiting outside the chapel. In those two chairs, my Lady Maria Esmond and Mr. Sampson placed themselves, going to Mr. Lyons's residence, escorted by the gentlemen we had just met.

Very soon after the capture, the Baroness Bernstein sent Mr. Case, her confidential servant, with a note to her niece, full of ardent affection but regretting that her heavy losses at cards rendered the payment of such a sum impossible. She had written immediately to Mrs. Pincott to entreat for time, promising to inform her dear unhappy niece as soon as she received an answer.

Mrs. Betty came

August 25th, 1756. Tunbridge Wells.

"My dear Lord March," Mr. Warrington wrote on that Saturday morning, "I am delighted to report that I have won all three of our bets. I arrived at Bromley just two minutes before the hour; my new horses maintained a capital pace. I drove them myself, with a postilion to guide me and my black man inside with Mrs. Betty. I trust they found the drive pleasant. We reached Tunbridge Wells at forty-five minutes past eleven, having been spared the trouble of stopping on Blackheath, despite two horsemen who rode up but turned away, disliking the look of our company. This victory allows me to settle our debt from yesterday's piquet, a game I shall be happy to replay to grant you your revenge. I remain, your most obliged and faithful servant, H. Esmond Warrington."

It was by this timely intervention that Lady Maria Esmond was able to surprise her aunt in her chambers that morning and escape her captivity. Having sent Mrs. Betty ahead to London, she had not anticipated the emissary's return on the very day of her flight. Late into the night, after a modest meal provided by the bailiff's wife, she and the chaplain had been playing cards when the sharp whirring of wheels approached the house. The sound caused the lady to drop her trumps, her heart hammering with sudden, violent emotion. The carriage halted directly at the door. After a brief exchange at the gate, Mrs. Betty emerged, her face radiant with joy though her eyes glistened with tears. Following her entered a tall young gentleman.

The chaplain slammed his cards down with a shout of triumph, while Lady Maria turned so pale she seemed to vanish, rising from her chair to totter forward a step before collapsing into her cousin's arms with a hysterical cry. How many kisses were exchanged? If they numbered in the thousands, I shall not recount them. He had come to rescue her. She knew he would; he was her champion, her deliverer from bondage and shame. She wept a genuine flood of tears upon his shoulder, and in that moment of release, she looked more beautiful than at any point in this entire history. She did not faint this time. She walked home, leaning lovingly on her cousin's arm, perhaps suffering a few more hysterical outbursts during the night, while Madame Bernstein slept soundly and remained unaware of the drama unfolding beside her.

"You are both free to go home," Harry said immediately. "Get my lady's hat and cloak, Betty, and Chaplain, we shall smoke a pipe together at our lodgings; it will refresh me after this ride." The chaplain, possessing a great deal of available sensibility, was utterly overcome. He burst into tears, seizing Harry's hand to kiss it and praying God to bless his dear, generous young patron. Mr. Warrington felt a thrill of pleasure course through his frame. It was good to alleviate suffering, to transform sorrow into joy. Proud and elated, the young champion marched beside his rescued princess, his hat cocked. His feelings seemed to materialize around him; beautiful happinesses with kind eyes and smiles danced before him, clothing him in a robe of honor and scattering flowers on his path. They led him up to the King's house and seated him in the hall of complacency upon cushions of comfort.

Yet, in truth, he had done little more than act kindly. He had merely reached into his pocket, used an easy talisman to dismiss the dragon guarding the gate, and caused the tyrant holding Lady Maria in execution to lay down his axe. Let his vanity puff itself up; he was good-natured. He had rescued two unfortunate souls and pumped tears of goodwill from their eyes. If he bragged tonight, swaggered before the chaplain, and spoke of London, Lord March, White's, and Almack's with the air of a macaroni, I do not believe we need dislike him any less.

Sampson remained prodigiously affected. This man possessed a nature easily worked upon, quick to receive pain and pleasure, tears, gratitude, laughter, hatred, and liking. In his preaching profession, he had trained his sensibilities to such an extent that they served him well; for the moment, he was exactly what he acted. He wept genuine tears, finding he could produce them freely. He loved those with whom he was present; he felt a real pang of grief mingling his sorrow with widows and orphans. Later, meeting Jack as he exited the door, he went to the tavern opposite and roared over a bottle. He gave money readily but never repaid debts. That night, he was in a rapture of gratitude and flattery toward Harry Warrington. In all London, perhaps, the unlucky Fortunate Youth could not have found a more dangerous companion.

In this grateful mood, full of enthusiasm for the benefactor who had released him from durance, Sampson's admiration grew with every bumper. He exalted Harry as the best and noblest of men, and the complacent young simpleton was disposed to accept these praises as well-deserved. "The younger branch of our family," said Mr. Harry with a superb air, "have treated you scurvily; but, by Jove, Sampson my boy, I'll stand by you!" At certain periods of Burgundian excitement, Mr. Warrington was always eloquent regarding the splendor of his lineage. "I am very glad I was enabled to help you in your strait. Count on me whenever you want me, Sampson. Did you not say you had a sister at boarding school? You will need money for her. Here is a bill which may help pay her schooling." The liberal young fellow passed a banknote across to the chaplain.

Once more, the man was brought to tears. Harry's generosity struck him deeply.

"Mr. Warrington," he said, pushing the banknote a short distance away, "I—I do not deserve your kindness—by George, I do not!" He swore an oath to corroborate his passionate assertion.

"Psha!" said Harry. "I have plenty more of them. There was no money in that confounded pocket-book which I lost last week."

"No, sir. There was no money!" said Mr. Sampson, dropping his head.

"Hallo! How do you know, Mr. Chaplain?" asked the young gentleman.

"I know because I am a villain, sir. I am not worthy of your kindness. I told you so. I found the book, sir, that night when you had too much wine at Barbeau's."

"And read the letters?" asked Mr. Warrington, starting up and turning very red.

"They told me nothing I did not know, sir," said the chaplain. "You have had spies about you whom you little suspect—from whom you are much too young and simple to keep your secret."

"Are those stories about Lady Fanny, and my cousin Will and his doings, true then?" inquired Harry.

"Yes, they are true," sighed the chaplain. "The house of Castlewood has not been fortunate, sir, since your honour's branch, the elder branch, left it."

"Sir, you don't dare for to breathe a word against my Lady Maria?" Harry cried out.

"Oh, not for worlds!" said Mr. Sampson, with a queer look at his young friend. "I may think she is too old for your honour, and that 'tis a pity you should not have a wife better suited to your age, though I admit she looks very young for hers, and hath every virtue and accomplishment."

"She is too old, Sampson, I know she is," said Mr. Warrington with much majesty; "but she has my word, and you see, sir, how fond she is of me. Go bring me the letters, sir, which you found, and let me try and forgive you for having seized upon them."

"My benefactor, let me try and forgive myself!" cried Mr. Sampson, and departed toward his chamber, leaving his young patron alone over his wine.

Sampson returned shortly thereafter, looking very pale. "What has happened, sir?" Harry asked with an imperious air.

The chaplain held out a pocket-book. "With your name in it, sir," he said.

"My brother's name in it," said Harry; "it was George who gave it to me."

"I kept it in a locked chest, sir, in which I left it this morning before I was taken by those people. Here is the book, sir, but the letters are gone. My trunk and valise have also been tampered with. And I am a miserable, guilty man, unable to make you the restitution which I owe you." Sampson looked the picture of woe as he uttered these sentiments. He clasped his hands together and almost knelt before Harry in an attitude of supreme pathos.

Who had been in the rooms during Mr. Sampson's and Mr. Warrington's absence? The landlady was ready to go on her knees, declaring that nobody had entered. Indeed, Mr. Warrington's chamber was not disturbed in the least, nor was anything abstracted from Mr. Sampson's scanty wardrobe and possessions except those papers of which he deplored the absence.

Whose interest was it to seize them? Lady Maria's? The poor woman had been a prisoner all day, and during the time when the capture was effected. She was certainly guiltless of the theft of the letters. The sudden seizure of the two documents—Case, the house-steward's secret journey to London, Case who knew the shoemaker at whose house Sampson lodged in London, and all the secret affairs of the Esmond family—these points, considered together and separately, might lead Mr. Sampson to believe that the Baroness Bernstein was at the bottom of this mischief. But why arrest Lady Maria? The chaplain knew nothing yet about the letter her ladyship had lost, for poor Maria had not thought it necessary to confide her secret to him.

As for the pocket-book and its contents, Mr. Harry was so swollen with self-satisfaction that evening—having won his three bets, rescued his two friends, and enjoyed a capital premature cold supper of partridges and ancient Burgundy sent over by obsequious Monsieur Barbeau—that he accepted Sampson's vows of contrition and solemn promises of future fidelity. He reached his gracious hand to the chaplain and condoned his offense. When the latter swore by his great gods that henceforth he would be Harry's truest, humblest friend and follower, ready to die for Mr. Warrington at any moment, Harry said, majestically, "I think, Sampson, you would; I hope you would. My family—the Esmond family—has always been accustomed to have faithful friends round about them—and to reward them too. The wine's with you, Chaplain. What toast do you call, sir?"

"I call a blessing on the house of Esmond-Warrington!" cried the chaplain, with real tears in his eyes.

"We are the elder branch, sir. My grandfather was the Marquis of Esmond," said Mr. Harry, in a voice noble but somewhat indistinct. "Here's to you, Chaplain—and I forgive you, sir—and God bless you, sir—and if you had been taken for three times as much, I'd have paid it. Why, what's that I see through the shutters? I am blest if the sun hasn't risen again! We have no need of candles to go to bed, ha, ha!" Extending his blessing once more to his chaplain, the young fellow went off to sleep.

About noon, Madame de Bernstein sent a servant to say she would be glad if her nephew would come over to drink a dish of chocolate with her. Our young friend rose and walked to his aunt's lodgings. She remarked, not without pleasure, some alteration in his toilette: in his brief sojourn in London, he had visited a tailor or two and been introduced by Lord March to some of his lordship's purveyors and tradesmen.

"Aunt Bernstein called him 'my dearest child,'" she thanked him for his noble, generous behavior to dear Maria. What a shock that seizure in church had been to her! A still greater shock that she had lost three hundred guineas on the Wednesday night to Lady Yarmouth and was quite a second to her. "Why," said the Baroness, "I had to send Case to London to my agent to get me money to pay—I could not leave Tunbridge in her debt."

"So Case did go to London?" said Mr. Harry.

"Of course he did: the Baroness de Bernstein can't afford to say she is court d'argent. Canst thou lend me some, child?"

"I can give your ladyship twenty-two pounds," said Harry, blushing very red; "I have but forty-four left till I get my Virginian remittances. I have bought horses and clothes, and been very extravagant, aunt."

"And rescued your poor relations in distress, you prodigal good boy. No, child, I do not want thy money. I can give thee some. Here is a note upon my agent for fifty pounds, vaurien! Go and spend it, and be merry! I dare say thy mother will repay me, though she does not love me." And she looked quite affectionate, holding out a pretty hand which the youth kissed.

"Your mother did not love me, but your mother's father did once. Mind, sir, you always come to me when you have need of me."

When bent on exhibiting them, nothing could exceed Beatrix Bernstein's grace or good humor. "I can't help loving you, child," she continued, "and yet I am so angry with you that I have scarce the patience to speak to you. So you have actually engaged yourself to poor Maria, who is as old as your mother? What will Madam Esmond say? She may live three hundred years, and you will not have wherewithal to support yourselves."

"I have ten thousand pounds from my father, of my own, now my poor brother is gone," said Harry, "that will go some way."

"Why, the interest will not keep you in card-money."

"We must give up cards," said Harry.

"It is more than Maria is capable of. She will pawn the coat off your back

The autumn air had finally cooled the feverish warmth of Tunbridge, and Madame de Bernstein's circle was restless, eager to trade the quiet countryside for the glittering chaos of Bath. Harry, with a reluctance that tasted like bile, promised to escort Lady Maria and the chaplain to Castlewood. Their route took them past Oakhurst, the village where Harry had once found genuine kindness, but the memory was quickly soured by Lady Maria's relentless commentary. She mocked the local young women, claiming they set their caps at Harry, and ridiculed the mother's obvious desire to secure him as a husband. Irritated and feeling the weight of her condescension, Harry declared he would pass their door without a glance. That evening, at the inn, the atmosphere was thick with tension. Lady Maria's forced smiles failed to thaw Harry's icy demeanor; her manufactured tears elicited nothing but a surly grunt from him. When she pressed for a private conversation, the chaplain, seemingly by some unseen decree, refused to leave the room, forcing her to retire with a heavy sigh. Harry bowed her out with a stiff, obstinate politeness, leaving her to the innkeeper's care.

Ten minutes after Lady Maria retired, a horse galloped out of the yard, its rider vanishing into the night. Later, when the maid Mrs. Betty entered to fetch smelling salts, she found the chaplain alone, smoking a pipe in the dim light. Harry was gone—perhaps for a moonlit walk, perhaps elsewhere. The truth, however, lay in the hills three miles from Oakhurst. There, leaning heavily on Harry's arm, Lady Maria had poured out a torrent of sentimental vows, calling herself his "Molinda" and promising eternal faithfulness. But as the sun warmed her face, revealing the fine lines of her twenty years, Harry felt the burden of her affection as an intolerable drag. He cursed the moonlight, the wine that had loosened his tongue, and the fatal pledge he had made. Her praises grated on his nerves; her claims to his image and hair, which Madame Bernstein had actually burned, struck him as absurd. It was then, as she leaned on him, that Harry suddenly jerked his arm away. In that instant of movement, Lady Maria felt the sharp pang of realization: she had lied, and she had been found out.

At Castlewood, the mood remained grim. Lord March was away, the ladies absent, and only Mr. Will, returning from partridge shooting, greeted them. He turned pale upon seeing his cousin, receiving a cold scowl in return. Yet, they met at supper, maintaining a veneer of civility. The conversation drifted to racing until Harry abruptly demanded to know about "my horse." Will, confused, asked what horse. Harry, his voice curt, specified the brown horse he had wagered against Will and won the night before Will departed. Will denied knowing anything of it. Harry summoned the chaplain to act as umpire. The chaplain confirmed Harry's claim. Will, grinning wryly, noted that Harry had sold the horse for a mere thirty shillings. Harry dismissed the insult as a trivial bet, offering chicken to Lady Maria, but the moment she rose, he followed her to the door, locking it behind her and pocketing the key.

Inside, the pretense shattered. Will, gripping a knife, asked what Harry meant by his behavior. Harry, feigning a bland smile, suggested a quarrel was inevitable and that servants should not witness disputes between gentlemen. He challenged Will regarding the fifty-guinea wager on the horse. Will denied it, laughing nervously. Harry accused him of lying as easily as cheating, stepping closer. "Hands off, Mr. Chaplain, and see fair play!" Harry shouted, his temper flaring. Before the insult could fully register, Will hurled a wine bottle at Harry's head. Harry ducked; the bottle smashed against the wainscot, shattering a portrait of an Esmond ancestor and splashing port wine over the chaplain's wig.

Gentlemen were not inclined to heed church commands. Seizing a large silver-handled knife, Will charged. Harry, recalling boxing techniques from Marybone, caught Will's wrist and delivered a rapid blow to his nose, sending him reeling against the oak panels. Will dropped his knife, which Harry's opponent kicked under the table. Undeterred, Will dashed forward like a battering ram, intending to drive his head into Harry's stomach. Harry, familiar with such brutal maneuvers from both the boxing ring and the plantations, sidestepped and struck Will's right ear with tremendous force. Will collapsed, his head striking the heavy oak table, and fell lifeless.

Harry, still trembling with adrenaline, declared the fight fair and called for the servants. They burst in to find two victims: the chaplain drenched in wine and Will sprawled in his own blood. Harry ordered his neckcloth undone and demanded a fleam to bleed him, but Will soon regained consciousness, his single functional eye rolling wildly before he began to swear and curse with articulate fury. Harry, adopting a stern humor, asked if he required more assistance. Will, recovering his strength, spat insults at the black servant Gumbo, who had tried to offer him water, before skulking off to bed, leaving a trail of curses in his wake.

The next morning, Harry's wit returned. He sent a note to Will, inviting him to ride to London or the Chocolate House, a jest that Will received with violent displeasure. Meanwhile, a simpering maid delivered a letter from Molinda, filled with declarations of undying love and pleas for reconciliation. Harry read it with a sigh, wondering where the golden tablets of his youth had faded. His dignity, however, forbade him to remain at Castlewood after such a scandal. He wrote a formal letter to Lord March, detailing the altercation and his decision to depart, with the chaplain supervising the document to ensure its propriety. Lady Maria wept at his departure, lamenting that he would find no one in London to love him as she did. Harry, however, was already cheering up, his spirits soaring as he crossed Castlewood Bridge, eager to return to the delights of London society.

Back in London, Harry's forty-four pounds from Tunbridge had vanished. Undeterred, he drew upon the five thousand pounds held in his and his brother's names, intending to replenish his funds through luck at the gaming tables. He settled into Bond Street, discarded his mourning attire for laced waistcoats and powdered wigs, and made his entrance into high society. Jack Morris introduced him to the fashionable crowd, and Harry, greedy for wine and pleasure, threw himself into the city's vibrant life.

Amidst this revelry, a letter arrived from the Honorable H.S. Conway, recounting a chaotic night at Vauxhall. Conway described Harry as a "young savage" making noise, winning money, and behaving with the enthusiasm of a child. He recounted how Harry had confronted him over rumors regarding the Esmond family and the Bernstein lineage, only to be pacified with punch and apologies. Conway noted Harry's presence at the club, alongside Lord March and himself, predicting that the three young men would soon fleece one another financially. The letter painted a picture of Harry as a whirlwind of energy and expense, a prodigal son enjoying the fruits of his inheritance while his mother prayed in the west and a tender heart beat in Oakhurst, unaware of the storm he had unleashed.

London, 1756. The city hummed with a restless energy, a cacophony of ambition and idleness that seemed to define the age. While the learned men of the universities—those guardians of the ancients—debated the merits of Greek philosophy and Latin verse, a quieter, more dangerous war was being waged in the hearts of the young. It was a war fought not with quills, but with wagers, duels, and the reckless pursuit of pleasure.

Harry Warrington sat in his lodgings on Bond Street, a figure of polished silk and youthful arrogance, yet his mind drifted far from the immediate glitter of the season. He was a man caught between two worlds: the stern, duty-bound Virginia of his inheritance and the intoxicating, chaotic freedom of London society. To the older generation, his behavior was a scandal; to the younger, it was the price of entry.

The contrast between the past and present was stark. One could look back a century and find a world teetering on the edge of moral collapse, a time when the "Lady of Quality" who lent her memoirs to the author of *Peregrine Pickle* was a living legend of depravity. Yet, here in 1756, the veneer of propriety was thinner still. The card tables at White's and the gambling dens of the West End were filled with lords and ladies who played with fortunes they did not possess, their faces flushed with gin and the thrill of the next hand. It was a society where swords were drawn over trifles, where taverns echoed with oaths, and where the line between honor and infamy was blurred by the fog of champagne.

Harry's life was a tapestry woven from these threads. He rode to Newmarket, where the aristocracy mixed with the jockeys in a frenzy of betting; he dined at the Shakespeare's Head, surrounded by men who spoke of glory and war while their hands trembled with the need for another drink. He was a member of the Club at White's, rubbing shoulders with the great figures of the day—Rockingham, Carlisle, Bolingbroke—men who shaped the destiny of nations while discussing the latest scandal at the opera.

Yet, beneath the surface of this dissipation lay a profound tension. Harry was not merely a rake; he was a son, a brother, and a heir. His correspondence with his mother in Virginia revealed a young man torn between the expectations of his station and the seductions of his environment. In his letters, he spoke of agriculture as the noblest pursuit, of his cousin William's violent temper, and of the tragic loss of his father. He wrote of his engagement to Lady Maria, a noblewoman whose family was as good as his own, unaware of the shadows that clung to her past. He believed in the purity of his intentions, convinced that he was acting for the honor of his family, even as he spent money he did not have and courted women whose hearts were perhaps not entirely his to command.

The truth of Harry's situation was illuminated by a letter from his aunt, Madame Beatrix, Baroness de Bernstein. Written with a mixture of affection and sharp warning, it painted a picture of a young man who was generous and bold, yet dangerously imprudent. She spoke of the narrowness of his income and the inevitable extravagance that would follow, a trap that had ensnared many a young lord before him. She warned of the "silly engagement" to Lady Maria, revealing secrets she had kept hidden from the young man himself. She knew of Maria's history, of her twenty years of seeking husbands, and of the promise Harry had made without fully understanding the weight of it.

Madame Beatrix's words were a mirror to Harry's own confusion. She urged his mother to intervene, to send more money, to protect her son from the financial ruin that awaited him. She spoke of the Duke's interest in Harry, of the possibility of a future in Virginia, of a governorship that could restore the family's standing. But for now, Harry was trapped in the London of his youth, a world where the only currency that mattered was reputation, and where the cost of maintaining it was often measured in gold and blood.

As the autumn winds swept through the streets of London, carrying the scent of rain and decay, Harry stood at a crossroads. He was a man of action, of passion, of the moment. But the shadow of his father's death, the weight of his inheritance, and the secrets of his own heart pressed upon him. The world of the ancients and the moderns, the clash of virtue and vice, the struggle between duty and desire—it all converged in the life of Harry Warrington, a young man who was about to discover that the progress of a rake's journey was often paved with the ruins of his own potential.

Harry Warrington stood firm in his resolve to honor the grim wager his cousin had wrung from him, though no benevolent observer would mistake this for a desire on the young man's part. He was eager to be rid of the engagement. Perhaps the beating inflicted upon poor Will was intended to hasten this resolution; Harry likely reasoned that a fistfight between them would inevitably drag the families into a feud. In such a chaos, Maria might side with her brother, leaving Harry isolated. He would offer no apology or retraction. Should Will then challenge him to settle the score by force, Harry would simply fight to determine the stronger man. Amidst the rising storm of family discord, the agreement would surely dissolve, freeing him once more.

Thus, honest Harry laid his trap and lit the fuse. Yet, when the explosion faded, the damage was minimal: William Esmond's nose was swollen and his eye blackened for a week. Will did not issue a challenge to his cousin, Harry Warrington, and consequently, neither man killed the other. Will was knocked down, but he rose again. How many sensible men would have done the same, had they been able to settle their grievances in private, away from prying eyes?

Maria did not take her family's side in the dispute; instead, she rallied behind her cousin, a stance supported by Lord Castlewood upon hearing of the disturbance. "Will struck the first blow," the Lord declared, citing the chaplain's provocation. It was not the first time he had been found quarreling while drunk. Mr. Warrington displayed proper spirit in resenting the insult, and it was for Will, not Harry, to seek pardon.

Harry insisted on accepting no apology until his horse was returned and his bet settled. While the chronicler cannot ascertain from surviving papers how the wager was finally resolved, it is certain that the cousins soon met in the homes of various friends, avoiding further physical altercation.

Maria's elder brother had initially been content to see his sister, who had remained unmarried for so many years, wed any gentleman who presented himself, especially one from Virginia. He envisioned her retiring to his wigwam in the forest, where she could be quietly disposed of. In the natural order of things, Harry would outlive his elderly bride and console himself as he saw fit after her departure.

However, following an interview with Aunt Bernstein upon arriving in London, the Lord changed his mind. He even attempted to dissuade Maria from the match, feigning pity for the young man condemned to a life of misery due to a foolish promise made at twenty-one.

"Miery, indeed!" Maria protested, confused by the sentiment. "Pity, forsooth?" Lord Castlewood had believed it was no pity at all. Maria understood the true meaning of pity. Her brother had confided in Aunt Bernstein, who had offered money to break off the match. She grasped the Lord's implication, yet she trusted Mr. Warrington as a man of honor.

On this, the Lord departed for White's or whatever haunt he frequented. It is probable his sister guessed accurately the nature of his conversation with Madame Bernstein.

"And so," he thought, "the end of my virtue is that the Mohock shall fall prey to others, rendering my sparing him useless. *Quem deus vult*—what was that schoolmaster's adage? If I do not have him, someone else will. My brother has had a slice; my dear sister intends to swallow the whole of him bodily. Here have I been at home respecting his youth and innocence, declining to play beyond the value of a sixpence, acting as his guardian and mentor. Why, I am but a fool fattening a goose for others to feed upon! Not many good actions have I performed in this life, and here is this one that benefits whom?—others. Talk of remorse! By all the fires and furies, the remorse I feel is for things I haven't done and might have done! Why did I spare Lucretia? She hated me ever after, and her husband met his predestined end. Why have I let this lad off?—that March and the rest, who do not want him, may pluck him! And I carry a bad repute; I am the man people point at, calling the wicked lord, against whom women warn their sons! Pardi, I am not a penny worse, only a great deal more unlucky than my neighbors, and it is only my cursed weakness that has been my greatest enemy!"

Here, the chronicler, in recording a speech a gentleman merely thought, may be accused of overdrawn narrative by the patient reader, who has a right to withhold full credulity. Yet, have not Livy, Thucydides, and countless other historians penned speeches for their heroes that the latter never actually delivered? How much more may we, knowing Lord Castlewood's character so intimately, declare what passed in his mind and transcribe his thoughts? What? A whole pack of wolves hunts this lamb, intending to make a meal of him, while one hungry old hunter stands by, denied a single cutlet? Who has not admired that noble speech of Lord Clive, when reproached upon returning from India for making too free with jaghires, lakhs, gold mohurs, diamonds, pearls, and the like? "Upon my life," said the hero of Plassy, "when I think of my opportunities, I am surprised I took so little!"

To tell disagreeable stories of a gentleman until one is forced to impart them is painful to a feeling mind. Hence, though I knew before the first page of this history was written the sort of person Lord Castlewood was and the esteem held by his contemporaries, I have withheld much that was unpleasant, allowing only the candid reader to perceive he was a nobleman who ought not to be liked. It is true that Lord March and other gentlemen of whom he complained would have bet with Mr. Warrington for his last shilling and taken their winnings without scruple, picking the bones of a chicken; they would seize any advantage in the game, the race, or their superior knowledge of the horses. In this, they followed the practice of all gentlemen: but when they played, they played fair, and when they lost, they paid.

Madame Bernstein was reluctant to reveal all she knew to her Virginian nephew regarding his family's discredit; she was even touched by the Lord's forbearance toward Harry upon his first arrival in Europe and pleased with his compliance with her wishes. However, in their conversation concerning Maria's designs on Harry, he spoke his mind with his usual cynicism. He voted himself a fool for sparing a lad whom no sparing would eventually keep from ruin, pointing out Mr. Harry's undeniable extravagances, his spendthrift associates, his nights at faro and hazard, and his rides to Newmarket. He asked why he alone should keep his hands off the young fellow.

In vain Madame Bernstein pleaded that Harry was poor. "Bah!" retorted the Lord. "He is heir to a principality which ought to have been his, Castlewood's, and might have restored our ruined family. Indeed, Madame Bernstein thought Mr. Warrington's Virginian property much greater than it was. Were there not money-lenders in the town who would lend him on post-obits in plenty?" Castlewood knew this to his cost; he had applied during his father's lifetime, and the cursed crew had eaten up two-thirds of his miserable income. He spoke with such desperate candor and ill-humor that Madame Bernstein became alarmed for her favorite and determined to caution him at the first opportunity.

That evening she began to pen a note to Mr. Warrington. But all her life she was slow with her pen and disliked using it. "I never knew any good come of writing more than *bon jour* or business," she used to say. "What is the use of writing ill, when there are so many clever people who can do it well? And even then, it were best left alone." So she sent one of her men to Mr. Harry's lodgings, bidding him come and drink a dish of tea with her the next day, when she proposed to warn him.

But the next morning she was indisposed and could not receive Mr. Harry when he came. She kept her chamber for a couple of days, and the next day there was a great engagement, and the day after that Mr. Harry was off on some expedition of his own. In the whirl of London life, what man sees his neighbor, what brother his sister, what schoolfellow his old friend? Many days passed before Mr. Warrington and his aunt had the confidential conversation she desired.

She began by scolding him mildly about his extravagance and madcap frolics (though, in truth, she was charmed with him for both). He replied that young men will be young men, and that it was in dutifully waiting in attendance on his aunt that he had made the acquaintance with whom he mostly lived at present. Then, with some prelude, she began to warn him regarding his cousin, Lord Castlewood. On this, he broke into a bitter laugh and said the good-natured world had told him plenty about Lord Castlewood already.

"To say of a man of his lordship's rank, or of any gentleman, 'Don't play with him,' is more than I like to do," continued the lady.

"Oh, you may say on, aunt!" said Harry, with something like an imprecation on his lips.

"And have you played with your cousin already?" asked the young man's worldly old monitress.

"And lost and won, madam!" answered Harry, gallantly. "It don't become me to say which. If we have a bout with a neighbor in Virginia, a bottle, or a pack of cards, or a quarrel, we don't go home and tell our mothers. I mean no offense, aunt!" And, blushing, the handsome young fellow went up and kissed the old lady. He looked very brave and brilliant, with his rich lace, his fair face and hair, his fine new suit of velvet and gold. On taking leave of his aunt, he gave his usual sumptuous benefaction to her servants, who crowded round him. It was a rainy wintry day, and the gentleman, to save his fine silk stockings, must come in a chair. "To White's!" he called out to the chairmen, and away they carried him to the place where he passed a great deal of his time.

Our Virginian's friends might have wished he had been a less sedulous frequenter of that house of entertainment; but so much may be said in favor of Mr. Warrington that, having engaged in play, he fought his battle like a hero. He was not flustered by good luck, and perfectly calm when the chances went against him. If Fortune is proverbially fickle to men at play, how many men are fickle to Fortune, running frightened from her advances and deserting her, who perhaps had never thought of leaving them but for their own cowardice?

"By George, Mr. Warrington," said Mr. Selwyn, waking up in a rare fit of enthusiasm, "you deserve to win! You treat your luck as a gentleman should, and as long as she remains with you, behave to her with the most perfect politeness. *Si celeres quatit pennas*—you know the rest, no? Well, you are not much the worse off—you will call her ladyship's coach and make her a bow at the step. Look at Lord Castlewood yonder, passing the box. Did you ever hear a fellow curse and swear so at losing five or six pieces? She must be a jade indeed if she long gives her favors to such a niggardly canaille as that!"

"We don't consider our family canaille, sir," said Mr. Warrington, "and my Lord Castlewood is one of them."

"I forgot. I forgot, and ask your pardon! And I make you my compliment upon my lord, and Mr. Will Esmond, his brother," said Harry's neighbor at the hazard-table. "The box is with me. Five's the main! Deuce Ace! my usual luck. *Virtute mea me involvo!*"—and he sank back in his chair.

Whether it was upon this occasion of taking the box that Mr. Harry threw the fifteen mains mentioned in one of those other letters of Mr. Walpole's, which have not come into his present learned editor's hands, I know not; but certain it is that on his first appearance at White's, Harry had five or six evenings of prodigious good luck and seemed more than ever the Fortunate Youth. The five hundred pounds withdrawn from his patrimonial inheritance multiplied into thousands. He bought fine clothes, purchased fine horses, gave grand entertainments, made handsome presents, lived as if he had been as rich as Sir James Lowther or his Grace of Bedford, and yet the five thousand pounds never seemed to diminish. No wonder he gave where giving was so easy; no wonder he was generous with Fortunatus's purse in his pocket. I say no wonder he gave, for such was his nature. Other Fortunati tie up the endless purse, drink small beer, and go to bed with a tallow candle.

During this vein of luck, what must Mr. Harry do but find out from Lady Maria what her ladyship's debts were and pay them off to the last shilling? Her stepmother and half-sister, who did not love her, he treated to all sorts of magnificent presents.

"Had you not better get yourself arrested, Will?" my lord sardonically said to his brother. "Although you bit him in that affair of the horse, the Mohock will certainly take you out of pawn." It was then that Mr. William felt a true remorse, although not of that humble kind which sent the repentant Prodigal to his knees. "Confound it," he groaned, "to think that I have let this fellow slip for such a little matter as forty pounds! Why, he was good for a thousand at least."

As for Maria, that generous creature accepted the good fortune sent her with a grateful heart and was ready to accept as much more as one pleased. Having paid off her debts to her various milliners, tradesmen, and purveyors, she forthwith proceeded to contract new ones. Mrs. Betty, her ladyship's maid, went round informing the tradespeople that her mistress was about to contract a matrimonial alliance with a

Mr. Harry Warrington of Virginia kept his lodgings in Bond Street, London, living upon the fat of the land and drinking bumpers of the finest wine. To the fashionable world, he was the Fortunate Youth, a title recognized with genuine envy. Young, wealthy, handsome, and blessed with fortune, he was welcomed by all. Let us not, my dear brethren, cry out too loudly against the selfishness of a world that is kind to the young and handsome while frowning upon the old, the ugly, and the miserable. If I have the right to choose my acquaintances—preferring at the club the company of a lively, well-dressed gentleman who amuses me over that of a slouching misanthrope or a ceaselessly prating coxcomb—has not society, the aggregate of you and me, the same right to such choice? Harry was liked because he was likeable; because he was rich, handsome, jovial, well-born, and brave; because with jolly topers he shared a song and a bottle; because with gentlemen sportsmen he loved any game on foot or horseback; because with ladies he possessed a modest, blushing timidity that rendered him intriguing; and because to those humbler than himself in degree, he was magnificently liberal and anxious to spare annoyance. Our Virginian was very grand, high and mighty, to be sure; but in those times, when the distinction of ranks still held sway, to be distant with inferiors brought no unpopularity to a gentleman. Remember that in those days, the Secretary of State knelt when he went to the king with his despatches, and the Under-Secretary never dared to sit in his chief's presence. If I were Secretary of State, I should not like to kneel before my audience; if Under-Secretary, I should dread standing while the Right Honourables looked over the papers. Yet there is a *modus in rebus*: certain lines must be drawn. I am only half pleased when Bob Bowstreet and Tom Garbage propose to join fellowship as brother literary men, slap me on the back, and call me "old boy" or by my Christian name.

As much pleasure as the town could offer in the winter season of 1756–57, Mr. Warrington had for the asking. There were operas, in which he took moderate delight, despite the prodigious satire brought against them for being foolish, Popish, and unmanly. There were the theatres with Mr. Garrick and Mrs. Pritchard, and Mrs. Clive. There were masquerades and ridottos frequented by fine society, and the private drums and assemblies of lords and ladies, which began and ended with cards. Mr. Warrington preferred White's, for the play there was neither so high nor so fair as at the club-table.

One day, his kinsman Lord Castlewood took him to court, presenting Harry to his Majesty, who had come to town from Kensington. But that gracious sovereign either disliked Harry's introducer or had other reasons for being sulky. His Majesty merely said, "Oh, heard of you from Lady Yarmouth. The Earl of Castlewood," turning to his lordship and speaking in German, "shall tell him that he plays too much!" And so saying, the Defender of the Faith turned his royal back.

Lord Castlewood shrank back, frightened at this cold reception.

"What does he say?" asked Harry.

"His Majesty thinks they play too high at White's, and is displeased," whispered the nobleman.

"If he does not want us, we had better not come again, that is all," said Harry, simply. "I never, somehow, considered that German fellow a real King of England."

"Hush! for Heaven's sake, hold your confounded colonial tongue!" cried my lord. "Don't you see the walls here have ears!"

"And what then?" asked Mr. Warrington. "Why, look at the people! Hang me, if it is not quite a curiosity! They were all shaking hands with me, bowing, and flattering me just now; and at present they avoid me as if I were the plague!"

"Shake hands, nephew," said a broad-faced, broad-shouldered gentleman in a scarlet-laced waistcoat and a great old-fashioned wig. "I heard what you said. I have ears like the wall, look you. And, now, if other people show you the cold shoulder, I'll give you my hand;" and so saying, the gentleman put out a great brown hand, grasping Harry's. "Something of my brother about your eyes and face. Though I suppose in your island you grow more wiry and thin. I am thine uncle, child. My name is Sir Miles Warrington. My lord knows me well enough."

My lord looked very frightened and yellow. "Yes, my dear Harry. This is your paternal uncle, Sir Miles Warrington."

"Might as well have come to see us in Norfolk, as dangle about playing the fool at Tunbridge Wells, Mr. Warrington, or Mr. Esmond—which do you call yourself?" said the Baronet. "The old lady calls herself Madam Esmond, don't she?"

"My mother is not ashamed of her father's name, nor am I, uncle," said Mr. Harry, rather proudly.

"Well said, lad! Come home and eat a bit of mutton with Lady Warrington at three, in Hill Street—that is if you can do without your White's kickshaws. You need not look frightened, my Lord Castlewood! I shall tell no tales out of school."

"I—I am sure Sir Miles Warrington will act as a gentleman!" said my lord, in much perturbation.

"Belike, he will," growled the Baronet, turning on his heel. "And thou wilt come, young man, at three; and mind, good roast mutton waits for nobody. Thou hast a great look of thy father. Lord bless us, how we used to beat each other! He was smaller than me, and in course younger; but many a time he had the best of it. Take it he was henpecked when he married, and Madam Esmond took the spirit out of him when she got him in her island. Virginia is an island. Ain't it an island?"

Harry laughed and said "No!" And the jolly Baronet, going off, said, "Well, island or not, thou must come and tell all about it to my lady. She'll know whether 'tis an island or not."

"My dear Mr. Warrington," said my lord, with an appealing look, "I need not tell you that in this great city every man has enemies, and that there is a great deal of detraction and scandal. I never spoke to you about Sir Miles Warrington precisely because I did know him, and because we have had differences together. Should he permit himself remarks to my disparagement, you will receive them *cum grano*, and remember that it is from an enemy they come." And the pair walked out of the King's apartments into Saint James's Street. Harry found the news of his cold reception at court had already preceded him to White's. The King had turned his back upon him. The King was jealous of Harry's favour with the favourite. Harry was *au mieux* with Lady Yarmouth. A score of gentlemen wished him a compliment upon his conquest. Before night it was a settled matter that this was amongst the other victories of the Fortunate Youth.

Sir Miles told his wife and Harry as much when the young man appeared at the appointed hour at the Baronet's dinner-table, rallying Harry in his simple rustic fashion. The lady, at first a grand and stately personage, told Harry that the reputation the world had made for him was so bad that at first she had given him but a frigid welcome. With the young ladies, Sir Miles's daughters, it was "How d'ye do, cousin?" and "No, thank you, cousin," and a number of prim curtseys to the Virginian as they greeted and left him. The little boy, the heir of the house, dined at table under the care of his governor; having his glass of port by papa after dinner, he gave a loose to his innocent tongue and asked many questions of his cousin. At last the innocent youth said, after looking hard in Harry's face, "Are you wicked, cousin Harry? You don't look very wicked!"

"My dear Master Miles!" expostulated the tutor, turning very red.

"But you know you said he was wicked!" cried the child.

"We are all miserable sinners, Miley," explained papa. "Haven't you heard the clergyman say so every Sunday?"

"Yes, but not so very wicked as cousin Harry. Is it true that you gamble, cousin, and drink all night with wicked men, and frequent the company of wicked women? You know you said so, Mr. Walker—and mamma said so, too, that Lady Yarmouth was a wicked woman."

"And you are a little pitcher," cried papa: "and my wife, nephew Harry, is a staunch Jacobite—you won't like her the worse for that. Take Miles to his sisters, Mr. Walker, and Topsham shall give thee a ride in the park, child, on thy little horse." The idea of the little horse consoled Master Miles; for when his father ordered him away to his sisters, he had begun to cry bitterly, bawling out that he would far rather stay with his wicked cousin.

"They have made you a sad reputation among 'em, nephew!" said the jolly Baronet. "My wife, you must know, of late years, and since the death of my poor eldest son, has taken to, to, hum—to Tottenham Court Road and Mr. Whitfield's preaching: and we have had one Ward about the house, a friend of Mr. Walker's yonder, who has recounted sad stories about you and your brother at home."

"About me, Sir Miles, as much as he pleases," cried Harry, warm with port: "but I'll break any man's bones who dares say a word against my brother! Why, sir, that fellow was not fit to buckle my dear George's shoe; and if I find him repeating at home what he dared to say in our house in Virginia, I promise him a second caning."

"You seem to stand up for your friends, nephew Harry," said the Baronet. "Fill thy glass, lad, thou art not as bad as thou hast been painted. I always told my lady so. I drink Madam Esmond Warrington's health, of Virginia, and will have a full bumper for that toast."

Harry, as in duty bound, emptied his glass, filled again, and drank Lady Warrington and Master Miles.

"Thou wouldst be heir to four thousand acres in Norfolk, did he die, though," said the Baronet.

"God forbid, sir, and be praised that I have acres enough in Virginia of my own!" said Mr. Warrington. He went up presently and took a dish of coffee with Lady Warrington; he talked to the young ladies of the house. He was quite easy, pleasant, and natural. There was one of them somewhat like Fanny Mountain, and this young lady became his special favourite. When he went away, they all agreed their wicked cousin was not near so wicked as they had imagined him to be; at any rate, my lady had strong hopes of rescuing him from the pit. She sent him a good book that evening, whilst Mr. Harry was at White's, with a pretty note praying that *Law's Call* might be of service to him. This despatched, she and her daughters went off to a rout at the house of a minister's lady. But Harry, before he went to White's, had driven to his friend Mr. Sparks in Tavistock Street and purchased more trinkets for his female cousins—"from their aunt in Virginia," he said. You see, he was full of kindness; he kindled and warmed with prosperity. There are men on whom wealth hath no such fortunate influence. It hardens base hearts; it makes those who were mean and servile, mean and proud. If it should please the gods to try me with ten thousand a year, I will, of course, meekly submit myself to their decrees, but I will pray them to give me strength enough to bear the trial. All the girls in Hill Street were delighted at getting the presents from Aunt Warrington in Virginia and addressed a collective note, which must have astonished that good lady when she received it in spring-time, when she and Mountain and Fanny were on a visit to grim deserted Castlewood, when the snows had cleared away and a thousand peach-trees flushed with blossoms. "Poor boy!" the mother thought. "This is some present he gave his cousins in my name, in the time of his prosperity—nay, of his extravagance and folly. How quickly his wealth has passed away! But he ever had a kind heart for the poor Mountain; and we must not forget him in his need. It behoves us to be more than ever careful of our own expenses, my good people!" And so, I dare say, they warmed themselves by one log, ate of one dish, and worked by one candle. And the widow's servants, whom the good soul began to pinch more and more, lied, stole, and cheated more and more; and what was saved in one way was stolen in another.

One afternoon, Mr. Harry sat in his Bond Street lodgings, arrayed in his dressing-gown, sipping his chocolate, surrounded by luxury, encased in satin, and yet enveloped in care. A few weeks previously, when the luck was with him and he was scattering his benefactions to and fro, he had royally told Parson Sampson to get together a list of his debts which he, Mr. Warrington, would pay. Accordingly Sampson had gone to work and got together a list, not of all his debts—no man ever does set down all—but such a catalogue as he thought sufficient to bring to Mr. Warrington, at whose breakfast-table the divine had humbly waited until his honour should choose to attend it.

Harry appeared at length, very pale and languid, in curl-papers, and scarce any appetite for his breakfast. The chaplain

The rejection of his peace-offerings had ignited a fire of indignation in the young American chief, a wrath directed not merely against Colonel Lambert but against the entire lineage of that gentleman. "He has humiliated me before the girls!" the young man fumed internally. "He and Mr. Wolfe, who were forever preaching morality and posturing with an air of superior protection, have once again held me up to the family as a scapegrace and prodigal. They are so virtuous they refuse to shake my hand; and when I attempt to show them a scrap of common gratitude, they fling my presents in my face!"

"Why, sir, the things must be worth a fortune!" observed Parson Sampson, his eyes gleaming with covetousness as he cast a glance at the two morocco boxes resting on white satin cushions, displaying Mr. Sparks's golden gewgaws.

"They cost some money, Sampson," admitted the young man. "Not that I would grudge ten times the amount to people who have been kind to me."

"No, faith, sir, not if I know your honour!" interjected Sampson, seizing every opportunity to praise his young patron.

"The repeater, they told me, was a great bargain, worth a hundred pounds at Paris. Little Miss Hetty said she longed for a repeating watch."

"Oh, what a love!" cried the chaplain, his voice rising. "With a little circle of pearls on the back and a diamond knob for the handle! Why, 'twould win any woman's heart, Sir!"

"There passes an apple-woman with a basket. I have a mind to fling the thing out to her!" Mr. Warrington shouted fiercely, his temper fraying under the weight of his own perceived slights.

When Harry departed on business that took him to the City and the Temple, his parasite did not follow him far into the Strand; he turned away, confessing a terror of Chancery Lane and its inhabitants. Mr. Warrington proceeded to his broker, and they walked to the Bank, conducting some minor business. After signing a trifling document or two, Harry departed with a bundle of crisp bank-notes in his pocket. The broker escorted him to one of the great dining-houses famous in the City, and afterwards showed him the Virginian walk upon 'Change. Harry passed through it with a certain shamefacedness. *What would a certain lady in Virginia say,* he thought, *if she knew that he was carrying off in that bottomless gambler's pocket a great portion of his father's patrimony?* *Those are all Virginia merchants,* he mused, imagining the whispers of the exchange. *They are all talking about me, saying, 'That is young Esmond, of Castlewood, on the Potomac, Madam Esmond's son; and he has been losing his money at play, selling out so much, and so much, and so much.'*

His spirits did not rise until he had passed under the traitors' heads of Temple Bar and was fairly out of the City. From the Strand, Mr. Harry walked home, glancing into St. James's Street by the way, but there was nobody there yet; the company did not arrive at the Chocolate-House until a later hour.

Arrived at home, Mr. Harry produced his bundle of bank-notes. He took three of them, placed them in a sheet of paper which he sealed carefully, having previously written within the sheet the words, "Much good may they do you. H. E. W." He directed this packet to the Reverend Mr. Sampson, leaving it on the chimney-glass with instructions to his servants to deliver it to the divine upon his arrival.

Now his honour's phaeton was brought to the door, and he stepped in, intending to drive round the park. But the rain began to fall, or the east wind blew, or some other reason arose, and his honour turned his horses' heads down St. James's Street, returning to White's at about three o'clock. Scarcely anybody had come in yet; it was the hour when folks were at dinner. However, there was his cousin Castlewood, lounging over the *Public Advertiser*, having just come off from his duty at Court.

Lord Castlewood yawned over the newspaper. "What shall they do?" he asked. "Shall we have a little piquet?" Harry had no objection to a little piquet. "Just for an hour," said Lord Castlewood. "I dine at Arlington Street at four." "Just for an hour," said Mr. Warrington, and they called for cards.

"Or shall we have 'em in upstairs?" suggested my lord. "Out of the noise?"

"Certainly, out of the noise," said Harry.

At five o'clock, a half-dozen gentlemen had come in after their dinner, sitting at cards, coffee, or talk. The folks from the ordinary had not left the table yet. There the gentlemen of White's would often sit till past midnight.

One toothpick pointed over the coffee-house blinds into the street. "Whose phaeton?" asked Toothpick 1 of Toothpick 2.

"The Fortunate Youth's," said No. 2.

"Not so fortunate the last three nights. Luck confoundedly against him. Lost, last night, thirteen hundred to the table. Mr. Warrington been here to-day, John?"

"Mr. Warrington is in the house now, sir. In the little tea-room with Lord Castlewood since three o'clock. They are playing at piquet," said John.

"What fun for Castlewood!" said No. 1, with a shrug.

The second gentleman growled out an execration. "Curse the fellow!" he said. "He has no right to be in this club at all. He doesn't pay if he loses. Gentlemen ought not to play with him. Sir Miles Warrington told me at court the other day that Castlewood has owed him money on a bet these three years."

"Castlewood," said No. 1, "doesn't lose if he plays alone. A large company flurries him, you see—that's why he doesn't come to the table." The facetious gentleman grinned, showing all his teeth, polished perfectly clean.

"Let's go up and stop 'em," growled No. 2.

"Why?" asked the other. "Much better look out the window. Lamplighter going up the ladder—famous sport. Look at that old putt in the chair: did you ever see such an old quiz?"

"Who is that just gone out of the house? As I live, it's Fortunatus! He seems to have forgotten that his phaeton has been here, waiting all the time. I bet you two to one he has been losing to Castlewood."

"Jack, do you take me to be a fool?" asked the one gentleman of the other. "Pretty pair of horses the youth has got. How he is flogging 'em!" And they saw Mr. Warrington galloping up the street, scared coachmen and chairmen clearing before him; presently my Lord Castlewood was seen to enter a chair and go his way.

Harry drove up to his own door. It was but a few yards, and those poor horses had been beating the pavement all this while in the rain. Mr. Gumbo was engaged at the door in conversation with a countrified-looking lass, who tripped off with a curtsey. Mr. Gumbo was always engaged with some pretty maid or other.

"Gumbo, has Mr. Sampson been here?" asked Gumbo's master from his driving-seat.

"No, sar. Mr. Sampson have not been here!" answered Mr. Warrington's gentleman. Harry bid him go upstairs and bring down a letter addressed to Mr. Sampson.

"Addressed to Mr. Sampson? Oh yes, sir," said Mr. Gumbo, who could not read.

"A sealed letter, stupid! on the mantelpiece, in the glass!" said Harry; and Gumbo leisurely retired to fetch that document. As soon as Harry had it, he turned his horses' heads towards St. James's Street, and the two gentlemen, still yawning out of the window at White's, beheld the Fortunate Youth, in an instant, back again.

As they passed out of the little tea-room where he and Lord Castlewood had had their piquet together, Mr. Warrington had seen that several gentlemen had entered the play-room and that there was a bank there. Some were already steadily at work, wearing their gaming jackets, which they kept at the club to put on when they intended to sit down to a regular night's play.

Mr. Warrington went to the clerk's desk, paid his account of the previous night, and, sitting down at the table, called for fresh counters. This had been decidedly an unlucky week with the Fortunate Youth, and tonight was no more fortunate than previous nights. He called for more counters, and more presently. He was a little pale and silent, though very easy and polite when talked to. But he could not win.

At last he got up. "Hang it! stay and mend your luck!" said Lord March, who was sitting by his side with a heap of counters before him, green and white. "Take a hundred of mine, and go on!"

"I have had enough for to-night, my lord," said Harry, and he rose and went away, eating a broiled bone in the coffee-room and walking back to his lodgings some time about midnight. A man after a great catastrophe commonly sleeps pretty well. It is the waking in the morning which is sometimes queer and unpleasant. Last night you proposed to Miss Brown; you quarrelled over your cups with Captain Jones, and valorously pulled his nose; you played at cards with Colonel Robinson, and gave him—oh, how many I O U's! These thoughts, with a fine headache, assail you in the morning watches. What a dreary, dreary gulf between to-day and yesterday! It seems as if you are years older. Can't you leap back over that chasm again, and is it not possible that Yesterday is but a dream? There you are, in bed. No daylight in at the windows yet. Pull your nightcap over your eyes, the blankets over your nose, and sleep away Yesterday. Psha, man, it was but a dream! Oh no, no! The sleep won't come. The watchman bawls some hour—what hour? Harry minded him that he had got the repeating watch under his pillow which he had bought for Hester. *Ting, ting, ting!* the repeating watch sang out six times in the darkness, with a little supplementary performance indicating the half-hour. Poor dear little Hester!—so bright, so gay, so innocent! he would have liked her to have that watch. What will Maria say? (Oh, that old Maria! what a bore she is beginning to be! he thought.) What will Madam Esmond at home say when she hears that he has lost every shilling of his ready money—of his patrimony? All his winnings, and five thousand pounds besides, in three nights. Could Castlewood have played him false? No. My lord knows piquet better than Harry does, but he would not deal unfairly with his own flesh and blood. No, no. Harry was glad his kinsman, who wanted the money, had got it. And for not one more shilling than he possessed, would he play. It was when he counted up his losses at the gaming-table, and found they would cover all the remainder of his patrimony, that he passed the box and left the table. But, O cursed bad company! O extravagance and folly! O humiliation and remorse! "Will my mother at home forgive me?" thought the young prodigal. "Oh, that I were there, and had never left it!"

The dreary London dawn peeped at length through shutters and curtains. The housemaid entered to light his honour's fire and admit the dun morning into his windows. Her Mr. Gumbo presently followed, who warmed his master's dressing-gown and set out his shaving-plate and linen. Then arrived the hairdresser to curl and powder his honour, whilst he read his morning's letters; and at breakfast-time came that inevitable Parson Sampson, with eager looks and servile smiles, to wait on his patron. The parson would have returned yesterday according to mutual agreement, but some jolly fellows had kept him to dinner at the St. Alban's, and, faith, they had made a night of it.

"Oh, Parson!" groaned Harry, "'twas the worst night you ever made in your life! Look here, sir!"

"Here is a broken envelope with the words, 'Much good may it do you,' written within," said the chaplain, glancing at the paper.

"Look on the outside, sir!" cried Mr. Warrington. "The paper was directed to you." The poor chaplain's countenance exhibited great alarm. "Has some one broke it open, sir?" he asked.

"Some one, yes. I broke it open, Sampson. Had you come here as you proposed yesterday afternoon, you would have found that envelope full of bank-notes. As it is, they were all dropped at the infernal macco-table last night."

"What, all?" said Sampson.

"Yes, all, with all the money I brought away from the city, and all the ready money I have left in the world. In the afternoon I played piquet with my cousin—with a gentleman at White's—and he eased me of all the money I had about me. Remembering that there was still some money left here, unless you had fetched it, I came home and carried it back and left it at the macco-table, with every shilling besides that belongs to me—and—great heaven, Sampson, what's the matter, man?"

"It's my luck, it's my usual luck," cried out the unfortunate chaplain, and fairly burst into tears.

"What! You are not whimpering like a baby at the loss of a loan of a couple of hundred pounds?" cried out Mr. Warrington, very fierce and angry. "Leave the room, Gumbo! Confound you! why are you always poking your woolly head

In the theater of human nature, there exists a peculiar species often mocked in fiction yet rarely encountered in reality: the pure religious hypocrite. These are the men who preach endlessly without believing a word of their own sermons, the infidels clad in broad-brimmed hats and sable cloaks who expound, exhort, and condemn with zero faith in their own paradise or fear of their own hell. One need only observe the candid throngs of hobnailed boots clumping toward church on a Sunday evening—the rustling maidservants in ribbons trailed by young apprentices, the little regiments of schoolboys, the trim maidens and staid matrons marching with glistening prayer-books as the chapel bell chinks. Consider them! How many are truly devout? Likely the maid is thinking of her sweetheart; the grocer calculates how to sell his sugar and whether the County Bank will accept his notes; the head boy recites Latin verses for Monday's exercise; the young rogue remembers the pie awaiting him after the sermon; the clerk calling out the psalm thinks of his daughter's troubles and drones through the responses unaware of their meaning; and the very moment the parson hides his face on his cushion, he ponders a bill due on Monday. These people are not heavenly-minded; they are of the world, deeply worldly, with their feet firmly planted upon it. Yet, they are not hypocrites. They possess their religion in a handy mental lock-up—a valuable medicine reserved for illness. A man administers his nostrum to his neighbor, recommending his private cure for the other's complaint. "My dear madam, you have spasms? These drops are infallible!" "You have been taking too much wine, my good sir? This pill will defy any evil consequences, allowing you to drink your port daily." Who are more eager dispensers of spiritual and bodily physic than women? Indeed, a century ago, every lady in the countryside maintained a still-room and medicine chest, stocked with pills, powders, and potions for the entire village.

Lady Warrington assumed charge of the consciences and digestions of her husband's tenants and family. She held the faith and health of the servants' hall in her keeping. Whether Heaven knew she doctor them rightly remains unknown, but whether pill or doctrine, she administered both with equal conviction in her own authority, and her disciples swallowed them obediently. She believed herself to be one of the most virtuous, self-denying, wise, and learned women in the world. By constantly dunning this opinion into the ears of everyone around her, she succeeded in convincing not a few to join her persuasion.

At Sir Miles's dinner, the sideboard of plate was so magnificent and the number of men in livery so great that it required a sharp mind to perceive the beer was of the smallest quality the butler brought in the splendid tankard, and that there was but one joint of mutton on the grand silver dish. When Sir Miles toasted the King's health and smacked his jolly lips over his wine, he eyed it and the company as if the liquor were ambrosia. He asked Harry Warrington if they had port of such quality in Virginia. He claimed it was nothing compared to the wine Harry should taste in Norfolk. He praised the wine so effusively that Harry almost believed it was good, winking into his own glass, trying to discern the merits his uncle perceived in the ruby nectar.

Much like many well-regulated families of the present century, the Warringtons possessed two paragons. Of the two grown daughters, one was the greatest beauty, the other the greatest genius and angel of any young lady alive, as Lady Warrington told Harry. The eldest, the Beauty, was engaged to dear Tom Claypool, a fact the fond mother shared with her cousin Harry in confidence. However, the second daughter, the Genius and Angel, was forever set upon our young friend to improve his wits and morals. She sang to him at the harpsichord—rather out of tune for an angel, Harry thought; she was ready with advice, instruction, and conversation—with almost too much instruction and advice, thought Harry, who would have far preferred the society of the little cousin who reminded him of Fanny Mountain at home. But the last-mentioned young maiden usually retired to her nursery after dinner. Beauty went off on her own avocations; mamma had to attend to her poor health or write her voluminous letters; papa dozed in his armchair; and the Genius remained to keep her young cousin company.

The calm of the house somehow pleased the young man, and he liked to take refuge there away from the riot and dissipation in which he ordinarily lived. Certainly, no welcome could be kinder than that which he received. The doors were opened to him at all hours. If Flora was not at home, Dora was ready to receive him. Within a few days of acquaintance, he and his little cousin Miles had gone for a galloping match in the Park, and Harry, who was kind and generous to every man alive who came near him, had in view the purchase of a little horse for his cousin, far superior to the one the boy rode, when circumstances occurred that brought all our poor Harry's coaches and horses to a sudden breakdown.

Though Sir Miles Warrington had imagined Virginia to be an island, the ladies were much better instructed in geography and anxious to hear from Harry all about his home and native country. He, on his part, was not averse to talking about it. He described to them the length and breadth of his estate, the rivers it coasted, and the produce it bore. Having had a little practice of surveying in his boyhood with a friend, he made a map of his county, marking fine towns here and there, which, in truth, were but log-huts (though, for the honor of his country, he desired they should wear as handsome a look as possible). Here was the Potomac; here was the James River; here were the wharves whence his mother's ships and tobacco were brought to the sea. In truth, the estate was as large as a county. He did not brag about the place overmuch. To see the handsome young fellow, in a fine suit of velvet and silver lace, making his draught, pointing out this hill and that forest or town, one might have imagined him a traveling prince describing the realms of the queen his mother. He almost fancied himself to be so at times. He had miles where gentlemen in England had acres. Not only Dora listened, but the beauteous Flora bowed her fair head and heard him with attention. Why, what was young Tom Claypool, their brother baronet's son in Norfolk, with his great boots, his great voice, and his heirloom to a poor five thousand acres, compared to this young American prince and charming stranger? Angel as she was, Dora began to lose her angelic temper and to twit Flora for being a flirt. Claypool, in his red waistcoat, would sit dumb before the splendid Harry in his ruffles and laces, talking of March and Chesterfield, Selwyn and Bolingbroke, and the whole company of macaronis. Mamma began to love Harry more and more as a son. She was anxious about the spiritual welfare of those poor Indians and those poor negroes in Virginia. What could she do to help dear Madam Esmond, a precious woman she knew, in the good work? She had a serious butler and housekeeper; they were delighted with the spiritual behavior and sweet musical gifts of Gumbo.

"Ah! Harry, Harry! you have been a sad wild boy! Why did you not come sooner to us, sir, and not lose your time amongst the spendthrifts and the vain world? But 'tis not yet too late. We must reclaim thee, dear Harry! Mustn't we, Sir Miles? Mustn't we, Dora? Mustn't we, Flora?"

The three ladies all looked up to the ceiling. They would reclaim the dear prodigal. It was a contest to see which should reclaim him most. Dora sat by and watched Flora. As for mamma, when the girls were away, she talked to him more and more seriously, more and more tenderly. She would be a mother to him in the absence of his own admirable parent. She gave him a hymn-book. She kissed him on the forehead. She was actuated by the purest love, tenderness, and religious regard toward her dear, wayward, wild, amiable nephew.

While these sentimentalities unfolded, it is presumed Mr. Warrington kept his own counsel about his affairs out-of-doors, which we have seen were in the very worst condition. He who had been favored by fortune for so many weeks was suddenly deserted by her, and a few days served to kick down all his heap of winnings. Did we say that my Lord Castlewood, his own kinsman, had dealt unfairly by the young Virginian, robbing him in the course of a couple of afternoons' closet practice? We would insinuate nothing so disrespectful to his lordship's character; but he had won from Harry every shilling which properly belonged to him, and would have played him for his reversions, but that the young man flung up his hands when he saw himself so far beaten, declaring he must continue the battle no more. Remembering that there still remained a spar out of the wreck, as it were—that portion he had set aside for poor Sampson—Harry ventured it at the gaming-table; but that last resource went down along with the rest of Harry's possessions, and Fortune fluttered off in the storm, leaving the luckless adventurer almost naked on the shore.

When a man is young, generous, and hearty, the loss of money scarce afflicts him. Harry would sell his horses and carriages and diminish his train of life. If he wanted immediate supplies of money, would not his Aunt Bernstein be his banker, or his kinsman who had won so much from him, or his kind Uncle Warrington and Lady Warrington, who were always talking virtue and benevolence and declaring they loved him as a son? He would call upon these, or any one of them whom he might choose to favor, at his leisure; meanwhile, Sampson's story of his landlord's distress touched the young gentleman, and, in order to raise a hasty supply for the clergyman, he carried off all his trinkets to a certain pawnbroker's shop in St. Martin's Lane.

Now this broker was a relative or partner of that very Mr. Sparks of Tavistock Street, from whom Harry had purchased—or rather, taken the trinkets he had intended to present to his Oakhurst friends—and it chanced that Mr. Sparks came to visit his brother-tradesman very soon after Mr. Warrington had disposed of his goods. Recognizing immediately the little enamelled diamond-handled repeater which he had sold to the Fortunate Youth, the jeweller broke out into expressions regarding Harry which I will not mention here, being already accused of speaking much too plainly. A gentleman who is acquainted with a pawnbroker may be sure has a bailiff or two amongst his acquaintances; and those bailiffs have followers who, at the bidding of the impartial Law, will touch with equal hand the fiercest captain's epaulet or the finest macaroni's shoulder. The very gentlemen who had seized upon Lady Maria at Tunbridge were set upon her cousin in London.
