They easily learned from the garrulous Gumbo that his honor was at Sir Miles Warrington's house in Hill Street, and whilst the black was courting Mrs. Lambert's maid at the adjoining mansion, Mr. Costigan and his assistant lay in wait for poor Harry, who was enjoying the delights of intercourse with a virtuous family circle assembled round his aunt's table. Never had Uncle Miles been more cordial, never had Aunt Warrington been more gracious, gentle, and affectionate; Flora looked unusually lovely, Dora had been more than ordinarily amiable. At parting, my lady gave him both her hands and called benedictions from the ceiling down upon him. Papa had said in his most jovial manner, "Hang it, nephew! when I was thy age I should have kissed two such fine girls as Do and Flo ere this, and my own flesh and blood too! Don't tell me! I should, my Lady Warrington! Odds-fish! 'tis the boy blushes, and not the girls! I think—I suppose they are used to it. He, he!"

"Papa!" cried the virgins.

"Sir Miles!" said the august mother at the same instant.

"There, there!" said papa. "A kiss won't do no harm, and won't tell no tales: will it, nephew Harry?" I suppose, during the utterance of the above three brief phrases, the harmless little osculatory operation had taken place, and blushing cousin Harry had touched the damask cheeks of cousin Flora and cousin Dora.

As he went downstairs with his uncle, mamma made a speech to the girls, looking, as usual, up to the ceiling, and saying, "What precious qualities your poor dear cousin has! What shrewdness mingled with his simplicity, and what a fine genteel manner, though upon mere worldly elegance I set little store. What a dreadful pity to think that such a vessel should ever be lost! We must rescue him, my loves. We must take him away from those wicked companions, and those horrible Castlewoods—not that I would speak ill of my neighbors. But I shall hope, I shall pray, that he may be rescued from his evil courses!" And again Lady Warrington eyed the cornice in a most determined manner as the girls wistfully looked toward the door behind which their interesting cousin had just vanished.

His uncle would go downstairs with him. He called, "God bless you, my boy!" most affectionately; he pressed Harry's hand and repeated his valuable benediction at the door. As it closed, the light from the hall within having sufficiently illuminated Mr. Warrington's face and figure, two gentlemen, who had been standing on the opposite side of the way, advanced rapidly, and one of them took a strip of paper out of his pocket, putting his hand upon Mr. Warrington's shoulder and declaring him his prisoner. A hackney-coach was in attendance, and poor Harry went to sleep in Chancery Lane.

Oh, to think that a Virginian prince's back should be slapped by a ragged bailiff's follower—that Madam Esmond's son should be in a spunging-house

A profound remorse for his past follies seized Harry Warrington the moment he realized he was a prisoner in that dismal lock-up house, mingled with a sharp wrath at the indignity of arrest. Yet, beneath the present misery, he clung to the certainty that his confinement was merely momentary. He possessed twenty friends who would surely release him; the question remained only to whom he should appeal. There was Mr. Draper, the man of business, who had been so obsequious; his kind uncle, the Baronet, who offered his home as Harry's sanctuary; his cousin Castlewood, who had drained him of so much gold; his noble associates at the Chocolate-House; and his good Aunt Bernstein. Any of these would undoubtedly provide aid, though some might administer a stern scolding for his imprudence. The paramount concern was discretion. Mr. Warrington was anxious that as few members of the public as possible should witness a gentleman of his prodigious importance subjected to such a vulgar process as arrest.

As if the public does not eventually learn everything it cares to know. As if the dinner I shall have today, or the hole in the stocking I wear while writing this, can remain hidden from some prying enemy, even if my boots are on and my door locked! I mention the stocking merely as an example. The world can pry out whatever it wishes to know. But there is a consolation men rarely accept in their own cases: the world does not care. Consider the sheer volume of scandal it has endured; how weary and blasé it must be of such intelligence. You are taken to prison, imagining yourself indelibly disgraced? You are bankrupt under odd circumstances? You strike a queer bargain and are found out, convinced the world will punish you? Psha! Your shame is merely vanity. Go and talk to the world as if nothing had happened. Tumble down, brush the mud from your clothes, appear with a smiling countenance, and nobody cares. Do you suppose Society will produce its pocket-handkerchief and be inconsolable when you die? Why should it care whether your worship graces or disgraces itself? Whatever happens, it talks, meets, jokes, yawns, and dines pretty much as before. Therefore, do not be so conceited as to fancy your private affairs are of such importance, *mi fili*. Yet, Mr. Harry Warrington chafed and fumed as though the entire world was tingling with the touch of the hand that had rested on his sublime shoulder.

"A pretty sensation my arrest must have created at the club!" Harry thought. "I suppose Mr. Selwyn will be cutting all sorts of jokes about my misfortune, plague take him! Everyone round the table will have heard of it. March will tremble about the bet I owe him, and faith, 'twill be difficult to pay him when I lose. They will all be setting up a whoop of congratulation at the Savage, calling me 'the Savage' because I was taken prisoner. How shall I ever appear in the world again? Whom shall I ask to come to my help?" No, he decided with his mingled acuteness and simplicity. He would not write to his relations or his noble friends at White's initially. He required Sampson's counsel. The chaplain had often been in similar predicaments and would know how to advise him.

Accordingly, as soon as the light of dawn appeared—after an almost intolerable delay, for it seemed to Harry as if the sun had forgotten to visit Cursitor Street that morning—and as soon as the inmates of the house of bondage were stirring, Mr. Warrington despatched a messenger to his friend in Long Acre, acquainting the chaplain with the calamity and beseeching his advice and consolation.

Mr. Warrington did not know that sending such a message to the parson was akin to saying, "I am fallen amongst the lions. Come down, my dear friend, into the pit with me." Harry likely thought Sampson's difficulties were over, or was so engrossed in his own perplexities that he bestowed little thought on his neighbor's. Having sent the missive, the captive's mind was somewhat more at ease, and he condescended to call for breakfast. The attendant serving him asked if he would order dinner or dine at Mrs. Bailiff's table with other gentlemen. No. Mr. Warrington would not order dinner. He informed the chamberlain that he intended to quit the place before dinner-time. The man departed, thinking this was not the first young gentleman who had announced such an intention within two hours. "Well, if your honour stays, there is good beef and carrot at two o'clock," the sceptic said, closing the door on Mr. Harry and his solitary meditations.

Harry's messenger returned with a note from Mr. Sampson stating he would arrive as soon as possible. But ten o'clock came, then eleven, then noon, and no Sampson. About twelve, however, Gumbo arrived with a portmanteau of his master's clothes, flinging himself, roaring with grief, at Harry's feet. With a thousand vows of fidelity, he expressed readiness to die, to sell himself into slavery again, to do anything to rescue his beloved Master Harry from this calamitous position. Harry was touched by the lad's affection and told him to rise from the ground where he was groveling. "All you have to do, sir, is give me my clothes to dress, and hold your tongue about this business. Mind you, not a word to anybody!" Mr. Warrington commanded severely.

"Oh no, sir, never to nobody!" Gumbo replied solemnly, proceeding to dress his master carefully. Harry needed a change and a toilette after his sudden capture and dismal night. Gumbo flung a dash of powder into Harry's hair and arrayed him so elegantly that Mr. Warrington looked as fine and splendid as if he were stepping into his chair to go to St. James's.

Indeed, all that love and servility could do, Gumbo faithfully did for his master, whom he held in extreme regard. But there were things beyond Gumbo's power. He could not undo what was already done, nor help lying and excusing himself when pressed on disagreeable points. The language of slaves is lies—I mean both black and white. The creature slinks away and hides with subterfuges, as a hunted animal runs to his covert at the sight of the tyrant. Strange relics of feudality, consequences of our ever-so-old social life! Our domestics (are they not men, too, and brethren?) are all hypocrites before us. They never speak naturally or the whole truth. We should be indignant; we should say, confound their impudence, and turn them out. But *quo me rapis*, O my unbridled hobby?

The truth was, an oath to say not a word about his master's arrest was impossible to keep for Gumbo. With a heart full of grief but a tongue that never ceased wagging, bragging, joking, and lying, he had already announced the woeful circumstance to a prodigious number of acquaintances, chiefly gentlemen of the shoulder-knot and worsted lace. We have seen how he carried the news to Colonel Lambert's and Lord Wrotham's servants; he had proclaimed it at the footman's club frequented by the nobility; he had subsequently partaken of ale in Sir Miles Warrington's butler's room, repeating and embellishing the story. Then he had gone to Madame Bernstein's people, informing that domestic circle of his grief and his master's capture, noting there was no call for his personal services that evening. Finally, he had stepped up to Lord Castlewood's, informing the gentry there of the incident. So, when laying his hand on his heart and with gushing tears, Gumbo replied to his master's injunction, "Oh no, master! nebber to nobody!" we are in a condition to judge the credibility of his statement.

The black had long completed his master's toilet; the dreary breakfast was over. Slow as the hours went to the prisoner, they passed one after another, but no Sampson came. At length, some time after noon, there arrived not Sampson, but a billet from him, sealed with a moist wafer and with the ink almost wet. The unlucky divine's letter ran as follows:

"Oh, sir, dear sir, I have done all that a man can at the command and in the behalf of his patron! You did not know, sir, to what you were subjecting me, did you? Else, if I was to go to prison, why did I not share yours, and why am I in a lock-up house three doors off?

"Yes. Such is the fact. As I was hastening to you, knowing full well the danger to which I was subject:—but what danger will I not affront at the call of such a benefactor as Mr. Warrington hath been to me?—I was seized by two villains who had a writ against me, and who have lodged me at Naboth's, hard by, and so close to your honour, that we could almost hear each other across the garden walls of the respective houses where we are confined.

"I had much and of importance to say, which I do not care to write down on paper regarding your affairs. May they mend! May my cursed fortunes, too, better themselves, is the prayer of—

"Your honour's afflicted Chaplain-in-Ordinary, J. S."

And now, as Mr. Sampson refused to speak, it will be our duty to acquaint the reader with those matters whereof the poor chaplain did not care to discourse on paper.

Gumbo's loquacity had not reached so far as Long Acre, and Mr. Sampson was ignorant of the extent of his patron's calamity until he received Harry's letter and messenger from Chancery Lane. The divine was still ardent with gratitude for the service Mr. Warrington had just conferred on him, and eager to find some means to succour his distressed patron. He knew what a large sum Lord Castlewood had won from his cousin, had dined in company with his lordship the day before, and now ran to Lord Castlewood's house, hoping to arouse him to some pity for Mr. Warrington. Sampson made a very eloquent and touching speech to Lord Castlewood about his kinsman's misfortune, speaking with real kindness and sympathy, which, however, failed to touch the nobleman to whom he addressed himself.

"My lord peevishly and curtly put a stop to the chaplain's passionate pleading. 'Did I not tell you, two days since, when you came for money, that I was as poor as a beggar, Sampson,' said his lordship, 'and has anybody left me a fortune since? The little sum I won from my cousin was swallowed up by others. I not only can't help Mr. Warrington, but, as I pledge you my word, not being in the least aware of his calamity, I had positively written to him this morning to ask him to help me.' And a letter to this effect did actually reach Mr. Warrington from his lodgings, whither it had been despatched by the penny post.

'I must get him money, my lord. I know he had scarcely anything left in his pocket after relieving me. Were I to pawn my cassock and bands, he must have money,' cried the chaplain.

'Amen. Go and pawn your bands, your cassock, anything you please. Your enthusiasm does you credit,' said my lord; and resumed the reading of his paper, whilst, in the deepest despondency, poor Sampson left him.

My Lady Maria meanwhile had heard that the chaplain was with her brother and conjectured the subject of their talk. She seized upon the parson as he issued from his fruitless interview with my lord. She drew him into the dining-room; the strongest marks of grief and sympathy were in her countenance. 'Tell me, what is this has happened to Mr. Warrington?' she asked.

'Your ladyship, then, knows?' asked the chaplain.

'Have I not been in mortal anxiety ever since his servant brought the dreadful news last night?' asked my lady. 'We had it as we came from the opera—from my Lady Yarmouth's box—my lord, my Lady Castlewood, and I.'

'His lordship, then, did know?' continued Sampson.

'Benson told the news when we came from the playhouse to our tea,' repeats Lady Maria.

The chaplain lost all patience and temper at such duplicity. 'This is too bad,' he said, with an oath; and he told Lady Maria of the conversation he had just had with Lord Castlewood, of the latter's refusal to succour his cousin after winning great sums from him, and with much eloquence and feeling, of Mr. Warrington's most generous behaviour to himself.

Then my Lady Maria broke out with a series of remarks regarding her own family, which were by no means complimentary to her own kith and kin. Although not accustomed to tell the truth commonly, yet, when certain families fall out, it is wonderful what a number of truths they will tell about one another. With tears, imprecations, and language stronger than I care to repeat, Lady Maria burst into a furious and impassioned tirade, touching upon the history of almost all her noble family. She complimented the men and ladies alike; she shrieked out interrogatories to Heaven, inquiring why it had made such [she named her brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, parents]; and, emboldened with wrath, she dashed at her brother's library door, so shrill in her outcries, so furious in her demeanour, that the alarmed chaplain, fearing the scene which might ensue, made for the street.

My lord, looking up from his book, regarded the furious woman with some surprise and selected a good strong oath to fling at her to check her onset.

But, when roused, we have seen how courageous Maria could be. Afraid as she was ordinarily of her brother, she was not in a mood to be frightened now by any language of abuse or sarcasm at his command.

"So, my lord!" she called out, "you sit down with him in private to cards, and pigeon him! You get the poor boy's last shilling, and

The generous and compassionate nature of Mr. Gumbo had succeeded in softening the storm within his master's heart. Harry's second night in the spunging-house was less bitter than the first, for at least one soul remained to offer aid and pity. Yet, this single thread of kindness could not mend the fabric of his spirit. Towards the rest of the world, Harry's heart remained iron-hard and proud. He viewed them all—his pious Aunt Warrington, his lordly friend March, his cynical cousin Castlewood—as selfish and ungenerous failures. He had tested them all and found them wanting. He would not stoop to beg another favor from any of them, nor would he endure twenty years of prison for their sake. He was a fool, he thought bitterly, to have believed their empty promises and trusted in their feigned friendship. There was no friendship in this cold, cursed country, only transaction and betrayal.

He resolved to leave. He would trust no Englishman, whether great or small. His mind raced with escape routes: he might go to Germany to fight alongside the King, or return to Virginia to bury himself in the wilderness, hunting all day and becoming his mother's mere factor and land-steward. He would marry Polly Broadbent or Fanny Mountain, turn to the soil as a tobacco grower, and do anything rather than remain among these English "fine gentlemen." Thus, he rose with a cheerful mask upon his face, though his spirit burned with anger.

Early in the morning, the faithful Gumbo appeared in his master's chamber, having traveled from Bond Street. "I sought to bring more clothes, sir," the honest black man said, "but Mr. Ruff, the landlord, refused to let me take any more."

Harry showed no interest in the letters Gumbo carried. He opened one, then two, then three; they were all demands for payment. A fourth revealed the landlord's ultimatum: no more of Mr. Warrington's belongings would leave the house until the bill was settled, or else the goods would be sold and the black man forced to sleep elsewhere. Harry hesitated to let Gumbo remove his own clothes and portmanteau. The servant explained he had found refuge with friends at Lord Wrotham's house.

"With Colonel Lambert's people," Gumbo observed, his eyes searching his master's face intently. "And Miss Hetty fainted when she heard you were taken up. Mr. Lambert is a good man; he told me this morning that if you need him, I should tell you to send for him, and he would come."

Harry felt a pang of gratitude hearing that Hetty had been distressed by his misfortune. He did not fully believe Gumbo's account of her fainting, accustomed as he was to filtering his servant's speech for exaggeration. But when Gumbo mentioned the Colonel, the young Virginian's spirit darkened anew. "I shall send for Lambert," he thought, grinding his teeth. "The man who insulted me and threw my gifts back in my face! Even if I were starving, I would not ask him for a crust!"

Dressed and ready for breakfast, Mr. Warrington summoned Gumbo to deliver a brief note to Mr. Draper in the Temple, demanding the attorney's immediate attendance.

"The note was written with the haughtiness of a lord addressing a serf, not a freeborn English gentleman," Draper remarked later, though he had always tolerated Harry's insufferable condescension. "It is all very well for a fine gentleman to give himself airs, but for a fellow in a spunging-house? Hang him! I have a mind not to go." Nevertheless, Mr. Draper complied. He found Mr. Warrington in his misfortune even more arrogant than in the days of his utmost prosperity. The young man sat upon his bed like a monarch, draped in a splendid gown with his hair meticulously dressed, motioning for a chair for his servant.

"Excuse me, madam, but such haughtiness and airs I am not accustomed to!" the outraged attorney declared.

"Take a chair and proceed with your story, my good Mr. Draper!" Madame de Bernstein smiled, amused by the lawyer's indignation. She delighted in her nephew's insolence in adversity.

The course of action Draper was to pursue had been arranged the previous day between the Baroness and her man of business. Draper was an able man, usually capable of serving a client well, but he failed here, piqued by anger or simply unable to comprehend the gentleman he faced. One might say that the reader, being gentle, has perhaps noticed how non-gentlemen offend those who are, without understanding why. They do or say something that provokes scorn; the offender perceives this scorn, rages, and interprets natural speech as sneering indifference.

"Gumbo, fetch a chair for Mr. Draper!" Mr. Warrington commanded, folding his brocaded dressing gown around his legs as he sat on the dingy bed. "Sit down, if you please, and let us discuss my business. Much obliged for coming so promptly. Have you heard of this ill-luck?"

Draper had heard. "Bad news travels quickly, Mr. Warrington," he replied. "I was eager to offer my humble services the moment you required them. Your friends and family will be deeply pained that a gentleman of your rank should be in such a position."

"I have been imprudent, Mr. Draper. I have lived beyond my means." (Draper bowed.) "I gambled with gentlemen much richer than myself, and a cursed run of bad luck has carried away all my ready money, leaving me with liabilities exceeding five hundred pounds."

"Five hundred pounds currently in the office," Draper noted gravely.

"Well, this is such a trifling sum that I thought by contacting one or two friends yesterday, I could have paid my debt and gone home without further ado. I was mistaken. I shall thank you to assist me in raising the funds as soon as possible."

Draper made a sound of disapproval and pulled a long, grave face.

"Why, sir, it can be done!" Mr. Warrington stared at the lawyer, expecting agreement.

Indeed, it could be done. Draper had proposed to Madame Bernstein the day before to pay the money instantly and release Mr. Warrington. The lady had declared her intention to make the young gentleman her heir. Like everyone else, Draper believed Harry's hereditary property in Virginia to be vast in both value and extent. He held notes in his pocket and the Baroness's order to pay them under specific conditions. Yet, when Harry declared, "It can be done!" Draper's face lengthened. "It can be done in time, sir; but it will require considerable time. To access the property in England belonging to Mr. George Warrington upon his death, we must prove the event and release the trustees. Who will do either? Lady Esmond Warrington in Virginia, of course, will not allow her son to remain in prison, but we must wait six months for her response. Does your Bristol agent have authority to honor your drafts?"

"He is authorized to pay me only two hundred pounds a year," said Mr. Warrington. "I suppose I have no resource but to apply to my aunt, Madame de Bernstein. She will be my security."

"Her ladyship will do anything for you, sir; she has said so often," the lawyer assured him. "If she gives the word at this moment, you can walk out of this place."

"Then go to her, Mr. Draper. I did not wish to trouble my relations, but rather than continue in this horrible, needless imprisonment, I must speak to her. Tell her where I am and what has befallen me. Disguise nothing! Tell her I confide in her affection and kindness to release me from this... this disgrace," Mr. Warrington's voice trembling slightly as he wiped his eyes.

"Sir," Draper said, eyeing the young man, "I was with her ladyship yesterday when we discussed this most unpleasant business."

"What do you mean, sir? Does Madame de Bernstein know of my misfortune?" Harry asked.

"Every circumstance, sir; including the pawning of the watches and all."

Harry turned a burning red. "It is an unfortunate business, the pawning of watches and things you had never paid for," the lawyer continued. The young man sprang up from the bed, looking so fierce that Draper felt a flicker of alarm.

"It may lead to litigation and unpleasant remarks in court, sir. Those barristers respect nothing; and when they get a fellow in the box—"

"Great Heaven, sir, you do not suppose a gentleman of my rank cannot take a watch on credit without intending to cheat the tradesman?" Harry cried, agitated.

"Of course you meant everything honorable; only, the law may not think so," Draper winked. ("Hang the supercilious beast; I touch him there!") "Your aunt says it is the most imprudent thing she has ever heard of—to call it by no worse name."

"You call it by no worse name yourself, Mr. Draper?" Harry asked, speaking slowly, trying to maintain command of himself.

Draper disliked his looks. "Heaven forbid I should say anything between gentlemen—but between me and my client, it is my duty to say, 'Sir, you are in a very unpleasant scrape,' just as a doctor would tell his patient, 'Sir, you are very ill.'"

"And you cannot help me pay this debt, coming only to tell me I may be accused of roguery?" Harry demanded.

"Of obtaining goods under false pretenses? Most undoubtedly, yes. I cannot help it, sir. Do not look as if you will knock me down. A young gentleman with only two hundred a year from his mother orders diamonds and watches and takes them to a pawnbroker. You ask me what people will think, and I tell you honestly. Do not be angry, Mr. Warrington."

"Go on, sir!" Harry groaned.

The lawyer thought the day was his own. "But you ask if I cannot help pay this debt? And I say Yes—and here is the money in my pocket to do it now, if you like—not mine, sir, but my honored client's, your aunt, Lady Bernstein. However, she has a right to impose conditions, and I have brought them."

"Tell them, sir," Harry said.

"They are not hard. They are for your own good. If you agree, we can call a hackney coach and go to Clarges Street together, which I have promised to do regardless. Mr. Warrington, I name no names, but there was a question of marriage between you and a certain party."

"Ah!" Harry's countenance brightened.

"To that marriage my noble client, the Baroness, is most averse—having other views for you and believing it will be your ruin to marry a party of noble birth and title, yet, excuse me, not of first-rate character and much older than yourself. You had given an imprudent promise to that party."

"Yes; and she has it still," Harry admitted.

"It has been recovered. She dropped it by accident at Tunbridge," Draper explained. "My client informed me; indeed, her ladyship showed it to me. It was written in blue ink—"

"Never mind, sir!" Harry cried, turning almost as red as the ink he had used to write his absurd promise, the madness and folly of which had smote him a thousand times with shame.

"At the same time, letters compromising a noble family were recovered," the lawyer continued. "You had lost them. It was no fault of yours; you were away when they were found again. You may say that that noble family, and yourself, have a friend such as few young men possess. Well, sir, there is no earthly promise binding you—only idle words spoken over a bottle, which any gentleman may forget. Say you will not proceed with this marriage—give me and my noble friend your word of honor. Cry off, Mr. W.! Do not be such a fool, saving your presence, as to marry an old woman who has jilted scores of men in her time. Say the word, and I will step downstairs, pay every shilling owed in the office, and put you in my coach, either at your aunt's or at White's Club, with two hundred pounds in your pocket. Say yes; give us your hand! There is no use sitting grinning behind these bars all day!"

Thus far, Mr. Draper had dominated the conversation. Harry merely longed to be rid of the engagement from which his aunt wished to free him. His foolish flame for Maria Esmond had died long ago. If she would release him, how thankful he would be! "Come! Give us your hand and say done!" the lawyer urged with a knowing wink. "Do not stand shilly-shallying, sir. Law bless you, Mr. W., if I had married everyone I promised, I should be like the Grand Turk or Captain Macheath in the play!"

The lawyer's familiarity disgusted Harry, who shrank from Draper, scarcely realizing he was doing so. He folded his dressing gown tighter and stepped back from the proffered hand. "Give me a little time to think of the matter, if you please, Mr. Draper," he said. "Have the goodness to come to me again in an hour."

"Very good, sir, very good, sir!" the lawyer bit his lips, turning red as he seized his hat. "Most parties would not want an hour to consider such an offer. But I suppose my time must be yours. I will come again to see whether you are to go or stay. Good morning, sir, good morning," and he descended the stairs, growling curses beneath his breath. "Won't take my hand, won't he? Will tell me in an hour! Hang his impudence! I'll show him what an hour is!"

Draper returned to his chambers in a dudgeon, bullied his clerks, sent a messenger to the Baroness reporting that the young gentleman had demanded time for consideration—a formality, he was sure—and then saw clients and dined leisurely. Finally, he turned toward Cursitor Street. "He'll be at home when I call, the ha

Mr. Draper, still seething with the indignity of his morning's confrontation with Harry, fancied he heard the young prisoner muttering behind him. In truth, Harry had risen, a half-sob caught in his throat to summon the lawyer back. But pride was a heavy armor for the young man; he checked his words, and Draper, offended, refused to halt. To humble himself before the lawyer, to yield solely because of a lack of coin, wounded Harry's spirit deeply. "An hour hence will suffice," he muttered, sinking sulkily back onto the bed.

"No," he whispered to the empty room, "I do not care for Maria Esmond!" The shame of his entrapment burned hotter than any anger. That woman, cunning and seasoned, had preyed upon his boyish ardor, exploiting him just as her brother had exploited him at the gaming table. They were his own flesh and blood, yet they had betrayed the sanctity of hospitality, turning the trusting kinsman into a victim for their selfish ends. His heart felt bruised, his head fell back against the pillow, and bitter tears soaked the linen. "Had they come to Virginia," he thought, his voice breaking, "I would have offered them a different welcome!"

This despondency was shattered by the grinning face of Gumbo at the door. "A lady has come to see Master Harry," the servant announced. Behind him stood the lady in the capuchin, the very woman they had just discussed. Harry sat up, pale and haggard. The lady, overcome with emotion, rushed toward the prisoner before the servant could retreat. With a sob, she threw her arms around his neck, embracing him with a maternal tenderness that pierced the gloom of the cell. She sobbed over his feverish cheek, kissing it amidst a flood of tears.

"Oh, my Harry! Did I ever, ever think to see thee here?"

Harry recoiled, startled by her sudden presence, but she sank to her knees beside the bed, seizing his burning hand and clutching his knees. There was genuine regard in her eyes; the wretched state of her kinsman filled her heart with sincere pity.

"I—I thought none of you would come!" Harry groaned.

More tears, more kisses of his hot young hand, more desperate clasps were her reply for a moment.

"Oh, my dear! My dear! I cannot bear to think of thee in misery!" she sobbed.

Though hardened by circumstance, her heart was not entirely stone; her life was not a barren desert. Her love for him surpassed even that of his own mother, her tones more tender than any he had known.

"Some of these debts," she confessed, her voice trembling, "were owing to my own extravagance! You bought trinkets and jewels to please me. Oh, how I hate them now! I little thought I could ever feel such regret! I have brought them all with me, and more—here! And here! And every guinea I possess in the world!"

She poured a cascade of brooches, rings, a watch, and a score of gold coins into Harry's lap. The sight stirred him profoundly, touching him to his core.

"Dearest, kindest cousin!" he sobbed.

His lips failed him, yet his expression spoke volumes of gratitude and affection. Soon, a strange light returned to his eyes. He smiled as he sorted through the gifts, planning which trinkets to send to Maria, and recounted the peril he had fallen into by selling goods on credit, and how the lawyer had just insulted him over it. He would not accept Maria's money—he had enough for the present—but he valued her twenty guineas as if they were twenty thousand. He vowed never to forget her kindness; it had buoyed him when he stood on the brink of total despair. He must tell his mother of her goodness. Heaven bless her for it!

The dark day seemed brighter after Maria's visit; the imprisonment felt less crushing. The world was not entirely cold and selfish. Here was a creature who truly loved him. Even Castlewood was not as terrible as he had imagined. He expressed profound grief at his inability to assist his kinsman, noting that the Baron was hopelessly in debt, losing every shilling he won the next day. Yet, he promised to do anything in his power. He would soon see Mr. Warrington, who was currently in waiting, a prisoner just as Harry was. Thus, the cousins conversed cheerfully and affectionately until twilight deepened. Then, with a sigh, Maria took her leave.

Scarcely had the door closed upon her when it swung open again to admit Draper.

"Your humble servant, sir," the attorney said. His voice grated on Harry's nerves, his presence an affront.

"I had expected you some hours ago, sir," Harry replied curtly.

"A lawyer's time is not always his own, sir," Draper retorted, having just consulted with a bottle of port at the Grecian. "Never mind, I am at your orders now. Presume it is settled, Mr. Warrington? Packed your trunk? Why, you are still in your bedgown. Let me go down and finalize matters while you summon your black man to freshen up. I have a coach at the door, and we shall dine with the old lady."

"Are you going to dine with the Baroness de Bernstein, pray?"

"Not me—no such honor. I have already eaten. It is you who are dining with your aunt, I suppose?"

"Mr. Draper, you suppose far more than you know," Mr. Warrington said, his voice fierce and tall as he wrapped his brocade dressing-gown tighter.

"Good heavens, sir, what do you mean?" Draper asked, confused.

"I mean, sir, that I have given my word to a faithful and honorable lady, and it does not become me to withdraw it."

"Confound it, sir!" shrieked the lawyer. "I tell you she has lost the paper! There is nothing binding you—nothing! Why, she is old enough to be—"

"Enough, sir!" Mr. Warrington stamped his foot. "You seem to think you are speaking to some other pettifogger. I take it, Mr. Draper, you are not accustomed to dealing with men of honor."

"Pettifogger, indeed!" Draper cried, his face purple with rage. "Men of honor, indeed! Let me inform you, Mr. Warrington, that I am as good a man of honor as you. I may not know so many gamblers and horse-jockeys. I have not gambled away my patrimony, nor lived as a nobleman on two hundred a year. I have not bought watches on credit and pawned them—touch me if you dare, sir!" The lawyer lunged for the door.

"That is the way out, sir. You cannot go through the window, for it is barred," Mr. Warrington said calmly.

"And the answer I take to my client is No, then!" Draper screamed.

Harry stepped forward, fists clenched. "If you utter another word," he warned, "I'll—" The door slammed shut before he could finish, and Draper departed in a fury to Madame de Bernstein. Though he delivered the most damning version of his story, he received only fiercer language from the Baroness than he had from Mr. Warrington himself.

"What? Shall she trust me, and I desert her?" Harry paced his room, his brocade gown rustling loudly. "Dear, faithful, generous woman! If I lie in prison for years, I shall remain true to her."

Once the lawyer was dismissed after the stormy interview, the desolate old woman was forced to sit down to the meal she had hoped to share with her nephew. The chair remained empty before her, the glasses gleaming beside the silver. Dish after dish was placed before her by the silent major-domo, tasted, and pushed away. Finally, the man pressed his mistress. "It is eight o'clock," he said. "You have eaten nothing all day. It is good for you to eat." She could not eat. She demanded coffee. Let Case fetch it. The lacquies cleared the table, leaving their mistress sitting alone before the vacant chair.

Soon, the old servant re-entered without the coffee, his face etched with strange fear. "Mr. WARRINGTON!" he cried.

The old woman gasped, rising from her armchair only to sink back, trembling violently. "So you are come, sir, are you?" she asked, her voice shaking. "Bring back the—Ah!" She screamed, "Gracious God, who is it?" Her eyes widened in wild terror; her white face looked ghastly beneath her rouge. Clinging to the arms of her chair for support, she watched as the visitor approached.

A gentleman entered whose face and figure were strikingly identical to Harry Warrington, his voice carrying tones strangely familiar. He bowed to the Baroness.

"You expected my brother, madam?" he said. "I have only just arrived in London. I went to his house and met his servant at your door, bearing this letter for you. I thought I would deliver it to your ladyship before proceeding to him," he added, placing a letter before Madame Bernstein.

"Are you"—the Baroness gasped—"are you my nephew, that we supposed was—?"

"Was killed—and is alive! I am George Warrington, madam. I ask your kinsfolk, what have you done with my brother?"

"Look, George!" the bewildered old lady exclaimed. "I expected him here tonight—that chair was set for him! I have waited for him, sir, until now, until I am quite faint. I do not like—I do not like being alone. Do stay and sup with me!"

"Pardon me, madam. Please God, my supper will be with Harry tonight!"

"Bring him back! Bring him back here on any conditions! It is but five hundred pounds! Here is the money, sir, if you need it!"

"I have no want, madam. I carry money that can be employed nowhere better than in my brother's service."

"And you will bring him to me, sir! Say you will bring him to me!"

Mr. Warrington made a stately bow in reply and left the room, passing the amazed domestics and calling with an air of authority for Gumbo to follow him.

Had Mr. Harry received no letters from home? Master Harry had not opened all his correspondence in the last day or two. Had he received no letter announcing his brother's escape from the French settlements and return to Virginia? Oh, no! No such letter had come; otherwise, Master Harry certainly would have told Gumbo. Quick, horses! Quick to the Strand, to Temple Bar! Here comes the house of Captivity and the Deliverer to the rescue!

The hackney-coach horses flew with a frantic, rattling speed, tearing George Warrington through the Strand and Fleet Street toward the rescue of his imprisoned brother. To any who recall Hogarth's grim depictions of London's thoroughfares in that era, the weariness of the journey is palpable: scarce a light save those held by link-boys, coaches poorly hung, pavements treacherous, and vast quagmires of winter mud swallowing the wheels. The drive from Piccadilly to Fleet Street stretched before the young man as endlessly as the road from Marlborough to London had that morning.

George had written to Harry announcing his arrival in Bristol, and previously, he had penned the great news of his existence and his return from captivity. Yet, war raged between England and France; French privateers were ever on the lookout, seizing British merchant-ships often within sight of port. The letter bearing intelligence of George's restoration must have fallen into the hands of one of the many American vessels captured by the French. The missive telling of George's arrival in England remained unopened by poor Harry. It lay undisturbed in his apartments, reaching him on the third morning after his captivity, only to be ignored when the angry Mr. Ruff refused to surrender a single item of his lodger's property.

It was to these very apartments that George first went upon his arrival in London, seeking his brother. The maid-servant who opened the door screamed at the likeness between the two men and fled back to her mistress. The mistress, unwilling to own that poor Harry was actually a prisoner at her husband's suit, lied, claiming Mr. Warrington had simply left his lodgings. George knew Clarges Street was near Bond Street; he had studied the London map often. Aunt Bernstein would tell him where Harry was. Perhaps she held him at that very moment. George recalled Harry's letters to Virginia detailing Aunt Bernstein's kindness. Even Madam Esmond had been softened by it, particularly by a letter from the Baroness that had once driven George post-haste to Europe. He hoped and trusted that Madam Beatrix had found occasion to repent of her former ways; it was time, indeed, at her age, though Heaven knew she had much to repent of. There were harmless souls of eighty still stoned by irreproachable ladies for slips made centuries prior, yet Rachel Esmond never mentioned her eldest daughter, and Madam Esmond Warrington never mentioned her sister. In spite of the order for remission of the sentence, there remained a crime some folks never would pardon, regarding which female virtue, especially, was inexorable.

Perhaps the Virginians' agent at Bristol had told George fearful stories of his brother's doings. Gumbo, whom he met at his aunt's door, had stammered out a few words of his young master's whereabouts and pitiable condition once the lad recovered from his terror at the sudden reappearance of the master he supposed dead. Hence, Mr. George's stern demeanor when he presented himself to the old lady. It seemed to him a matter of course that his brother in difficulty should be rescued by his relations. Oh, George, how little you know about London and London ways! Whenever you take your walks abroad, how many poor you meet—if a philanthropist were to rescue all of them, not all the wealth of all the provinces of America would suffice him!

Yet, the feeling and agitation displayed by the old lady touched her nephew's heart as George jolted through the dark streets toward the house of his brother's captivity. "She does feel my poor Harry's misfortune," he thought to himself, "I have been too hasty in judging her." Again and again in his life, Mr. George had to rebuke himself for the crime of being too hasty. How many of us have not? And alas, the mischief done, there is no repentance that can mend it. "Quick, coachman!" he urged. "We are almost as slow as you are in getting from Clarges Street to the Temple." Poor Gumbo knew the way to the bailiff's house well enough.

Again the bell rang. The first door opened to George and his negro, then locked warily upon them, leaving them in a little passage with a little Jewish janitor. A second door unlocked, and they entered the house. The janitor stared, his flaring tallow-torch illuminating a second Mr. Warrington. "Come to see that gentleman?" he asked. "Yes. But wait a moment. This is Mr. Warrington's brother from America. Gumbo must go and prepare his master first. Step into this room. There's a gentleman already there about Mr. W.'s business, and another upstairs with him now. There's no end of people who have been about him."

The room into which George was introduced was a small apartment known as Mr. Amos's office. By a guttering candle and the light of the porter, a stout gentleman in a cloak and laced hat sat talking to the bailiff. The young porter carried his candle, preceding Mr. George, ensuring sufficient light.

"We are not angry any more, Harry!" the stout gentleman said in a cheery voice, rising and advancing with an outstretched hand to the newcomer. "Thank God, my boy! Mr. Amos here says there will be no difficulty about James and me being your bail, and we will do your business by breakfast-time. Why... Angels and ministers of grace! Who are you?" He started back as the other grasped his hand.

But the stranger held it more strongly. "God bless you, sir!" he said. "I know who you are. You must be Colonel Lambert, of whose kindness to him my poor Harry wrote. And I am the brother whom you have heard of, sir; who was left for dead in Mr. Braddock's action; and came to life again after eighteen months amongst the French; and live to thank God and thank you for your kindness to my Harry," the lad continued with a faltering voice.

"James! James! Here is news!" cried Mr. Lambert to a gentleman in red who now entered the room. "Here are the dead come alive! Here is Harry Scapegrace's brother come back, and with his scalp on his head, too!" George had taken his hat off and stood by the light. "This is my brother-bail, Mr. Warrington! This is Lieutenant-Colonel James Wolfe, at your service. You must know there has been a little difference between Harry and me, Mr. George. He is pacified, is he, James?"

"He is full of gratitude," said Mr. Wolfe, bowing to Mr. Warrington.

"Harry wrote home about Mr. Wolfe, too, sir," said the young man. "And I hope my brother's friends will be so kind as to be mine."

"I wish he had none other but us, Mr. Warrington. Poor Harry's fine folks have been too fine for him, and have ended by landing him here."

"Nay, your honours, I have done my best to make the young gentleman comfortable; and, knowing your honour before, when you came to bail Captain Watkins, and that your security is perfectly good—if your honour wishes, the young gentleman can go out this very night, and I will make it all right with the lawyer in the morning," said Harry's landlord, recognizing the rank and respectability of the two gentlemen offering bail.

"The debt is five hundred and odd pounds, I think?" said Mr. Warrington. "With a hundred thanks to these gentlemen, I can pay the amount at this moment into the officers' hands, taking the usual acknowledgment and caution. But I can never forget, gentlemen, that you helped my brother at his need, and, for doing so, I say thank you, and God bless you, in my mother's name and mine."

Meanwhile, Gumbo had gone upstairs to his master's apartment. Harry would probably have scolded the negro for returning that night, but the young gentleman was very much soothed and touched by the conversation he had had with the friend who had just left him. He sat over his pipe of Virginia in a sad mood; somehow, even Maria's goodness and affection, as she had just exhibited them, had not altogether consoled him. He had thought, with a little dismay, of certain consequences to which that very kindness and fidelity bound him. Then Mr. Wolfe's homely features and eager outstretched hand came to cheer the prisoner. He heard how Mr. Lambert was below and the errand upon which the two officers had come. In spite of himself, Lambert would be kind to him. In spite of Harry's ill-temper, needless suspicion, and anger, the good gentleman was determined to help him if he might—even against Mr. Wolfe's own advice.

"For you were wrong, Mr. Warrington," said the Colonel. "And you wouldn't be set right; and you, a young man, used hard words and unkind behaviour to your senior, and what is more, one of the best gentlemen who walks God's earth. You see, sir, what his answer hath been to your wayward temper. Will you bear with a friend who speaks frankly with you? Martin Lambert hath acted in this as he always doth, as the best Christian, the best friend, the most kind and generous of men. Nay, if you want another proof of his goodness, here it is: He has converted me, who, as I don't care to disguise, was angry with you for your treatment of him, and has absolutely brought me down here to be your bail. Let us both cry *Peccavimus*! Harry, and shake our friend by the hand! He is sitting in the room below. He would not come here till he knew how you would receive him."

"I think he is a good man!" groaned out Harry. "I was very angry and wild at the time when he and I met last, Colonel Wolfe. Nay, perhaps he was right in sending back those trinkets, hurt as I was at his doing so. Go down to him, will you be so kind, sir? and tell him I am sorry, and ask his pardon, and—and, God bless him for his generous behaviour." And here the young gentleman turned his head away, rubbing his hand across his eyes.

"Tell him all this thyself, Harry!" cried the Colonel, taking the young fellow's hand. "No deputy will ever say it half so well. Come with me now."

"You go first, and I'll—I'll follow,—on my word I will. See! I am in my morning-gown! I will but put on a coat and come to him. Give him my message first. Just—just prepare him for me!" said poor Harry, who knew he must do it, but yet did not much like that process of eating humble-pie.

Wolfe went out smiling, understanding the lad's scruples well enough. As he opened the door, Mr. Gumbo entered; almost forgetting to bow to the gentleman, profusely courteous as he was on ordinary occasions, his eyes glaring round, his great mouth grinning, himself in a state of such high excitement and delight that his master remarked his condition.

"What, Gum? What has happened to thee? Hast thou got a new sweetheart?"

"No, Gum had not got no new sweetheart, master."

"Give me my coat. What has brought thee back?"

Gum grinned prodigiously. "I have seen a ghost, mas'r!" he said.

"A ghost! And whose, and where?"

"Whar? Saw him at Madame Bernstein's house. Come with him here in the coach! He downstairs now with Colonel Lambert!" Whilst Gumbo spoke, putting on his master's coat, his eyes rolled, his head wagged, his hands trembled, and his lips grinned.

"Ghost—what ghost?" said Harry, in a strange agitation. "Is anybody—is—my mother come?"

"No, sir; no, Master Harry!" Gumbo's head rolled nearly off its violent convolutions, and his master, looking oddly at him, flung the door open and went rapidly down the stairs.

He was at the foot of them just as a voice within the little office, of which the door was open, was saying, "and for doing so, I say thank you, and God bless you, in my mother's name and mine."

"Whose voice is that?" called out Harry Warrington, with a strange cry in his own voice.

"It's the ghost's, mas'r!" said Gumbo from behind; and Harry ran forward to the room. There, if you please, we will pause a little minute before we enter. The two gentlemen who were there turned their heads away. The lost was found again. The dead was alive. The prodigal was on his brother's heart—his own full of love, gratitude, repentance.

"Come away, James! I think we are not wanted any more here," said the Colonel. "Good-night, boys. Some ladies in Hill Street won't be able to sleep for this strange news. Or will you go home and sup with 'em, and tell them the story?"

No, with many thanks, the boys would not go and sup that night. They had stories of their own to tell. "Quick, Gumbo, with the trunks! Good-bye, Mr. Amos!" Harry felt almost unhappy when he went away.

When we were first presented to Sir Miles Warrington at the King's drawing-room in St. James's Palace, I confess that I, for one, gazing upon his jovial rotund face, his broad waistcoat, and his hearty, rustic manner, expected to have finally found an eligible and agreeable acquaintance. I was prepared to become intimate with that noblest specimen of the human race, the bepraised subject of songs and men: the good old English country gentleman. In truth, to be a good old country gentleman is to occupy a station nearest the gods, the summit of earthly felicity. To possess a large, unencumbered rent-roll, collected regularly by adoring farmers who bless their stars for such a landlord; to have no tenant withhold payment save perhaps one, solely to provide an occasion for the Good Old Country Gentleman to display his sublime charity and universal benevolence; to hunt three days a week, love the sport above all else, and maintain perfect health and appetite in consequence; to enjoy not only a good appetite but a good dinner; to sit in church amidst a chorus of blessings from the villagers, the first man in the parish, the benefactor of the parish, with a consciousness of consummate desert, saying, "Have mercy upon us, miserable sinners," merely for form's sake, because the words are written in the book, and to set an example—a G.O.C.G., a miserable sinner! So healthy, so wealthy, so jolly, so respected by the vicar, so honoured by the tenants, so beloved and admired by his family, amongst whom his stories of grouse in the gunroom cause laughter from generation to generation—this perfect being, a miserable sinner! Allons donc! Give any man good health and temper, five thousand a year, the adoration of his parish, and the love and worship of his family, and I defy you to make him so heartily dissatisfied with his spiritual condition as to set himself down a miserable anything. If you were a Royal Highness, attending church in perfect health and comfort, with the parson waiting to begin the service until your arrival, would you believe yourself a miserable creature? You might only when racked with gout, in solitude, the fear of death before your eyes, the doctor having cut off your bottle of claret and ordered arrowroot and a little sherry; you might then be humiliated, acknowledging your own shortcomings and the vanity of things. But in high health, sunshine, and spirits, that word "miserable" is only a form. You cannot think in your heart that you are to be pitied much for the present. If you are to be miserable, what is Colin Ploughman, with the ague, seven children, two pounds a year rent to pay for his cottage, and eight shillings a week? No: a healthy, rich, jolly country gentleman, if miserable, has a very supportable misery; if a sinner, has very few people to tell him so.

It may be he becomes somewhat selfish; but at least he is satisfied with himself. Except my lord at the castle, there is nobody for miles and miles round so good or so great. His admirable wife ministers to him and to the whole parish; his children bow before him; the vicar reverences him; he is respected at quarter-sessions; he causes poachers to tremble; off go all hats before him at market; and round about his great coach, in which his spotless daughters and sublime lady sit, all the country-town tradesmen cringe, bareheaded, and the farmers' wives drop innumerable curtseys. From their cushions in the great coach, the ladies look down beneficently, smiling on the poorer folk. They buy a yard of ribbon with affability; they condescend to purchase an ounce of salts or a packet of flower-seeds; they deign to cheapen a goose. Their drive is like a royal progress; a happy people is supposed to press round them and bless them. Tradesmen bow, farmers' wives bob, town-boys, waving their ragged hats, cheer the red-faced coachman as he drives the fat bays, crying, "Sir Miles for ever! Throw us a halfpenny, my lady!"

But suppose the market-woman should hide her fat goose when Sir Miles's coach comes, out of terror lest my lady, spying the bird, should insist on purchasing it at a bargain? Suppose no coppers ever come out of the royal coach window? Suppose Sir Miles regales his tenants with notoriously small beer and his poor with especially thin broth? This may be our fine old English gentleman's way. There have been not a few fine English gentlemen and ladies of this sort; who patronized the poor without ever relieving them, who called out "Amen!" at church as loud as the clerk; who went through all the forms of piety and discharged all the etiquette of old English gentlemanhood; who bought virtue a bargain, as it were, and had no doubt they were honouring her by the purchase. Poor Harry in his distress asked help from his relations; his aunt sent him a tract and her blessing; his uncle had business out of town and could not, of course, answer the poor boy's petition. How much of this behaviour goes on daily in respectable life, think you? You can fancy Lord and Lady Macbeth concocting a murder, and coming together with some little awkwardness, perhaps, when the transaction was done and over; but my Lord and Lady Skinflint, when they consult in their bedroom about giving their luckless nephew a helping hand, and determine to refuse, and go down to family prayers, and meet their children and domestics, and discourse virtuously before them, and then remain together, and talk nose to nose—what can they think of one another? And of the poor kinsman fallen among the thieves, and groaning for help unheeded? How can they go on with those virtuous airs? How can they dare look each other in the face?

Dare? Do you suppose they think they have done wrong? Do you suppose Skinflint is tortured with remorse at the idea of the distress which called to him in vain, and of the hunger which he sent empty away? Not he. He is indignant with Prodigal for being a fool; he is not ashamed of himself for being a curmudgeon. What? A young man with such opportunities throw them away? A fortune spent amongst gamblers and spendthrifts? Horrible, horrible! Take warning, my child, by this unfortunate young man's behaviour, and see the consequences of extravagance. According to the great and always Established Church of the Pharisees, here is an admirable opportunity for a moral discourse and an assertion of virtue. "And to think of his deceiving us so!" cries out Lady Warrington.

"Very sad, very sad, my dear!" says Sir Miles, wagging his head.

"To think of so much extravagance in one so young!" cries Lady Warrington. "Cards, bets, feasts at taverns of the most wicked profusion, carriage and riding horses, the company of the wealthy and profligate of his own sex, and, I fear, of the most iniquitous persons of ours."

"Hush, my Lady Warrington!" cries her husband, glancing towards the spotless Dora and Flora, who held down their blushing heads at the mention of the last naughty persons.

"No wonder my poor children hide their faces!" mamma continues. "My dears, I wish even the existence of such creatures could be kept from you!"

"They can't go to an opera, or the park, without seeing 'em, to be sure," says Sir Miles.

"To think we should have introduced such a young serpent into the bosom of our family! And have left him in the company of that guileless darling!" and she points to Master Miles.

"Who's a serpent, mamma?" inquires that youth. "First you said cousin Harry was bad: then he was good: now he is bad again. Which is he, Sir Miles?"

"He has faults, like all of us, Miley, my dear. Your cousin has been wild, and you must take warning by him."

"Was not my elder brother, who died—my naughty brother—was not he wild too? He was not kind to me when I was quite a little boy. He never gave me money, nor toys, nor rode with me, nor—why do you cry, mamma? Sure I remember how Hugh and you were always fight—"

"Silence, sir!" cry out papa and the girls in a breath. "Don't you know you are never to mention that name?"

"I know I love Harry, and I didn't love Hugh," says the sturdy little rebel. "And if cousin Harry is in prison, I'll give him my half-guinea that my godpapa gave me, and anything I have—yes, anything, except—except my little horse—and my silver waistcoat—and—and Snowball and Sweetlips at home—and—and, yes, my custard after dinner." This was in reply to a hint of sister Dora. "But I'd give him some of it," continues Miles, after a pause.

"Shut thy mouth with it, child, and then go about thy business," says papa, amused. Sir Miles Warrington had a considerable fund of easy humour.

"Who would have thought he should ever be so wild?" mamma goes on.

"Nay. Youth is the season for wild oats, my dear."

"That we should be so misled in him!" sighed the girls.

"That he should kiss us both!" cries papa.

"Sir Miles Warrington, I have no patience with that sort of vulgarity!" says the majestic matron.

"Which of you was the favourite yesterday, girls?" continues the father.

"Favourite, indeed! I told him over and over again of my engagement to dear Tom—I did, Dora—why do you sneer, if you please?" says the handsome sister.

"Nay, to do her justice, so did Dora too," said papa.

"Because Flora seemed to wish to forget her engagement with dear Tom sometimes," remarks the sister.

"I never, never, never wished to break with Tom! It's wicked of you to say so, Dora! It is you who were for ever sneering at him: it is you who are always envious because I happen—at least, because gentlemen imagine that I am not ill-looking, and prefer me to some folks, in spite of all their learning and wit!" cries Flora, tossing her head over her shoulder, and looking at the glass.

"Why are you always looking there, sister?" says the artless Miles junior. "Sure, you must know your face well enough!"

"Some people look at it just as often, child, who haven't near such good reason," says papa, gallantly.

"If you mean me, Sir Miles, I thank you," cries Dora. "My face is as Heaven made it, and my father and mother gave it me. 'Tis not my fault if I resemble my papa's family. If my head is homely, at least I have got some brains in it. I'm not envious of Flora, indeed, because she has found favour in the sight of poor Tom Claypool! I should as soon be proud of captivating a ploughboy!"

"Pray, miss, was your Mr. Harry, of Virginia, much wiser than Tom Claypool? You would have had him for the asking!" exclaims Flora.

"And so would you, miss, and have dropped Tom Claypool into the sea!" cries Dora.

"I wouldn't."

"You would."

"I wouldn't;"—and da capo goes the conversation—the shuttlecock of wrath being briskly battled from one sister to another.

"Oh, my children! Is this the way you dwell together in unity?" exclaims their excellent female parent, laying down her embroidery. "What an example you set to this Innocent!"

"Like to see 'em fight, my lady!" cries the Innocent, rubbing his hands.

"At her, Flora! Worry her, Dora! To it again, you little rogues!" says facetious papa. 'Tis good sport, ain't it, Miley?"

"Oh, Sir Miles! Oh, my children! These disputes are unseemly. They tear a fond mother's heart," says mamma, with majestic action, though bearing the laceration of her bosom with much seeming equanimity. "What cause for thankfulness ought we to have that watchful parents have prevented any idle engagements between you and your misguided cousin. If we have been mistaken in him, is it not a mercy that we have found out our error in time? If either of you had any preference for him, your excellent good sense, my loves, will teach you to overcome, to eradicate, the vain feeling. That we cherished and were kind to him can never be a source of regret. 'Tis a proof of our good-nature. What we have to regret, I fear, is, that your cousin should have proved unworthy of our kindness, and, coming away from the society of gamblers, play-actors, and the like, should have brought contamination—pollution, I had almost said—into this pure family!"

"Oh, bother mamma's sermons!" says Flora, as my lady pursues a harangue of which we only give the commencement here, but during which papa, whistling, gently quits the room on tiptoe, whilst the artless Miles junior winds his top and pegs it under the robes of his sisters. It has done humming, and staggered and tumbled over, and expired in its usual tipsy manner, long ere Lady Warrington has finished her sermon.

"Were you listening to me, my child?" she asks, laying her hand on her darling's head.

"Yes, mother," says he, with the whipcord in his mouth, and proceeding to wind up his sportive engine. "You was a-saying that Harry was very poor now, and that we oughtn't to help him. That's what you was saying; wasn't it, madam?"

"My poor child, thou wilt understand me better when thou art older!" says mamma, turning towards that ceiling to which her eyes always have recourse.
