Across the way, if the gracious reader will deign to follow, he will find our young gentlemen at Lord Wrotham's residence, a property lent to the General for the duration of his stay. The little family party, familiar to us from Oakhurst and Tunbridge Wells, is assembled within. James Wolfe has pledged his attendance for dinner; yet James is currently attending upon Miss Lowther with such devoted fervor that he would trade the finest culinary creations of Lord Wrotham's kitchen, or the promised desserts, for a single glance from her eyes. You shall occupy the sixth seat; you may confidently assume Mr. Wolfe's place, for his absence is assured. As for me, I shall stand sentinel by the sideboard to chronicle the conversation.

First, observe the radiant countenances of the women. Recall when Harry Warrington was seized by the bailiffs; I had intended to recount how Mrs. Lambert, upon hearing of her son's plight, rushed to her husband. She implored, insisted, and beseeched that her Martin intervene. "Forget his recent rebellion," she argued, "forget his anger regarding the returned presents—anyone would be angry, especially a spirited lad like Harry! Disregard our poverty and the need for funds for the boys at college; there must be a way to extricate him. Did you not rescue Charles Watkins two years ago? He repaid every halfpenny, and your benevolence made a whole family happy. Blessed be God, Mrs. Watkins prays for you daily, and our fortunes have prospered since. Surely, this act will secure your promotion to Major-General!"

Martin Lambert, requiring little persuasion to perform a kindness, yielded readily. Having resolved to seek James Wolfe and post bail for Harry, he donned his hat, squeezed Theo's hand—who seemed to divine his purpose—or perhaps the sensible mother had inadvertently revealed it—and kissed little Hetty's flushed cheek before departing. Yet, the mother followed him to the doorway.

Once alone with him, the enthusiastic matron could no longer restrain her emotions. She threw her arms around her husband's neck, kissing him a hundred and twenty-five times in rapid succession, calling upon God to bless him, and weeping profusely upon his shoulder. In this display of conjugal sentimentality, she was discovered by Old Mrs. Quiggett, the lord's housekeeper, who bustled about the house and presumably found the scene astonishing.

"We have had a tiff and are making it up! Do not spread tales out of school, Mrs. Quiggett!" the gentleman declared, walking away.

"Well, I never!" Mrs. Quiggett exclaimed, emitting a shrill, strident laugh reminiscent of a venerable old cockatoo—a white, hook-nosed, long-lived bird she strongly resembled. "Well, I never!" she laughed again, shaking her old sides until her keys and, one might imagine, her ribs clattered and jingled.

"Oh, Quiggett!" sobbed Mrs. Lambert, "what a man that is!"

"You've been quarrelling, mum, and now you're making it up? That is right."

"Quarrel with him? He never told a greater story. My General is an angel, Quiggett. I should like to worship him. I should like to fall down at his boots and kiss them! There has never been a man so good as my General. What have I done to deserve such a husband? How dare I possess such a good man?"

"My dear, I think there is a pair of you," the old cockatoo replied. "And what would you like for your supper?"

When Lambert returned very late to the meal, announcing that Harry was free and that his brother had come to his senses to rescue him, one can imagine the commotion that ensued among those present! If Mrs. Lambert's General was an angel before, what office of humble devotion would she prefer in the evening? Little Hetty nestled silently against her father, drinking a drop from his glass. Theo and her mother's faces beamed with happiness, like two moons of brightness. After supper, the four of them fell to their knees at a certain signal, paying glad homage in awful mirth-rejoicing, with such pure joy as angels experience for the sinner who repents. Then came a great knocking at the door. My lord was miles away in the country; it was past midnight, so late had they talked. Mrs. Lambert likely guessed the visitor.

"This is George," a young gentleman announced, ushering another in. "We have been to Aunt Bernstein's. We could not go to bed without coming to thank you too. You dear, dear, good..." Speech ceased as Aunt Lambert kissed Harry, Theo snatched up Hetty—who was as pale as death—and hugged her back to life. George Warrington stood with his hat removed, and upon the conclusion of Harry's transaction, approached to kiss Mrs. Lambert's hand; the General passed his hand across his eyes. They were all in a tender, happy state. Generous hearts often feel this way when wrong is forgiven, peace restored, and love returns thought lost.

"We came from Aunt Bernstein's; we saw lights here and could not sleep without saying good-night," Harry explained. "Could we not, George?"

"'Tis certainly a famous nightcap you have brought us, boys," the General remarked. "When are you to dine with us? Tomorrow?" No, they must visit Madame Bernstein's tomorrow.

Then the next day? Yes, they would come the following day—the very day we are writing about, and the very dinner at which my gracious reader has just been invited to sit.

Why sit? Not to a mere Barmecide feast, but to hear the statement of Mr. George Esmond Warrington, which he was about to deliver. Here they all sat—not in the grand dining-room, but in the snug study or parlour before. The cloth was withdrawn, the General had toasted the King, the servants had departed, and the guests sat *conticentes*. After a moment of hemming and blushing, Mr. George proceeded:

"I recall sitting at the General's table when a little Philadelphia agent, whose wit and shrewdness we had noted at home, voiced objections to the conduct of the campaign, the disastrous outcome proving his justice. 'Of course,' he said, 'your Excellency's troops, once before Fort Duquesne, will never be able to resist such a general, such an army, such artillery. But do you calculate on the difficulty of reaching the place? Your march will be through woods almost untrodden, over roads you must make yourself, with a line four miles long. This slender column, forced through the forest, will face endless attacks in front, rear, and flank from enemies unseen, practiced in the dexterous laying of ambuscades.'

"'Psha, sir!' the General retorted. 'The savages may frighten your raw American militia—but the Indians will never make any impression on his Majesty's regular troops.'

"'I heartily hope not, sir,' said Mr. Franklin, sighing. Of course, the gentlemen of the General's family sneered at the postmaster as a pert civilian offering opinions beyond his comprehension.

"We despised the Indians on our own side, and our commander made light of them and their service. Our officers disgusted the allied chiefs with outrageous behavior toward their women. Only seven or eight remained with our force. Had we had a couple of hundred in our front on that fatal ninth of July, the event must have been vastly different. They would have repelled the French Indians, preventing the surprise and panic that ensued. It is known now that the French were ready to surrender, never dreaming of defense, and that the French Indians themselves remonstrated against the audacity of attacking such an overwhelming force.

"I was with the General and the main body when firing began. Aide-de-camp after another was sent forward. Initially, the enemy's attack was answered briskly; our men huzzahed with good heart. But soon our fire slackened, while from behind every tree and bush came single shots, laying man after man low. We marched in orderly line, skirmishers ahead, colors and two small guns in the center, baggage bringing up the rear, moving over open ground for a mile or two, flanked by thick, tangled brushwood. After brief frontal firing, the ambush opened from both sides of the surrounding wood. Men dropped rapidly, officers falling in greater numbers than the rank and file.

"At first, cheering and answering fire, our guns even opened on the wood, seemingly silencing the French ambush. But the hidden rifle-fire resumed. Men halted, huddled together, ignoring shouts and orders to advance, firing wildly into the brushwood with no effect. Those in front ran back to the main body, frightened and wounded, reporting five thousand Frenchmen and a legion of yelling Indian devils, scalping our people as they fell. We heard their cries as our men dropped. No one could be induced to move forward. One aide-de-camp after another was sent and never returned. Finally, it was my turn. I was sent with a message to Captain Fraser of Halkett's in front, which he never received, nor did I deliver.

"I had not gone thirty yards when a rifle-ball struck my leg, and I fell straightway. I recall a rush of Indians and Frenchmen, the former crying fiendish war-cries, the latter as fierce as their savage allies. I was amazed and mortified to see so few whitecoats; not above a score passed me, indeed fewer than fifty in the accursed action where two of the bravest British regiments were routed.

"One of them, half Indian, half Frenchman, wearing mocassins and a white uniform coat with a cockade, saw me prostrate. Turning back, he ran toward me, his musket clubbed to dash my brains out and plunder me. I had my little fusil, given to me by Harry before the campaign, fallen nearby. Seizing it, I felled the Frenchman dead at six yards. Saved for the moment, I bled heavily and fainted while trying to load, the weapon dropping from my lifeless hand.

"Scarcely in my senses, yells and shots ringing dimly, I saw an Indian busy over the Frenchman's body, glancing toward me as I lay bleeding. He rifled the corpse, tore open the coat, felt in the pockets, then scalped him. With his bleeding knife in his mouth, he advanced. I saw him coming through a film, in a dream, powerless to move or resist.

"He put his knee upon my chest. With one bloody hand, he seized my long hair, lifting my head. As he raised it, I saw a French officer rapidly advancing behind him.

'Good God! It was young Florac, my second in the duel at Quebec,' I cried. 'A moi, Florac! C'est Georges! aide moi!'

"He started, ran up at my cry, laid his hand on the Indian's shoulder, and commanded him to hold. But the savage did not understand French, or chose not to. Clutching my hair firmer, he waved his dripping knife, motioning the French lad to leave me to my prey. I could only cry out pitifully, 'A moi!'

''Ah, canaille, tu veux du sang? Prends!' said Florac, cursing. The next moment, with an ugh, the Indian fell over my chest dead, pierced by Florac's sword.

"My friend looked around. 'Eh! la belle affaire! Where art thou wounded? In the leg?' He bound my leg tightly with his sash. 'The others will kill thee if they find thee here. Ah, tiens! Put me on this coat, and this hat with the white cockade. Call out in French if any of our people pass. They will take thee for one of us. Thou art Brunet of the Quebec Volunteers. God guard thee, Brunet! I must go forward. 'Tis a general debacle, and the whole of your redcoats are on the run, my poor boy.' Ah, what a rout! What a day of disgrace for England!

"Florac's rough application stopped the bleeding. The kind creature helped me rest against a tree and load my fusil, placing it within reach to protect me from other marauders. He gave me the gourd of the unlucky French soldier I had slain, and the drink refreshed and invigorated me. Taking a mark of the tree and noting the bearings, the young lad hastened to the front. 'Thou seest how much I love thee, George,' he said, 'that I stay behind in a moment like this.' I forget whether I told thee, Harry, that Florac owed me money. I had won it from him at cards in Quebec, playing at his entreaty, and there was a difficulty in payment. I remitted his debt to me, and lighted my pipe with his note-of-hand. You see, sir, you are not the only gambler in the family.

"At evening, when the dismal pursuit ended, the faithful fellow returned with two Indians, each bearing reeking scalps. He informed them I was a Frenchman, his brother, wounded early in the day, to be carried back to the fort. They laid me in a blanket and carried me, groaning, with trusty Florac by my side. Had he left me, they would surely have plundered me and added my hair to the spoils hanging at their girdles. He promised brandy at the fort if they brought me safely there. I have but a dim recollection of the journey; the anguish of my wound was extreme, and I fainted more than once.

"We reached the fort's end. I was taken to the officer's log-house and laid upon Florac's own bed. Happy for me was my insensibility. I was brought in as a wounded French soldier of the garrison. I learned later that during my delirium, the few prisoners made on the day of our disaster had been brought under the walls of Duquesne by their savage captors, there horribly burned, tortured, and butchered by the Indians under the garrison's eyes.

"As George spoke, a thrill of horror seemed to run through his sympathetic audience. Theo took Hetty's hand, looking at George with alarm. Harry struck his fist upon the table, crying, 'The bloody, murderous, red-skinned villains! There will never

Months bled into one another, a weary gray stretch of time spent within the stone walls of the fort. Life there was a cycle of friction and truce between the commandant and myself, punctuated by greasy card games and dismal musical duets—his wheezing flute battling my cracked guitar. The poor Fawn endured the dual burdens of her master's whims, accepting beatings and cans of liquor as they came, while simultaneously nursing her papoose, her gout-stricken lord, or a prisoner shivering with ague. This rhythm held until the onset of last autumn, when a hunter arrived bearing news that ignited the garrison with a feverish excitement.

The Marquis de Montcalm had dispatched a substantial detachment to reinforce French-held forts and seize new positions within British territory. Troops had departed Quebec and Montreal, descending the St. Lawrence and navigating the lakes in bateaux, laden with artillery and vast stores of war supplies. Rumors swirled that Museau would soon be replaced by an officer of superior rank—a replacement who might exchange me for a prisoner or surrender me to the Indians in retaliation for cruelties inflicted upon enemy officers. The men of the fort hungered for these reinforcements; they dreamed of marching into Pennsylvania and New York, seizing Albany and Philadelphia, driving the "Rosbifs" into the sea, and claiming all America from the Mississippi to Newfoundland.

Yet, amidst this triumphant rhetoric, a shadow lingered in Commandant Museau's satisfaction. The prospect of French conquest did not bring him joy.

"Eh, commandant!" I said, breaking the silence. "'Tis fort bien, but meanwhile, where is your farm in Normandy? Where is the pot of cider and the trippes à la mode de Caen?"

"Yes; 'tis all very well, my garcon," he replied, his voice dropping. "But consider: when poor old Museau is superseded, where will you be? Other officers are not companions like me. Few men possess my humanity. If a great garrison arrives, will my successors grant you the indulgences honest Museau has bestowed? You will be kept in a sty like a pig ready for slaughter. As surely as one of our officers falls into the hands of your frontier brigands and suffers, so surely must you pay with your skin. You will be handed over to our red allies—to the brethren of La Biche yonder. Did you see, last year, what they did to your countrymen captured at Braddock? Roasting was merely the smallest punishment, ma foi—was it not, La Biche?"

He launched into a vivid, jocular catalog of tortures: eyes burned out, teeth and nails wrenched loose, limbs and bodies gashed. You turn pale, dear Miss Theo! Well, I shall have pity and spare you the graphic details Museau recounted with such cheerful relish.

La Biche, however, was not so easily shaken. She had witnessed such horrors in her own time. Hailing from the Senecas, whose villages lay near the great cataract between Ontario and Erie, her people had fought both for and against the English. In the battles between our races, it was difficult to declare which skin—white or red—proved most savage.

"They may chop me into cutlets and broil me," I said coolly. "But again, I say, you will never have the farm in Normandy."

"Go get the whisky-bottle, La Biche," Museau commanded.

"And it is not too late, even now. I will reward the guide who takes me home generously. I promise, as a man of honor, ten thousand livres to anyone who brings me a token—say, my watch and seal with my grandfather's arms, which I believe are hidden in a chest somewhere in this fort."

"Ah, scelerat!" roared the commandant, his laughter turning hoarse. "Thou hast eyes, thou! All is good prize in war."

"Think of a house in your village, of a fine field with a half-dozen cows, of an orchard heavy with fruit."

"And Javotte at the door with her wheel, and a rascal of a child or two with cheeks as red as the apples! O my country! O my mother!" the commandant whimpered. "Quick, La Biche, the whisky!"

That night, the commandant sat deep in thought, and so did La Biche. She remained silent and melancholy, sitting apart from us while nursing her child. Whenever my gaze met hers, I saw a fixed intensity. The infant began to cry, and Museau, with his usual foul tongue, ordered the child away to the building La Biche occupied. Once she was gone, we spoke freely. I laid out reasons before him that his cupidity could not resist.

"How do you know," he asked, "that this hunter will serve you?"

"That is my secret," I replied. Yet, since we were not bound by honor, I might reveal it. When hunters came to the settlements for trade, they often stayed a day or two for rest, drink, and company. Our new friend loved these things. He gambled with the men, traded his furs for liquor, and enjoyed the fort's atmosphere, singing and dancing. I believe the men liked my songs; for lack of better entertainment, I often sang and scraped my guitar. We held many concerts, the men joining in chorus or dancing to my rough music, until interrupted by the drums and the retreat.

Our guest, the hunter, attended one or two of these gatherings. I decided to test if he understood English. After exhausting our stock of French songs, I declared, "My lads, I will give you an English song." To the tune of "Over the hills and far away"—a favorite air my grandfather once hummed in Marlborough's camp—I improvised some doggerel: "This long, long year, a prisoner drear; Ah, me! I'm tired of lingering here: I'll give a hundred guineas gay, To be over the hills and far away."

"What is it?" the hunter asked. "I don't understand."

"'Tis a girl to her lover," I answered. But I saw the twinkle in his eye; he understood.

The next day, when no men were within hearing, the trapper confirmed my suspicion. As he passed me, he hummed in a low, perfect English tone the burden of my previous verse: "Over the hills and far away."

"If you are ready," he said, "I am ready. I know your people and the way to them. Talk to the Fawn; she will tell you what to do. What! You will not play with me?" He pulled out some cards just as two soldiers approached. "Milor est trop grand seigneur? Bonjour, my lord!"

The man offered a mock bow and walked away, shrugging his shoulders, ready to seek other players.

I knew then that La Biche was to be the agent, and that Museau had accepted my offer. The poor Fawn performed her part faithfully and dexterously. She had long been allowed free communication with me, tending to my wounds and illnesses, helping with my chamber duties and cooking. She was permitted to leave the fort, wandering to the river and fields where the garrison's corn and garden produce were gathered.

Having gambled away most of the money earned from his peltries, the trapper gathered his store of flints, powder, and blankets, and took his leave. Three days after his departure, the Fawn signaled that the time for my trial of freedom had arrived.

When first wounded, I had been taken by my kind Florac and placed on his bed in the officers' room. When the fort was emptied of all officers except the old lieutenant left in command, I was allowed to remain in my quarters, sometimes left free, sometimes locked up and fed prisoners' rations, and sometimes invited to share his mess by my tipsy gaoler.

This officers' house, or room, was constructed of logs like the half-dozen others within the fort, mounting only four small-caliber guns, one of which stood on the bastion behind my cabin. Looking westward over this gun, one could see a small island at the confluence of the Ohio and Monongahela rivers, where Duquesne was situated. On the shore opposite this island stood some trees.

"You see those trees?" my poor La Biche asked me the day before, speaking in her French jargon. "He waits for you behind those trees."

During the day, the door to my quarters remained open, and La Biche was free to come and go. On the eve of my escape, she returned from the fields carrying a pick and a basket of vegetables and potherbs for soup. She sat on a bench at my door, the pick resting against it, the basket beside her. I stood talking to her for a while; I was so distracted by my condition that I never would have thought to use the pick had she actually pushed it into my open door, causing it to fall into my room. "Hide it," she said. "Want it soon." That afternoon, she pointed out the trees to me.

The following day, she appeared pretending to be furious, calling out, "My lord! My lord! Why do you not come to the commandant's dinner? He is very bad! Entendez-vous?" Peering into the room as she spoke, she threw a coil of rope at me.

"I am coming, La Biche," I said, hobbling after her on my crutch. As I entered the commandant's quarters, she whispered, "Pour ce soir." Then I knew the time had come.

As for Museau, he knew nothing of the matter. Not he! He growled at me, claiming the soup was cold. He looked me steadily in the face, talking of this and that, not only while his servant was present but afterwards as we smoked our pipes and played piquet, while the poor La Biche sat cowering in a corner.

My friend's whisky bottle was empty. With a knowing look, he said he needed another glass—that we both needed a glass that night. Rising from the table, he stumped to the inner room where he kept his fire-water under lock and key, leaving the poor La Biche behind, who could not resist that temptation.

As he turned his back, La Biche rose. He was no sooner gone than she was at my feet, kissing my hand, pressing it to her heart, and bursting into tears over my knees. I confess I was so troubled by this silent testimony of her attachment and fondness—an extent I had scarcely suspected before—that when Museau returned, I had not fully recovered my equanimity, though the poor Fawn was back in her corner, shrouded in her blanket.

He seemed to notice nothing strange in either of our behaviors. We sat down to our game, though my thoughts were so preoccupied that I scarcely knew what cards faced me.

"I gain everything from you tonight, milor," he said grimly. "We play upon parole."

"And you may count upon mine," I replied.

"Eh! 'Tis all that you have!" he countered.

"Monsieur," I said, "my word is good for ten thousand livres;" and we continued the game.

Finally, he claimed a headache and retired to bed, signaling that I should also retire. "I wish you a good night, mon petit milor," he said. "Stay, you will fall without your crutch," his eyes twinkling, his face wearing a sarcastic grin. In the agitation of the moment, I had forgotten I was lame and walked away at a pace as good as a grenadier's.

"What a vilain night!" he muttered, looking out. Indeed, a tempest raged abroad, a great roaring and wind. "Bring a lantern, La Tulipe, and lock my lord comfortably into his quarters!" He stood a moment looking at me from his own door, and I caught a glimpse of the poor La Biche behind him.

The night was so rainy that the sentries preferred their boxes and did not disturb me in my work. The log-house was built with upright posts deeply fixed in the ground and horizontal logs laid upon them. I had to dig beneath these, working a hole sufficient for my body to pass. I began in the dark, shortly after tattoo. It was some time after midnight before my work was done; lifting my hand under the log, I felt the rain falling from without. I had to work very cautiously for two hours after that, then creep through to the parapet and silently fling my rope over the gun. My heart trembled lest a sentry should see me and send a charge of lead into my body.

The wall was but twelve feet high, and my fall into the ditch was easy enough. I waited there a while, looking steadily under the gun, trying to discern the river and the island. I heard the sentry pacing above, humming a tune. The darkness cleared somewhat as the moon rose, revealing the shining river and the dark rocks and trees of the island rising from the waters.

I made for this mark as swiftly as I could, heading for the clump of trees to which I had been directed. Oh, what a relief I felt when I heard a low voice humming there, "Over the hills and far away!"

When Mr. George reached this part of his narrative, Miss Theo, seated by a harpsichord, turned and dashed off the tune on the instrument, while the entire little company broke out into the merry chorus.

"Our way," the speaker continued, "lay through a level tract of forest familiar to my guide, along the right bank of the Monongahela. By daylight, we reached a clearer country, and my trapper—Silverheels was the name by which he went—asked if I had ever seen the spot before. It was the fatal field where Braddock had fallen, and whence I had been wonderfully rescued the summer of the previous year. Now, the leaves were beginning to tint themselves with the magnificent hues of autumn."

"Ah, brother!" cried Harry, seizing his brother's hand. "I was gambling and making a fool of myself at the Wells and in London, when my George was flying for his life in the wilderness! Oh, what a miserable spendthrift I have been!"

"But I think thou art not unworthy to be called thy mother's son," said Mrs. Lambert,

The tale George Warrington had spun for Madame de Bernstein the night before was, in essence, the same story we have just heard. Yet, the reception differed vastly from the warm applause that greeted him in Hill Street. There, Hetty's wide-eyed wonder, Theo's sympathetic gaze, and their parents' gentle encouragement had fueled his modest eloquence. In contrast, the old lady at the Court End had nodded off repeatedly, only rousing herself to declare the narrative "most interesting" and demand its continuation. George, however, had stumbled through it—hemming, hawing, blushing, and speaking far less fluently than he did for his friendly audience. His aunt, the General, later remarked that his mother's performance during the telling was comparable to a professional tragedienne hired solely to weep in the front boxes, a sentiment that likely influenced our decision to stage George's first public performance at Lord Wrotham's house. We wished him to speak with dignity, free from the cynicism and sleepiness of that elderly listener.

"Very good and most interesting, I am sure, my dear sir," Madame Bernstein purred, lifting three lace-covered fingers to mask a convulsive twitch of her mouth. "And your mother must have been delighted to see you."

George offered a slight shrug and a low bow as his aunt raised her keen, aged eyes to meet his.

"She was delighted," she continued dryly, "and undoubtedly killed the fatted calf. Though I confess, nephew George, I struggle to understand why I say 'calf.' You were never the prodigal son. I might as well address my poor Harry: 'Thou hast been amongst the swine sure enough.' Evil companions have stripped you of both your money and your coat."

"He came to his family in England, madam," George retorted with rising heat, "and his friends were your ladyship's."

"They could not have chosen worse advisers," the old lady declared, tossing her head with theatrical flair. "Had my sister written to me through him, I would have informed her sooner. 'Hey! hey!' she cried last night to her maid while preparing for the rout. 'This young gentleman's mother is half sorry he has returned to life; I can see it in his face. She is half sorry, and I am perfectly furious! Why did he not lie still beneath the tree, and why did that young Florac carry him to the fort?'"

She paused, her mind drifting to the past. "I knew those Floracs in Paris, during the time of Monsieur le Regent. They were of the Floracs of Ivry—a house of no great consequence before Henri IV. His ancestor was the king's favorite. His ancestor—he! he!--his ancestress! Brett! *Entendez-vous?* Give me my card-purse. I dislike the grand airs of this Monsieur George, yet he bears a striking resemblance to his grandfather—the same look, and sometimes the same tones. You recall Colonel Esmond from my youth? This boy possesses his eyes. I suppose I favored the Colonel because he loved me."

Shortly thereafter, having concluded her card party—an amusement she pursued relentlessly regardless of the day of the week or the Sabbath—as long as she possessed the strength to hold trumps or sit upright, the old lady dismissed her two nephews. To the elder, George, she offered a couple of fingers and a stiff, stately curtsey. To Harry, she gave two hands and a kindly pat upon the cheek.

"My poor child, now that thou art disinherited, thou shalt see how differently the world treats thee!" she proclaimed. "In all of London, there is but one wicked, heartless old woman who will treat thee as before. Here is a pocket-book for you, child! Do not lose it at Ranelagh tonight. That suit of yours does not become your brother half so well as it did upon you! You shall present your brother to everyone and pace the room for at least two hours. Were I in your shoes, I would retreat to the Chocolate-House and play as if nothing had occurred. While you are there, your brother may return to dine with me. My Lady Flint serves wretched suppers, and I wish to discuss your mother's letter with him. *Au revoir*, gentlemen!" With that, she departed toward her toilette, her chairmen and flambeaux already waiting at the door.

The gentlemen proceeded to Ranelagh, where only a handful of Harry's acquaintances were present. They strolled the circular walk, encountered Mr. Tom Claypool with his country friends, listened to the music, and drank tea in a private box. Harry, acting as master of ceremonies, introduced his brother to the curiosities of the pleasure palace. George, however, proved even more excited than Harry had been on his initial visit. George possessed a profound love for music, having heard a full orchestra for the first time and witnessed a satisfactory performance of a work by Mr. Handel. It was a testament to Harry's humility and regard for his elder brother that he could respect George's passion for music at a time when fiddling was deemed effeminate and unmanly in England, and when patriotic prints urged Britons to sneer at the frivolous accomplishments of the "Squallinis" and "Monsieurs." Indeed, the spirit of the age had shifted; no longer was ignorance a source of pride, nor was there room for dullness or arrogance. Art had secured her naturalization, living here on terms of near-equality. Even if Mrs. Thrale chose to marry a music-master today, her friends would not shudder; with a good fortune and a competent cook, people would dine with her despite the misalliance, treating Mr. Piozzi with civility.

Following Ranelagh, and adhering to Madame Bernstein's counsel, George returned to her ladyship's house, while Harry presented himself at the club, where gentlemen assembled nightly to sup and then gamble. Naturally, no one alluded to Mr. Warrington's brief disappearance. Mr. Ruff, his former landlord, waited upon him with grave civility, as if no rift had ever existed between them. Mr. Warrington had indeed had his trunks and belongings removed from Bond Street that morning, and he and his brother were now established in separate apartments.

Once supper concluded and the gentlemen prepared to ascend to the macco-table, Harry announced he would not play further. He had already burned his fingers and could afford no further extravagance.

"Why," Mr. Morris remarked in a flippant tone, "you must have won more than you have lost, Mr. Warrington, after all is said and done."

"And of course I do not know my own business as well as you, Mr. Morris," Harry replied sternly, recalling the other's behavior upon hearing of his arrest. "But I have another reason. A few months or days ago, I was heir to a great estate and could afford to lose a little money. Now, thank God, I am heir to nothing." He glanced around, blushing slightly, at the knot of gentlemen lounging at the tables or gathered by the fire.

"How do you mean, Mr. Warrington?" cried Lord March. "Have you lost Virginia, too? Who has won it? I always fancied playing you myself for that stake."

"And grow an improved breed of slaves in the colony," added another.

"The rightful owner has won it. You have heard me speak of my twin elder brother?"

"Who was killed in the affair of Braddock two years ago! Yes. Gracious goodness, my dear sir, I hope in heaven he has not come back to life?"

"He arrived in London two days since. He was a prisoner in a French fort for eighteen months; he escaped only a few months ago and left our house in Virginia shortly after his release."

"You haven't had time to order mourning, I suppose, Mr. Warrington?" asked Mr. Selwyn, with a good-natured simplicity that Harry failed to grasp until his brother explained the jest.

"By Jove, I believe the fellow is absolutely glad of the reappearance of his confounded brother!" Lord March exclaimed as the conversation continued after the young Virginian took his leave.

"These savages practice the simple virtues of affection—they are barely civilized in America yet," yawned Selwyn.

"They love their kin and scalp their enemies," simpered Mr. Walpole. "It is not Christian, but natural. Would you not like to attend a scalping match, George, and watch a fellow skinned alive?"

"A man's elder brother is his natural enemy," Mr. Selwyn stated placidly, arranging his money and counters.

"Torture is like broiled bones and pepper. You would not relish simple hanging afterwards, George!" continued Horry.

"I'm hanged if there is any man in England who would like to see his elder brother alive," Lord March declared.

"No, nor his father either, my lord!" cried Jack Morris.

"First time I ever knew you had one, Jack. Give me counters for five hundred."

"I say, 'tis all mighty fine about dead brothers coming to life again," Jack continued. "Who is to know that this was not a scheme arranged between these two fellows? Here comes a young fellow calling himself the Fortunate Youth, claiming to be a Virginian Prince and the devil knows what else, who enters our society..."

A great laugh erupted at Jack's phrase "our society."

"Who is to know that this was not a cross?" Jack pressed on. "The younger one comes first. He marries an heiress, secures her fortune, and then the elder brother rises! When did this elder brother appear? Only when the younger's scheme was blown and all was lost for him! Who shall tell me that the fellow has not been living in Seven Dials or a cellar, dining on tripe and cow-heel until my younger gentleman was disposed of? Dammy, as gentlemen, I think we ought to take notice: that this Mr. Warrington has taken the most outrageous liberty with the entire club."

"Who put him up? It was March, I think, who put him up?" asked a bystander.

"Yes. But my lord thought he was putting up a very different person. Didn't you, March?"

"Hold your confounded tongue and mind your game!" the nobleman addressed snapped. Yet, Lord March's opinion found few supporters. Many agreed that it was indecorous for Mr. Harry Warrington to have ever believed in his brother's death; that there was something suspicious about the young man's first appearance and subsequent actions; and, in fine, that regarding such foreigners, adventurers, and the like, we ought to exercise extreme caution.

Though he was now out of prison and difficulty, though he held his aunt's liberal donation in his pocket, and though his dearest brother was restored to him—a return Harry never once thought to deplore, contrary to his friends at White's assumption; and though Maria had shown herself in such a favorable light during his misfortune—Harry, when alone, felt far from cheerful. He smoked his pipe of Virginia with a troubled mind. It was not that he was deposed from his principality; the loss of it never vexed him, for he knew his brother would share as he would have done. But after all those struggles and doubts within his own mind, to find himself poor, yet irrevocably bound to his elderly cousin! Yes, she was elderly, there was no doubt about it. When she had descended into that horrible den in Cursitor Street and the tears had washed her rouge away, she looked as old as his mother! Her face was wrinkled and yellow, and thinking of her brought on a qualm similar to the one he had felt when she fell ill in the coach on their road to Tunbridge. What would his mother say when he brought her home? Lord, what battles there would be between them! He would go to live on one of the plantations—the farther from home the better—and have a few negroes, farming as best he might and hunting often. But at Castlewood, or in the home he could make for her, what a life for poor Maria, who had been accustomed to court, cards, balls, and assemblies every night! If he could merely be the overseer of the estates—oh, he would be an honest factor, trying to make amends for his useless life and extravagance of recent days! Five thousand pounds, all his patrimony and the accumulations of his long minority, squandered in six months! He was a beggar, save for dear George's kindness, with nothing left to him but an old wife—a pretty beggar, dressed out in velvet and silver lace, forsooth! The poor lad was arrayed in his best clothes, a fine figure he had made in Europe, and yet what a wretched end he had come to! With all his fine friends at White's and Newmarket, with all his extravagance, had he been happy a single day since arriving in Europe? Yes, three days, four days, yesterday evening, when he had been with dear dear Mrs. Lambert, those affectionate kind girls, and that brave good Colonel. And the Colonel was right when he rebuked him for his spendthrift follies; he had been a brute to be angry as he had been, and God bless them all for their generous exertions in his behalf! Such were the thoughts Harry poured into his pipe, smoking them while he waited for his brother's return from Madame Bernstein.

The maternal grandfather of our Virginians, Colonel Esmond, had spent a significant portion of his long retirement in the New World composing memoirs of his early life. In these volumes, Madame de Bernstein—then known as Mrs. Beatrice Esmond—played a considerable role. George Warrington, having read his grandfather's manuscript countless times, knew his kinswoman intimately long before he ever laid eyes upon her. He knew the lady of half a century prior: young, beautiful, and wilful. Now, he observed her in the decline of her days. When cheeks fade and eyes grow dim, is it sorrow or delight for a woman who is no longer a beauty to recall the bloom of her youth? When the heart withers, does it not ache to remember how it once beat with warmth? When spirits grow languid, do we not long for the buoyant hope and eager enjoyment of other days? Thus fall the buds of prime, the roses of beauty, the florid harvests of summer—leaving only naked branches to shiver in the winter.

"And that was a beauty once!" George thought as his aunt, adorned in rouge and diamonds, entered from her evening rout. "And that ruin was once a splendid palace. Crowds of lovers have sighed before those decrepit feet and been bewildered by the brightness of those eyes." His mind drifted to a firework display at Williamsburg on the King's birthday, recalling the skeleton-wheel and the sockets of exploded Roman candles. The dazzling brilliance of Aunt Beatrice's early career flashed before him as he reflected on his grandsire's journals. Honest Harry had witnessed those times too, yet Harry, not being a scholar, had not scrutinized the manuscript with such intensity. Moreover, unlike his melancholy senior, Harry possessed little inclination for moralizing.

Mr. Warrington deemed it unnecessary to inform his aunt of his intimate knowledge of her early history and thus remained silent. After their meal, she pointed her cane toward her escritoire, instructing her attendant to retrieve a letter lying beneath the inkstand. George recognized the superscription immediately; it was the correspondence he had carried from home.

"It appears by this letter," the old lady remarked, fixing a sharp gaze upon her nephew, "that since your return, differences have arisen between you and my sister."

"Indeed?" George replied. "I was unaware that Madam Esmond had alluded to them."

The Baroness adjusted a large pair of spectacles over eyes that once kindled passions unknown, glanced over the letter, and handed it to George. He read aloud:

"RICHMOND, VIRGINIA, December 26th, 1756.

"HONOURED MADAM! AND SISTER!—I acknowledge receipt of your ladyship's favor via the Rose packet of October 23rd. I answer at a season meant for goodwill and peace, yet one wherein Heaven decrees we must still bear our share of earthly sorrow. My reply shall be delivered by my eldest son, Mr. Esmond Warrington, who returned to us miraculously from the Valley of the Shadow of Death—as our previous letters informed my poor Henry—and who desires, with my consent, to visit Europe, though he has been among us but briefly.

"I grieve to think that my dearest Harry appeared at home—in England—under false pretenses, presented to His Majesty, our family, and his own as his father's heir, while my dear son George was still alive, though dead to us. Ah, madam! During the eighteen months of his captivity, what anguish his mother's and brother's hearts endured! My Harry's is the tenderest of any man's now living. In the joy of seeing Mr. Esmond Warrington restored to life, he will forget the worldly misfortune that befalls him. He will return to comparative poverty without a pang. The most generous and obedient of human beings, of sons, he will gladly yield to his elder brother that inheritance which was his own but for the accident of birth and the providential return of my son George.

"Your beneficent intentions toward dearest Harry will be more than ever welcome, now he is reduced to a younger brother's slender portion! Many years ago, an advantageous opportunity arose to provide for him in this province; by now, he would have owned a noble estate and negroes, capable of making a figure here, had my wishes been complied with and his father's small portion, currently yielding little interest in British funds, been invested in this excellent purchase. But legal formalities and, I grieve to admit, my elder son's scruples prevailed, causing me to lose this admirable opportunity. Harry will find his savings carefully accumulated—may he live long to enjoy them! May Heaven bless you, dear sister, for whatever you may add to his modest store! As I gather from your letter that the sum allowed him has proven insufficient for his expenses in fine company—and the grandson of the Marquis of Esmond, one who nearly succeeded his lordship, surely claims equality with any nobleman in Great Britain—I entrust a sum I had always intended for the poor child's establishment to my eldest son. To do him justice, he possesses a most sincere regard for his brother, and I charge him to invest it for Harry's best advantage."

"It took him out of prison yesterday, madam," George interjected at this juncture. "I believe that was the best use to which we could put it."

"Nay, sir, I know nothing of the sort! Why not keep it to buy a pair of colors for him, or assist toward another estate and some negroes if he has a fancy for home?" cried the old lady. "Besides, I had a fancy to pay that debt myself."

"I hope you will allow his brother to handle that. I request leave to act as my brother's banker in this matter, considering I have borrowed so much from my mother, to be repaid to my dear Harry."

"Do you say so, sir? Give me a glass of wine! You are an extravagant fellow! Read on; you will see your mother thinks so. I drink to your health, nephew George! 'Tis good Burgundy. Your grandfather never loved Burgundy; he preferred claret, the little he drank."

George continued reading:

"This remittance will, I trust, amply cover any expenses incurred by dearest Harry owing to the mistake regarding his position. I wish I could trust his elder brother's prudence as confidently as I trust my Harry's! Yet I fear that even in captivity, Mr. Esmond W. has learned little of the humility becoming all Christians, which I have ever endeavored to teach my children. Should you chance to show him these lines when, by Heaven's blessing on those who go down to the sea in ships, the Great Ocean divides us, he will know that a fond mother's blessing and prayers follow both her children. There is no act I have ever done, no desire I have ever expressed—however little he may have been inclined to obey it—but hath been dictated by the fondest wishes for my dearest boys' welfare."

"There is a scratch with a penknife and a great blot upon the letter, as if water had fallen on it," George's aunt observed kindly. "Your mother writes well, George. I suppose you and she had a difference?"

"Yes, ma'am, many," the young man answered sadly. "The last concerned a question of money—a ransom I promised to the old lieutenant of the fort who aided my escape. I told you he had a mistress, a poor Indian woman who helped me and was kind to me. Six weeks after my arrival home, the poor thing appeared at Richmond, having found her way through the woods by much the same track I followed, bringing me the token Museau promised to send when he connived at my flight. A commanding officer and considerable reinforcement had arrived at Duquesne. Charges of peculation, though his messenger could not express herself clearly, had been brought against Museau. He was arrested, attempted escape, but, less fortunate than myself, was shot on the rampart. He sent the Indian woman to me with my grandfather's watch and a line scrawled in his prison on his deathbed, begging me to send *ce que je scavais* to a notary at Havre de Grace in France to be transmitted to his relatives at Caen in Normandy. My friend Silverheels, the hunter, assisted my poor Indian companion on her journey. I know not how she would have escaped scalping otherwise. But at home, they received her sternly, hardly granting her a welcome. I won't detail the suspicions they harbored regarding her and me. The poor wretch fell to drinking whenever she could find means. I ordered food and shelter, yet she became the jest of our negroes and the subject of scandal and gossip among the old fools in our little town. Our Governor, fortunately, was a man of sense; I made interest with him and procured a pass to send her back to her people. Her grief at parting with me only confirmed the suspicions against her. A fellow preached against me from the pulpit, I believe; I had to treat another with a cane. And I had a violent dispute with Madam Esmond—a difference not yet healed—because I insisted on paying the heirs Museau designated the money I had promised for my deliverance. You see that scandal flourishes at the borders of the wilderness and in the New World as well as the Old."

"I have suffered from it myself, my dear!" said Madame Bernstein demurely. "Fill thy glass, child! A little dash of cherry-brandy! 'Twill do thee all the good in the world."

"As for my poor Harry's marriage," the letter continued, "though I know too well, from sad experience, the dangers to which youth is subject, and would keep my boy, at any price, from them, though I should wish him to marry a person of rank as becomes his birth, yet my Lady Maria Esmond is out of the question. Her age is almost the same as mine; and I know my brother Castlewood left his daughters with the very smallest portions. My Harry is so obedient that I know a desire from me will suffice to cause him to give up this imprudent match. Some foolish people once supposed that I myself once considered a second union with a person of rank very different from ours. No! I knew what was due to my children. As succeeding to this estate after me, Mr. Esmond W. is amply provided for. Let my task now be to save for his less fortunate younger brother: and, as I do not love to live quite alone, let him return without delay to his fond and loving mother.

"The report your ladyship gave of my Harry fills my heart with warmest gratitude. He is all indeed a mother may wish. A year in Europe will have given him a polish and refinement he could not acquire in our homely Virginia. Mr. Stack, one of our invaluable ministers in Richmond, has a letter from Mr. Ward—my darling's tutor of early days—who knows my Lady Warrington and her excellent family, and says that my Harry has lived much with his cousins of late. I am grateful to think that my boy has the privilege of being with his good aunt. May he follow her counsels and listen to those around him who will guide him on the way of his best welfare! Adieu, dear madam and sister! For your kindness to my boy, accept the grateful thanks of a mother's heart. Though we have been divided hitherto, may these kindly ties draw us nearer and nearer. I am thankful that you should speak of my dearest father so. He was, indeed, one of the best of men! He, too, thanks you, I know, for the love you have borne to one of his children; and his daughter subscribes herself—with sincere thanks, your ladyship's most dutiful and grateful sister and servant, RACHEL ESMOND WN.

"P.S.—I have communicated with my Lady Maria; but there will be no need to tell her and dear Harry that his mother or your ladyship hope to be able to increase his small fortune. The match is altogether unsuitable."

"As far as regards myself, madam," George said, laying down the paper, "my mother's letter conveys no news to me. I always knew that Harry was the favorite son with Madam Esmond, as he deserves indeed to be. He has a hundred good qualities which I have not the good fortune to possess. He has better looks—"

"Nay, that is not your fault," the old lady said slyly, looking at him. "And, but that he is fair and you are brown, one might almost pass for the other."

Mr. George bowed, and a faint blush tinged his pale cheek.

"His disposition is bright, and mine is dark," he continued. "Harry is cheerful, and I am otherwise, perhaps. He knows how to make himself beloved by everyone, and it has been my lot to find but few friends."

"My sister and you have pretty little quarrels. There were such in old days in our family," the Baroness said. "And if Madam Esmond takes after our mother—"

"My mother has always described hers as an angel upon earth," George interjected.

"Eh! That is a common character for people when they are dead!" cried the Baroness. "And Rachel Castlewood was an angel, if you like—at least your grandfather thought so. But let me tell you, sir, that angels are sometimes not very commodious to live with. It may be they are too good to live with us sinners, and the air down below here doesn't agree with them. My poor mother was so perfect she never could forgive me for being otherwise. Ah, mon Dieu! how she used to oppress me with those angelical airs!"

George cast down his eyes, thinking of his own melancholy youth. He did not care to submit more of his family secrets to the cynical inquisition of this old worldling, who seemed, however, to understand him despite his reticence.

"I quite comprehend you, sir, though you hold your tongue," the Baroness continued. "A sermon in the morning; a sermon at night; and two or three on a Sunday. That is what people call being good. Every pleasure cried fie upon; all us worldly people excommunicated; a ball an abomination of desolation; a play a forbidden pastime; and a game of cards perdition! What a life! Mon Dieu, what a life!"

"We

The two young men had spent their initial hours exchanging the intimate details of their separate worlds, recounting the history of their households and the comings and goings of their families. Harry spoke eagerly of his dogs, the spirited little Dempster, and the steadfast old Nathan, asking after the health of Mountain and the blossoming beauty of Fanny. He relayed news of Parson Broadbent's daughter, Polly, who was soon to wed Tom Barker of Savannah and depart for Georgia. Harry confessed with a flush of shame that he had once been deeply infatuated with Polly, squandering pocket money at cards and consuming excessive spirits with her father merely to secure her company. Yet, he noted with relief that Madam Esmond would never have permitted such a union, deeming it a waste of her son's future.

In contrast, George described Colonel Washington's wife as a woman of considerable charm, good nature, and substantial fortune. He recounted the stiff, almost theatrical ceremony of introducing her to Madam Esmond in Richmond. With a twinkle in his eye, George recalled his mother's biting wit during the encounter: "Never mind, George, my dear!" she had declared, dismissing the Colonel's new bride. "The Colonel has taken another wife, but I feel certain that at one time two young gentlemen I know of ran a very near chance of having a tall stepfather six feet two in his boots." Mrs. Mountain, ever the matchmaker, seemed to envision a lifelong connection between any two people who shared a meal or a game of cards. It was she, the gossipy instigator, who had spread the rumor concerning the Indian woman, Biche. Madam Esmond had met the accusation with scornful disdain when Parson Stack delivered it, declaring she would sooner suspect Mr. Esmond of stealing silverware or marrying a servant from the kitchen. However, despite her refusal to believe Biche guilty and her gratitude for the woman's care during her son's illness, Madam Esmond treated her with such icy hauteur that the Indian woman retreated to the servants' quarters, drowning her disappointment in drink.

George painted a bleak picture of his two months at home. "The birthright is mine, Harry," he lamented, "but thou art the favourite, and God help me! I think my mother almost grudges it to me. Why should I have taken the pass, and preceded your worship into the world? Had you been the elder, you would have possessed the finest cellar, ridden the best horse, and been the most popular man in the country. As for me, I have not a word to say for myself, and frighten people with my glum visage. I should have been content as a second son, setting up as a lawyer in England, earning degrees, and saying grace at your honour's table. The time is out of joint, sir. O cursed spite, that ever I was born to set it right!"

"Why, Georgy, you are reciting verses, I protest!" Harry exclaimed.

"I believe someone else spoke those lines before me," George smiled.

"It is from one of your books," Harry cried, laughing. "You know every book ever written, I swear! Though I admit I cared little for their contents, lacking the wit to appreciate them fully. But I remembered how my dear old George used to speak of them, and that is why I took the trouble to see the authors at Tunbridge. I removed my hat to them, though not out of reverence for their works, but because of my affection for you." His voice choked slightly. "To see you again feels like a dream. Think of that bloody Indian with a knife at your throat! I wish I could offer Monsieur de Florac something for saving you, but I possess little now—merely my gold knee-buckles, which are hardly worth two guineas."

"You hold half of what I possess, child," George replied gently. "We shall divide it as soon as I have settled the debt to the Frenchman."

At this, Harry erupted into a torrent of blessings and oaths, expressing his profound love and relief. He swore that no brother in the world could compare to George. For several days following his arrival, Harry's eyes followed his brother constantly. He would pause mid-meal, drop his knife and fork, or abandon his newspaper to burst into laughter. Walking together on the Mall or in Hyde Park, Harry would gaze around at the assembled crowd as if presenting a trophy, thinking, *Behold, gentlemen! This is he. This is my brother, who was dead and is now alive again! Can any man in Christendom boast such a sibling?*

Harry firmly believed that George must honor his promise to pay Museau's heirs the ransom sum. This obligation had caused George significant distress at home. Upon Museau's death, Madam Esmond had argued with fierce eagerness and rancor that the bargain was void, freeing her son. She refused to pay the wages of iniquity. While Mr. Esmond possessed a small independence and might squander his patrimony, his mother would not be complicit in such extravagance. She would not subscribe to the wickedness of giving twelve thousand livres to a band of peasant farmers in Normandy, enemies of England, who would likely funnel the money to the priests and the Pope. Instead, if George wished to spend his father's money, he should give it to his own flesh and blood—to poor Harry, who had suddenly lost his inheritance—rather than to a set of priest-ridden peasants in a hostile nation. This dispute had raged between mother and son throughout George's final days in Virginia. On the morning of his departure, after a sleepless night, Madam Esmond had visited his bedside to ask if he still intended to throw away his father's property. George, filled with grief and perplexity, replied that his word was given and he must act according to his honor. She answered that she would continue to pray for Heaven to soften his proud heart and enable her to bear her trials. Her last look at her son was one of pale, tearless resignation before she slowly withdrew from his chamber.

"Where didst thou learn the art of winning everyone to thy side, Harry?" George continued, shifting the conversation. "How is it that you and the entire world begin as friends? Teach me a few lessons in popularity. Nay, I do not know that I require them; indeed, when I discover certain people hate me, I am often more pleased than angry."

He recounted his early days in Richmond. Mr. Esmond Warrington, the sole survivor of Braddock's defeat, had been a favorite of the townsfolk, receiving private and public kindness. The parson had glorified his escape in a sermon, neighbors visited the fugitive, and the family carriage was dispatched for reciprocal calls. George recalled that some had even set pretty little caps for him. But his mother had routed these admirers away with prodigious haughtiness, and his popularity waned before the events that sealed his fate occurred. He was not jovial enough for the officers, who preferred their drinking bouts, dice, and swearing; nor was he warm enough for the ladies, whose tea and gossip stupefied him as much as the men's bluster. He felt profoundly lonely amidst the scandal and squabbles, regretting his prison and longing for the freedom of thought and silent ease of Duquesne. He admitted to being shy, speaking unreservedly to very few, often sitting in utter silence before others. At home, it had always been Harry who dominated the table conversation, eliciting smiles from their mother, while George and his mother had little in common, speaking only to dispute matters of law and divinity.

Consequently, the gentlemen deemed him supercilious and dull, an opinion George believed was justified. The ladies found him cold and sarcastic, unable to discern if he was in earnest, generally voting him a disagreeable fellow before his reputation collapsed entirely with the appearance of the poor Biche. "Oh, a nice character they made for me, my dear!" George cried in a transport of wrath. "And a pretty life they led me after Museau's unlucky messenger appeared among us! The boys hooted the poor woman if she appeared in the street; the ladies dropped half-curtseys and crossed to the other side. That precious clergyman went from tea-table to tea-table preaching on the horrors of seduction and the lax principles young men learned in popish countries. The poor Fawn's appearance at home a few weeks after my return was declared a scheme between her and me; the best-informed agreed she had waited on the other side of the river for my signal to join me in Richmond. The officers bantered me at the coffee-house, cracking clumsy jokes about the woman I had selected. Oh, the world is a nice, charitable world! I was so enraged that I considered fleeing to Castlewood to live alone—for our mother finds the place dull and relies on Mr. Stack's ministry—until news arrived of your female perplexity, and I think we were all glad I had a pretext to come to Europe."

"I should like to see any of the infernal scoundrels who spoke against you," Harry roared, pacing the room, "and break their rascally bones!"

"I had to do something similar for Bob Clubber."

"What! That little sneaking, backbiting, toad-eating wretch who hangs about my lord at Greenway Court, spunging on every gentleman in the country? If you whipped him, George, I hope you whipped him well!"

"We were bound over to keep the peace," George explained. "I offered to go to Maryland with him to settle our difference there, and of course, the good folk remarked that having made free with the seventh commandment, I was inclined to break the sixth. By this and that, and being as innocent of the crime imputed to me as you are, I left home, my dear Harry, with as awful a reputation as ever a young gentleman earned."

Ah, what an opportunity for moralizing! If the esteemed reader and his humble servant could compile a book, illustrated with the lies told regarding each of them since reaching manhood, what a harrowing and thrilling work of fiction it would be! The world is informed of everything about you, and far more. Recently, a postman had delivered a paper containing a valuable critique stating, "This author states he was born in such and such a year. It is a lie. He was born in the year so and so." The critic knew better. Another warning from the same region advised, "Do not speak of New South Wales to him. He has a brother there, and the family never mentions his name." But this subject is too vast for a mere paragraph; it deserves a memoir, or perhaps a series of biographies penned by dear friends whom the subjects do not know.

Having related his exploits as champion and martyr, Harry was compelled to unbosom himself, laying before his elder brother an account of his private affairs. He detailed his dealings with the Castlewood family—not his lordship, for Harry was a sporting man who expected to pay when he lost and receive when he won, but for refusing to aid the chaplain in his necessity and dismissing him with false, heartless pretexts. Regarding Mr. Will, Harry had made up his mind after the horse-dealing incident, freely marking his displeasure on the man's eyes and nose. Speaking of the Countess and Lady Fanny, Harry was guarded but not favorable. He had heard all sorts of stories: the Countess was a card-playing old cat, and Lady Fanny a desperate flirt. He had heard these tales from someone who knew them both intimately. Indeed, in those days of confidence, Maria had freely imparted numerous anecdotes to her cousin regarding her stepmother and half-sister, none of which were in their favor.

However, regarding Lady Maria herself, the young man remained staunch and hearty. "It may be imprudent," he admitted to George. "I don't say no. I may be a fool; I think I am. I know there will be a dreadful piece of work at home, and that Madam and she will fight. Well! We must live apart. Our estate is big enough to live on without quarrelling, and I can go elsewhere than to Richmond or Castlewood. When you come to the property, you'll give me a bit—at any rate, Madam will let me off at an easy rent—or I'll make a famous farmer or factor. I cannot and will not part from Maria. She has acted so nobly by me that I should be a rascal to turn my back on her. Think of her bringing me every jewel she had in the world, dear brave creature! And flinging them into my lap with her last guineas—and—and—God bless her!" Harry dashed his sleeve across his eyes, stamped his foot, and declared, "No, brother, I won't part with her—not to be made Governor of Virginia tomorrow. And my dearest old George would never advise me to do so, I know that."

"I am sent here to advise you," George replied. "I am sent to break the marriage off, if I can: and a more unhappy one I cannot imagine. But I cannot counsel you to break your word, my boy."

"I knew you couldn't! What's said is said, George. I have made my bed, and must lie on it," Harry said gloomily.

Such had been the settlement between the two young worthies regarding Harry's love affair. But after George's conversation with his aunt and his further knowledge of her family, gained through the information of that keen old woman of the world, Mr. Warrington, who was naturally of a skeptical turn, began to doubt Lady Maria, as well as her brothers and sister. He viewed Harry's engagement with increased distrust and alarm. Was it for his wealth that Maria wanted Harry? Was it his handsome young person that she longed after? Were those stories true which Aunt Bernstein had told? Certainly, he could not advise Harry to break his word; but he might cast about in his mind for some scheme to put Maria's affection to the test. His ensuing conduct, which appeared not very amiable, presumably resulted from this deliberation.

Lord Castlewood's residence in Kensington Square was a sprawling edifice designed to house his entire noble clan and their retinue, situated conveniently near the palace for when the King resided there. While Lady Castlewood hosted her evening gatherings and card parties here, the location felt remote to the Londoners of a century prior. George Selwyn, for one, harbored a distinct dread of venturing out at night, fearing robbery by footpads draped in crape or by ladies in rouge at the quadrille table—though the latter threat remained a matter of speculation.

About noon, the day following Harry's dramatic reappearance at White's, the virtuous kinfolk assembled for breakfast, even Mr. Will, who was scheduled to begin his service as a footman later that afternoon. The ladies arrived first for their chocolate, joined by Will in his court suit. Finally, Lord Castlewood entered, languid in his bedgown and nightcap, having not yet donned his wig for the day. This was the news Will had brought from the Star and Garter the previous evening, having heard it from men who had witnessed it at White's and Ranelagh.

"Heard what? Seen what?" the head of the house asked, picking up his *Daily Advertiser*.

"Ask Maria!" Lady Fanny interjected. My lord turned to his elder sister, whose face wore an expression of portentous sadness, pale as a tablecloth.

"'Tis one of Will's usual elegant and polite inventions," Maria dismissed.

"No," Will swore, punctuating his denial with several oaths. "It was no invention of his. Tom Claypool of Norfolk saw them both at Ranelagh; and Jack Morris came out of White's, where he heard the story straight from Harry Warrington's own lips. Curse him, I'm glad of it!" Will roared, slapping the table. "What do you think of your Fortunate Youth, your Virginian, whom your lordship made so much of, turning out to be a second son?"

"The elder brother not dead?" my lord queried.

"No more dead than you are. Never was. It's my belief that it was a cross between the two."

"Mr. Warrington is incapable of such duplicity!" Maria cried out.

"I never encouraged the fellow; I am sure you will do me justice there," Lady Castlewood replied. "Nor did Fanny: not we, indeed!"

"Not we, indeed!" echoed Lady Fanny.

"The fellow is only a beggar, and, I dare say, has not paid for the clothes on his back," Will continued. "I'm glad of it, for, hang him, I hate him!"

"You don't regard him with favourable eyes; especially since he blacked yours, Will!" my lord grinned. "So the poor fellow has found his brother, and lost his estate!" He turned toward his sister Maria, who, despite looking the picture of woe, must have suggested something ludicrous to the humorist beside her. After gazing at her for a minute, he burst into a shrill laugh, causing the poor lady's face to flush and her eyes to overflow with tears.

"It's a shame! It's a shame!" she sobbed, hiding her face in her handkerchief. Maria's stepmother and sister exchanged glances.

"We never quite understand your lordship's humour," the former lady remarked gravely.

"I don't see there is the least reason why you should," my lord said coolly. "Maria, my dear, pray excuse me if I have said—or done anything—to hurt your feelings."

"Done anything! You pillaged the poor lad in his prosperity, and laugh at him in his ruin!" Maria rose from the table, glaring around at her family.

"Excuse me, my dear sister, I was not laughing at him," my lord said gently.

"Oh, never mind at what or whom else, my lord! You have taken from him all he had to lose. All the world points at you as the man who feeds on his own flesh and blood. And now you have his all, you make merry over his misfortune!" With a rustle of defiance, she left the room, casting looks of anger at the assembled party.

"Tell us what has happened, or what you have heard, Will, and my sister's grief will not interrupt us." Will recounted the story of George Warrington's sudden apparition at great length, filled with immense exultation at Harry's discomfiture. Lord Castlewood feigned sorrow for Harry, calling him a good, brave lad whom he liked as much as certain worldly folks liked each other. To be sure, he had played Harry at cards and taken advantage of the market upon him; but why not? The peach which other men would certainly pluck, he might as well devour. *Eh! if that were all my conscience had to reproach me with, I need not be very uneasy!* my lord thought. "Where does Mr. Warrington live?"

Will expressed readiness to enter upon a state of reprobation if he knew or cared.

"He shall be invited here, and treated with every respect," my lord declared.

"Including piquet, I suppose!" Will growled.

"Or will you take him to the stables, and sell him one of your bargains of horseflesh, Will?" my lord asked. "You would have won of Harry Warrington fast enough, if you could; but you cheat so clumsily at your game that you got paid with a cudgel. I desire, once more, that every attention may be paid to our cousin Warrington."

"And that you are not to be disturbed, when you sit down to play, of course, my lord!" cried Lady Castlewood.

"Madam, I desire fair play, for Mr. Warrington, and for myself, and for every member of this amiable family," my lord retorted fiercely.

"Heaven help the poor gentleman if your lordship is going to be kind to him," the stepmother said with a curtsey. There is no knowing how far this family dispute might have been carried had not, at that moment, a phaeton driven up to the house, in which sat the two young Virginians.

It was the carriage the prodigal had purchased in the days of his prosperity. He still drove it; George sat by his side, their negroes behind them. Harry had been meekly giving the whip and reins to his brother, ceding the whole property to him. "What business has a poor devil like me with horses and carriages, Georgy?" Harry had humbly said. "Beyond the coat on my back, and the purse my aunt gave me, I have nothing in the world. You take the driving-seat, brother; it will ease my mind if you will take the driving-seat." George laughingly said he did not know the way, and Harry did; and that, as for the carriage, he would claim only a half of it, as he had already done with his brother's wardrobe. "But a bargain is a bargain; if I share thy coats, thou must divide my breeches' pocket, Harry; that is but fair dealing!" Again and again Harry swore there never was such a brother on earth. How he rattled his horses over the road! How pleased and proud he was to drive such a brother! They arrived at Kensington in famous high spirits, and Gumbo's thunder upon Lord Castlewood's door was worthy of the biggest footman in all St. James's.

Only Lady Castlewood and her daughter Lady Fanny were in the room into which the young gentlemen were ushered. Will had no particular fancy to face Harry; my lord was not yet dressed; Maria had her reasons for being away, at least until her eyes were dried. When we drive up to friends' houses nowadays in our coaches-and-six, when John carries up our noble names, when, finally, we enter the drawing-room with our best hat and best Sunday smile foremost, does it ever happen that we interrupt a family row? That we come simpering and smiling in, stepping over the delusive ashes of a still-burning domestic heat? That in the interval between the hall-door and the drawing-room, Mrs., Mr., and the Misses Jones have grouped themselves in a family tableau? This girl artlessly arranging flowers in a vase; that one reclining over an illuminated work of devotion; mamma on the sofa, with the butcher's and grocer's book pushed under the cushion, some elegant work in her hand, and a pretty little foot pushed out advantageously; while honest Jones, far from saying, "Curse that Brown, he is always calling here!" holds out a kindly hand, shows a pleased face, and exclaims, "What, Brown my boy, delighted to see you! Hope you've come to lunch!" I say, does it ever happen to us to be made the victims of domestic artifices, the spectators of domestic comedies got up for our special amusement? Oh, let us be thankful, not only for faces, but for masks! Not only for honest welcome, but for hypocrisy, which hides unwelcome things from us! Whilst I am talking, for instance, in this easy, chatty way, what right have you, my good sir, to know what is really passing in my mind? It may be that I am racked with gout, or that my eldest son has just sent me in a thousand pounds' worth of college-bills, or that I am writhing under an attack of the Stoke Pogis Sentinel, which has just been sent me under cover, or that there is a dreadfully scrappy dinner, the evident remains of a party to which I didn't invite you, and yet I conceal my agony, I wear a merry smile; I say, "What! come to take pot-luck with us, Brown my boy! Betsy! put a knife and fork for Mr. Brown. Eat! Welcome! Fall to! It's my best!" I say that humbug which I am performing is beautiful self-denial—that hypocrisy is true virtue. Oh, if every man spoke his mind, what an intolerable society ours would be to live in!

As the young gentlemen were announced, Lady Castlewood advanced toward them with perfect ease and good humour. "We have heard, Harry," she said, looking at the latter with special friendliness, "of this most extraordinary circumstance. My Lord Castlewood said at breakfast that he should wait on you this very day, Mr. Warrington, and, cousin Harry, we intend not to love you any the less because you are poor."

"We shall be able to show now that it is not for your acres that we like you, Harry!" Lady Fanny said, following her mother's lead.

"And I to whom the acres have fallen?" Mr. George said, with a smile and a bow.

"Oh, cousin, we shall like you for being like Harry!" replied the arch Lady Fanny.

Ah! Who that has seen the world has not admired that astonishing ease with which fine ladies drop you and pick you up again? Both the ladies now addressed themselves almost exclusively to the younger brother. They were quite civil to Mr. George: but with Mr. Harry they were fond, softly familiar, gently kind, affectionately reproachful. Why had Harry not been for days and days to see them?

"Better to have had a dish of tea and a game at piquet with them than with some other folks," Lady Castlewood said. "If we had won enough to buy a paper of pins from you we should have been content; but young gentlemen don't know what is for their own good," said mamma.

"Now you have no more money to play with, you can come and play with us, cousin!" cried fond Lady Fanny, lifting up a finger, "and so your misfortune will be good fortune to us."

George was puzzled. This welcome of his brother was very different from that to which he had looked. All these compliments and attentions paid to the younger brother, though he was without a guinea! Perhaps the people were not so bad as they were painted? The Blackest of all Blacks is said not to be of quite so dark a complexion as some folks describe him.

This affectionate conversation continued for some twenty minutes, at the end of which period my Lord Castlewood made his appearance, wig on head, and sword by side. He greeted both the young men with much politeness: one not more than the other. "If you were to come to us—and I, for one, cordially rejoice to see you—what a pity it is you did not come a few months earlier! A certain evening at piquet would then most likely never have taken place. A younger son would have been more prudent."

"Yes, indeed," said Harry.

"Or a kinsman more compassionate. But I fear that love of play runs in the blood of all of us. I have it from my father, and it has made me the poorest peer in England. Those fair ladies whom you see before you are not exempt. My poor brother Will is a martyr to it; and what I, for my part, win on one day, I lose on the next. 'Tis shocking, positively, the rage for play in England. All my poor cousin's bank-notes parted company with me within twenty-four hours after I got them."

"I have played, like other gentlemen, but never to hurt myself, and never indeed caring much for the sport," remarked Mr. Warrington.

"When we heard that my lord had played with Harry, we did so scold him," cried the ladies.

"But if it had not been I, thou knowest, cousin Warrington, some other person would have had thy money. 'Tis a poor consolation, but as such Harry must please to take it, and be glad that friends won his money, who wish him well, not strangers, who cared nothing for him, and fleeced him."

"Eh! a tooth out is a tooth out, though it be your brother who pulls it, my lord!" said Mr. George, laughing. "Harry must bear the penalty of his faults, and pay his debts, like other men."

"I am sure I have never said or thought otherwise. 'Tis not like an Englishman to be sulky because he is beaten," said Harry.

"Your hand, cousin! You speak like a man!" cried my lord, with delight. The ladies smiled to each other.
