Madame de Bernstein was hardly less delighted than her nephews by the conclusion of Harry's final audience with Lady Maria. That evening, George dispatched a note to his aunt detailing the proceedings. Soon after, Lord Castlewood, whose visits to his aunt were typically infrequent, arrived to pay his respects. With the business between Maria and Harry now concluded, there was no necessity for reticence or hypocrisy; my Lord Castlewood was a man who knew precisely when to be frank. The game had been played and was over; he had no objection to discussing its various moves, stratagems, and finesse.

"She is my own sister," said my Lord, speaking with affection. "She will not have many more such opportunities to marry and establish herself. While I might not approve of the match in every respect, and I might pity your ladyship's young Virginian favorite, such a stroke of good fortune could not be thrown away. I was bound to stand by my own flesh and blood."

"Your candour does your lordship honour," Madame de Bernstein replied, "and your love for your sister is truly edifying!"

"Nay, we have lost the game, and I speak without rancour. It is not for you, who have won, to bear malice," my Lord added with a bow.

Madame de Bernstein protested that she had never been in better humour. "Confess now, Eugene," she pressed, "that Maria's visit to Harry at the spunging-house—that touching surrender of all his presents to her—was a stroke of your invention?"

"Pity for the young man, and a sense of what was due from Maria to her friend, her affianced lover, in misfortune; surely these were sufficient motives to make her act as she did," Lord Castlewood replied demurely.

"But you advised her, my good nephew?"

With a shrug of his shoulders, Castlewood admitted that he had indeed advised his sister to see Mr. Henry Warrington. "However," he continued, "we should have won, in spite of your ladyship, had not the elder brother made his appearance. I have been trying to console my poor Maria by showing her what a piece of good fortune it is, after all, that we lost."

"Suppose she had married Harry, and then cousin George had made his appearance?" remarked the Baroness.

"Effectivement," cried Eugene, taking a pinch of snuff. "Let us be thankful to the grave for disgorging its dead in time! I must say that Mr. George Warrington seems a man of sense, and not more selfish than other elder sons and men of the world. My poor Molly fancied he might be a greenhorn, perhaps like his younger brother. She fondly hoped he might be inclined to share everything with Harry junior. In which case, so infatuated was she about the young fellow, I believe she would have taken him. 'Harry Warrington with half a loaf might do very well,' I said, 'but Harry Warrington with no bread, my dear!'"

"How no bread?" asked the Baroness.

"Well, no bread except at his brother's side-table. The elder said as much."

"What a hard-hearted wretch!" cried Madame de Bernstein.

"Ah, bah! I play with you, aunt, *cartes sur table*! Mr. George only did what everybody else would do; and we have no right to be angry with him, really we haven't. Molly herself acknowledged as much after her first burst of grief subsided, and I brought her to listen to reason. The silly old creature! to be so wild about a young lad at her time of life!"

"'Twas a real passion, I almost do believe," said Madame de Bernstein.

"You should have heard her take leave of him. *C'était touchant*, ma parole d'honneur! I cried. Before George, I could not help myself. The young fellow, with muddy stockings and his hair falling over his eyes, threw himself amongst us at dinner; he made his offer to Molly in a very frank and noble manner, and in good language too; and she replied. *Begad*, it put me in mind of Mrs. Woffington in the new Scotch play written by Lord Bute's man—*Douglas*, what d'ye call it? She clung round the lad; she bade him adieu in heartrending accents. She stepped out of the room in a stately despair—no more chocolate, thank you. If she had made a *mauvais pas*, no one could retire from it with more dignity. 'Twas a masterly retreat after a defeat. We were starved out of our position, but we retired with all the honours of war."

"Molly won't die of the disappointment!" said my Lord's aunt, sipping her cup.

My Lord snarled a grin and showed his yellow teeth. "He, he!" he said. "She has once or twice before had the malady very severely, and recovered perfectly. It doesn't kill, as your ladyship knows, at Molly's age."

How should her ladyship know? She did not marry Doctor Tusher until she was advanced in life, nor did she become Madame de Bernstein until still later. As the poet Old Dido remarked, one is not ignorant of misfortune until one learns to have compassion on the wretched.

In the little world, as I have been told, people quarrel, fight, and abuse one another for ages without reconciliation. But people in the great world are surely wiser in their generation. They have differences; they cease seeing each other. They make it up and come together again, and no questions are asked. A stray prodigal, or a stray puppy-dog, is thus brought in under the benefit of an amnesty, though you know he has been away in ugly company. For six months past, ever since the Castlewoods and Madame de Bernstein had been battling for possession of poor Harry Warrington, these two branches of the Esmond family had remained apart. Now, the question being settled, they were free to meet again, as though no difference had ever separated them. Madame de Bernstein drove her great coach to Lady Castlewood's rout, and the Esmond ladies appeared smiling at Madame de Bernstein's drums, loving each other just as much as they previously had done.

"So, sir, I hear you have acted like a hard-hearted monster about your poor brother Harry!" said the Baroness, delighted, and menacing George with her stick.

"I acted but upon your ladyship's hint, and desired to see whether it was for himself or his reputed money that his kinsfolk wanted to have him," replied George, turning rather red.

"Nay, Maria could not marry a poor fellow who was utterly penniless, and whose elder brother said he would give him nothing!"

"I did it for the best, madam," said George, still blushing.

"And so thou didst, O thou hypocrite!" cried the old lady.

"Hypocrite, madam! And why?" asked Mr. Warrington, drawing himself up in much state.

"I know all, my infant!" said the Baroness in French. "Thou art very like thy grandfather. Come, that I embrace thee! Harry has told me all, and that thou hast divided thy little patrimony with him!"

"It was but natural, madam. We have had common hearts and purses since we were born. I but feigned hard-heartedness in order to try those people yonder," said George, with filling eyes.

"And thou wilt divide Virginia with him too?" asked the Bernstein.

"I don't say so. It were not just," replied Mr. Warrington. "The land must go to the eldest born, and Harry would not have it otherwise: and it may be I shall die, or my mother outlive the pair of us. But half of what is mine is his: and he, it must be remembered, only was extravagant because he was mistaken as to his position."

"But it is a knight of old, it is a Bayard, it is the grandfather come to life!" cried Madame de Bernstein to her attendant as she retired for the night. That evening, when the lads left her, it was to poor Harry she gave the two fingers, and to George the rouged cheek, who blushed, for his part, almost as deep as that often-dyed rose, at such a mark of his old kinswoman's favour.

Although Harry Warrington was the least envious of men, and did honour to his brother as in all respects his chief, guide, and superior, yet no wonder a certain feeling of humiliation and disappointment oppressed the young man after his deposition from his eminence as Fortunate Youth and heir to boundless Virginian territories. Our friends at Kensington might promise and vow that they would love him all the better after his fall; Harry made a low bow and professed himself very thankful; but he could not help perceiving, when he went with his brother to the state entertainment with which my Lord Castlewood regaled his new-found kinsman, that George was all in all to his cousins. Had all the talk, compliments, and *petits soins* for himself, whilst of Harry no one took any notice save poor Maria, who followed him with wistful looks, pursued him with eyes conveying dismal reproaches, and, as it were, blamed him because she had left him. "Ah!" the eyes seemed to say, "'Tis mighty well of you, Harry, to have accepted the freedom which I gave you; but I had no intention, sir, that you should be so pleased at being let off." She gave him up, but yet she did not quite forgive him for taking her at her word. She would not have him, and yet she would. Oh, my young friends, how delightful is the beginning of a love-business, and how undignified, sometimes, the end! What a romantic vista is before young Damon and young Phillis (or middle-aged ditto ditto) when, their artless loves made known to each other, they twine their arms round each other's waists and survey that charming *pays du tendre* which lies at their feet! Into that country, so linked together, they will wander from now until extreme old age. There may be rocks and roaring rivers, but will not Damon's strong true love enable him to carry Sweetheart over them? There may be dragons and dangers in the path, but shall not his courageous sword cut them down? Then at eve, how they will rest cuddled together, like two pretty babes in the wood, the moss their couch, the stars their canopy, their arms their mutual pillows! This is the wise plan young folks make when they set out on the love journey; and—O me!--they have not got a mile when they come to a great wall and find they must walk back again. They are squabbling with the post-boy at Barnet (the first stage on the Gretna Road, I mean), and, behold, perhaps Strephon has not got any money, or here is papa with a whacking horsewhip, who takes Miss back again, and locks her up crying in the schoolroom. The parting is heart-breaking; but, when she has married the banker and had eight children, and he has become, it may be, a prosperous barrister—it may be, a seedy raff who has gone twice or thrice into the Gazette; when, I say, in after years Strephon and Delia meet again, is not the meeting ridiculous? Nevertheless, I hope no young man will fall in love, having any doubt in his mind as to the eternity of his passion. 'Tis when a man has had a second or third amorous attack that he begins to grow doubtful; but some women are romantic to the end, and from eighteen to eighty-five (for what I know) are always expecting their hearts to break. In fine, when you have been in love and are so no more, when the King of France, with twenty thousand men, with colours flying, music playing, and all the pomp of war, having marched up the hill, then proceeds to march down again, he and you are in an absurd position.

This is what Harry Warrington, no doubt, felt when he went to Kensington and encountered the melancholy, reproachful eyes of his cousin. Yes! it is a foolish position to be in; but it is also melancholy to look into a house you have once lived in, and see black casements and emptiness where once shone the fires of welcome. Melancholy? Yes; but, ha! how bitter, how melancholy, how absurd to look up as you pass sentimentally by No. 13, and see somebody else grinning out of window, and evidently on the best terms with the landlady. I always feel hurt, even at an inn which I frequent, if I see other folks' trunks and boots at the doors of the rooms which were once mine. Have those boots lolled on the sofa which once I reclined on? I kick you from before me, you muddy, vulgar highlows!

So considering that his period of occupation was over, and Maria's rooms, if not given up to a new tenant, were, at any rate, to let, Harry did not feel very easy in his cousin's company, nor she possibly in his. He found either that he had nothing to say to her, or that what she had to say to him was rather dull and commonplace, and that the red lip of a white-necked pipe of Virginia was decidedly more agreeable to him now than Maria's softest accents and most melancholy moue. When George went to Kensington, then, Harry did not care much about going, and pleaded other engagements.

At his uncle's house in Hill Street the poor lad was no better amused, and indeed was treated by the virtuous people there with scarce any attention at all. The ladies did not scruple to deny themselves when he came; he could scarce have believed in such insincerity after their caresses, their welcome, their repeated vows of affection; but happening to sit with the Lamberts for an hour after he had called upon his aunt, he saw her ladyship's chairmen arrive with an empty chair, and his aunt step out and enter the vehicle, and not even blush when he made her a bow from the opposite window. To be denied by his own relations—to have that door which had

Our Virginians, displaying a wisdom rare in youth, had embraced strong Jacobite sentiments, professing a profound devotion to the exiled royal family. The banished prince had recognized Madam Esmond's father as Marquis of Esmond, and she felt no ill will toward a lineage so eager to honor her house. Scandals regarding her sister, Madame de Bernstein, and the Old Chevalier were dismissed with scorn; she maintained with perfect truth that the first two monarchs of the House of Hanover were no more virtuous in domestic matters than any Stuart. Yet, the king *de facto* was king, crowned and anointed, having decisively defeated the king *de jure* in battle. In her clear judgment, her sons owed it to themselves and the sovereign to appear at his court. If the King offered a lucrative post or a ribbon of blue or red, she would not be surprised. She was certain the King knew the Virginian Esmonds as well as any nobleman. Thus, the lads were commanded to present themselves at court. Had their mother known that George had taken Harry's laced coat for the day he bowed at Kensington, she might have been angry, but she was absent from the scene.

A century prior, the King's drawing-room was open daily to his nobility and gentry. Loyalty, especially since the war began, found satisfaction a dozen times a month in the august sight of the sovereign. A prudent avoidance of enemy ships and a gracious acknowledgment of the potential loss of the royal person at sea caused the monarch to forego visits to his beloved Hanover, compelling him to remain, albeit unwillingly, among his loving Britons. A Hanoverian lady, whose virtues endeared her to the prince, strove to console him for his enforced absence from Herrenhausen. Through the Countess of Walmoden, the revered Defender of the Faith could hear the accents of his native home.

Mr. Warrington requested his uncle, an assiduous courtier, to present him. Since Mr. Lambert also needed to attend court to thank the King for his promotion, the two gentlemen traveled to Kensington together, hiring a hackney-coach as my Lord Wrotham's carriage was required by its rightful owner, who had returned to town. They alighted at the Kensington Palace Gate, where sentries saluted the good General, and proceeded on foot to the summer residence. Walking under the portico, they entered the gallery leading to the great black marble staircase, richly decorated by Mr. Kent, passing through rooms hung with tapestry and adorned with pictures and busts until they reached the King's great drawing-room. Here, amidst masterpieces including Titian's "Venus" and Rubens' "St. Francis adoring the infant Saviour," the gentlemen waited for the King to issue from his private apartments, where he was in conference with his ministers.

George Warrington, never having seen a palace before, had leisure to admire the surroundings and the people. He beheld fine pictures for the first time, delighting in Sir Anthony Van Dyck's portrait of King Charles the First and his family, and Tintoret's "Esther before Ahasuerus," where figures wore magnificent Venetian attire. So enraptured was he by these works that he scarce heard his friend the General whispering the names of the surrounding personages.

"Yonder," said Mr. Lambert, "are two Lords of the Admiralty, Mr. Gilbert Elliot and Admiral Boscawen—the Boscawen whose fleet fired the first gun in your waters two years ago. That stout gentleman belted with gold is Mr. Fox, former Minister, now Paymaster with a great salary."

"He carries the *auri fames* on his person. Why, his waistcoat is a perfect Potosi!" exclaimed George.

*"Aliena appetens"—how goes the text? He loves to get money and to spend it,* continued General Lambert. *That is my Lord Chief Justice Willes, talking to my Lord of Salisbury, Doctor Headley, who, if he serves his God as he serves his King, will be translated to high promotion in Heaven. He belongs to your grandfather's time, loved by Dick Steele and hated by the Dean. With them is my Lord of London, the learned Doctor Sherlock. My lords of the lawn sleeves have lost half their honors now. I remember when I was a boy in my mother's hand, she made me kneel to the Bishop of Rochester; him who went over the water to become Minister to a nameless Perkin. That handsome fair man is Admiral Smith, president of poor Byng's court-martial, who strove in vain to save him; 'Tom of Ten Thousand' they call him in the fleet. The French Ambassador had him broken when he was a lieutenant for making a French man-of-war lower topsails to him, yet the King made Tom a captain the next day. That tall, haughty-looking man is my Lord George Sackville; now that I am a Major-General myself, he will treat me somewhat better than a footman. I wish my stout old Blakeney were here; he is the soldier's darling, as kind and brave as yonder poker of a nobleman is brave. I am your lordship's very humble servant. This is a young gentleman just from America, involved in Braddock's sad business two years ago."*

"Oh, indeed!" said the poker of a nobleman. "I have the honor of speaking to Mr.—?"

"To Major-General Lambert, at your lordship's service, and who served in his Majesty's army before you entered it. That, Mr. Warrington, is the first commoner in England, Mr. Speaker Onslow. Where is your uncle? I shall have to present you myself if Sir Miles delays." As he spoke, the General addressed himself entirely to his young friend, ignoring his colleague, who stalked away with a scared look, amazed at the other's audacity. A hundred years ago, a nobleman was a nobleman, expected to be admired as such.

Sir Miles's red waistcoat appeared shortly, and many cordial greetings passed between him, his nephew, and General Lambert, for Sir Miles was the most affectionate of men. Was the General leaving my Lord Wrotham's house? It was time, as his lordship wished to occupy it. Very good; but consider what a loss for the neighbors!

"We miss you, we positively miss you, my dear General," cried Sir Miles. "My daughters were in love with those lovely young ladies—upon my word, they were; and my Lady Warrington and my girls debated endlessly how to make acquaintance with your charming family. We feel as if we were old friends already; indeed we do, General, if you permit me; and we love you, if I may speak frankly, on account of your friendship and kindness to our dear nephews: though we were a little jealous, I own a little jealous of them, because they went so often to see you. Often have I said to my Lady Warrington, 'My dear, why don't we make acquaintance with the General? Why don't we ask him and his ladies to dine with some other plain country gentlefolks?' Carry my most sincere respects to Mrs. Lambert, I pray, sir; and thank her for her goodness to these young gentlemen. My own flesh and blood, sir; my dear, dear brother's boys!" He passed his hand across his manly eyes, choking almost with generous emotion.

While they discoursed—George Warrington restraining his laughter with admirable gravity—the door of the King's apartments opened, and pages entered, preceding his Majesty. He was followed by his burly son, the Duke, a very corpulent Prince with a coat and face of blazing scarlet. Behind them came various gentlemen and officers of state; among whom George immediately recognized the famous Mr. Secretary Pitt, by his tall stature, eagle eye, and beak, his grave and majestic presence. As I see that solemn figure passing, even a hundred years later, I protest I feel a present awe, a desire to take off my hat. I am not frightened at George the Second, nor dazzled by the portentous appearance of his Royal Highness the Duke of Culloden and Fontenoy; but the Great Commoner, the terrible Cornet of Horse! His figure bestrides our narrow isle of a century back like a Colossus; and I hush as he passes in his gouty shoes, his thunderbolt hand wrapped in flannel. Perhaps, as we see him issuing with dark looks from the royal closet, angry scenes have passed between him and his august master. He has been boring that old monarch for hours with prodigiously long speeches, full of eloquence and noble phrases on commonest topics, utterly repulsive to the little shrewd old gentleman "at whose feet he lays himself," who has the most thorough dislike for fine boody and fine brose! The sublime Minister passed solemnly through the crowd; the company ranged respectfully round the wall; and his Majesty walked round the circle, his royal son lagging a little behind, engaging select individuals in conversation.

The monarch was a little, keen, fresh-colored old man with very protruding eyes, attired in plain, old-fashioned, snuff-colored clothes and brown stockings, his only ornament the blue ribbon of the Order of the Garter. He spoke in a German accent, but with ease, shrewdness, and simplicity, addressing those he wished to notice or passing on with a bow. He knew Mr. Lambert well, who had served under his Majesty at Dettingen and with his royal son in Scotland, and congratulated him good-humoredly on his promotion.

"It is not always," his Majesty said, "that we can do as we like; but I was glad when, for once, I could give myself that pleasure in your case, General; for my army contains no better officer as you."

The veteran blushed and bowed, deeply gratified. Meanwhile, the Best of Monarchs looked at Sir Miles Warrington, whom he knew perfectly as the eager recipient of all favors, and at the young gentleman by his side.

"Who is this?" the Defender of the Faith asked, pointing toward George Warrington, who stood before his sovereign in a respectful attitude, clad in poor Harry's best embroidered suit.

With the deepest reverence, Sir Miles informed his King that the young gentleman was his nephew, Mr. George Warrington, of Virginia, who asked leave to pay his humble duty.

"This, then, is the other brother?" the Venerated Prince observed. "He came in time, else the other brother would have spent all the money. My Lord Bishop of Salisbury, why do you come out in this bitter weather? You had much better stay at home!" And with this, the revered wielder of Britannia's sceptre passed on to other lords and gentlemen. Sir Miles Warrington was deeply affected by the royal condescension. He clapped his nephew's hands. "God bless you, my boy," he cried; "I told you that you would see the greatest monarch and the finest gentleman in the world. Is he not so, my Lord Bishop?"

"That, that he is!" cried his lordship, clasping his ruffled hands and turning his fine eyes to the sky, "the best of princes and of men."

"That is Master Louis, my Lady Yarmouth's favorite nephew," said Lambert, pointing to a young gentleman surrounded by a crowd; and presently the stout Duke of Cumberland came up to their little group.

His Royal Highness held out his hand to his old companion-in-arms. "Congratulate you on your promotion, Lambert," he said good-naturedly. Sir Miles Warrington's eyes were ready to burst with rapture.

"I owe it, sir, to your Royal Highness's good offices," said the grateful General.

"Not at all; not at all: ought to have had it a long time before. Always been a good officer; perhaps there'll be some employment for you soon. This is the gentleman whom James Wolfe introduced to me?"

"His brother, sir."

"Oh, the real Fortunate Youth! You were with poor Ned Braddock in America—a prisoner, and lucky enough to escape. Come and see me, sir, in Pall Mall. Bring him to my levee, Lambert." And the broad back of the Royal Prince turned to their friends.

"It is raining! You came on foot, General Lambert? You and George must come home in my coach. You must and shall come home with me, I say. By George, you must! I'll have no denial," cried the enthusiastic Baronet. He drove George and the General back to Hill Street, presenting the latter to my Lady Warrington and his darlings, Flora and Dora, and insisting they partake of a collation, as they must be hungry after their ride. "What, there is only cold mutton? Well, an old soldier can eat cold mutton. And a good glass of my Lady Warrington's own cordial, prepared with her own hands, will keep the cold wind out. Delicious cordial! Capital mutton! Our own, my dear General," said the hospitable Baronet, "our own from the country, six years old if a day. We keep a plain table; but all the Warringtons since the Conqueror have been remarkable for their love of mutton; and our meal may look a little scanty, and is, for we are plain people, and I am obliged to keep my rascals of servants on board-wages. Can't give them seven-year-old mutton, you know."

Sir Miles, in his nephew's presence, described George's reception at court in such flattering terms that George hardly knew himself, or the scene he had witnessed, or how to look his uncle in the face, or how to contradict him before his family amidst the astonishing narrative. Lambert sat by with open eyes. He, too, had been at Kensington, yet he had seen none of the wonders Sir Miles described.

"We are proud of you, dear George. We love you, my dear nephew—we all love you, we are all proud of you—"

"Yes; but I like Harry best," said a little voice.

Life, in its raw and unvarnished reality, offers the novelist scant material for a narrative. When dealing with the profession of arms, where courage is tested and danger is tangible, the writer can draw upon vivid circumstances and heroic deeds. But for the rest of existence—the mundane drudgery of commerce, law, or tailoring—there is little to recount. To chronicle the daily sale of sugar or the poring over of dusty legal volumes would be to write a tedious history of hobnails and pennies, a tale no reader could endure. Even in the romanticized past, poets depicted shepherds in absurd finery, dancing before flocks with flageolets tied in satin ribbons, ignoring the truth of their labor. Thus, the novelist is forced to admit that, save for war, the actual affairs of life remain beyond the scope of fiction. We can only depict men removed from their trades, caught in the throes of passion, love, laughter, and hatred, while their professions remain a silent, subaudient backdrop.

Consequently, our characters are rarely seen in their workplaces. We find them only in the theater lobbies, coffee houses, pleasure grounds, and fair booths, drifting away from their humdrum labors. Corydon carts litter and threshes barley only to make love to Phillis; Ancillula dresses the nursery and waits on breakfast before catching a fleeting moment to speak with Boopis, the policeman. All day, their feet beat the stale pavement; only in stolen moments, away from toil, do we glimpse them.

Poor Harry Warrington found himself increasingly shunned by the macaronis and fine gentlemen of White's and Arthur's. The Ring, the Mall, and the gaming tables knew him no more. Madame de Bernstein, his aunt, attempted to brace him against the world's indifference, vowing that courage would conquer it. Yet Harry, too honest to wear a mask of smiling compliance when discontented, could not parry slights with adroit flattery.

"You pull a long face, Harry," the old lady chided, "and complain of the world's treatment. Fiddlededee, sir! Everyone must put up with impertinences. If you get a box on the ear because you are poor and cast down, you must bear it with a smile and seek revenge ten years hence. Moi qui vous parle! Do you suppose I have not eaten humble-pie? We all must swallow it. Now that you are no longer the Fortunate Youth, be the Clever Youth. Win back your place. Go to every rout and party. Be civil to everyone, especially women. Show your spirit, of which you have plenty. With economy and your brother's generosity, you can still make a genteel figure. With your handsome person, you cannot fail to attract a rich heiress. Go to the merchants in the City; they won't know you are out of fashion at Court. When did you visit my Lady Yarmouth? She took a fancy to you. Be constant at her evenings!"

Thus, the woman who once loved Harry with such eagerness turned against him. Instead of smiles, she met him with coldness, becoming peevish and patronizing. She cast gibes at him before her guests, flushing his honest face with humiliation and awakening sharp pangs of grief in his gentle heart. Her servants, once eager to respect him, now ignored him. My Lady was often indisposed when he called; her people did not press him to stay or offer dinner as they had when he was the Fortunate Youth.

Despairing, Harry carried his woes to Mrs. Lambert. In a passion of sorrow, he recounted his aunt's cruelty. Stricken by the world's fickleness, he sat glum in a window-seat while the good lady and her daughters bustled about their household cares.

"I know you are the best people alive," he told them, "and the kindest. I must be the dullest company in the world—yes, that I am."

"Well, you are not very lively, Harry," said Miss Hetty, beginning to command him, perhaps wondering, "Is this the hero I took him for?"

"If he is unhappy, why should he be lively?" asked Theo, gently. "He has a good heart and is pained by his friends' desertion. Surely there is no harm in that?"

"I would have too much spirit to show I was hurt," cried Hetty, clenching her fists. "I would smile, though that horrible old painted woman boxed my ears. She is horrible, Mamma. You think so yourself, Theo! Admit it! You said so last night, acting her coming in on her crutch and grinning at the company."

"I mayn't like her," said Theo, turning red. "But there is no reason to call Harry's aunt names before his face."

"You provoking thing! You are always right!" Hetty cried, angry. "Indeed, Harry, it was very wrong of me to make rude remarks about your relations."

"I don't care about the others, Hetty," Harry replied, his voice trembling. "But it seems hard that this one should turn upon me. I had grown very fond of her. It makes me mad when people I love turn away or act unkindly."

"Suppose George were to do so?" Hetty asked.

"You are very clever and lively, and may suppose many things," Harry snapped, standing up with resolute anger. "But not that, Hetty, if you please! You don't know my brother as I know him—or you wouldn't take such a liberty as to suppose my brother George could do anything unkind or unworthy!" Harry flushed deeply as he spoke.

Hetty turned pale, looked up at Harry, and said nothing.

Before leaving, Harry added simply, "I am very sorry, Hetty, and beg your pardon if I said anything rough. But I always fight up if anyone says anything against George."

Hetty offered no answer from her pale lips, only giving him her hand and dropping a prim curtsey.

Later, when Hetty and Theo shared curl-paper confidences, she sighed, "Oh! I thought it would be so happy to see him every day. Now that I do see him, I keep offending him. I can't help it. And I know he isn't clever, Theo. But oh! Isn't he good, kind, and brave? Didn't he look handsome when he was angry?"

"You silly little thing," Theo replied, "you are always trying to make him look handsome."

Among these young people were Theo and Hetty, Harry and George. Perhaps General Lambert applied the monosyllable "Bo" to his wife as a rebuke for her inveterate love of sentiment and propensity for match-making—a hint that she was a goose if she fancied the two Virginian lads would fall for the Lambert daughters. Little Het might have her fancies; little girls will. But they grow out of them. "And you know, Molly," the General noted, "you fancied somebody else before you fancied me." Harry, however, had evidently not been smitten by Hetty. Now superseded by his elder brother, he could not even claim the coat on his back as his own. Master Harry was no great catch.

"Oh yes," Mrs. Lambert said, "now he is poor we will show him the door, as the rest of the world does."

"That is what I always do, isn't it, Molly? Turn my back on my friends in distress?" the General asked.

"No, my dear! I am a goose, now, and that I own, Martin!" the wife admitted, reaching for her pocket-handkerchief.

"Let the poor boy come to us and welcome. Ours is almost the only house in this selfish place where so much can be said for him. He is unhappy, and to be with us puts him at ease. In God's name, let him be with us!" the kind-hearted officer declared. Accordingly, whenever crestfallen Hal wanted a dinner or an evening's entertainment, Mr. Lambert's table had a corner for him. George was welcome too. Though he did not initially feel the cordiality Harry did, George was colder and more mistrustful. Yet, the goodness and friendliness of the family touched him. Soon, George learned to love them for their own sake, as well as for their kindness to his brother. He saw Harry's sadness and pitied his depression. In his sarcastic way, George would often take himself to task before his brother for coming to life again, saying, "Dear Harry, I am George the Unlucky, though you have ceased to be Harry the Fortunate. Florac would have done much better not to pass his sword through that Indian's body and leave my scalp as an ornament for the fellow's belt. I say he would, sir! At White's, people would have respected you. Our mother would have wept over me as a defunct angel instead of being angry with me for again supplanting her favorite—you are her favorite, you deserve to be everybody's favorite. Only, if I had not come back, your favorite, Maria, would have insisted on marrying you. That is how the gods would have revenged themselves upon you for your prosperity."

"I never know whether you are laughing at me or yourself, George," Harry said. "I never know whether you are serious or jesting."

"Precisely my own case, Harry, my dear!" George replied.

"But this I know: there never was a better brother in the world; and never better people than the Lamberts."

"Never was truer word said!" cried George, taking his brother's hand.

"And if I'm unhappy, 'tis not your fault—nor theirs—nor perhaps mine, George," the younger continued. "'Tis fate, you see. 'Tis having nothing to do. I must work; and how, George? That is the question."

"We will see what our mother says. We must wait till we hear from her," George said.

"I say, George! Do you know, I don't think I should much like going back to Virginia?" Harry asked in a low, alarmed voice.

"What! In love with one of the lasses here?"

"Love 'em like sisters—with all my heart, of course, dearest, best girls! But, having come out of that business, thanks to you, I don't want to go back. No! No! It is not for that I fancy staying in Europe better than going home. But, you see, I don't fancy hunting, duck-shooting, tobacco-planting, whist-playing, and going to sermon, over and over again, for all my life, George. And what else is there to do at home? What on earth is there for me to do at all? That's what makes me miserable. It would not matter for you to be a younger son; you are so clever you would make your way anywhere. But for a poor fellow like me, what chance is there? Until I do something, George, I shall be miserable, that's what I shall!"

"Have I not always said so? Art thou not coming round to my opinion?"

"What opinion, George? You know pretty much whatever you think, I think, George!" the dutiful junior replied.

"That Florac had best have left the Indian to take my scalp, my dear!"

At which Harry burst away with an angry exclamation, and they continued to puff their pipes in friendly union.

They lived together, each going his own gait, with little intercourse save that of affection. Harry never ventured to meddle with George's books, sitting dumb as a mouse at the lodgings while his brother studied. They soon moved from the Court end of the town, Madame de Bernstein pishing and pshaing at their change of residence. George took a great fancy to frequenting Sir Hans Sloane's new reading-room and museum at Montagu House, taking cheerful lodgings in Southampton Row, Bloomsbury, overlooking the delightful fields toward Hampstead. Lord Wrotham's family coming to Mayfair, and Mr. Lambert having business detaining him in London, also changed houses, engaging furnished apartments in Soho, not far from the young men's dwelling. It was with the Lamberts that Harry, night after night, took refuge.

George was often with them too. As the acquaintance ripened, he frequented their house with increasing assiduity, finding their company more to his taste than Aunt Bernstein's polite circle of gamblers, Sir Miles Warrington's port and mutton, or the daily noise of the coffee-houses. Being strangers in London alike, he and the Lambert ladies partook of its pleasures together, visiting Vauxhall, Ranelagh, Marybone Gardens, the play, and the Tower, wherever there was honest amusement to be had. Martin Lambert loved that his children should have all the innocent pleasure he could procure, and Mr. George, of a generous disposition, liked to treat his friends, especially those who had been so kindly to his brother.

With all the passion of his heart, Mr. Warrington loved a play. He had never enjoyed this amusement in Virginia, only once or twice at Quebec, but when he came to London, where the two theaters were in their full glory, he thought he could never have enough of the delightful entertainment. Anything he liked, he naturally wished to share. No wonder he was eager to take his friends to the theater; the young countryfolk were not unwilling. Should it be Drury Lane or Covent Garden, ladies? There was Garrick and Shakespeare at Drury Lane. Yet, would it be believed, the ladies wanted to hear the famous new author whose piece was being played at Covent Garden?

At this time, a star of genius had risen, blazing with dazzling brilliance. The great Mr. John Home of Scotland had produced a tragedy, than which, since the days of the ancients, there had been nothing more classic and elegant. What had Mr. Garrick meant by refusing such a masterpiece for his theater? Say what you will about Shakespeare; in the works of that undoubted great poet—who had begun to grow vastly more popular in England since Monsieur Voltaire attacked him—there were many barbarisms that could not but shock a polite auditory. Whereas, Mr. Home, the modern author, knew how to be refined in the very midst of grief and passion. The performances concluded, and our friends departed in a carriage for Mr. Warrington's lodging, where the Virginians had arranged an elegant supper. Mr. Warrington, eager to treat them with the utmost distinction, had secured the hospitality of the General and his wife, who gladly accepted the invitation of the two bachelors, delighted at the prospect of bringing joy to their young companions. The gathering comprised the General and Mrs. Lambert, their son recently returned from college, their two vibrant daughters, and Mr. Spencer of the Temple—a new acquaintance George had met at the coffee-house. All partook cheerfully of the landlady's fare, though the precise arrangement of their seating remains somewhat obscure to me. It seems, however, that Miss Theo found herself seated beside the chickens, while Mr. George Warrington shared the table with Miss Hetty and a ham, the latter dividing the attentions of Mr. Harry. Mrs. Lambert likely sat to George's right, leaving the three remaining seats for the General, his son, and the Templar to be deduced.

Mr. Spencer had attended the rival theatre, where he had previously introduced George to the greenroom. Conversation naturally turned to the play, with several members of the party insisting they had been thoroughly delighted.

"As for what our gentlemen say, sir," Mrs. Lambert exclaimed, addressing Mr. Spencer, "you must not believe a word of it. 'Tis a delightful piece, and my husband and Mr. George behaved as ill as possible."

"We laughed in the wrong places and wept when we ought to have cried," the General admitted. "That is the truth."

"You caused every soul in the boxes around us to glance about and cry 'Hush!' You made the pit shout, 'Silence in the boxes, yonder!' Such conduct I have never witnessed, and I quite blushed for you, Mr. Lambert!"

"Mamma thought it was a tragedy, and we thought it was merely fun," the General replied. "George and I behaved perfectly well, didn't we, Theo?"

"Not when I was looking your way, Papa!" Theo retorted. At this, the General asked, "Was there ever such a saucy baggage seen?"

"You know, sir, I did not speak until I was bid," Theo continued, modestly. "I confess I was deeply moved by the play, and by the beauty and acting of Mrs. Woffington. I was sorry that the poor mother should find her child and then lose him. I am sorry, too, Papa, if I ought not to have been sorry!" she added, offering a smile.

"Women are not so clever as men, you know, Theo," Hetty called out from the end of the table, casting a sly glance at Harry. "Next time we go to the play, please, brother Jack, pinch us when we ought to cry, or give us a nudge when it is right to laugh."

"I wish we could have seen the fight," General Lambert remarked. "The combat between little Norval and the gigantic Norwegian—that would have been rare sport. You should write, Jack, and suggest it to Mr. Rich, the manager."

"I have not seen that," Harry said gravely. "But I saw Slack and Broughton at Marybone Gardens!" He wondered if he had struck a witty remark, as the entire company laughed. "It would require no giant," he added, "to knock over yonder little fellow in the red boots. I, for one, could throw him over my shoulder."

"Mr. Garrick is a small man. But there are times when he appears a giant," Mr. Spencer observed. "How grand he was in *Macbeth*, Mr. Warrington! How awful that dagger scene was! You should have seen our host, ladies! I presented Mr. Warrington in the greenroom to Mr. Garrick and Mrs. Pritchard, and Lady Macbeth did him the honor of taking a pinch out of his box."

"Did the wife of the Thane of Cawdor sneeze?" the General asked in an awe-struck tone.

"She thanked Mr. Warrington in tones so hollow and tragic that he started back, nearly upsetting his rappee, for Macbeth sneezed thrice."

"Macbeth, Macbeth, Macbeth!" cried the General.

"And the great philosopher standing by Mr. Johnson said, 'You must mind, Davy, lest thy sneeze should awaken Duncan!' who, by the way, was conversing with the three witches as they sat against the wall."

"What! Have you been behind the scenes at the play? Oh, I would give worlds to go behind the scenes!" Theo exclaimed.

"And see the ropes pulled, and smell the tallow-candles, and look at the pasteboard gold, the tinsel jewels, and the painted old women, Theo? No. Do not look too close," the skeptical young host said demurely, drinking a glass of hock. "You were angry with your papa and me."

"Nay, George!" the girl cried.

"Nay? I say, yes! You were angry with us because we laughed when you were disposed to cry. If I may speak for you, sir, as well as myself," George said, bowing to his guest, the General Lambert, "I think we were not inclined to weep, like the ladies, because we stood behind the author's scenes of the play, as it were. Looking closely at the young hero, we saw how much of him was mere rant and tinsel; and as for the pale, tragical mother, her pallor was but white chalk, and her grief her pocket-handkerchief. Own now, Theo, you thought me very unfeeling?"

"If you find it out, sir, without my owning it—what is the good of my confessing?" Theo replied.

"Suppose I were to die?" George continued. "And you saw Harry in grief? You would be witnessing genuine affliction, a real tragedy; you would grieve too. But you would not be affected if you saw the undertaker in weepers and a black cloak!"

"Indeed, but I should, sir!" Mrs. Lambert declared. "And so, I promise you, would any daughter of mine."

"Perhaps we might find weepers of our own, Mr. Warrington," Theo suggested.

"Would you?" George cried, and his cheeks and Theo's flushed simultaneously with red; I suppose because they both noticed Hetty's bright young eyes watching them.

"The elder writers understood but little of the pathetic," Mr. Spencer, the Temple wit, remarked.

"What do you think of Sophocles and *Antigone*?" Mr. John Lambert called out.

"Faith, our wits trouble themselves little about him unless an Oxford gentleman reminds us of him! I did not mean to go back farther than Mr. Shakespeare, who, as you will all agree, does not understand the elegant and pathetic as well as the moderns. Has he ever approached Belvidera, or Monimia, or Jane Shore? Or can you find in his comic female characters the elegance of Congreve?" The Templar offered snuff to the right and left.

"I think Mr. Spencer himself must have tried his hand?" someone asked.

"Many gentlemen of leisure have. Mr. Garrick, I own, has had a piece of mine and returned it."

"And I confess that I have four acts of a play in one of my boxes," George said.

"I'll be bound to say it's as good as any of 'em," Harry whispered to his neighbor.

"Is it a tragedy or a comedy?" Mrs. Lambert asked.

"Oh, a tragedy, and two or three dreadful murders at least!" George replied.

"Let us play it, and let the audience look to their eyes! Yet my chief humor is for a tyrant," the General said.

"The tragedy, the tragedy! Go and fetch the tragedy this moment, Gumbo!" Mrs. Lambert called to the black servant. Gumbo made a low bow and said, "Tragedy? Yes, madam."

"In the great cowskin trunk, Gumbo," George said gravely.

Gumbo bowed and said, "Yes, sir," with still superior gravity.

"But my tragedy is at the bottom of I don't know how much linen, packages, books, and boots, Hetty."

"Never mind, let us have it, and fling the linen out of the window!" Miss Hetty cried.

"And the great cowskin trunk is at our agent's in Bristol: so Gumbo must get post-horses, and we can keep it up till he returns the day after tomorrow," George said.

The ladies groaned a comical "Oh!" and Papa, perhaps more seriously, said, "Let us be thankful for the escape. Let us be thinking of going home too. Our young gentlemen have treated us nobly, and we will all drink a parting bumper to Madam Esmond Warrington of Castlewood, in Virginia. Suppose, boys, you were to find a tall, handsome stepfather when you got home? Ladies as old as she have been known to marry before now."

"To Madam Esmond Warrington, my old schoolfellow!" Mrs. Lambert cried. "I shall write and tell her what a pretty supper her sons have given us: and, Mr. George, I won't say how ill you behaved at the play!" With this last toast, the company took leave; the General's coach and servant, with a flambeau, being in waiting to carry his family home.

After such an entertainment as that which Mr. Warrington had given, what could be more natural or proper than a visit from him to his guests, to inquire how they had reached home and rested? Why, their coach might have taken the open country behind Montague House, in the direction of Oxford Road, and been waylaid by footpads in the fields. The ladies might have caught cold or slept ill after the excitement of the tragedy. In a word, there was no reason why he should make any excuse at all to himself or them for visiting his kind friends; and he shut his books early at the Sloane Museum, and perhaps thought, as he walked away thence, that he remembered very little about what he had been reading.

Pray, what is the meaning of this eagerness, this hesitation, this pshawing and shilly-shallying, these doubts, this tremor as he knocks at the door of Mr. Lambert's lodgings in Dean Street, and surveys the footman who comes to his summons? Does any young man read? Does any old one remember? Does any wearied, worn, disappointed pulseless heart recall the time of its full beat and early throbbing? It is ever so many hundred years since some of us were young; and we forget, but do not all forget. No, madam, we remember with advantages, as Shakespeare's Harry promised his soldiers they should do if they survived Agincourt and that day of St. Crispin. Worn old chargers turned out to grass, if the trumpet sounds over the hedge, may we not kick up our old heels, and gallop a minute or so about the paddock, till we are brought up roaring? I do not care for clown and pantaloon now, and think the fairy ugly, and her verses insufferable: but I like to see children at a pantomime. I do not dance, or eat supper any more; but I like to watch Eugenio and Flirtilla twirling round in a pretty waltz, or Lucinda and Ardentio pulling a cracker. Burn your little fingers, children! Blaze out little kindly flames from each other's eyes! And then draw close together and read the motto (that old namby-pamby motto, so stale and so new!)—I say, let her lips read it, and his construe it; and so divide the sweetmeat, young people, and crunch it between you. I have no teeth. Bitter almonds and sugar disagree with me, I tell you; but, for all that, shall not bonbons melt in the mouth?

We followed John upstairs to the General's apartments and entered with Mr. George Esmond Warrington, who made a prodigious fine bow. There was only one lady in the room, seated near a window: there is not often much sunshine in Dean Street; the young lady in the window is no especial beauty: but it is spring-time, and she is blooming vernally. A bunch of fresh roses was flushing in her honest cheek. I suppose her eyes are violets. If we lived a hundred years ago, and wrote in the *Gentleman's* or the *London Magazine*, we should tell Mr. Sylvanus Urban that her neck was the lily, and her shape the nymph's: we should write an acrostic about her, and celebrate our Lambertella in an elegant poem, still to be read between a neat new engraved plan of the city of Prague and the King of Prussia's camp, and a map of Maryland and the Delaware counties.

Here is Miss Theo blushing like a rose. What could Mamma have meant an hour since by insisting that she was very pale and tired, and had best not come out to-day with the rest of the party? They were gone to pay their compliments to my Lord Wrotham's ladies, and thank them for the house in their absence; and Papa was at the Horse Guards. He is in great spirits. I believe he expects some command, though Mamma is in a sad tremor lest he should again be ordered abroad.

"Your brother and mine are gone to see our little brother at his school at the Chartreux. My brothers are both to be clergymen, I think," Miss Theo continued. She was assiduously hemming some article of boyish wearing apparel as she talked. A hundred years ago, young ladies were not afraid either to make shirts, or to name them. Mind, I don't say they were the worse or the better for that plain stitching or plain speaking: and have not the least desire, my dear young lady, that you should make puddings or I should black boots.

So Harry has been with them? "He often comes, almost every day," Theo said, looking up in George's face. "Poor fellow! He likes us better than the fine folks, who don't care for him now—now he is no longer a fine folk

The loyal hearts of Britain bristled with a mixture of awe and indignation as they read of Mr. George Warrington's treatment of a gallant Prince, the beloved son of the greatest monarch and Captain-General of the British army. What an unfathomable favor had the youth spurned? What a golden ladder to promotion had he discarded? Will Esmond, whose tongue was a fountain of blasphemy, hurled his most venomous curses at his cousin's behavior, reveling in the thought that the confounded young Mohock was merely cutting his own throat. Cousin Castlewood offered a charitable defense, suggesting that a savage gentleman possessed the right to scalp himself if he chose, or perhaps that Mr. Warrington had heard too much of the war-whoop at Braddock's defeat and simply lacked the stomach for further fighting. Will rejoiced that the younger brother had gone to the deuce, and he took even greater pleasure in imagining the elder following close behind. Upon their first meeting, Will declared he would ensure Mr. George understood exactly what he thought of him.

"If you intend to insult George, at least ensure his brother Harry is out of hearing!" cried Lady Maria, a warning that seemed to summon fresh torrents of curses from Mr. Will regarding his twin kinsfolk.

"Ta, ta, ta!" my lord interjected, dismissing the squabbling. "We cannot be warriors all around the family!"

"I never heard your lordship claim to be one!" Maria retorted.

"Never, my dear; quite the opposite! Will is our champion, and one is sufficient for the house. So I dare say with the two Mohocks—George is the student, and Harry is the fighting man. When you intended to quarrel, Will, what a pity it was you had George instead of the other to your hand!"

"Your lordship's hand is famous—at piquet," Will's mother remarked.

"It is a pretty one," my lord replied, examining his fingers with a simpering air. "My Lord Hervey's glove and mine were of a size. Yes, my hand, as you say, is more fitted for cards than for war. Yours, my Lady Castlewood, is equally dexterous. How I bless the day when you bestowed it on my lamented father!" In this playful exchange of sarcasm, as in other games of skill, his lordship found satisfaction, possessing a cool head and the ability to outmaneuver his entire family.

Madame de Bernstein, upon hearing of Mr. Warrington's blunder, was furious, storming and scolding her household. She would have scolded George as well, but age had softened her resolve, and she harbored a lingering fear of her nephew, treating him with a respectful caution she once lacked. "You will never make your fortune at court, nephew!" she groaned when the young gentleman visited her shortly after his discomfiture.

"It was never my wish, madam," Mr. George replied in a stately tone.

"Your wish was to aid Harry? You might have been of service to your brother had you accepted the Duke's offer. Princes do not relish having their favors refused, and I do not wonder his Royal Highness was offended."

"General Lambert said the same," George confessed, flushing slightly. "And I see now that I was wrong. But you must remember I had never seen a court before, and I doubt I shall shine in one."

"I think possibly not, my good nephew," the aunt said, taking a pinch of snuff.

"And what then?" George asked. "I never sought that kind of glory, and I can find contentment without it. When his Royal Highness spoke to me so kindly, my thought was that I shall make a very bad soldier, while my brother would be excellent. He possesses a hundred qualities for the profession in which I am deficient; he would serve a commanding officer far better than I ever could. Say the Duke is in battle and his horse is shot, as my poor chief's was at home—would he not be better mounted on a beast of courage and strength to bear him anywhere, than on one that cannot carry his weight?"

"Au fait. His Royal Highness's charger must be a strong one, my dear!" the old lady observed.

"Expende Hannibalem," George muttered with a shrug. "Our Hannibal weighs no trifle."

"I do not quite follow you, sir, nor your Hannibal," the Baroness remarked.

"When Mr. Wolfe and Mr. Lambert remonstrated with me as you have done, madam," George rejoined with a laugh, "I made this same defense. I told them I offered the Prince the best soldier in the family, and the two gentlemen allowed my blunder had at least some excuse. Who knows but they may set me right with his Royal Highness? The taste I have had of battles reveals how little my genius inclines that way. We saw the Scotch play everyone discussed last night. When the hero, young Norval, spoke of longing to follow some warlike lord to the field, I thought to myself, 'how like my Harry is to him, except that he does not brag.' Harry is pining for a red coat now, and if we do not mind, he will take the shilling. He keeps the map of Germany perpetually before his eyes and follows the King of Prussia everywhere. He fears neither men nor gods. As for me, I love my books and quiet above all, preferring to read of battles in Homer or Lucan."

"Then what made a soldier of you at all, my dear? And why did you not send Harry with Mr. Braddock instead of going yourself?" Madame de Bernstein asked.

"My mother loved her younger son the best," George said darkly. "Besides, with the enemy invading our country, it was my duty, as the head of our family, to go on the campaign. Had I been a Scotchman twelve years ago, I should have been a..."

"Hush, sir! Or I shall be more angry than ever!" the old lady commanded, her face perfectly pleased.

George's explanation might appease Madame de Bernstein, an elderly woman whose principles we fear were somewhat loose; but to the loyal hearts of Sir Miles Warrington and his lady, the young man's conduct delivered a severe blow. "I should have thought," her ladyship said, "from my sister Esmond Warrington's letter, that my brother's widow was a woman of good sense and judgment, and that she had educated her sons in a becoming manner. But what, Sir Miles, what, my dear Thomas Claypool, can we think of an education that has resulted so lamentably for both these young men?"

"The elder seems to know a power of Latin, though, and speaks French and German too. I heard him with the Hanover Envoy at the Baroness's rout," Mr. Claypool noted. "The French he jabbered quite easily; and when he was at a loss for High Dutch, he and the Envoy began in Latin and talked away until the whole room stared."

"It is not language, but principles, Thomas Claypool!" the virtuous matron exclaimed. "What must Mr. Warrington's principles be when he could reject an offer made by his Prince? Can he speak High Dutch? So much the more ought he to have accepted his Royal Highness's condescension and made himself useful in the campaign! Look at our son, look at Miles!"

"Hold up thy head, Miley, my boy!" cried papa.

"I trust, Sir Miles, that as a member of the House of Commons and an English gentleman, you will attend his Royal Highness's levee tomorrow and say that if such an offer had been made to us for that child, we would have taken it, though our boy is but ten years of age."

"Faith, Miley, thou wouldst make a good little drummer or fifer!" papa replied. "Shouldst like to be a little soldier, Miley?"

"Anything, sir, anything! A Warrington ought to be ready at any moment to have himself cut in pieces for his sovereign!" the matron cried, pointing to the boy, who, upon comprehending his mother's proposal, protested with a loud roar before being removed by Screwby. In obedience to these conjugal orders, Sir Miles attended his Royal Highness's levee the next day, making a protest of his love and duty which the Prince graciously accepted, remarking:

"Nobody ever supposed that Sir Miles Warrington would ever refuse any place offered to him."

A compliment indeed, repeated everywhere by Lady Warrington as proof of how implicitly the august royal family could rely on the loyalty of the Warringtons.

Consequently, when this worthy couple saw George, they received him with a ghastly commiseration, the sort of pity our dear relatives sometimes extend when we have done something fatal or clumsy in life; when we have come badly out of a lawsuit; when we enter a room just as the company has been abusing us; when our banker has broken; or when, for our sad part, we have had to figure in the commercial columns of the London Gazette. Who does not know that face of pity? Whose dear relations have not so deplored him, not dead, but living? Not yours? Then, sir, if you have never been in scrapes; if you have never sown a handful of wild oats; if you have always been fortunate, good, and careful, and butter has never melted in your mouth, and an imprudent word has never escaped; if you have never sinned and repented, been a fool and been sorry—then, sir, you are a wiseacre who won't waste your time over an idle novel, and it is not *de te* that the fable is narrated.

It was not entirely just for Sir Miles to turn upon George and be angry with his nephew for refusing the promotion offered by his Royal Highness, for Sir Miles himself had agreed with George's view of pursuing a career quite other than military, a plan approved by Madam Esmond in her letters from Virginia. George had announced his intention to enter the Temple, qualifying himself for the magisterial and civil duties he would naturally fulfill. Nor could anyone applaud his resolution more cordially than his uncle Sir Miles, who introduced George to a lawyer of reputation, under whose guidance we may imagine the young gentleman reading leisurely. Madam Esmond from home signified her approval of her son's course, fully agreeing with Sir Miles (to whom and his lady she begged to send her grateful remembrances) that the British Constitution was the envy of the world and the proper object of every English gentleman's admiring study. The chief point to which George's mother objected was the notion that Mr. Warrington should sit down in the Temple dinner-ball, cutting at a shoulder of mutton and drinking small-beer out of tin pannikins by the side of rough students wearing gowns like the parish-clerk. George's loyal younger brother shared this repugnance. Anything was good enough for him, Harry said; he was a younger son and prepared to rough it. But George, in a gown, dining in a mess with three nobody's sons off dirty pewter platters! Harry could never relish this condescension on his brother's part, or fancy George in his proper place at any table except the high one; and he was sorry that a plan Madam Esmond hinted at in her letters was not feasible—namely, that an application should be made to the Master of the Temple, informing him that Mr. George Warrington was a gentleman of most noble birth and of great property in America, and ought only to sit with the very best company in the Hall. To Harry's discomfiture, when he communicated his own and his mother's ideas to the gentlemen's new coffee-house friend, Mr. Spencer, Mr. Spencer received the proposal with roars of laughter; and I cannot learn, from the Warrington papers, that any application was made to the Master of the Temple on this subject.

Besides his literary and historical pursuits, which were those he most especially loved, Mr. Warrington studied the laws of his country, attended the courts at Westminster, where he heard a Henley, a Pratt, a Murray, and those other great famous schools of eloquence and patriotism, the two houses of parliament.

Gradually, Mr. Warrington made acquaintance with some members of the House and the Bar. When they came to know him, they spoke of him as a young gentleman of good parts and good breeding, in terms so generally complimentary that his good uncle's heart relented toward him, and Dora and Flora began once more to smile upon him. This reconciliation dated from the time when his Royal Highness the Duke, after having been defeated by the French in the affair of Hastenbeck, concluded the famous capitulation with the French, which his Majesty George II. refused to ratify. His Royal Highness, as 'tis well known, flung up his commissions after this disgrace, laid down his commander's baton—which, it must be confessed, he had not wielded with much luck or dexterity—and never again appeared at the head of armies or in public life. The stout warrior would not allow a word of complaint against his father and sovereign to escape his lips; but, as he retired with his wounded honor and would have no interest or authority more, nor any places to give, it may be supposed that Sir Miles Warrington's anger against his nephew diminished as his respect for his Royal Highness diminished.

As our two gentlemen walked in St. James's Park one day with their friend Mr. Lambert, they met his Royal Highness in plain clothes and without a star, and made profound bows to the Prince, who was pleased to stop and speak to them.

He asked Mr. Lambert how he liked my Lord Ligonier, his new chief at the Horse Guards, and the new duties there in which he was engaged? And, recognizing the young men with that fidelity of memory for which his Royal race hath ever been remarkable, he said to Mr. Warrington:

"You did well, sir, not to come with me when I asked you in the spring."

"I was sorry, then, sir," Mr. Warrington said, making a very low reverence, "but I am more sorry now."

On which the Prince said, "Thank you, sir," and,

If Harry Warrington possessed a fervor for martial pursuits, the European continent offered ample fuel for his ambition. The continent buzzed with the echoes of war; the House of Hanover had suffered defeat, yet the Protestant Hero, the King of Prussia, filled the world with his glory, securing astonishing victories. It was fortunate, in my own estimation, that my poor Harry did not take part in these campaigns. Had he stood at Rossbach on that famous Gunpowder Fete-day, the fifth of November, 1757, or at the tremendous slaughter of Leuthen a month later, my veracious biographer would have been forced to narrate battles described by no other pen. I am glad, therefore, that Harry Warrington was spared the Rossbach and Leuthen; for these prodigious actions will be narrated in other volumes, which I and all the world are eager to behold. Would you have this history compete with yonder book? Could my jaunty, yellow park-phaeton run counter to that grim chariot of thundering war? Could my meek little jog-trot Pegasus meet the shock of yon steed of foaming bit and flaming nostril? Dear, kind reader—with whom I love to talk from time to time, stepping down from the stage where our figures perform, attired in the habits and using the parlance of past ages—my kind, patient reader! It is a mercy for both of us that Harry Warrington did not follow the King of the Borussians, as he was minded to do, for then I should have had to describe battles which Carlyle is going to paint; and I don't wish you should make odious comparisons between me and that master.

Harry Warrington not only did not join the King of the Borussians, but he pined and chafed at not going. He led a sulky, useless life, that is the fact. He dangled about the military coffee-houses. He cared for nothing save a newspaper. His turn was not literary. He even thought novels were stupid; and, as for the ladies crying their eyes out over Mr. Richardson, he could not imagine how they could be moved by any such nonsense. He used to laugh in a very hearty, jolly way, but a little late, and some time after the joke was over. Pray, why should all gentlemen have a literary turn? And do we like some of our friends the worse because they never turned a couplet in their lives? Ruined, perforce idle, dependent on his brother for supplies, if he read a book falling asleep over it, with no fitting work for his great strong hands to do—how lucky it is that he did not get into more trouble! Why, in the case of Achilles himself, when he was sent by his mamma to the court of King What-d'ye-call-'em in order to be put out of harm's reach, what happened to him amongst a parcel of women with whom he was made to idle his life away? And how did Pyrrhus come into the world? A powerful, mettlesome young Achilles ought not to be leading-stringed by women too much; is out of his place dawdling by distaffs or handing coffee-cups; and when he is not fighting, depend on it, is likely to fall into much worse mischief.

Those soft-hearted women, the two elder ladies of the Lambert family, with whom he mainly consorted, had an untiring pity and kindness for Harry, such as women only—and only a few of those—can give. If a man is in grief, who cheers him; in trouble, who consoles him; in wrath, who soothes him; in joy, who makes him doubly happy; in prosperity, who rejoices; in disgrace, who backs him against the world, and dresses with gentle unguents and warm poultices the rankling wounds made by the slings and arrows of outrageous Fortune? Who but woman, if you please? You who are ill and sore from the buffets of Fate, have you one or two of these sweet physicians? Return thanks to the gods that they have left you so much of consolation. What gentleman is not more or less a Prometheus? Who has not his rock (ai, ai), his chain (ea, ea), and his liver in a deuce of a condition? But the sea-nymphs come—the gentle, the sympathising; they kiss our writhing feet; they moisten our parched lips with their tears; they do their blessed best to console us Titans; they don't turn their backs upon us after our overthrow.

Now Theo and her mother were full of pity for Harry; but Hetty's heart was rather hard and seemingly savage towards him. She chafed that his position was not more glorious; she was angry that he was still dependent and idle. The whole world was in arms, and could he not carry a musket? It was harvest-time, and hundreds of thousands of reapers were out with their flashing sickles; could he not use his, and cut down his sheaf or two of glory?

"Why, how savage the little thing is with him!" says papa, after a scene in which, according to her wont, Miss Hetty had been firing little shots into that quivering target which came and set itself up in Mrs. Lambert's drawing-room every day.

"Her conduct is perfectly abominable!" cries mamma; "she deserves to be whipped, and sent to bed."

"Perhaps, mother, it is because she likes him better than any of us do," says Theo, "and it is for his sake that Hetty is angry. If I were fond of—of some one, I should like to be able to admire and respect him always—to think everything he did right—and my gentleman better than all the gentlemen in the world."

"The truth is, my dear," answers Mrs. Lambert, "that your father is so much better than all the world, he has spoiled us. Did you ever see any one to compare with him?"

"Very few, indeed," owns Theo, with a blush.

"Very few. Who is so good-tempered?"

"I think nobody, mamma," Theo acknowledges.

"Or so brave?"

"Why, I dare say Mr. Wolfe, or Harry, or Mr. George, are very brave."

"Or so learned and witty?"

"I am sure Mr. George seems very learned, and witty too, in his way," says Theo; "and his manners are very fine—you own they are. Madame de Bernstein says they are, and she hath seen the world. Indeed, Mr. George has a lofty way with him, which I don't see in other people; and, in reading books, I find he chooses the fine noble things always, and loves them in spite of all his satire. He certainly is of a satirical turn, but then he is only bitter against mean things and people. No gentleman hath a more tender heart I am sure; and but yesterday, after he had been talking so bitterly as you said, I happened to look out of window, and saw him stop and treat a whole crowd of little children to apples at the stall at the corner. And the day before yesterday, when he was coming and brought me the Moliere, he stopped and gave money to a beggar, and how charmingly, sure, he reads the French! I agree with him though about Tartuffe, though 'tis so wonderfully clever and lively, that a mere villain and hypocrite is a figure too mean to be made the chief of a great piece. Iago, Mr. George said, is near as great a villain; but then he is not the first character of the tragedy, which is Othello, with his noble weakness. But what fine ladies and gentlemen Moliere represents—and—but oh, I don't dare to repeat the verses after him."

"But you know them by heart, my dear?" asks Mrs. Lambert.

And Theo replies, "Oh yes, mamma! I know them by... Nonsense!"

I here fancy osculations, palpitations, and exit Miss Theo, blushing like a rose. Why had she stopped in her sentence? Because mamma was looking at her so oddly. And why was mamma looking at her so oddly? And why had she looked after Mr. George when he was going away, and looked for him when he was coming? Ah, and why do cheeks blush, and why do roses bloom? Old Time is still a-flying. Old spring and bud time; old summer and bloom time; old autumn and seed time; old winter time, when the cracking, shivering old tree-tops are bald or covered with snow.

A few minutes after George arrived, Theo would come downstairs with a fluttering heart, may be, and a sweet nosegay in her cheeks, just culled, as it were, fresh in his honour; and I suppose she must have been constantly at that window which commanded the street, and whence she could espy his generosity to the sweep, or his purchases from the apple-woman. But if it was Harry who knocked, she remained in her own apartment with her work or her books, sending her sister to receive the young gentleman, or her brothers when the elder was at home from college, or Doctor Crusius from the Chartreux gave the younger leave to go home. And what good eyes Theo must have had—and often in the evening, too—to note the difference between Harry's yellow hair and George's dark locks—and between their figures, though they were so like that people continually were mistaking one for the other brother. Now it is certain that Theo never mistook one or t'other; and that Hetty, for her part, was not in the least excited, or rude, or pert, when she found the black-haired gentleman in her mother's drawing-room.

Our friends could come when they liked to Mr. Lambert's house, and stay as long as they chose; and, one day, he of the golden locks was sitting on a couch there, in an attitude of more than ordinary idleness and despondency, when who should come down to him but Miss Hetty? I say it was a most curious thing (though the girls would have gone to the rack rather than own any collusion), that when Harry called, Hetty appeared; when George arrived, Theo somehow came; and so, according to the usual dispensation, it was Miss Lambert, junior, who now arrived to entertain the younger Virginian.

After usual ceremonies and compliments we may imagine that the lady says to the gentleman:

"And pray, sir, what makes your honour look so glum this morning?"

"Ah, Hetty!" says he, "I have nothing else to do but to look glum. I remember when we were boys—and I a rare idle one, you may be sure—I would always be asking my tutor for a holiday, which I would pass very likely swinging on a gate, or making ducks and drakes over the pond, and those do-nothing days were always the most melancholy. What have I got to do now from morning till night?"

"Breakfast, walk—dinner, walk—tea, supper, I suppose; and a pipe of your Virginia," says Miss Hetty, tossing her head.

"I tell you what, when I went back with Charley to the Chartreux, t'other night, I had a mind to say to the master, 'Teach me, sir. Here's a boy knows a deal more Latin and Greek, at thirteen, than I do, who am ten years older. I have nothing to do from morning till night, and I might as well go to my books again, and see if I can repair my idleness as a boy.' Why do you laugh, Hetty?"

"I laugh to fancy you at the head of a class, and called up by the master!" cries Hetty.

"I shouldn't be at the head of the class," Harry says, humbly. "George might be at the head of any class, but I am not a bookman, you see; and when I was young neglected myself, and was very idle. We would not let our tutors cane us much at home, but, if we had, it might have done me good."

Hetty drubbed with her little foot, and looked at the young man sitting before her—strong, idle, melancholy.

"Upon my word, it might do you good now!" she was minded to say. "What does Tom say about the caning at school? Does his account of it set you longing for it, pray?" she asked.

"His account of his school," Harry answered simply, "makes me see that I have been idle when I ought to have worked, and that I have not a genius for books, and for what am I good? Only to spend my patrimony when I come abroad, or to lounge at coffee-houses or racecourses, or to gallop behind dogs when I am at home. I am good for nothing, I am."

"What, such a great, brave, strong fellow as you good for nothing?" cries Het. "I would not confess as much to any woman, if I were twice as good for nothing!"

"What am I to do? I ask for leave to go into the army, and Madam Esmond does not answer me. 'Tis the only thing I am fit for. I have no money to buy. Having spent all my own, and so much of my brother's, I cannot and won't ask for more. If my mother would but send me to the army, you know I would jump to go."

"Eh! A gentleman of spirit does not want a woman to buckle his sword on for him or to clean his firelock! What was that our papa told us of the young gentleman at court yesterday?—Sir John Armytage—"

"Sir John Armytage? I used to know him when I frequented White's and the club-houses—a fine, noble young gentleman, of a great estate in the North."

"And engaged to be married to a famous beauty, too—Miss Howe, my Lord Howe's sister—but that, I suppose, is not an obstacle to gentlemen?"

"An obstacle to what?" asks the gentleman.

"An obstacle to glory!" says Miss Hetty. "I think no woman of spirit would say 'Stay!' though she adored her lover ever so much, when his country said 'Go!' Sir John had volunteered for the expedition which is preparing, and being at court yesterday his Majesty asked him when he would be ready to go?

George Warrington managed his legal studies with a singular disregard for the rigors of the profession, ensuring they never impinged upon his comfort, his pleasures, or, most critically, his precious health. Madam Esmond, in her correspondence, had repeatedly admonished him that while he donned the student's gown and sat among nameless commoners in the hall, he possessed a name of ancient lineage to uphold. She insisted he study as a gentleman, not as a mere professional drudge. The young man complied with sufficient obedience to avoid the rank and file of the law, positioning himself instead as a volunteer in her service, akin to the young gentlemen of the era who treated the law as a secondary pursuit. Though the law a century prior was a jealous mistress demanding exclusive attention—allowing her disciples far more leisure, punch, and coffee-house sociability than she permits today—George treated her with decent respect. Yet, his heart belonged elsewhere; the black-letter of Chaucer held infinitely more charm for him than the Gothic pages of Hale and Coke.

In those quaint times, letters were revered, and authors held sway as authorities. Gentlemen appealed to Virgil or Lucan in Courts and Parliament. What did Statius or Juvenal decree on such matters? Their reign has long since passed; the worship of Jupiter and Juno is no more fashionable than the cultivation of Pagan poetry. The age of economists and calculators has superseded the ancients; Tooke's Pantheon is deserted and ridiculed.
