Occasionally, a Stanley may kill a kid, a Gladstone a wreath, or a Lytton burn incense in honor of the Olympians, but who cares at Lambeth or Birmingham for ancient rites? Who are the Muses, and what use is Greek rubbish? What is Elicon, and who seeks Thalia? As for Melpomene, does her name bear three or four syllables? And from whose design did I steal the figure of Tragedy that adorns the initial G of this chapter?

It is recorded that in his youth, during the long leisure of his home and his imprisonment in the French fort on the Monongahela, George courted Melpomene. The union produced a tragedy, omitted from Bell's Theatre, though I suspect it rivals the worst pieces printed there. Young men often pay their respects to the Tragic Muse first, falling in love with women older than themselves. Let the candid reader admit that, possessing a literary turn, his ambition was of the highest order. In his riper age, he might have settled for translating Horace or versifying Waller, but his green, unknowing youth engaged only in tragedy and epic, deeming no prize but the highest worthy of him.

Upon arriving in London, George attended performances at both houses, frequented theatrical coffee-houses, and absorbed the opinions of critics. He might be seen at the Bedford between plays or supping at the Cecil with wits and actors. Here, he acquainted himself with the players and poets. The tough old Macklin, the frolicsome Foote, the vivacious Hippisley, and the sprightly Garrick himself occasionally graced these circles. Through his wit, modesty, and evident wealth, George became beloved in coffee-house society. Actors drank punch with him; critics supped at his expense with affability. To hob-nob with Bobadil or Henry the Fifth, to accept a pinch from Aristarchus's box, or to escort Juliet and Monimia, were privileges delighting to the poetic young man. George loved the theatre, finding satisfaction in the fact that his mother only half-approved of such forbidden fruit. He hosted elegant entertainments for the players, and it was rumored that distinguished geniuses had condescended to borrow money from him.

As he polished his masterpiece, seeking advice from friends, he received applause and counsel. Mr. Spencer, a new acquaintance of the Temple, hosted a breakfast in Fig Tree Court where George read portions of his play. The gentlemen pronounced it of uncommon merit. Even the learned Mr. Johnson, invited to the gathering, conceded the piece showed talent. It warred against the unities, to be sure, but these had been violated by others; Mr. Warrington might sacrifice them as well. The tragedy contained elements reminiscent of *Coriolanus* and *Othello*. "Two very good things, sir!" the author pleaded. "Well, well," Mr. Spencer replied, "your catastrophe is terrible, just, and being partly true, is not the less awful."

The plot was replete with battle and murder. A favorite book of George's grandfather had been the life of George Frundsberg of Mindelheim, a colonel at Pavia and during the wars of the Constable Bourbon. One of Frundsberg's companions, Carpzow, became the tragedy's hero. The first act, as it stood in Sir George Warrington's manuscript, took place before a convent on the Rhine besieged by Lutherans under Carpezan. These godless men had pulled friars' beards and torn nuns' veils. Inside, a score of religious women trembled; the garrison promised surrender unless succours arrived by midday. An armistice prevailed as soldiers gambled on the grass. Twelve o'clock struck. No succours came. The warder opened the gates to the famous Protestant hero, the terror of Turks and Papists—Colonel Carpezan. Clad in steel, hammer over shoulder, flags displayed, trumpets blowing, he entered. "No rudeness, my men," Carpezan declared. "The wine is yours, the larder good, the church plate to be melted. Any garrison member joining Gaspar Carpezan is welcome. No insult to the religious ladies! I promised them safe-conduct; he who touches them hangs." The Provost Marshal, a huge fellow in a red doublet, nodded.

"We shall see more of that Provost Marshal," Mr. Spencer explained to his guests. "A very agreeable acquaintance," Mr. Johnson added, wagging his head over his tea. "This scene of mercenaries and wild sports is novel and stirring. The Colonel enters the convent?"

The Abbess and her oldest ladies appeared before the conqueror. Despite his title, they heard him in their sacred halls, recalling his violent behavior in other establishments. His hammer had smashed sacred images; his melting of plate was legendary. The Abbess-Princess of St. Mary's, a lady of violent prejudices and noble birth, disliked the lowborn heretic lordling her convent. She challenged Carpezan, a scene the audience at the Temple greatly enjoyed. Though terrible in war, Carpezan was initially shaken by the Abbess's brisk verbal charge, seeming conquered by his prisoner. Yet, an old soldier was not to be beaten ultimately by a woman. "Madam," he asked, "how many ladies are there for whom my people shall provide conveyance?" The Abbess, troubled and angry, counted twenty-three. "Ha! Why this hesitation?" asked Captain Ulric, one of Carpezan's gayest officers.

The dark chief pulled a letter from his pocket. "I require the body of the noble lady Sybilla of Hoya," he said sternly. "Her brother was my favorite captain, slain by my side in the Milanese. By his death, she becomes heiress. It is said a greedy uncle immured her here. She shall pronounce her fate: remain a cloistered sister or return to liberty." The Abbess, haughty, denied any Lady Sybil existed, claiming Sister Agnes had been professed and her wealth reverted to the Order. "Give me straightway the body of Lady Sybilla!" roared Carpezan. "If not, I signal my Reiters and give you and your convent up to war."

"Faith, if I lead the storm," said Captain Ulric, "I'd choose some plump, smiling, red-lipped maid rather than your Lady Abbess." As he looked under the veils of two attendant nuns, the stern Abbess cried, "Silence, fellow! The lady you seek is passed away from sin three days since; our Sister Agnes died." The chaplain confirmed the burial. Too much! In his coat of mail, Carpezan found a letter from Sister Agnes announcing she was to be buried in an oubliette, to starve or live on water and bread. Seizing the Abbess by the arm, while Ulric choked the chaplain, the Colonel blew his horn. Furious Lanzknechts crashed the convent walls. Amidst flames and screams, Sybilla herself was brought in, fainting on Carpezan's shoulder, having been guided to the dungeon by the very nun with the red lips.

"The convent is suppressed with a vengeance," Mr. Warrington noted. "We end the first act with the burning, the roars of triumph, and the nuns' outcries. They must change dresses immediately; they will be court ladies in the next act." The gentlemen cast the roles: Mrs. Pritchard as the Abbess, Miss Pritchard as Sybilla, Miss Gates as the nun, and Mr. Garrick, despite his slight height, as Carpezan. Mr. Johnson deemed Woodward excellent as Ulric. The audience already saw the play on the boards.

In the second act, Carpezan married Sybilla. Ennobled by the Emperor and living in state on the Danube, he was not happy. Perhaps remorse haunted him for his wild life as a condottiere; perhaps his rough manners clashed with his imperious, highborn bride. She taunted him with his low birth and vulgar companions, leading him to wish he had never rescued the quarrelsome vixen from the oubliette. This quiet act passed in quarreling until horns announced the young King of Bohemia and Hungary's approach, offering preferment: Count to Carpezan, General-in-Chief to his wife.

"Oh, stay—I have it," Mr. Johnson interjected. "'Tis in *Meteranus*, in the *Theatrum Universum*. Carpezanus or Carpzoff..." "That is the fourth act," corrected Mr. Warrington. The King's attentions toward Sybilla grew marked, but her husband, battling jealousy, refused to yield until her criminality was proven. The act closed with the terrible tragedy that actually happened: convinced of her guilt, Carpezan ordered the executioner to slay her in her own palace. The curtain fell in a side-chamber illuminated by moonlight through an oriel window, where the King played a song—the signal between him and his guilty victim. Mr. Johnson praised this song as a happy imitation of Waller, noting its gay repetition deepened the tragic gloom.

"But whatever came afterwards?" Johnson asked. "I recall Carpezan being taken into favor by Count Mansfield." Here, the poet departed from history. In the fifth act, King Louis, terror-stricken by the sanguinary end of his intrigue, received word of the Ottoman invasion. Two noblemen related how the injured Carpezan rushed into the royal presence, broke his sword, and threw it at the King's feet along with a glove he dared the King to wear. The rebel fled Prague, reportedly joining the Turks and assuming the turban. The King, preparing for battle at Mohacz, dismissed his generals, keeping an aged knight by his side to express repentance for his past crimes and determination to fight like a man.

"What is this field called?"
"Mohacz, my liege!" the old warrior replied. "Ere set of sun, Mohacz will see a battle bravely won."

Trumpets sounded; the cymbals and barbaric music of the Janissaries signaled the Turkish camp. There walked the Sultan's friend, the conqueror of Rhodes, the Grand Vizier. Who was the warrior in Eastern habit with a glove in his cap? It was Carpezan. Solyman knew his courage. Carpezan prayed for a command near the traitor King Louis. "Tis well," said the grim Vizier. "Our invincible Emperor surveys the battle from yonder tower."

Signal-guns fired. Christian knights and Turkish warriors clashed. Carpezan, glove in cap and hammer in hand, raged about the field, calling for King Louis. About to slay a warrior, he recognized young Ulric, his ex-captain, dropped his hammer, and bid him fly. Softened by memories of their shared Protestant conquests, Ulric urged him to return, but Carpezan knew it was impossible. They fought; Ulric fell under the hammer. The renegade melted in sight of his wounded comrade until King Louis appeared, plumes torn, sword hacked. The guilty monarch tried to turn away, but Carpezan was on him. All softness gone, he roared, "An equal fight! A traitor against a traitor! Stand, King Louis!" He tore the token from his cap and flung it at the King.

They set to, and the monarch fell under the terrible arm of the man he had injured. Dying, he uttered incoherent words of repentance. Carpezan, leaning on his mace, spoke a heartbroken soliloquy over the corpse. The Turkish warriors gathered. The dark Vizier surveyed the renegade. "Christian renegade!" he said. "Allah has given us a great victory. The Christian King is slain by you."
"Peace to his soul! He died like a good knight," gasped Ulric, dying himself.
"In this day's battle," the Vizier continued, "no man hath comported himself more bravely than you. You are made Bassa of Transylvania! Advance bowmen—Fire!"

An arrow quivered in Carpezan's breast.
"Bassa of Transylvania, you were a traitor to your King, who lies murdered by your hand!" the Vizier declared. "You contributed more than any soldier to this victory. 'Tis thus my sublime Emperor meetsly rewards you. Sound trumpets! We march for Vienna to-night!"

The curtain dropped as Carpezan crawled to his dying comrade, kissing his hands and gasping, "Forgive me, Ulric!"

When Mr. Warrington finished reading, he turned to Mr. Johnson, modestly asking, "What say you, sir? Is there any chance for me?" But the eminent critic had been asleep and frankly admitted losing the latter part of the play. The little auditory stirred.

The faithful Gumbo could find no solace in the departure of his beloved master. To judge by his initial tears and howls upon hearing the news of Mr. Harry's enlistment, one might have believed the negro's heart shattered at the separation. No wonder he sought sympathy among the maid-servants at Mr. Lambert's lodgings. Wherever that dusky youth appeared, he found comfort in the company of females. Their fair and tender bosoms possessed a capacity for pity that transcended prejudice; the darkness of Gumbo's complexion held no more repulsion for them than Othello's did for Desdemona. Indeed, Europe had never been so squeamish regarding Africa as in that certain respected quarter. Nay, some Africans—witness the Chevalier de St. Georges, for instance—had been notorious favorites with the fair sex.

In his humbler station, Mr. Gumbo found kinship among the Lambert servants, who wept freely in his company. The maids regarded him not merely as Mr. Harry's man, but as their brother. Hetty could not help laughing when she discovered Gumbo roaring because his master had gone a volunteer, as he termed it, and had not taken him along. He was ready to save Master Harry's life any day, and would have done so, even if it meant being cut into twenty thousand pieces, for Master Harry. Yet, nature required support, and he condescended to fortify it with large supplies of beer and cold meat in the kitchen. That he was greedy, idle, and prone to lying was certain; yet Hetty gave him half a crown and treated him with especial kindness. Her tongue, usually so pert, grew gentle now, as if it had never made a joke. She moved about the house meek and mum. She was humble to her mother, thankful to John and Betty when they waited at dinner, patient with Polly when the latter pulled her hair while combing it, long-suffering when Charley from school trod on her toes or deranged her workbox, and silent in her father's company. Oh, such a transmogrified little Hetty! If her father had ordered her to roast the leg of mutton or walk to church arm-in-arm with Gumbo, she would have curtseyed and said, "Yes, if you please, dear papa!" Leg of mutton! What sort of meal were some poor volunteers having, with cannonballs flying about their heads? Church! When it came to the prayer in time of war, oh, how her knees smote together as she knelt, hiding her head in the pew! She held her head down when the parson read, "Thou shalt do no murder," from the communion rail, fancying he must be looking right at her. How she thought of all travelers by land or by water! How she sickened as she ran to the paper to read if there was news of the Expedition! How she watched her father when he came home from his Ordnance Office, searching his face for good or bad tidings! Was he well? Was he made a General yet? Was he wounded and made a prisoner? Ah me! Or, perhaps, were both his legs taken off by one shot, like that pensioner they had seen in Chelsea Garden the other day? She would go on wooden legs all her life if his could but bring him home safely; at least, she ought never to rise from her knees until he was returned. "Haven't you heard of people, Theo," she said, "whose hair has grown grey in a single night? I shouldn't wonder if mine did—I shouldn't wonder in the least." And she looked in the glass to ascertain that phenomenon.

"Hetty dear, you used not to be so nervous when papa was away in Minorca," remarked Theo.

"Ah, Theo! One may very well see that George is not with the army, but safe at home," rejoined Hetty; whereat the elder sister blushed and looked very pensive. After all, if Mr. George had been in the army, that would have been another pair of boots. Meanwhile, let us not harrow anyone's kind feelings further, but state that Harry was, for the present, as safe as any officer of the Life Guards at Regent's Park Barracks.

The first expedition in which our gallant volunteer was engaged may be called successful, but certainly not glorious. The British Lion, or any other lion, cannot always have a worthy enemy to combat, or a battle-royal to deliver. Suppose he goes forth in quest of a tiger who won't come, and lays his paws on a goose, and gobbles him up? Lions, we know, must live like any other animals. But suppose, advancing into the forest in search of the tiger aforesaid, and bellowing his challenge of war, he espies not one but six tigers coming towards him? This manifestly is not his game at all. He puts his tail between his royal legs and retreats into his own snug den as quickly as he may. Were he to attempt to fight six tigers, you might write that Lion down an Ass.

Now, Harry Warrington's first feat of war was in this wise. He and about 13,000 other fighting men embarked in various ships and transports on the 1st of June from the Isle of Wight, and at daybreak on the 5th the fleet stood in to the Bay of Cancale in Brittany. For a while, he and the gentlemen volunteers had the pleasure of examining the French coast from their ships, whilst the Commander-in-Chief and the Commodore reconnoitered the bay in a cutter. Cattle were seen, and some dragoons who trotted off into the distance; and a little fort with a couple of guns had the audacity to fire at his Grace of Marlborough and the Commodore in the cutter. By two o'clock the whole British fleet was at anchor, and signal was made for all the grenadier companies of eleven regiments to embark on board flat-bottomed boats and assemble round the Commodore's ship, the Essex. Meanwhile, Mr. Howe, hoisting his broad pennant on board the Success frigate, went in as near as possible to shore, followed by the other frigates, to protect the landing of the troops. Now, with Lord George Sackville and General Dury in command, the gentlemen volunteers, the grenadier companies, and three battalions of guards pulled to shore.

The gentlemen volunteers could do no heroic deed upon this occasion, because the French, who should have stayed to fight them, ran away. The frigates having silenced the fire of the little fort which had disturbed the reconnaissance of the Commander-in-Chief, the army presently assaulted it, taking the whole garrison prisoner and shooting him in the leg. Indeed, he was but one old gentleman who gallantly had fired his two guns, and who told his conquerors, "If every Frenchman had acted like me, you would not have landed at Cancale at all."

The advanced detachment of invaders took possession of the village of Cancale, where they lay upon their arms all night. Our volunteer was joked by his comrades about his eagerness to go out upon the war-path and bring in two or three scalps of Frenchmen. None such, however, fell under his tomahawk; the only person slain on the whole day being a French gentleman who was riding with his servant and was surprised by volunteer Lord Downe, marching in the front with a company of Kingsley's. My Lord Downe offered the gentleman quarter, which he foolishly refused, whereupon he, his servant, and the two horses were straightway shot.

Next day the whole force was landed and advanced from Cancale to St. Malo. All the villages were emptied through which the troops passed, and the roads were so narrow in many places that the men had to march single file, and might have been shot down from behind the tall leafy hedges had there been any enemy to disturb them.

At nightfall the army arrived before St. Malo and were saluted by a fire of artillery from that town, which did little damage in the darkness. Under cover of this, the British set fire to the ships, wooden buildings, pitch and tar magazines in the harbor, and made a prodigious conflagration that lasted the whole night.

This feat was achieved without any attempt on the part of the French to molest the British force. But, as it was confidently asserted that there was a considerable French force in the town of St. Malo, though they wouldn't come out, his Grace the Duke of Marlborough and my Lord George Sackville determined not to disturb the garrison, marched back to Cancale again—and so got on board their ships.

If this were not a veracious history, don't you see that it would have been easy to send our Virginian on a more glorious campaign? Exactly four weeks after his departure from England, Mr. Warrington found himself at Portsmouth again and addressed a letter to his brother George, with which the latter ran off to Dean Street so soon as ever he received it.

"Glorious news, ladies!" cried he, finding the Lambert family all at breakfast. "Our champion has come back. He has undergone all sorts of dangers, but has survived them all. He has seen dragons—upon my word, he says so."

"Dragons! What do you mean, Mr. Warrington?"

"But not killed any—he says so, as you shall hear. He writes:

"'DEAREST BROTHER—I think you will be glad to hear that I am returned, without any commission as yet; without any wounds or glory; but, at any rate, alive and hearty. On board our ship, we were almost as crowded as poor Mr. Holwell and his friends in their Black Hole at Calcutta. We had rough weather, and some of the gentlemen volunteers, who prefer smooth water, grumbled not a little. My gentlemen's stomachs are dainty; and after Braund's cookery and White's kick-shaws, they don't like plain sailor's rum and biscuit. But I, who have been at sea before, took my rations and can of flip very contentedly, being determined to put a good face on everything before our fine English macaronis and show that a Virginia gentleman is as good as the best of 'em. I wish, for the honor of old Virginia, that I had more to brag about. But all I can say in truth is that we have been to France and come back again. Why, I don't think even your tragic pen could make anything of such a campaign as ours has been. We landed on the 6th at Cancale Bay, we saw a few dragons on a hill...'

"There! Did I not tell you there were dragons?" asked George, laughing.

"Mercy! What can he mean by dragons?" cried Hetty.

"Immense, long-tailed monsters, with steel scales on their backs, who vomit fire and gobble up a virgin a day. Haven't you read about them in *The Seven Champions*?" said Papa. "Seeing St. George's flag, I suppose, they slunk off."

"I have read of 'em," said the little boy from Chartreux, solemnly. "They like to eat women. One was going to eat Andromeda, you know, Papa; and Jason killed another who was guarding the apple-tree."

"... A few dragons on a hill," George resumed, "who rode away from us without engaging. We slept under canvas. We marched to St. Malo and burned ever so many privateers there. And we went on board ships again, without ever crossing swords with an enemy or meeting any except a few poor devils whom the troops plundered. Better luck next time! This hasn't been very much nor particularly glorious; but I have liked it for my part. I have smelt powder, besides a good deal of rosin and pitch we burned. I've seen the enemy; have slept under canvas, and been dreadfully crowded and sick at sea. I like it. My best compliments to dear Aunt Lambert, and tell Miss Hetty I wasn't very much frightened when I saw the French horse.—Your most affectionate brother, H. E. WARRINGTON."

We hope Miss Hetty's qualms of conscience were allayed by Harry's announcement that his expedition was over and that he had so far taken no hurt. Far otherwise. Mr. Lambert, in the course of his official duties, had occasion to visit the troops at Portsmouth and the Isle of Wight, and George Warrington bore him company. They found Harry vastly improved in spirits and health from the excitement produced by the little campaign, quite eager and pleased to learn his new military duties, active, cheerful, and healthy, and altogether a different person from the listless, moping lad who had dawdled in London coffee-houses and Mrs. Lambert's drawing-room. The troops were under canvas; the weather was glorious, and George found his brother a ready pupil in a fine, brisk open-air school of war. Not a little amused, the elder brother, arm-in-arm with the young volunteer, paced the streets of the warlike city, recalled his own brief military experiences of two years back, and saw here a much greater army than that ill-fated one of which he had shared the disasters. The expedition, such as we have seen it, was certainly not glorious, and yet the troops and the nation were in high spirits with it. We were said to have humiliated the proud Gaul. We should have vanquished as well as humbled him had he dared to appear. What valour, after all, is like British valour? I dare say some such expressions have been heard in later times. Not that I would hint that our people brag much more than any other, or more now than formerly. Have not these eyes beheld the battle-grounds of Leipzig, Jena, Dresden, Waterloo, Blenheim, Bunker's Hill, New Orleans? What heroic nation has not fought, has not conquered, has not run away, has not bragged in its turn? Well, the British nation was much excited by the glorious victory of St. Malo. Captured treasures were sent home and exhibited in London. The people were so excited that more laurels and more victories were demanded, and the enthusiastic army went forth to seek some.

With this new expedition went a volunteer so distinguished that we must give him precedence of all other amateur soldiers or sailors. This was our sailor

What endless vanity grips the great powers, and the French in particular? Can it truly be believed that following the skirmish at St. Cast—a mere affair of severing a rear guard, as you know—they proceeded to waste countless pounds of powder at the Invalides in Paris, boasting and blustering over our misfortune? Is there any true magnanimity in cheering and huzzahing because five or six hundred brave souls were trapped by ten thousand on a shoreline, meeting the fate that often awaits the last man? I once felt a sudden urge to paint a vivid picture of the rejoicings in London celebrating our glorious triumph at St. Malo. I imagined the polished cannons dragged in procession by our gallant tars; the sturdy horse-grenadiers prancing alongside; the mob waving hats and roaring cheers, while our friends watched from a balcony in Fleet Street, blessing this scene of British glory. But now that the French Invalides have grown so vulgar as to mimic the Tower, setting their St. Cast against our St. Malo, I scorn to touch upon such a stale subject. I say *Nolo*, not *Malo*; content, for my part, if Harry has returned from one expedition and another with his skin intact. Have I ever claimed he was bruised? Have I not, for fear of alarming my fair young readers, insisted he was as well as ever in his life? The sea air had merely bronzed his cheek, and the whistling ball had spared his side-curl. The ocean had wet his gaiters and garments without swallowing his body. True, he had shown the lapels of his coat to the enemy, but only for the briefest moment, withdrawing from their sight as quickly as possible. And what are lapels but reverses? Coats possess them, as do men; and our duty is to wear them with courage and good humor.

"I can tell you," said Harry, "we were all forced to run for it. When our line broke, luck belonged to whoever could reach the boats first. The French horse and foot pursued us down to the sea, mingling among us, cutting our men down and bayoneting them where they fell. Poor Armytage was shot ahead of me and fell; I picked him up and staggered through the surf to a boat. It was fortunate the sailors in our vessel were not afraid, for the shots whistled past their ears, shattered their oars, and riddled their flag. Yet the officer in command remained as cool as if he were drinking a bowl of punch at Portsmouth, which we shared upon landing, I can promise you. Poor Sir John was less fortunate than I. He never reached the ship, and the service has lost a fine soldier, while Miss Howe has lost a true gentleman to her husband. Such casualties must happen; and his brother receives the promotion—the baronetcy."

"It is the poor lady I am thinking of," said Miss Hetty, to whom our volunteer was recounting his tale. "And the King. Why did the King encourage Sir John Armytage to go? A gentleman could not refuse a command from such a quarter. And now the poor gentleman is dead! Oh, what a state his Majesty must be in!"

"I have no doubt his Majesty will be in a deep state of grief," replied Papa, wagging his head.

"Now you are laughing! Do you mean, sir, that when a gentleman dies in his service, almost at his feet, the King of England feels nothing?" Hetty asked. "If I thought that, I vow I would support the Pretender!"

"The sauce-box would make a pretty little head for Temple Bar," remarked the General, seeing the tumult of remorse, consternation, and gratitude beating in Miss Hetty's little heart as the danger passed. "No, my dear. Were kings to weep for every soldier, what a life you would make for them! I think better of his Majesty than to suppose him so weak; and if Miss Hester Lambert secured her Pretender, I doubt she would be any happier. That family was never famous for excessive feeling."

"But if the King sent Harry—I mean Sir John Armytage—actually to the war in which he lost his life, ought not his Majesty to repent greatly?" the young lady pressed.

"If Harry had fallen, no doubt the court would have gone into mourning: as it is, gentlemen and ladies wore colored clothes yesterday," the General noted.

"Why should we not make bonfires for a defeat and don sackcloth and ashes after a victory?" asked George. "I protest I do not wish to thank Heaven for helping us burn the ships at Cherbourg."

"Yes, you do, George! Not that I have a right to speak, nor are you ever so clever. But when your country wins, you are glad—I know I am. When I run away before the French, I am ashamed; I cannot help it, though I did it," Harry admitted. "It does not seem right somehow that Englishmen should have to do it," he added gravely. George smiled but chose not to ask his brother what, on the other hand, was the Frenchman's opinion.

"'Tis a bad business," Harry continued seriously, "but it is lucky it was no worse. The story is that their Governor, the Duke of Aiguillon, was rather what you call a moistened chicken. Our entire retreat might have been cut off, only we ourselves were in a mighty hurry to move. The French local militia behaved famously, I am happy to say, and there were many gentlemen volunteers with them who showed, as they ought, in the front. They say the Chevalier of Tour d'Auvergne engaged in spite of the Duke of Aiguillon's orders. Officers told us who came off with a list of prisoners and wounded to General Bligh and Lord Howe. He is a lord now, since the news of his brother's death reached home, George. He is a brave fellow, whether lord or commoner."

"And his sister, who was to have married poor Sir John Armytage; think what her state must be!" sighed Miss Hetty, who had lately grown sentimental.

"And his mother!" cried Mrs. Lambert. "Have you seen her ladyship's address in the papers to the electors of Nottingham? 'Lord Howe being now absent upon the publick service, and Lieutenant-Colonel Howe with his regiment at Louisbourg, it rests upon me to beg the favour of your votes and interests that Lieutenant-Colonel Howe may supply the place of his late brother as your representative in Parliament.' Isn't this a gallant woman?"

"A laconic woman," said George.

"How can sons help being brave who have been nursed by such a mother as that?" asked the General.

Our two young men looked at each other.

"If one of us were to fall in defense of his country, we have a mother in Sparta who would think and write so too," said George.

"If Sparta is anywhere Virginia way, I reckon we have," remarked Mr. Harry. "And to think that we should both of us have met the enemy, and both of us been whipped by him, brother!" he added pensively.

Hetty looked at him, thinking of him only as he was the other day, tottering through the water toward the boats, his comrade bleeding on his shoulder, the enemy in pursuit, the shot flying around. And it was she who had driven him into that danger! Her words had provoked him. Now that he was returned, he never rebuked her. Except when asked, he scarcely spoke of his adventures at all. He was very grave and courteous with Hetty; with the rest of the family, especially frank and tender. But those taunts of hers had wounded him. "Little hand!" his looks and demeanor seemed to say, "thou shouldst not have been lifted against me! It is ill to scorn anyone, much more one who has been so devoted to you and all yours. I may not be over quick of wit, but insofar as the heart goes, I am the equal of the best, and the best of my heart your family has had."

Harry's wrong, and his magnanimous endurance of it, served him to regain in Miss Hetty's esteem the place he had lost during the previous months of inglorious idleness. The respect the fair paid to the brave she gave him. She was no longer pert in her answers or sarcastic in her observations regarding his conduct. In a word, she was a humiliated, an altered, an improved Miss Hetty.

And all the world seemed to change toward Harry, as he changed toward the world. He was no longer sulky and indolent; he no longer desponded about himself or defied his neighbors. The colonel of his regiment reported his behavior as exemplary and recommended him for one of the commissions vacated by the casualties during the expedition. Unlucky as its termination was, it was at least fortunate for him. His brother-volunteers, when they returned to St. James's Street, reported highly of his behavior. These volunteers and their actions became the theme of everybody's praise. Had he been a general commanding, slain in the moment of victory, Sir John Armytage could scarce have had more sympathy than that which the nation showed him. The papers teemed with letters about him, and men of wit and sensibility vied with each other in composing epitaphs in his honor. The fate of his affianced bride was bewailed. She was, as we have said, the sister of the brave Commodore who had just returned from this unfortunate expedition and succeeded to the title of his elder brother, an officer as gallant as himself, who had just fallen in America.

My Lord Howe was heard to speak in special praise of Mr. Warrington, so he received a handsome share of the fashion and favor the town now bestowed on the volunteers. Doubtless there were thousands of men employed who were as good as they, but the English ever love their gentlemen, and love that they should distinguish themselves; and these volunteers were voted Paladins and heroes by common accord. As our young noblemen will, they accepted their popularity very affably. White's and Almack's illuminated when they returned, and St. James's embraced its young knights. Harry was restored to full favor amongst them. Their hands were held out eagerly to him again. Even his relations congratulated him; and there came a letter from Castlewood, whither Aunt Bernstein had by this time betaken herself, containing praises of his valor and a pretty little bank-bill as a token of his affectionate aunt's approbation. This was under my Lord Castlewood's frank, who sent his regards to both his kinsmen and an offer of the hospitality of his country-house if they were minded to come to him. Besides this, there came to him a private letter through the post—not very well spelt, but in a handwriting Harry smiled to see again—in which his affectionate cousin, Maria Esmond, told him she always loved to hear his praises (which were now in everybody's mouth) and sympathized in his good or evil fortune; and that whatever occurred to him, she begged to keep a little place in his heart. Parson Sampson, she wrote, had preached a beautiful sermon about the horrors of war and the noble actions of men who volunteered to face battle and danger in the service of their country. Indeed, the chaplain wrote himself, presently, a letter full of enthusiasm, in which he saluted Mr. Harry as his friend, his benefactor, his glorious hero. Even Sir Miles Warrington despatched a basket of game from Norfolk; and one bird (shot sitting), with love to my cousin, had a string and paper round the leg and was sent as the first victim of young Miles's fowling-piece.

And presently, with joy beaming in his countenance, Mr. Lambert came to visit his young friends at their lodgings in Southampton Row and announced to them that Mr. Henry Warrington was forthwith to be gazetted as Ensign in the Second Battalion of Kingsley's, the 20th Regiment, which had been engaged in the campaign and which now, at this time, was formed into a separate regiment, the 67th. Its colonel was not with his regiment during its expedition to Brittany. He was away at Cape Breton, engaged in capturing those guns at Louisbourg, of which the arrival in England had caused such exultation.

It is a custom among my kind readers to visit the celebrated gardens of Regent's Park, where nature's creatures—finned, feathered, and four-footed alike—are housed in exchange for our amusement and instruction. Amidst the bustle of such a place, where business and private thought inevitably mingle with the surrounding life, I found myself gazing into an aquarium, yet my mind remained firmly anchored on our friends, the Virginians.

Among the specimens, one creature particularly caught my eye. A master of motion, he swept through his green bath in harmonious curves, flashing a black, glistening back before revealing a fair, white chest. Every movement was active and graceful. Yet, this was none other than our old, homely acquaintance, the flounder—a beauty we had previously overlooked while gobbling him up at Greenwich, unaware of his potential.

As is often the case with mankind, so it is with flounders. Viewed in their proper element, they appear agile, healthy, and comely. Remove them from their depth, however, and their beauty vanishes; their motions become disgraceful as they flap their tails against the unfeeling ground, gasping out their feeble lives. But take such a creature tenderly and return him to the Thames, and he revives.

This proverb of the "fish out of water" seemed strikingly applicable to Harry Warrington. For a long time, he had been floundering, displaced from his natural habitat. Yet, the moment he found his footing, health, strength, and spirit surged back into him. With the tap of an epaulet on his shoulder, he sprang up an entirely altered being. He delighted in his new profession, mastering the details of military life with eager quickness. Had I possessed the skill of my friend Lorrequer, I would have followed Harry into camp, sharing his carouses under the tents and explaining the maneuvers of war alongside him. Since I cannot, I ask the reader to use his imagination to fill in the colors of this picture: envision Mr. Harry Warrington in his new red coat and yellow facings, radiant with happiness to bear the King's colours and eager to perform the duties of his new trade.

While Harry embraced the excellence of battle, George, his brother, found a different, yet equally fulfilling, path. Proud of Harry's success and rejoicing in his restored fortune, George wrote an affectionate letter to his mother in Virginia. He recounted the praises Harry had earned, noting that his brother's modesty would never allow him to boast of them himself. George described how Harry had secured his first step in the army and declared his intention to ask his mother's permission to share the expense of purchasing a higher rank for him.

Nothing brought George greater delight than the ability to assist his brother, especially since Harry's sudden return to prosperity had inadvertently deprived him of an inheritance he had legitimately considered his own. Having labored under the misconception that he was the heir, Harry had incurred expenses he would never have dared as a younger son. George viewed his contribution not merely as fair compensation, but as a thank-offering for his own deliverance from financial ruin.

Having settled matters regarding Harry, George turned his pen to his own affairs, addressing a point of deep personal concern to his honored mother. He reminded her of the kindness shown to them by Mr. and Mrs. Lambert, true friends who had stood by them when their own blood relations proved worldly and unfeeling. The General was respected throughout the army, and Mrs. Lambert's affection for the Esmond children was unparalleled. Now, George wrote, he had formed an attachment for the elder Miss Lambert, a bond upon which he believed his entire happiness depended. He had made no formal offers yet, but he felt bound to confess that his sentiments were clear, and that both the young lady and her parents appeared favorable. Describing her as a model of perfection and an exemplary daughter, George expressed his firm conviction that his future lay solely in possessing or losing her.

Why, one might ask, does the editor withhold this letter? Why not reveal the secrets of a young man's love, his incoherent vows and wild raptures? Because it is cruel to babble such confidences. To overhear a lover's sighs, to bottle his tears, or to lay a stethoscope upon a delicate breast to feel the throbbing of passion is a violation of sanctity. Love is sacred. Whether it shoots suddenly from two pairs of eyes, glances sadly from one, or descends from a mother to a child, it demands reverence. To kiss and tell is wrong; to tell about kisses is worse. Let us respect the privacy of the heart.

While Harry's love for battle led him to rush toward the reluctant dragons of war, George pursued an amusement far more peaceful: the art of courtship. He penned sonnets to his mistress's eyebrow, paced beneath her window watching the lamp in her chamber, and found endless pretexts to send notes that required no immediate answer but always received one. He culled verses from his favorite poets and gathered flowers from Covent Garden for her adornment. He walked to St. James's Church, singing along with the Prayer-book while ignoring the sermon, his mind elsewhere. He was prodigiously affectionate to Miss Theo's relations—her siblings at school, her brother at college, her witty cousin Hetty, and even her mother, who, according to Martin Lambert, was already half in love with him. For if fathers may grow sulky at the prospect of a son-in-law, mothers often become sentimental, loving their own loves anew.

Gumbo and Sady were perpetually on the move between Southampton Row and Dean Street, devising summer junketings and proposing excursions to Ranelagh, Hampstead, Vauxhall, and Marylebone Gardens. George desired that Miss Theo copy a famous tragedy for the stage, admiring her beautiful Italian hand. As sheets passed between them, accompanied by notes of thanks, interrogation, and admiration, a tender intimacy grew. These virgin words, whispered for one ear alone, were too sacred for public gaze. Years later, a husband might read them with sweet pangs of remembrance, but to expose them now would be sacrilege. Let kind readers trust our word: the young lady's letters were modest and pure, the gentleman's respectful and tender. In these few months, Mr. George Warrington had decided he had found the woman of women. She may not be the most beautiful—Cousin Flora, Coelia, and Ardelia were far more handsome—but her sweet face pleased him more than any other. She may not be the most clever, but her voice was the dearest to hear. In her company, he felt clever, eloquent, and generous; he was so noble and witty that he delighted in her presence. And regarding the young lady, we may be sure, as Heaven knows we do not suppose women to be devoid of virtue, that she endowed her young hero with wit, wisdom, beauty, valour, and goodness in equal measure.

When George's letter reached home, excitement rippled through the circle around Madam Esmond's fireside. He was in love and wished to marry! It was natural, and it promised to keep him out of harm's way. If he intended to unite with a well-bred Christian woman, Madam saw no objection.

"I knew they would be setting their caps at him," said Mountain. "They fancy his wealth equals his estate. He does not say whether the young lady has money. I fear otherwise."

"People would set their caps at him here, I dare say," replied Madam Esmond, grimly regarding her dependent. "They would try to catch Mr. Esmond Warrington for their own daughters, who are no richer than Miss Lambert may be."

"I suppose your ladyship means me!" said Mountain. "My Fanny is poor, as you say; and 'tis kind of you to remind me of her poverty!"

"I said people would set their caps at him. If the cap fits you, *tant pis!* as my papa used to say."

"You think, madam, I am scheming to keep George for my daughter? I thank you, on my word! A good opinion you seem to have of us after the years we have lived together!"

"My dear Mountain, I know you much better than to suppose you could ever fancy your daughter would be a suitable match for a gentleman of Mr. Esmond's rank and station," said the mistress of Castlewood with dignity.

"Fanny Parker was as good as Molly Benson at school, and Mr. Mountain's daughter is as good as Mr. Lambert's!" cried Mrs. Mountain.

"Then you did think of marrying her to my son! I shall write to Mr. Esmond Warrington and say how sorry I am that you should be disappointed!" declared the mistress. And we may suppose that Mrs. Mountain was indeed disappointed, harboring some ambitious views for her daughter, which explains her anger at the notion of Mr. Warrington's marriage to another.

In reply, Madam Esmond wrote that she was pleased with the fraternal love George exhibited. It was right, she noted, to compensate Harry, whose expectations had led him to adopt a costly lifestyle he would not have chosen had he known he was only a younger son. Regarding the purchase of his promotion, she offered to halve the expense with Harry's elder brother, grateful that his own gallantry had won him his first step. She added that this bestowal of George's money was far more satisfactory than other extravagances she would not detail.

The other extravagance alluded to was the payment of the ransom to the French captain's family—a tax George's mother never would have submitted to. Possessing a determined spirit of her own, which her son inherited, she viewed his persistence as pride and obstinacy. What she thought of her own pertinacity, her distant biographer does not pretend to say. Only one can assume that people a hundred years ago resembled their modern descendants in loving to have their own way and making others follow it.

After paying his own ransom, his brother's debts, and half the price for his promotion, George calculated that a significant portion of his private patrimony would be consumed. Nevertheless, he made the sacrifice with a perfect good heart. His good mother always enjoined him to remember his grandfather and support the dignity of his family. She gave him commissions to purchase goods in England, and though she had sent only trifling remittances, she constantly alluded to the exalted rank of the Esmonds. She desired that he do nothing unworthy of that illustrious family, advising him peremptorily to appear in the first society, frequent the court where his ancestors moved, and conduct himself in a manner worthy of his name. George made no doubt that his mother's money would be forthcoming when his own ran short, and he generously obeyed her injunctions regarding his style of life.

In the Esmond papers of this period, I find bills for genteel entertainments, tailors' bills for court suits, liveries for his negro servants and chairmen, horse-dealers' receipts, and the like. Thus, it appears the elder of our Virginians was also living at considerable expense. Yet, he was not wild or extravagant like his brother. There was no talk of gambling or racehorses against Mr. George; his table was liberal, his equipages handsome, and his purse always full. The estate to which he was heir was known to be immense. I mention these circumstances because they likely influenced the conduct of George and his friends regarding the matter of his marriage.

The young heir of Virginia was traveling for pleasure and improvement in foreign kingdoms. The Queen, his mother, maintained daily correspondence with his Highness, constantly enjoining him to act as became his lofty station. There could be no doubt from her letters that she desired him to live liberally and magnificently. He was perpetually making purchases at her order. She had not yet settled the accounts; on the contrary, she had written by the last mail for twelve new sets of waggon harness and an organ capable of playing fourteen specified psalm-tunes. George dutifully ordered these items. She had not paid as yet, and might not today or tomorrow, but eventually, of course, she would. Mr. Warrington never troubled his friends with these calculations or discussed his mother's domestic affairs. They, on their side, took for granted that he was in a state of competence and ease. Without being mercenary, Mr. and Mrs. Lambert were pleased to see an attachment growing between their daughter and a young gentleman of such good principles, talents, family, and expectations. There was honesty in all Mr. Esmond Warrington's words and actions, and in his behavior to the world a certain grandeur and simplicity that marked him as a true gentleman. Somewhat cold and haughty in his demeanor to strangers, especially the great, he was not supercilious; he was perfectly courteous to women and, with those he loved, kind, amiable, lively, and tender.

No wonder that one young woman came to think him the best man in all the world—alas! not even excepting her father. A great love felt by a man towards a woman makes him better, as regards her, than all other men. We have said that George used to wonder how witty, eloquent, and wise he became when talking with the fair young creature whose heart had become all his. We will not again listen to their love whispers. Those soft words do not bear being written down. If you please, good sir or madam, who are sentimentally inclined, lay down the book and think over certain things for yourself. You may be ever so old now; but you remember. It may be all dead and buried; but in a moment, it springs out of its grave, looking, smiling, and whispering as of yore when it clung to your arm and dropped fresh tears on your heart. Is it here, and alive? O far, far away! O lonely hearth and cold ashes! Here is the vase, but the roses are gone; here is the shore, and yonder the ship was moored; but the anchors are up, and it has sailed away forever.

*Et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.* This, however, is mere sentimentality; as regards George and Theo, it is neither here nor there. What I mean to say is that the young lady's family were perfectly satisfied with the state of affairs between her and Mr. Warrington. Though he had not yet asked the

James Wolfe, Harry's new Colonel, returned from America a few weeks after our Virginian had joined his regiment. Wolfe had previously served as Lieutenant-Colonel of Kingsley's, and a second battalion had been formed and placed under his command in recognition of his distinguished gallantry and services at Cape Breton. Harry approached his new commander with unfeigned respect and cordiality, for the eyes of the world were now turned upon him; the common opinion held that he was destined to become a great general. In the recent affairs in France, several officers of great previous repute had been tried and found lamentably wanting. The Duke of Marlborough had shown himself no worthy descendant of his great ancestor, and doubts existed even before his unhappy behavior at Minden prevented a great victory regarding Lord George Sackville's military genius. The nation was longing for military glory, and the Minister was anxious to find a general who might gratify the eager desire of the people. With Mr. Wolfe and Mr. Lambert's business keeping them both in London, the friendly intercourse between those officers was renewed, no one being more delighted than Lambert at his younger friend's good fortune.

When Harry was away from his duty, he was never tired of hearing Mr. Wolfe's details of the military operations of the last year, about which Wolfe talked very freely and openly. Whatever thought was in his mind, he appeared to have spoken it out generously. He possessed that heroic simplicity which distinguished Nelson afterwards; he talked frankly of his actions. Some of the fine gentlemen at St. James's might wonder and sneer at him, but amongst our little circle of friends we may be sure he found admiring listeners. The young General had the romance of a boy on many matters. He delighted in music and poetry. On the last day of his life, he said he would rather have written Gray's Elegy than have won a battle. We may be sure that with a gentleman of such literary tastes, our friend George would become familiar; and as they were both in love, and both accepted lovers, and both eager for happiness, no doubt they must have had many sentimental conversations together which would be very interesting to report could we only have accurate accounts of them. In one of his later letters, Warrington writes:

"I had the honour of knowing the famous General Wolfe, and seeing much of him during his last stay in London. We had a subject of conversation then which was of unfailing interest to both of us, and I could not but admire Mr. Wolfe's simplicity, his frankness, and a sort of glorious bravery which characterized him. He was much in love, and he wanted heaps and heaps of laurels to take to his mistress. 'If it be a sin to covet honour,' he used to say with Harry the Fifth (he was passionately fond of plays and poetry), 'I am the most offending soul alive.' Surely on his last day he had a feast which was enough to satisfy the greediest appetite for glory. He hungered after it. He seemed to me not merely like a soldier going resolutely to do his duty, but rather like a knight in quest of dragons and giants. My own country has furnished of late a chief of a very different order, and quite an opposite genius. I scarce know which to admire most. The Briton's chivalrous ardour, or the more than Roman constancy of our great Virginian."

As Mr. Lambert's official duties detained him in London, his family remained contentedly with him, and I suppose Mr. Warrington was so satisfied with the rural quiet of Southampton Row and the beautiful flowers and trees of Bedford Gardens, that he did not care to quit London for any long period. He made his pilgrimage to Castlewood, and passed a few days there, occupying the chamber of which he had often heard his grandfather talk, and which Colonel Esmond had occupied as a boy, and he was received kindly enough by such members of the family as happened to be at home. But no doubt he loved better to be in London by the side of a young person in whose society he found greater pleasure than any which my Lord Castlewood's circle could afford him, though all the ladies were civil, and Lady Maria especially gracious, and enchanted with the tragedy which George and Parson Sampson read out to the ladies. The chaplain was enthusiastic in its praises, and indeed it was through his interest and not through Mr. Johnson's after all, that Mr. Warrington's piece ever came on the stage. Mr. Johnson, it is true, pressed the play on his friend Mr. Garrick for Drury Lane, but Garrick had just made an arrangement with the famous Mr. Home for a tragedy from the pen of the author of Douglas. Accordingly, Carpezan was carried to Mr. Rich at Covent Garden, and accepted by that manager.

On the night of the production of the piece, Mr. Warrington gave an elegant entertainment to his friends at the Bedford Head, in Covent Garden, whence they adjourned in a body to the theatre; leaving only one or two with our young author, who remained at the coffee-house, where friends from time to time came to him with an account of the performance. The part of Carpezan was filled by Barry, Shuter was the old nobleman, Reddish, I need scarcely say, made an excellent Ulric, and the King of Bohemia was by a young actor from Dublin, Mr. Geoghegan, or Hagan as he was called on the stage, and who looked and performed the part to admiration. Mrs. Woffington looked too old in the first act as the heroine, but her murder in the fourth act, about which great doubts were expressed, went off to the terror and delight of the audience. Miss Wayn sang the ballad which is supposed to be sung by the king's page, just at the moment of the unhappy wife's execution, and all agreed that Barry was very terrible and pathetic as Carpezan, especially in the execution scene. The grace and elegance of the young actor, Hagan, won general applause. The piece was put very elegantly on the stage by Mr. Rich, though there was some doubt whether, in the march of Janissaries in the last, the manager was correct in introducing a favorite elephant, which had figured in various pantomimes, and by which one of Mr. Warrington's black servants marched in a Turkish habit. The other sat in the footman's gallery, and uproariously wept and applauded at the proper intervals.

The execution of Sybilla was the turning-point of the piece. Her head off, George's friends breathed freely, and one messenger after another came to him at the coffee-house, to announce the complete success of the tragedy. Mr. Barry, amidst general applause, announced the play for repetition, and that it was the work of a young gentleman of Virginia, his first attempt in the dramatic style.

We should like to have been in the box where all our friends were seated during the performance, to have watched Theo's flutter and anxiety whilst the success of the play seemed dubious, and have beheld the blushes and the sparkles in her eyes, when the victory was assured. Harry, during the little trouble in the fourth act, was deadly pale—whiter, Mrs. Lambert said, than Barry, with all his chalk. But if Briareus could have clapped hands, he could scarcely have made more noise than Harry at the end of the piece. Mr. Wolfe and General Lambert huzzayed enthusiastically. Mrs. Lambert, of course, cried: and though Hetty said, "Why do you cry, mamma? I you don't want any of them alive again; you know it serves them all right"—the girl was really as much delighted as any person present, including little Charley from the Chartreux, who had leave from Dr. Crusius for that evening, and Miss Lucy, who had been brought from boarding-school on purpose to be present on the great occasion. My Lord Castlewood and his sister, Lady Maria, were present; and his lordship went from his box and complimented Mr. Barry and the other actors on the stage; and Parson Sampson was invaluable in the pit, where he led the applause, having, I believe, given previous instructions to Gumbo to keep an eye upon him from the gallery, and do as he did.

Be sure there was a very jolly supper of Mr. Warrington's friends that night—much more jolly than Mr. Garrick's, for example, who made but a very poor success with his Agis and its dreary choruses, and who must have again felt that he had missed a good chance, in preferring Mr. Home's tragedy to our young author's. A jolly supper, did we say?—Many jolly suppers. Mr. Gumbo gave an entertainment to several gentlemen of the shoulder-knot, who had concurred in supporting his master's masterpiece: Mr. Henry Warrington gave a supper at the Star and Garter, in Pall Mall, to ten officers of his new regiment, who had come up for the express purpose of backing Carpezan; and finally, Mr. Warrington received the three principal actors of the tragedy, our family party from the side box, Mr. Johnson and his ingenious friend, Mr. Reynolds the painter, my Lord Castlewood and his sister, and one or two more. My Lady Maria happened to sit next to the young actor who had performed the part of the King. Mr. Warrington somehow had Miss Theo for a neighbour, and no doubt passed a pleasant evening beside her. The greatest animation and cordiality prevailed, and when toasts were called, Lady Maria gaily gave "The King of Hungary" for hers. That gentleman, who had plenty of eloquence and fire, and excellent manners, on as well as off the stage, protested that he had already suffered death in the course of the evening, hoped that he should die a hundred times more on the same field; but, dead or living, vowed he knew whose humble servant he ever should be. Ah, if he had but a real crown in place of his diadem of pasteboard and tinsel, with what joy would he lay it at her ladyship's feet! Neither my lord nor Mr. Esmond were over well pleased with the gentleman's exceeding gallantry—a part of which they attributed, no doubt justly, to the wine and punch, of which he had been partaking very freely. Theo and her sister, who were quite new to the world, were a little frightened by the exceeding energy of Mr. Hagan's manner—but Lady Maria, much more experienced, took it in perfectly good part. At a late hour coaches were called, to which the gentlemen attended the ladies, after whose departure some of them returned to the supper-room, and the end was that Carpezan had to be carried away in a chair, and that the King of Hungary had a severe headache; and that the Poet, though he remembered making a great number of speeches, was quite astounded when half a dozen of his guests appeared at his house the next day, whom he had invited overnight to come and sup with him once more.

As he put Mrs. Lambert and her daughters into their coach on the night previous, all the ladies were flurried, delighted, excited; and you may be sure our gentleman was with them the next day, to talk of the play and the audience, and the actors, and the beauties of the piece, over and over again. Mrs. Lambert had heard that the ladies of the theatre were dangerous company for young men. She hoped George would have a care, and not frequent the greenroom too much.

George smiled, and said he had a preventive against all greenroom temptations, of which he was not in the least afraid; and as he spoke he looked in Theo's face, as if in those eyes lay the amulet which was to preserve him from all danger.

"Why should he be afraid, mamma?" asks the maiden simply. She had no idea of danger or of guile.

"No, my darling, I don't think he need be afraid," says the mother, kissing her.

"You don't suppose Mr. George would fall in love with that painted old creature who performed the chief part?" asks Miss Hetty, with a toss of her head. "She must be old enough to be his mother."

"Pray, do you suppose that at our age nobody can care for us, or that we have no hearts left?" asks mamma, very tartly. "I believe, or I may say, I hope and trust, your father thinks otherwise. He is, I imagine, perfectly satisfied, miss. He does not sneer at age, whatever little girls out of the schoolroom may do. And they had much better be back there, and they had much better remember what the fifth commandment is—that they had, Hetty!"

"I didn't think I was breaking it by saying that an actress was as old as George's mother," pleaded Hetty.

"George's mother is as old as I am, miss!--at least she was when we were at school. And Fanny Parker--Mrs. Mountain who now is--was seven months older, and we were in the French class together; and I have no idea that our age is to be made the subject of remarks and ridicule by our children, and I will thank you to spare it, if you please! Do you consider your mother too old, George?"

"I am glad my mother is of your age, Aunt Lambert," says George, in the most sentimental manner.

Strange infatuation of passion--singular perversity of reason! At some period before his marriage, it not unfrequently happens that a man actually is fond of his mother-in-law! At this time our good General vowed, and with some reason, that he was jealous. Mrs. Lambert made much more of George than of any other person in the family. She dressed up Theo to the utmost advantage in order to meet him; she was for ever caressing her, and appealing to her when he spoke. It was, "Don't you think he looks well?"--"Don't you think he looks pale, Theo, to-day?"--"Don't you think he has been sitting up over his books too much at night?" and so forth. If he had a cold, she would have liked to make gruel for him and see his feet in hot water. She sent him recipes of her own for his health. When he was away, she never ceased talking about him to her daughter. I dare say Miss Theo liked the subject well enough. When he came

The human heart recoils from the thought of separation, and so I shall spare you the description of Harry Warrington's sorrow as he prepares to depart. Are there not thousands of men in the same predicament? Did not Mr. Wolfe have a mother to kiss—his brave father having passed away during his son's absence at the siege of Louisbourg—and a beloved sweetheart to hold in a final embrace? Did not the stout Admiral Holmes, before sailing his squadron westward aboard *The Dublin*, bid farewell to Mrs. Holmes and his daughters? Was Admiral Saunders, who departed the following day, immune to human feeling? Away went William and his crew of jovial sailors, cutting through the tumbling waves, while poor Black-eyed Susan stood on the shore, watching the vessel shrink until it vanished into the sunset.

It faded into the West. Night fell darkly over the ocean. They were gone, yet their hearts remained at home for a while longer. In silence, with a tenderness beyond expression, each man pondered those he had left behind. What a chorus of pitiful prayers rose to the Father, from the sea and the shore, on that night of parting: by the vacant bedside where a wife knelt in tears; around the hearth where mothers and children poured out their supplications; or on the deck, where the sailor gazed upward at the stars as the ship cleaved the roaring midnight waters. Tomorrow, the sun would rise upon our common life again, and we would resume our daily tasks of toil and duty.

George accompanied his brother, staying with him at Portsmouth while they waited for a favorable wind. He shook Mr. Wolfe's hand, looked upon his pale face one last time, and watched the vessels depart amidst the clamor of bells and the thunder of cannon from the shore. The next day, George returned to his home, to that occupation which is surely one of the most selfish and absorbing in the world, to which nearly every man of thirty has apprenticed himself. A pang of sadness struck him as he peered into the lodgings and saw the little room Harry had occupied, noting the half-burned papers still lingering in the grate. Soon, however, he was on his way to Dean Street again, whispering by the fitful firelight to his clinging sweetheart. She was exceedingly happy—oh, so happy!—at his return, though she felt ashamed of it. Was it not heartless to be so glad when poor Hetty was so melancholy? Poor little Hetty! Indeed, it was selfish to rejoice while she suffered. It made one quite wretched to witness her distress. "Don't, sir! Well, I ought to be wretched, and it is very, very wicked of me if I am not," said Theo, and one could understand her soft-hearted repentance. What she meant by "Don't" was unclear; I had noted the room was dark and the fire burned fitfully, and "Don't" was likely uttered in one of those shadowy moments. Servants entered with supper and lights; the family arrived, and conversation became general. The destination of the fleet was now known to all. The force aboard was deemed sufficient to defeat the French in Canada, and under an officer like Wolfe, to rectify the blunders of previous campaigns. He looked dreadfully ill, indeed, but possessed a great soul within a feeble body. The ministers and the country placed their highest hopes in him. After supper, as was custom, Mr. Lambert gathered his modest household, of whom George Warrington formed a significant part; as he prayed for all travelers by land and water, Theo and her sister knelt together. Thus, as the ship sped farther into the West, these fond thoughts pursued it; the night passed, and the sun rose.

A day or two more, and everyone returned to their books or usual work. As for George Warrington, that celebrated dramatist was busy with another composition. When the tragedy of *Carpezan* had run some thirty or forty nights, other persons of genius took possession of the theater.

There may have been those who wondered how the town could be so fickle as to tire of such a masterpiece, unable to bear seeing the actors in other costumes reciting other men's verses. But George, of a skeptical turn of mind, accepted the fate of his tragedy philosophically, pocketing the proceeds with quiet satisfaction. From Mr. Dodsley, the bookseller, he received the customary hundred pounds; from the theater manager, two hundred or more; and with such praise from critics and friends, he set to work preparing another piece, hoping to achieve even greater success.

Over these studies and other charming pursuits, months passed. Happy times! The happiest season of youth and life, when love is first spoken and returned; when the dearest eyes shine daily with welcome, and the fondest lips never tire of whispering sweet secrets; when the parting glance accompanying "Good night!" offers delightful promise of tomorrow; when the heart overflows with love and happiness, leaving nothing to spare for the world; when days close with glad prayers and open with joyful hopes; when doubt seems cowardice, misfortune impossible, and poverty merely a sweet trial of constancy! Theo's elders, thankfully recalling their own prime, sat softly by to witness this pretty comedy performed by their young people. In one of his later letters, dutifully written to his wife during a temporary absence, George Warrington recorded how he had looked up at the windows of the dear old house in Dean Street, wondering who sat in the chamber where he and Theo had been so happy.

Meanwhile, we may learn how time passed and what occupied our friends through extracts from George's letters to his brother.

"From the old window opposite Bedford Gardens, August 20, 1759.

"Why have you returned to rugged rocks, bleak shores, burning summers, and nipping winters at home, when you might have been cropping laurels in Germany? Kingsley's are returning covered with them as Jack-a-Green on May-day. Our six regiments did wonders; our horse would have done too, had my Lord George Sackville only allowed it. But when Prince Ferdinand shouted 'Charge!' his lordship could not hear, or could not translate the German word for 'Forward,' and so we only beat the French, without utterly annihilating them as we might have, had Lord Granby or Mr. Warrington commanded. My lord has returned to town and is shouting for a Court-Martial. He held his head high enough in prosperity; in misfortune, he displays such a constancy of arrogance that one almost admires him. He looks as if he rather envied poor Mr. Byng, and the fact that he was not shot was a *manque d'égards* toward him.

"The Duke has received notice to prepare for departure from this world of grandeur, victories, downfalls, and disappointments. An attack of palsy has visited His Royal Highness, and *pallida mors* has just peeped in at his door, saying, 'I will call again.' Tyrant as he was, this prince has been noble in disgrace; and no king has ever had a truer servant than ours has found in his son. Why do I always favor the losing side, and am I disposed to revolt against the winners? Your famous Mr. P----, your chief's patron and discoverer, I have heard speak in the House of Commons twice or thrice. I revolt against his magniloquence. I wish some little David would topple that swelling giant. His thoughts and language are always attitudinizing. I like Barry's manner best, though the other is the more awful actor.

"*Pocahontas* is progressing well. Barry likes his part as Captain Smith; and though he insists he wear a red coat with blue facings and an epaulet, I fancy dressing him exactly like one of the pictures of Queen Elizabeth's gentlemen at Hampton Court: with a ruff, a square beard, and square shoes. 'And Pocahontas—would you like her to be tattooed?' asks Uncle Lambert. Hagan's part as the warrior who loves her, and seeing her partiality for the captain, nobly rescuing him from death, I trust will prove a hit. A strange fish is this Hagan: his mouth full of stage-plays and rant, but good, honest, and brave, if I do not err. He is angry at having been cast recently for Sir O'Brallaghan in Mr. Macklin's new farce, *Love A-la-mode*. He says he does not care to disgrace his tongue with imitations of that rascal's brogue. As if there were any need for imitation, when he has such an admirable twang of his own!

"Shall I tell you? Shall I hide the circumstance? Shall I hurt your feelings? Shall I set you in a rage of jealousy and cause you to ask leave to return to Europe? Know then, that though *Carpezan* is long since dead, cousin Maria is forever coming to the playhouse. Tom Spencer has spied her out night after night in the gallery, and she comes on the nights when Hagan performs. Quick, Burroughs, Mr. Warrington's boots and portmanteau! Order a chaise and four for Portsmouth immediately! The letter I burned one morning at breakfast (I may let the cat out of the bag now that puss has such a prodigious way to run) was from cousin M., hinting that she wished me to tell no tales about her: but I cannot help whispering to you that Maria is currently busy consoling herself as fast as possible. Shall I spoil the sport? Shall I tell her brother? Is the affair any business of mine? What have the Esmonds done for you and me but win our money at cards? Yet I like our noble cousin. It seems to me that he would be good if he could—or rather, he would have been once. He has been set on a wrong path of life, from which 'tis now probably too late to rescue him. O *beati agricolae*! Our Virginia was dull, but let us thank Heaven we were bred there. We were made little slaves, but not slaves to wickedness, gambling, or bad male and female company. It was not until my poor Harry left home that he fell among thieves. I mean thieves *en grand*, such as waylaid him and stripped him on English highroads. I consider you none the worse because you were the unlucky one and had to deliver your purse. And now you are going to retrieve yourself, make a good name, and kill more 'French dragons,' becoming a great commander. Our mother will talk of her son the Captain, the Colonel, the General, and have his picture painted with all his stars and epaulets, while poor I shall be but a dawdling poetaster, or, if we may hope for the best, a snug placeman with a little box at Richmond or Kew, and a half-score of little picaninnies who will come to bob curtseys at the garden-gate when their uncle the General rides up on his great charger, his aide-de-camp's pockets filled with gingerbread for the nephews and nieces. 'Tis for you to brandish the sword of Mars. As for me, I look forward to a quiet life: a quiet little home, a quiet little library full of books, and a little *Some one dulce ridentem, dulce loquentem* on the other side of the fire as I scribble away at my papers. I am so pleased with this prospect, so utterly contented and happy, that I feel afraid lest it should escape me; and even to my dearest Hal, I am shy of speaking of my happiness. What is ambition to me with this certainty? What do I care for wars, with this beatific peace smiling near?

"Our mother's friend, Mynheer Van den Bosch, has been away on a tour to discover his family in Holland, and, strange to say, has found one. Miss (who was intended by maternal solicitude to be a wife for your worship) has had six months at Kensington School and is coming out with a hundred pretty accomplishments to complete her as a perfect fine lady. Her papa brought her to make a curtsey in Dean Street, and a mighty elegant curtsey she made. Though she is scarce seventeen, no dowager of sixty can be more at her ease. She conversed with Aunt Lambert on an equal footing, treated the girls as chits—to Hetty's wrath and Theo's amusement. She talked politics with the General and the last routs, dresses, operas, fashions, and scandal with such perfect ease that, but for a blunder or two, you might have fancied Miss Lydia was born in Mayfair. At the Court end of the town she will live, she says, and has no patience with her father, who has a lodging in Monument Yard. For those who love a brown beauty, a prettier little *mignonne* creature cannot be seen. But my taste, you know, dearest brother, and..."

Here follows a page of raptures and quotations of verse, which, out of regard for the reader and the writer's memory, the editor of these pages declines to reprint. Gentlemen and ladies of a certain age may remember the time when they indulged in these rapturous follies on their own accounts; when the praises of the charmer were forever warbling from their lips or trickling from their pens; when the flowers of life were in full bloom, and all the birds of spring were singing. The twigs are now bare, perhaps, and the leaves have fallen; but, for all that, shall we not remember the vernal time? As for you, young people, whose May (or April, is it?) has not commenced yet, you need not be detained over other folks' love-rhapsodies; depend on it, when your spring-season arrives, kindly Nature will warm all your flowers into bloom and rouse your glad bosoms to pour out their full song.

Despite the previous friction between my Lord Castlewood and Harry, the two men had reconciled, meeting with a cordiality that belied their past. George Warrington, finding in his cousin a willing patron, eagerly accepted the promise of assistance in securing a position within the House of Lords. This offer was particularly appealing to George, who had grown increasingly weary of the stifling atmosphere of Virginia. There, he felt less a master and more a subject, bound by the rigid hierarchy of his mother's household. The prospect of returning to a life of tedious subordination, marked by petty jealousies and domestic friction, held no allure for him. In contrast, London offered him the freedom he craved, a society that matched his wit, and the potential for distinction. He preferred the uncertainty of poverty in England to the certain weariness of his plantation home.

My Lord Castlewood, in turn, proved surprisingly gracious upon learning of George's engagement to Miss Lambert. He visited the Lamberts with such charm and wit that he effectively erased his notorious reputation in their eyes. To the good-hearted Mrs. Lambert and her family, he appeared as a man transformed, leaving his worldliness behind like a heavy cloak until he departed. He spoke openly of his admiration for Miss Theo, claiming it was a genuine sentiment, albeit one that did not trouble his sleep or threaten to break his heart. Yet, in a moment of vulnerability, he confessed that he wished he had met such an innocent soul in his youth, suggesting that her purity might have spared him from the harms of his own nature. When Mrs. Lambert gently urged him that it was never too late to repent, he responded with a melancholy grace, acknowledging the weight of his past while expressing a profound, if distant, respect for her virtue. He saw himself as a man bound by fate, unable to change his nature, yet he found comfort in the kindness of those who remained unaware of his true depths.

While the Lambert family viewed him with hopeful charity, seeing in him a sinner capable of redemption, the reality of his character remained complex. Their kindness, however, did no harm, and an intimacy developed between the households.
