If Mr. Lambert was a man of spirit and honour, as he was represented to be, Madam Esmond scarcely supposed that, after her representations, he would persist in desiring this match. She would not lay commands upon her son, whose temper she knew; but for the sake of Miss Lambert's own reputation and comfort, she urged that the dissolution of the engagement should come from her family, and not from the just unwillingness of Rachel Esmond Warrington of Virginia.

"God help us, George!" the General said, "and give us all strength to bear this grief, and these charges which it has pleased your mother to bring! They are hard, but they don't matter now. What is of most importance, is to spare as much sorrow as we can to my poor girl. I know you love her so well, that you will help me and her mother to make the blow as tolerable as we may to that poor gentle heart. Since she was born she has never given pain to a soul alive, and 'tis cruel that she should be made to suffer." And as he spoke he passed his hand across his dry eyes.

"It was my fault, Martin! It was my fault!" weeps the poor mother.

"Your mother spoke us fair, and gave her promise," said the father.

"And do you think I will withdraw mine?" cried I; and protested, with a thousand frantic vows, what they knew full well, that I was bound to Theo before Heaven, and that nothing should part me from her."

"She herself will demand the parting. She is a good girl, God help me! and a dutiful. She will not have her father and mother called schemers, and treated with scorn. Your mother knew not, very likely, what she was doing, but 'tis done. You may see the child, and she will tell you as much. Is Theo dressed, Molly? I brought the letter home from my office last evening after you were gone. The women have had a bad night. She knew at once by my face that there was bad news from America. She read the letter quite firmly. She said she would like to see you and say good-bye. Of course, George, you will give me your word of honour not to try and see her afterwards. As soon as my business will let me we will get away from this, but mother and I think we are best all together. 'Tis you, perhaps, had best go. But give me your word, at any rate, that you will not try and see her. We must spare her pain, sir! We must spare her pain!" And the good man sate down in such deep anguish himself that I, who was not yet under the full pressure of my own grief, actually felt his, and pitied it. It could not be that the dear lips I had kissed yesterday were to speak to me only once more. We were all here together; loving each other, sitting in the room where we met every day; my drawing on the table by her little workbox; she was in the chamber upstairs; she must come down presently.

Who is this opens the door? I see her sweet face. It was like our little Mary's when we thought she would die of the fever. There was even a smile upon her lips. She comes up and kisses me. "Good-bye, dear George!" she says. Great Heaven! An old man sitting in this room,—with my wife's workbox opposite, and she but five minutes away, my eyes grow so dim and full that I can't see the book before me. I am three-and-twenty years old again. I go through every stage of that agony. I once had it sitting

Once the initial shock of our reunion had settled, the little maid, Hetty, launched immediately into her tirade.

"So you have finally arrived to inquire after Theo, and you feel remorse that your neglect has rendered her so ill? For six weeks she has languished, and you have uttered not a single word regarding her! How very kind of you, Mr. George, I am certain!"

"Kind!" Mr. Warrington gasped, the word tearing from his throat.

"I suppose you deem it kind to attend her day and night for a year, only to vanish without a whisper?"

"My dear child, you recall my pledge to your father?" I replied.

"Pledge!" Miss Hetty scoffed, rolling her eyes. "A magnificent pledge, indeed, to render my darling sick, and then, on a sudden, one fine morning, to bid her 'Good-bye, Theo,' and depart forever. Gentlemen make such vows, I suppose, because they intend to honor them. I would not toy with a poor child's heart and abandon her afterward if I were a man. What has she ever done to you but be foolish and too fond of you? Pray, sir, by what right do you seize her from all of us, and then desert her because an elderly woman in America disapproves of her? She was content with us before your arrival. She adored her sister—there was never such a devoted sibling—until she saw you. And now, because your mother believes a young gentleman might fare better elsewhere, you must leave her, forsooth!"

"Heavens, child!" I cried, exasperated by her misguided logic. "Was it I who retreated? Am I not the one forbidden your household? Did not your father demand, upon my honor, that I cease seeing her?"

"Honor!" Hetty exclaimed. "You are the men who claim superiority, and we are the ones meant to revere you! I declare, George Warrington, you ought to return to your schoolroom in Virginia, have your black nurse tuck you in, and beg permission from your mother to step outside. Oh, George! I little imagined my sister was surrendering her heart to a man lacking the spirit to stand by her; yet, at the first obstacle, he fled! When Doctor Heberden mentioned attending to you, I resolved to visit, and you do appear quite ill, which brings me relief. I assume it is your mother you fear. But I shall not inform Theo of your sickness. She cannot cease caring for you. She cannot abandon her solemn engagements and stride into the world the next day as if nothing occurred! That is reserved for men, our superiors in courage and wisdom; to desert an angel—yes, an angel ten thousand times too pure for you; an angel who loved me until she saw you, and was the blessing of our lives—is what you term honor? Do not tell me, sir! I despise you all! Are we to worship and wait upon you? I care not for your wit, your tragedies, or your verses; I find them often tedious. I will not spend nights copying your manuscripts nor waste hours gazing from a window to catch a glimpse of your worship walking with your hat cocked! If you are departing, and welcome, give me back my sister, I say! Return my darling of the old days, who loved every one of us until she saw you. And you leave her because your mother thinks she can secure a richer match for you! Oh, brave gentleman! Go marry the person your mother chooses, and let my dear die here deserted!"

"Great heavens, Hetty!" I cried, stunned by the ferocity of her reasoning. "Is it I who wish to leave your sister? Did I not offer to uphold my promise, and was it not your father who refused me, compelling me to vow never to seek her again? What remains to me but my word and my honor?"

"Honor, indeed! You keep your word to him, yet break it to her! Pretty honor! If I were a man, I would soon reveal my thoughts on your honor! Only I forgot—you are bound to maintain the peace and must not... Oh, George, George! Do you not see the agony I endure? I am distraught, scarcely knowing what I speak. You must not leave my darling. They do not know at home. They do not believe it, but I know her best of all, and she will perish if you abandon her. Say you will not! Have pity upon me, Mr. Warrington, and restore my dearest to me!" Thus the warm-hearted, frantic creature oscillated between scorn and supplication, from anger to tears. Was my little physician correct in describing the plight of her dear patient? Was there no other remedy than what Hetty cried out for? Had not others felt the cruel pain of amputation, endured the subsequent exhaustion and fever, lain hopeless of anything but death, and yet recovered, limping through life thereafter? Why, but that love is selfish, heedless of others' griefs and passions, or that ours was so intense and unique that we deemed no other lovers could suffer as we did; here, in this passionate young advocate for her sister, we might have witnessed an instance that a fond heart could be struck by the love malady, silently endure it, and eventually recover. What had transpired in Hetty's own case? My sister and I, in our easy triumph and confidential chatter, had often discussed this matter, and, egotists as we were, perhaps derived a secret zest and security from her less fortunate attachment. It was like sitting by the fireside while winter howled without; it was like walking beside the great river, watching a ship toss at sea. We clung to each other more tightly, and wrapped in our own happiness, viewed others' misfortunes with complacent pity. Be the truth as it may. Grant that we might have been sundered and, after a while, survived the separation—so much my skeptical old age may admit. Yet, at that time, I was eager to share my ardent little Hetty's terrors and apprehensions, willingly choosing to believe that the life dearest to me in the world would be sacrificed if separated from mine. Was I wrong? I would not say so now. I may doubt myself (or not doubt, I know), but of her, never; and Hetty found in me a quite willing sharer in her alarms and terrors. I was inclined to impart some of these feelings to our doctor; but the good gentleman shut my mouth. "Hush," he said, with a comical look of fright. "I must hear none of this. If two people who happen to know each other chance to meet and talk in my patients' room, I cannot help myself; but as for match-making and love-making, I am your humble servant! What will the General do when he returns to town? He will have me behind Montagu House as sure as I am a living doctor, and alive I wish to remain, my good sir!" And he skipped into his carriage, leaving me there to meditate. "And you and Miss Hetty must have no further meetings here, mind you," he had previously warned.

Oh, no! Of course we would have none! We are gentlemen of honor, and so forth, and our word is our bond. Besides, to have seen Hetty was not that an inestimable boon, and would we not be forever grateful? I was so refreshed by that drop of water I had consumed that I thought I could endure for a very long time. I walked away with Hetty to Soho, never once considering arranging a new meeting with her. But the little emissary was more thoughtful, and she asked me if I intended to go to the Museum to read. I replied, "Oh yes, sometimes, my dear; but I am too wretched for reading now; I cannot discern what is on the paper. I do not care about my books. Even Pocahontas is wearisome to me. I..." I might have continued far longer when, "Nonsense!" she said, stamping her little foot. "Why, I declare, George, you are more stupid than Harry!"

"How do you mean, my dear child?" I asked.

"When do you go? You depart at three o'clock. You strike across the road to Tottenham Court. You walk through the village and return by the Green Lane that leads back toward the new hospital. You know you do! If you walk for a week there, it can do you no harm. Good morning, sir! Please do not follow me any farther." And she dropped a curtsey and walked away, her face veiled.

That Green Lane, lying to the north of the new hospital, is now built over with houses. In my time, when good old George II. was yet king, it was a shabby rural outlet of London; so dangerous that the City folk who visited their villas and junketing houses at Hampstead and the outlying villages would return in parties at night, escorted by waiters with lanterns to defend them from the footpads who prowled the town outskirts. Hampstead and Highgate churches, each crowning its hill, filled the background of the view as you turned your back to London; and for one, two, three days Mr. George Warrington had the pleasure of gazing upon this landscape, walking back in the direction of the new hospital.

Along the lane stood sundry small houses of entertainment; and I remember at one place, where they sold cakes and beer, at the sign of the Protestant Hero, a decent woman smiling at me on the third or fourth day, curtseying in her clean apron as she said, "It appears the lady does not come, sir! Your honor had best step in and take a can of my cool beer."

At length, as I returned through Tottenham Road on the 25th of May—an O day to be marked with the whitest stone!—a little way beyond Mr. Whitefield's Tabernacle, I saw a landau before me, and on the box-seat by the driver sat my young friend Charley, who waved his hat and called out, "George! George!" I ran up to the carriage, my knees knocking together so violently I thought I should fall by the wheel; and inside I saw Hetty, and by her my dearest Theo, propped with a pillow. How thin the little hand had become since last it was laid in mine! The cheeks were flushed and wasted, the eyes strangely bright, and the thrill of the voice when she spoke a word or two smote me with a pang, I know not of grief or joy, so intimately were they blended.

"I am taking her an airing to Hampstead," Hetty said demurely. "The doctor says the air will do her good."

"I have been ill, but I am better now, George," Theo said. There came a great burst of music from the people in the chapel hard by as she spoke. I held her hand in mine. Her eyes looked into mine once more. It seemed as if we had never been parted.

I can never forget the tune of that psalm. I have heard it throughout my life. My wife has touched it on her harpsichord, and her little ones have warbled it. Now, do you understand, young people, why I love it so? Because it was the music played at our *amoris redintegratio*. Because it sang hope to me during the period of my existence the most miserable. Yes, the most miserable: for that dreary confinement of Duquesne had its tendernesses and kindly associations connected with it; and many a time in after days I have thought with fondness of the poor Biche and my tipsy jailor, and the reveille of the forest birds and the military music of my prison.

Master Charley looked down from his box-seat upon his sister and me engaged in beatific contemplation, and Hetty listening too to the music. "I think I should like to go and hear it. And that famous Mr. Whitfield, perhaps he is going to preach this very day! Come in with me, Charley—and George can drive for half an hour with dear Theo towards Hampstead and back."

Charley did not seem to possess a very strong desire for witnessing the devotional exercises of good Mr. Whitfield and his congregation, and proposed that George Warrington should take Hetty in; but Hetty was not to be denied. "I will never help you in another exercise as long as you live, sir," cries Miss Hetty, "if you don't come on,"—while the youth clambered down from his box-seat, and they entered the temple together.

Can any moralist, bearing my previous promises in mind, excuse me for jumping into the carriage and sitting down once more by my dearest Theo? Suppose I did break them? Will he blame me much? Reverend sir, you are welcome. I broke my promise; and if you would not do as much, good friend, you are welcome to your virtue. Not that I for a moment suspect my own children will ever be so bold as to think of having hearts of their own, and bestowing them according to their liking. No, my young people, you will let papa choose for you; be hungry when he tells you; be thirsty when he orders; and settle your children's marriages afterwards.

And now, of course, you are anxious to hear what took place when papa jumped into the landau by the side of poor little mamma, propped up by her pillows. "I am come to your part of the story, my dear," I said, looking over to my wife as she plied her needles.

"To what, pray?" said my lady. "You should skip all that part, and come to the grand battles, and your heroic defense of—"

"Of Fort Fiddlededee in the year 1778, when I pulled off Mr. Washington's epaulet, gouged General Gates's eye, cut off Charles Lee's head, and pasted it on again!"

"Let us hear all about the fighting," said the boys. Even the Captain condescended to own he would listen to any military details, though only from a militia officer.

"Fair and softly, young people! Everything in its turn. I am not yet arrived at the war. I am only a young gentleman, just stepping into a landau, by the side of

"You, Captain Miles Warrington, possess the rare distinction of winning the favor of a lady—indeed, of several ladies, including the Duchess of Devonshire, Mrs. Crew, Mrs. Fitzherbert, the Queen of Prussia, the Goddess Venus, and Mademoiselle Hillisberg of the Opera. Let us not concern ourselves with the specific identity. Now, if you have secured a lady's good graces, do you invariably proceed to the mess to recount the details?"

"Not such a fool, Squire!" replied the Captain, examining his sideburns in the mirror.

"Have you, Miss Theo, disclosed every word spoken to Mr. Joe Blake, junior, in the shrubbery this morning?"

"Joe Blake, indeed!" cried Theo junior.

"And you, mademoiselle? Regarding that scented billet-doux delivered under Sir Thomas's frank, have you revealed its entire contents? Observe how she blushes! As crimson as the curtain, I swear! No, mademoiselle, we all possess our secrets" (the Squire added, executing his finest French bow).

"No, Theo, there was nothing in the shrubbery—merely nuts, my child! No, Miles, my son, we do not reveal everything, even to the most indulgent of fathers—and if I recount what transpired in a landau on the Hampstead Road on the twenty-fifth of May, 1760, may the Chevalier Ruspini extract every tooth from my head!"

"Pray tell, papa!" urged mamma. "Or, since Jobson, who drove us, is now in your service, perhaps you will summon him from the stables! I insist upon your telling!"

"What is, then, this mystery?" asked mademoiselle, in her charming French accent, addressing my wife.

"Eh, ma fille!" whispered the lady. "Thou wouldst ask me what I said? I said 'Yes!'—behold, that is all I said." Thus, it was my wife who had betrayed us, not I; and this was the entirety of our conversation as the carriage, faster than I deemed prudent, galloped toward Hampstead and returned swiftly. Theo had not agreed to defy her honored parents—such a notion was unthinkable. Yet, we would marry no other; not even the Prince of Wales himself could command her hand. Her heart had been given away with her father's consent—nay, his order—it was not hers to reclaim. Such a benevolent father must eventually relent; and if George kept his promise—whether now, in twenty years, or in another world—she knew she would never break hers.

Hetty's face beamed with delight when, upon my brief interview concluding, she observed Theo's countenance wearing a sweet tranquility. "All the doctor's medicine has not done her so much good," the devoted sister remarked. The girls departed home following their act of disobedience. I relinquished the position I had held during a fleeting period of happiness beside my dear invalid. Hetty skipped back into her seat, and Charley mounted to his box. He later informed me that it was a remarkably dull, stupid sermon he had attended. The little chap was too orthodox to appreciate dissenting preachers' sermons.

Hetty was not the sole family member to notice her sister's altered demeanor and improved spirits. I am told that upon the girls' return, their mother embraced both, especially the invalid, with more than usual ardor. "There was nothing like a country ride," Aunt Lambert declared, "for restoring her dear Theo. She had traveled the road to Hampstead, had she? She must undertake another ride tomorrow. Heaven be praised, my Lord Wrotham's horses were at our orders three or four times weekly, and the sweet child might avail herself of them!" As for the notion that Mr. Warrington might have encountered the children during their drive, Aunt Lambert never once entertained it—at least, she never spoke of it. I leave it to anyone interested to conjecture whether Mrs. Lambert could possibly have suspected that her daughter and her sweetheart might ever reunite. Do women assist one another in matters of love? Do women scheme, intrigue, devise little plans, utter little falsehoods, create amorous opportunities, hang up the rope-ladder, coax, wheedle, mystify the guardian or Abigail, and divert their attention while Strephon and Chloe coo in the twilight or whisk away in the postchaise to Gretna Green? My dear young folks, some individuals are of this nature; and some kind souls, having loved tenderly and truly in their own time, continue thereafter to be kindly and tenderly disposed toward their young successors as they commence playing the same delightful game.

Miss Prim does not. If she hears of two young persons attached to one another, she snarls at them as fools or imagines every conceivable evil. Because she possesses a humpback herself, she seeks to bite everyone else's. I believe if she witnessed a pair of turtles cooing in a wood, she would cast her eyes downward or throw a stone to frighten them; yet I am speaking, you see, young ladies, of your grandmother, Aunt Lambert, who was one great syllabub of human kindness. Moreover, regarding the affair currently under discussion, how am I ever to determine whether she knew anything concerning it or not?

Thus, all she tells Theo upon her return home is, "My child, the country air has done you all the good in the world, and I hope you will take another drive tomorrow, and another, and another, and so on."

"Do you not think, papa, the ride has done the child wonderful good, and must she not be made to go out in the air?" Aunt Lambert asks the General when he arrives for supper.

"Yes, certainly, if a coach-and-six will do his little Theo good, she shall have it," Lambert replies, "or he will drag the landau up Hampstead Hill himself if there are no horses;" and so the good man would have freely spent his guineas, his breath, or his blood to grant his child pleasure. He was charmed by his girl's altered countenance; she picked at a piece of chicken with appetite; she drank a little negus, which he prepared for her; indeed, it seemed superior to the kind doctor's best medicine, which, God knows, had hitherto been of little benefit. Mamma was gracious and happy. Hetty was radiant and rident. It was quite like an evening at home at Oakhurst. Never for months past, never since that fatal, cruel day that no one spoke of, had they spent an evening so delightful.

However, if the other women chose to coax and cajole the good, simple father, Theo herself was too honest to sustain that sweet and fond delusion for long. When, for the third or fourth time, he returned to the delightful theme of his daughter's improved health and asked, "What has done it? Is it the country air? Is it the Jesuit's bark? Is it the new medicine?"

"Can't you think, dear, what it is?" she said, laying a hand upon her father's, with a tremor in her voice, perhaps, but eyes that were quite open and bright.

"And what is it, my child?" asked the General.

"It is because I have seen him again, papa!" she replied.

The other two women turned pale, and Theo's heart too began to palpitate, her cheek whitening as she continued to gaze into her father's terrified face.

"It was not wrong to see him," she continued more quickly; "it would have been wrong not to tell you."

"Great God!" groaned the father, drawing his hand back, with such dreadful grief in his countenance that Hetty ran to her almost swooning sister, clasped her to her heart, and cried out rapidly, "Theo knew nothing of it, sir! It was my doing—it was all my doing!"

Theo lay on her sister's neck, kissing it twenty, fifty times.

"Women, women! Are you playing with my honour?" cried the father, bursting forth with a fierce exclamation.

Aunt Lambert sobbed wildly, "Martin! Martin! Don't say a word to her!" Hetty called out again, falling back herself staggering toward the wall, for Theo had fainted upon her shoulder.

I was taking my breakfast the next morning with whatever appetite I might possess when my door opened and my faithful black announced, "General Lambert." Immediately, by the General's face, I saw that the transaction of the previous day was known to him. "Your accomplices did not confess," the General said as soon as my servant had left us, "but sided with you against their father—a proof of how desirable clandestine meetings are. It was from Theo herself I heard that she had seen you."

"Accomplices, sir!" I said (perhaps not unwilling to turn the conversation from the real point at issue). "You know how fondly and dutifully your young people regard their father. If they side against you in this instance, it must be because justice is against you. A man like you is not going to set up *sic volo sic jubeo* as the sole law in his family!"

"Psha, George!" cried the General. "For though we are parted, God forbid I should desire that we should cease to love each other. I had your promise that you would not seek to see her."

"Nor did I go to her, sir," I said, turning red, no doubt; for though this was truth, I own it was untrue.

"You mean she was brought to you?" said Theo's father, in great agitation. "Is it behind Hester's petticoat that you will shelter yourself? What a fine defense for a gentleman!"

"Well, I won't screen myself behind the poor child," I replied. "To speak as I did was an attempt at evasion, and I am ill-accustomed to dissemble. I did not infringe the letter of my agreement, but I acted against the spirit of it. From this moment I annul it altogether."

"You break your word given to me!" cried Mr. Lambert.

"I recall a hasty promise made suddenly at a moment of extreme excitement and perturbation. No man can be forever bound by words uttered at such a time; and what is more, no man of honor or humanity, Mr. Lambert, would try to bind him."

"Dishonor to me! sir," exclaimed the General.

"Yes, if the phrase is to be shuttlecocked between us!" I answered hotly. "There can be no question about love, or mutual regard, or difference of age, when that word is used: and were you my own father—and I love you better than a father, Uncle Lambert—I would not bear it! What have I done? I have seen the woman whom I consider my wife before God and man, and if she calls me I will see her again. If she comes to me, here is my home for her, and the half of the little I have. 'Tis you, who have no right, having made me the gift, to resume it. Because my mother taunts you unjustly, are you to visit Mrs. Esmond's wrong upon this tender, innocent creature? You profess to love your daughter, and you can't bear a little wounded pride for her sake. Better she should perish away in misery than an old woman in Virginia should say that Mr. Lambert had schemed to marry one of his daughters. Say that to satisfy what you call honor and I call selfishness, we part, we break our hearts well nigh, we rally, we try to forget each other, we marry elsewhere? Can any man be to my dear as I have been? God forbid! Can any woman be to me what she is? You shall marry her to the Prince of Wales tomorrow, and it is cowardice and treason. How can we, how can you, undo the promises we have made to each other before Heaven? You may part us: and she will die as surely as if she were Jephthah's daughter. Have you made any vow to Heaven to compass her murder? Kill her if you conceive your promise so binds you: but this I swear, that I am glad you have come, so that I may here formally recall a hasty pledge which I gave, and that, call me when she will, I will come to her!"

No doubt this speech was made with the flurry and agitation belonging to Mr. Warrington's youth, and with the firm conviction that death would infallibly carry off one or both of the parties if their worldly separation was inevitably decreed. Who does not believe his first passion eternal? Having watched the world since, and seen the rise, progress, and—alas, that I must say it—decay of other amours, I may smile now as I think of my own youthful errors and ardors; but if it be a superstition, I had rather hold it; I had rather think that neither of us could have lived with any other mate, and that, of all its innumerable creatures, Heaven decreed these special two should be joined together.

"We must come, then, to what I had fain have spared myself," said the General in reply to my outbreak; "to an unfriendly separation. When I meet you, Mr. Warrington, I must know you no more. I must order—and they will not do other than obey me—my family and children not to recognize you when they see you, since you will not recognize in your intercourse with me the respect due to my age, the courtesy of gentlemen. I had hoped so far from your sense of honor, and the idea I had formed of you, that in my present great grief and perplexity, I should have found you willing to soothe and help me as far as you might—for, God knows, I have need of everybody's sympathy. But instead of help, you fling obstacles in my way. Instead of a friend—a gracious Heaven pardon me!—I find in you an enemy! An enemy to the peace of my home and the honor of my children, sir! And as such I shall treat you, and know how to deal with you when you molest me!"

Waving his hand to me and putting on his hat, Mr. Lambert hastily quitted my apartment.

I was confounded and believed, indeed, there was war between us. The brief happiness of

Years later, sifting through the dusty archives of my home, I discovered a packet sealed with my mother's precise, familiar script, labeled "From London, April, 1760. My son's dreadful letter." When it finally became mine to keep, I burned it without hesitation. I refused to allow the chronicle of our domestic fracture to remain among the family annals, lest some future Warrington should gaze upon it with shame, or a rebellious son cite it as a precedent for his own defiance. For the same reasons, I have consigned to the flames the reply my mother dispatched to me during this season of tyranny, revolt, and irritation.

Blinded by the agony of separation from my mistress, and justly regarding Mrs. Esmond as the architect of the deepest misery I had ever known, I penned a letter to Virginia. It was a document of extreme gravity, though perhaps lacking in temper. I asserted that I knew not her motives, yet held her accountable for the wretchedness of my future, which she had wilfully marred. I accused her of severing the bond between me and a virtuous, innocent young woman, whose hopes and health had been irrevocably shattered by her interference. The deed was done; I offered no further comment on the perpetrator, who answered only to God, but I made no secret that the injury inflicted upon me was mortal. The tie of my allegiance was severed; I could never again be the dutiful, respectful son she had expected.

Madam Esmond's reply was a masterpiece of dignified silence. She uttered no reproach, no harsh word, but coldly referred the case to the awful tribunal of God, asking for counsel. She humbly submitted her own conduct to judgment and challenged me, as a son, to answer for myself before the Great Judge. Whether I had done my duty and honoured my parents? *O popoi!* My grandfather often quoted Homer, noting how in our troubles we invariably summon the gods. When pride, avarice, or the desire to dominate stirs within us, do we not forever pestilence Heaven to decide in our favour? Did we not, in our great American quarrel, appeal to the skies on both sides, singing Te Deum for victory and claiming the right must prevail? Was America right solely because she was victorious? Then surely Poland was wrong because she was defeated? How am I wandering into this digression of nations and wars, while my mind wanders to a little woman now gone, who appealed to Heaven with a thousand texts because her son sought a marriage she disliked? We appeal, we imprecate, we kneel and demand blessings; we shriek for legal sentence. Yet the great course of the world moves on. We pant, strive, struggle; we hate and rage and weep; we reconcile and race, winning and losing; we pass away, and other little strugglers succeed. Our days are spent, our nights come, and another morning rises that shines on us no more.

I showed a duplicate of my letter of revolt to Mr. Lambert, wishing him to understand the depth of my estrangement from my mother and my determination that my separation from Theo was forced, not voluntary. Whenever I could see her again, I would. My word was given *in secula seculorum*, binding as long as life endured. I implied the girl was similarly bound to me, and her poor father knew it well. He might separate us; he might even offer a dose of poison, and the gentle, obedient creature would take it and die; but the death or separation would be his doing. Let him answer for it. Now, he was tender to a fault, unable to subject any of his children—this one especially—to torture. We had tried to part; we could not. He had endeavoured to separate us; it was beyond his power. The bars were raised, but the maid within and the knight without still loved each other. The wall stood high, but Pyramus and Thisbe whispered on either side. Amidst his grief and perplexity, Uncle Lambert possessed plenty of humour; he could not but see that his role was a sorry one. Light was beginning to pierce the lime and rough plaster of the wall; the lovers were getting their hands through, then their heads through. Indeed, it was the wall's best business to retire.

I forget the stages and days of what followed; nor does it matter for the instruction of future ages. When my descendants encounter their own love scrapes, they will find their own means of escape. I believe I did not return to Dean Street, but that open-air driving was deemed most healthful for Miss Lambert. I procured a fine horse and rode beside her carriage. The old woman at Tottenham Court soon knew us both, nodding and winking in the most friendly manner as we passed. I fancy the old goody was not unaccustomed to taking an interest in young couples, having dispensed the hospitality of her roadside cottage to more than one pair.

The doctor and the country air effected a prodigious cure upon Miss Lambert. Hetty always attended as duenna, and sometimes, on his holidays, Master Charley rode my horse when I entered the carriage. What a deal of love-making Miss Hetty heard! With what exemplary patience she listened! I do not say she resumed attending Methodist sermons, but it is certain that when we had a closed carriage, she would very kindly and considerately look out of the window. Then, what heaps of letters! What running to and fro! Gumbo's bandy legs were forever on the trot from my quarters to Dean Street; and, on my account or her own, Mrs. Molly, the girl's maid, was forever bringing back answers to Bloomsbury. By the time the autumn leaves began to turn pale, Miss Theo's roses were in full bloom again, and my good Doctor Heberden pronounced his cure complete.

What else occurred during this blessed period? Mr. Warrington completed his great tragedy of *Pocahontas*, which was not only accepted by Mr. Garrick this time (his friend Dr. Johnson having spoken favourably of the work), but my friend and cousin, Hagan, was engaged by the manager to perform the part of the hero, Captain Smith. Hagan's engagement was secured precisely when it was needed. I had helped him and his family with means disproportioned, perhaps, to my power, especially considering my feud with Madam Esmond. Her answer to my angry missive of April arrived towards autumn, written from Virginia with war for war, controlment for controlment. These menaces frightened me little; my poor mother's thunder could not reach me. My conscience, or casuistry, supplied me with other interpretations for her texts of Scripture, so that her oracles held no weight to frighten me from my purpose. I informed neither my mother nor any other member of my maternal or paternal family, who had been bitter against my marriage, of how my new love was speeding. Of what use wrangling with them? It was better to *carpere diem* and its sweet loves and pleasures, leaving the railers to grumble or the seniors to advise at their ease.

Besides Madam Esmond, I must own, in the frantic rage of my temporary separation, I addressed notes of wondrous sarcasm to my Uncle Warrington, my Aunt Madame de Bernstein, and my Lord or Lady of Castlewood (I forget to which individually), thanking them for the trouble taken in preventing the dearest happiness of my life, and promising corresponding gratitude from my obliged relative. Business brought the jovial Baronet and his family to London somewhat earlier than usual, and Madame de Bernstein was never sorry to return to Clarges Street and her cards. I saw them. They found me perfectly well. They concluded the match was broken off, and I did not choose to undeceive them. The Baroness took heart at seeing how cheerful I was, making many sly jokes about my philosophy and my prudent behaviour as a man of the world. She was, as ever, bent upon finding a rich match for me; and I fear I paid many compliments at her house to a rich young soap-boiler's daughter from Mile End, whom the worthy Baroness wished to place in my arms.

"You court her with infinite wit and esprit, my dear," said my pleased kinswoman, "but she does not understand half you say, and the other half, I think, frightens her. This *ton de persiflage* is very well in our society, but you must be sparing of it, my dear nephew, amongst these roturiers."

Miss Badge married a young gentleman of royal dignity, though with shattered fortunes, from a neighbouring island; and I trust Mrs. Mackshane has ere this pardoned my levity. There was another person besides Miss at my aunt's house who did not understand my persiflage much better than Miss herself; and that was a lady who had seen James the Second's reign, and who was alive and as worldly as ever in King George's. I loved to be with her; but since my little folks have access to this volume, I could put down a hundred stories of the great old folks she had known in the great old days—of George the First and his ladies, of St. John and Marlborough, of his reigning Majesty and the late Prince of Wales, and the causes of their quarrel—but my modest muse pipes for boys and virgins. Son Miles does not care about court stories, or if he doth, has a fresh budget from Carlton House quite as bad as the worst of our old Baroness. No, my dear wife, thou hast no need to shake thy powdered locks at me! Papa is not going to scandalise his nursery with old-world gossip, nor bring a blush over our chaste bread-and-butter.

But this piece of scandal I cannot help. My aunt used to tell it with infinite gusto; for, to do her justice, she hated your would-be good people and sniggered over the faults of the self-styled righteous with uncommon satisfaction. In her later days she had no hypocrisy, at least; and in so far was better than some whitewashed... Well, to the story. My Lady Warrington, one of the tallest and most virtuous of her sex, who had goodness forever on her lips and "Heaven in her eye," like the woman in Mr. Addison's tedious tragedy (which has kept the stage, from which some others, which shall be nameless, have disappeared), had the world in her other eye and an exceedingly shrewd desire of pushing herself in it. What did she do, when my marriage with your ladyship yonder was supposed to be broken off, but attempt to play off on me those arts she had tried on my poor Harry with such signal ill success, and which failed with me likewise! It was not the Beauty—Miss Flora was for my master (and what a master! I protest I take off my hat at the idea of such an illustrious connexion!)—it was Dora, the Muse, who was set upon me to languish at me, pity me, read even my godless tragedy, applaud me, and console me. Meanwhile, how was the Beauty occupied? Will it be believed that my severe aunt gave a great entertainment to my Lady Yarmouth, presented her boy to her, and placed poor little Miles under her ladyship's august protection? That, so far, is certain; but can it be that she sent her daughter to stay at my lady's house, which our gracious lord and master daily visited, with the views which old Aunt Bernstein attributed to her? "But for that fit of apoplexy, my dear," Bernstein said, "that aunt of yours intended there should have been a Countess in her own right in the Warrington family!" [Compare Walpole's letters in Mr. Cunningham's excellent new edition. See the story of the supper at N. House, to show what great noblemen would do for a king's mistress, and the pleasant account of the waiting for the Prince of Wales before Holland House.—EDITOR.] My neighbour and kinswoman, my Lady Claypole, is dead and buried. Grow white, ye daisies, upon Flora's tomb! I can see my pretty Miles, in a gay little uniform of the Norfolk Militia, led up by his parent to the lady whom the King delighted to honour, and the good-natured old Jezebel laying her hand upon the boy's curly pate. I am accused of being but a lukewarm royalist; but sure I can contrast those times with ours, and acknowledge the difference between the late sovereign and the present, who, born a Briton, has given to every family in the empire an example of decorum and virtuous life. [The Warrington MS. is dated 1793.—ED.]

Thus my life sped in the pleasantest of all occupations; and, being so happy myself, I could afford to be reconciled to those who, after all, had done me no injury, but rather added to the zest of my happiness by the brief obstacle they had placed in my way. No specific plans were formed, but Theo and I knew that a day would come when we need say Farewell no more. Should the day befall a year hence—or ten years hence—we were ready to wait. Day after day we discussed our little plans, with Hetty for our confidante. On our drives we spied out pretty cottages that we thought might suit young people of small means; we devised all sorts of delightful schemes and childish economies. We were Strephon and Chloe to be sure. A cot and a brown loaf should content us! Gumbo and Molly should wait upon us (as indeed they have done from that day until this). At twenty, who is afraid of being poor? Our trials would only confirm our attachment. The "sweet sorrow" of every day's parting but made the morrow's meeting more delightful; and when we separated we ran home and wrote each other those precious letters which we and other young gentlemen and ladies write under such circumstances; but though my wife has them all in a great tin sugar-box in the closet in her bedroom, and, I own, I myself have looked at them once, and even thought some of them pretty—I hereby desire my heirs and executors to burn them all, unread, at our demise; specially desiring my son the Captain (to whom I know the perusal of MSS. is not pleasant) to perform this duty. Those secrets whispered to the penny-post, or delivered between Molly and Gumbo, were intended for us alone, and no ears

We who had participated in that guilty morning felt a treble guilt when we witnessed the profound effect our actions had wrought upon him, the man we loved and revered above all others. The shock inflicted upon the good man was strange, yet pitiful to behold for those who had delivered it. His beloved child had deceived and defied him; indeed, I confess now, my dear, that neither we nor anyone else could possibly repeat such a deed. His entire family had conspired against him. Oh, dear, kind friend and father! We know you have pardoned our transgression in that Heaven where you dwell among purified spirits who learned on earth the art of loving and forgiving. For that man, love and forgiveness were natural duties; beneficence flowed from him like a gentle stream, accompanied by a sweet, smiling humility. To wound either was to become savage and brutal, akin to torturing a child or striking a nursing mother. Once the deed was done, all of us, the guilty ones, groveled in the dust before the man we had injured.

I shall pass over the scenes of forgiveness, reconciliation, and our shared worship, concluding with the final separation when the good man departed for his government, leaving the ship to sail away before us, carrying him from the shore where I and Theo stood hand in hand—horribly abashed, silent, and burdened by guilt. My wife did not join me until her father had departed. During the interval between our marriage ceremony and his leaving, she remained at home, occupying her accustomed place beside her father and by her sister's side. He was as kind as ever, yet the women were almost speechless among themselves; Aunt Lambert, for once, was unkind and fretful in her temper; and little Hetty was feverish and strange, muttering, "I wish we were gone. I wish we were gone." Though admitted to the house and forgiven, I slunk away during those final days, seeing my wife only for a minute or two in the street or within the confines of her family. She was not truly mine until they were gone. We traveled to Winchester and Hampton for what may be termed our wedding—a dismal business indeed. For a while, we felt utterly lonely, grieving for our dear father as if we had buried him or driven him to the grave through our undutifulness.

I instructed Sampson to announce our marriage in the newspapers. (My wife used to hang her head low before the poor fellow afterwards.) I took Mrs. Warrington back to my old lodgings in Bloomsbury, where there was ample room for us, and our modest married life began. I wrote a letter home to my mother in Virginia, omitting all particulars save that Mr. Lambert was about to depart for his government and that, bound in honor, I intended to fulfill my promise to his dearest daughter. I also stated my intention to complete my studies for the Bar, qualifying myself for employment at home or in any colony. My good Mrs. Mountain answered this letter, acting on the desire of Madam Esmond, who deemed it best for the sake of peace that my communications be conducted through her. I found my relatives in a fury that was perfectly amusing to witness. The butler's face, as he curtly declared, "Not at home," at my uncle's house in Hill Street, was a blank tragedy that might have been studied by Garrick himself. My poor little wife rested on my arm, and we tripped away, laughing at the fellow's cold reception, only to encounter my lady in a street stoppage in her carriage. I removed my hat and made her the lowest possible bow, affectionately inquiring after my dear cousins. "I—I wonder you dare look me in the face!" Lady Warrington gasped out. "Nay, don't deprive me of that precious privilege!" I replied. "Move on, Peter," she screamed to her chairman. "Your ladyship would not impale your own husband's flesh and blood!" I retorted. She rattled the glass of her chair in a fury. I kissed my hand, removed my hat, and performed another of my finest bows.

Walking shortly afterward in Hyde Park with my dearest companion, I met my little cousin exercising on horseback with a groom behind him. As soon as he saw us, he galloped up, the groom powdering afterwards and bawling, "Stop, Master Miles, stop!"

"I am not to speak to my cousin," said Miles, "but telling you to send my love to Harry is not speaking to you, is it? Is that my new cousin? I'm not told not to speak to her. I'm Miles, cousin, Sir Miles Warrington Baronet's son, and you are very pretty!" "Now, duee now, Master Miles," said the groom, touching his hat to us, and the boy trotted away laughing, glancing back over his shoulder. "You see how my relations have determined to treat me," I said to my partner. "As if I married you for your relations!" said Theo, her eyes beaming with joy and love into mine. Ah, how happy we were! How brisk and pleasant the winter! How snug the kettle by the fire, where the abashed Sampson sometimes came to make the punch; how delightful the night at the theatre, for which our friends had procured tickets, and where we daily expected our new play of *Pocahontas* would rival the successes of all former tragedies.

The fickle old aunt of Clarges Street, who had received me on my first coming to London with my wife in a burst of scorn, mollified presently. As soon as she came to know Theo—who she had previously pronounced an insignificant little country-faced chit—she fell utterly in love with her, inviting her to tea and supper every day whenever there was no other company. "As for company, my dears," she would say, "I don't ask you. You are no longer *du monde*. Your marriage has put that entirely out of the question." Thus she would have us come to amuse her, entering and exiting by the back stairs. My wife was fine lady enough to feel only amused at this reception; and I must do justice to the Baroness's domestics, for had we been duke and duchess, we could not have been received with more respect. Madame de Bernstein was very much tickled and amused by my story of Lady Warrington and the chair. I acted it for her, recounting anecdotes of the pious Baronet's lady and her daughters, which pleased the mischievous, lively old woman.

The Dowager Countess of Castlewood, now established in her house at Kensington, gave us that kind of welcome which genteel ladies extend to their poorer relatives. We visited her ladyship's drawing rooms at Kensington once or twice; but, losing more money at cards and spending more on coach-hire than I cared to afford, we speedily gave up those entertainments. I dare say we were no more missed or regretted than other people in the fashionable world who are carried by death, debt, or other accident out of the polite sphere. My Theo did not in the least regret this exclusion. She had made her appearance at one of these gatherings, attired in some little ornaments her mother had left behind, which the good lady set some store by; but I thought her own white neck far prettier than these poor twinkling stones. There were dowagers whose wrinkled old bones blazed with rubies and diamonds, which I am sure they would gladly have exchanged for her modest parure of beauty and freshness. Not a soul spoke to her—except, to be sure, Beau Lothair, a friend of Mr. Will's, who prowled about Bloomsbury afterwards and even sent my wife a billet. I met him in Covent Garden shortly after and promised to break his ugly face if ever I saw him in the neighborhood of my lodgings, and Madam Theo was molested no further.

The only relative who came to see us (Madame de Bernstein never came; she sent her coach for us sometimes, or made inquiries regarding us by her woman or her major-domo) was our poor Maria, who, with her husband, Mr. Hagan, often took a share of our homely dinner. Then we had friend Spencer from the Temple, who admired our Arcadian felicity and gently asked for our sympathy regarding his less fortunate loves; and twice or thrice the famous Doctor Johnson came in for a dish of Theo's tea. A dish? A pailful! "And a pail the best thing to feed him, sar!" said Mr. Gumbo, indignantly; for the Doctor's appearance was not pleasant, nor his linen particularly white. He snorted, grew red, and sputtered while feeding; he flung his meat about and bawled out in contradiction, annoying my Theo, whom he professed to admire greatly, by declaring every time he saw her, "Madam, you do not love me; I see by your manner you do not love me; though I admire you, and come here for your sake. Here is my friend Mr. Reynolds that shall paint you: he has no ceruse in his paint-box that is as brilliant as your complexion." And so Mr. Reynolds, a most perfect and agreeable gentleman, would have painted my wife; but I knew what his price was and did not choose to incur that expense. I wish I had now, for the sake of the children, that they might see what yonder face was like some fifty years ago. To me, madam, 'tis the same now as ever; and your ladyship is always young!

What annoyed Mrs. Warrington with Dr. Johnson more than his contradictions, sputterings, and dirty nails was, I think, an unfavorable opinion he formed of my new tragedy. Hagan once proposed that he should read some scenes from it after tea.

"Nay, sir, conversation is better," said the Doctor. "I can read for myself, or hear you at the theatre. I had rather hear Mrs. Warrington's artless prattle than your declamation of Mr. Warrington's decasyllables. Tell us about your household affairs, madam, and whether his Excellency your father is well, and whether you made the pudding and the butter sauce. The butter sauce was delicious!" (He loved it so well that he had kept a large quantity in the bosom of a very dingy shirt.) "You made it as though you loved me. You helped me as though you loved me, though you don't."

"Faith, sir, you are taking some of the present away with you in your waistcoat," said Hagan, with much spirit.

"Sir, you are rude!" bawled the Doctor. "You are unacquainted with the first principles of politeness, which is courtesy before ladies. Having received a university education, I am surprised that you have not learned the rudiments of politeness. I respect Mrs. Warrington. I should never think of making personal remarks about her guests before her!"

"Then, sir," said Hagan, fiercely, "why did you speak of my theatre?"

"Sir, you are saucy!" roared the Doctor.

"De te fabula," said the actor. "I think it is your waistcoat that is saucy. Madam, shall I make some punch in the way we make it in Ireland?"

The Doctor, puffing and purple in the face, wiped the dingy shirt with a still more dubious pocket-handkerchief, which he then applied to his forehead. After this exercise, he blew a hyperborean whistle, as if to blow his wrath away. "It is de me, sir—though, as a young man, perhaps you need not have told me so."

"I drop my point, sir! If you have been wrong, I am sure I am bound to ask your pardon for setting you so!" said Mr. Hagan, with a fine bow.

"Doesn't he look like a god?" said Maria, clutching my wife's hand; and indeed Mr. Hagan did look like a handsome young gentleman. His color had risen; he had put his hand to his breast with a noble air; Chamont or Castalio could not present himself better.

"Let me make you some lemonade, sir; my papa has sent us a box of fresh limes. May we send you some to the Temple?"

"Madam, if they stay in your house, they will lose their quality and turn sweet," said the Doctor. "Mr. Hagan, you are a young sauce-box, that's what you are! Ho! ho! It is I have been wrong."

"Oh, my lord, my Polidore!" bleated Lady Maria when she was alone in my wife's drawing-room:

"'Oh, I could hear thee talk for ever thus,
Eternally admiring,—fix and gaze
On those dear eyes, for every glance they send
Darts through my soul, and fills my heart with rapture!'"

"Thou knowest not, my Theo, what a pearl and paragon of a man my Castalio is; my Chamont, my—oh, dear me, child, what a pity it is that in your husband's tragedy he should have to take the horrid name of Captain Smith!"

Upon this tragedy not only my literary hopes, but much of my financial prospects were founded. My brother's debts were to be discharged, my mother's drafts from home duly honored, my own expenses paid, which, though moderate, were not inconsiderable—pretty nearly the whole of my patrimony had been spent, and this auspicious moment I must choose for my marriage! I could raise money on my inheritance; that was not impossible, though certainly costly. My mother could not leave her eldest son without a maintenance, whatever our quarrels might be. I had health, strength, good wits, some friends, and reputation—above all, my famous tragedy, which the manager had promised to perform, and upon the proceeds of this I counted for my present support. What becomes of the arithmetic of youth? How do we then calculate that a hundred pounds is a maintenance and a thousand a fortune? How did I dare play against Fortune with such odds? I succeeded, I remember, in convincing my dear General, and he left home convinced that his son-in-law had for the present necessity at least a score of hundred pounds at his command. He and his dear Molly had begun life with less

The English public, unfamiliar with the true history of Pocahontas, knew her only through the lens of our Virginia affection for that simple, kindly soul. Seizing the opportunity, Mr. Warrington, urged on by his friends, composed a ballad about the Indian princess. Printed in the magazines just prior to the tragedy's premiere, this piece served as "ground-bait," a strategy the enthusiastic parson and Sampson hailed with great enthusiasm. They claimed the poem was already being debated and admired in coffee-houses, with some attributing it to Mr. Mason, Mr. Cowper, or even the renowned Mr. Gray. I suspect poor Sam himself spread these rumors; had Shakespeare been named the author of the tragedy, he would have declared *Pocahontas* among the Bard's finest achievements.

My connection to the story began in childhood, sitting at my grandfather's knee in his library, tracing the exploits of Captain Smith with my finger. I loved the tales of his travels, sufferings, and escapes across both America and Europe. The old man would paint vivid pictures for me: Smith battling Turks on the Danube, or being led by savages to his death. I particularly delighted in the account of his combat with Bonny Molgro, the last and most dreadful of the three Turkish champions. With his prodigious turban, scimitar, and whiskers, the Turk seemed a figure of terror. According to my favorite volume, after slaying his first two foes, Smith faced Bonny Molgro. Their battle-axes clashed with such force that neither rider could keep his seat, yet Smith, displaying great judgment and dexterity, pierced the Turk under the cutlets, through back and body. Though the Turk dismounted, he fell swiftly, losing his head as the others had. In reward, Duke Segismundus granted Smith a shield bearing three Turkish heads and a pension of three hundred ducats annually.

In my tragedy, I dared to transport these exploits to the banks of the Potomac and James River, disregarding time and place—a liberty poets alone possess. The "ground-bait" verses I wrote ran thus:

Wearied arm and broken sword
Wage in vain the desperate fight;
Round him press the countless horde,
He is but a single knight.
Hark! a cry of triumph shrill
Through the wilderness resounds,
As, with twenty bleeding wounds,
Sinks the warrior, fighting still.

Now they heap the fatal pyre,
And the torch of death they light;
Ah! 'tis hard to die of fire!
Who will shield the captive knight?
Round the stake with fiendish cry
Wheel and dance the savage crowd,
Cold the victim's mien and proud,
And his breast is bared to die.

Who will shield the fearless heart?
Who avert the murderous blade?
From the throng, with sudden start,
See, there springs an Indian maid.
Quick she stands before the knight,
'Loose the chain, unbind the ring,
I am daughter of the king,
And I claim the Indian right!'

Dauntlessly aside she flings
Lifted axe and thirsty knife;
Fondly to his heart she clings,
And her bosom guards his life!
In the woods of Powhattan,
Still 'tis told, by Indian fires,
How a daughter of their sires
Saved the captive Englishman."

I need not detail the full plot of my tragedy, for my children could peruse it at any time from the shelves. Nor shall I rush to read it again to my young folks, recalling how Captain Miles and the parson fell asleep last Christmas during a reading of two acts at my mother's request. However, anyone with a moderate acquaintance with plays and novels could easily construct a picture from the sketch above. The elements included an Indian king, a loving princess, her attendant enamored of the British captain's servant, a traitor within the English fort, a brave Indian warrior harboring an unhappy passion for Pocahontas, and a medicine-man and priest capable of every treason and crime, bent on the torture and death of the English prisoner. These characters, combined with the accidents of the wilderness, war-dances mimicked by Gumbo, and references to recent victories in Canada, seemed promising.

Yet, ill omens preceded the day. Peevish, jealous, and timid management threw obstacles in the piece's path, and violent prejudice existed in certain high quarters. Was it surprising, then, that *Pocahontas* failed to be a victory? I laughed at the malignity of critics who faulted the performance, calling Carpezan a masterpiece while sneering at my superior work. I insisted that Hagan acted so admirably that a certain actor-manager might well have been jealous, and that but for the cabal outside, the piece would have succeeded. Sampson declared the order had been given for failure. "The house swarmed with Macs, by George," the honest fellow swore, vowing that Mr. Garrick himself would not have allowed the piece to succeed. He was particularly enraged during the grand scene in the second act, where Smith, bound to the stake, was saved by Pocahontas, causing the entire house to thrill with applause and sympathy.

Those curious enough may refer to the published tragedy in the octavo or the subsequent quarto edition of my Collected Works. Can they say the scene lacks merit, or that the verses are not elegant, rich, and noble? One cause of failure was my fidelity to history. I had copied a figure of Sir Walter Raleigh from the Museum, complete with frill and beard, and with Theo providing some of her mother's finest lace for the ruff, we dressed Hagan accurately. No man could look better. Similarly, I dressed Miss Pritchard as a Red Indian, having seen enough of that costume in my own experience. Would it be believed that the house tittered when she first appeared? They eventually grew accustomed to her, but just as she rushed into the prisoner's arms, a fellow in the pit bawled, "Bedad! here's the Belle Savage kissing the Saracen's Head!" An impertinent roar of laughter erupted, breaking out in fitful explosions throughout the performance.

As the wag in Mr. Sheridan's *Critic* noted regarding morning guns, playwrights were not content with one joke but must fire two or three. Thus, this wretched pothouse joke of the Belle Savage struck—ignorant audiences unaware that Pocahontas herself was the very Belle Sauvage from whom the tavern took its name. My friend in the pit repeated it ad nauseam, saluting each new character with a tavern name: the English governor became the Goat and Boots, his lieutenant Barker the Bull and Mouth. The curtain descended amidst a shrill storm of whistles and hisses, especially assailing poor Hagan. Sampson spotted Master Will in the green boxes with pretty acquaintances, convinced he was a ringleader in the conspiracy. "I would have flung him over into the pit," the faithful fellow said, though he was forced to sheer off due to Mr. Nadab's followers prowling the lobby. Our hoped-for profits were broken, our poor hopes shattered.

Before the curtain rose, I looked in from the stage and saw the house fairly filled, notably Mr. Johnson in the front boxes with Mr. Reynolds, the latter unable to hear and the former unable to see, forming a duo to judge my tragedy. I spotted Lady Maria in the lower gallery, once more watching her beloved actor perform a principal role. As for Theo, she frankly admitted she preferred not to attend unless ordered, and I, knowing that witnessing her suffering would be intolerable pain, acquiesced to her desire to stay away.

Of a pretty equanimous disposition, I took a light dinner at the Bedford and arrived at the theatre shortly before the play began, intending to remain until victory or defeat was decided. I could not help sensing the gloomy, disastrous aspect of everything around. Miss Pritchard suffered from a headache; the barber who brought Hagan's wig had powdered it like a wretch; among the gentlemen and ladies in the greenroom, I saw only doubtful faces. The manager, a flippant and impertinent gentleman who looked as dismal as a mute at a funeral, insolently suggested, "For Heaven's sake, Mr. Warrington, go and get a glass of punch at the Bedford, and don't frighten us all here by your dismal countenance!"

"Sir," I replied, "I have a right, for five shillings, to comment upon your face, but I never gave you authority to make remarks upon mine." He retorted in a pet, "Sir, I most heartily wish I had never seen your face at all!" "Yours, sir!" I said, "has often amused me greatly; and when painted for Abel Drugger is exceedingly comic"—indeed, I have always thought Mr. G. unrivalled in low comedy. I bowed and walked off to the coffee-house, never speaking to the gentleman again for five years until he apologized at a nobleman's house. I feigned forgetfulness, noting that on a play's first night, both author and manager are flurried alike, adding, "After all, there is no shame in not being made for the theatre. Mr. Garrick—you were." He appeared pleased with the compliment.

Fidus Achates ran to me at the end of the first act to report things going pretty well, though he confessed to the titter upon Miss Pritchard's first appearance in her Indian princess attire. "I cannot help it, Sampson," I said, filling him a bumper of punch, "if Indians are dressed so." "Why," he asked, "would you have had Caractacus painted blue like an ancient Briton, or Bonduca with nothing but a cow-skin?" Indeed, fidelity to history may have caused the ridicule, in which case I am not ashamed of the defeat.

After the second act, my aide-de-camp returned with dismal news. Nervous before action, I became surprisingly cool and cheerful in disaster. "Are things going ill?" I asked. I called for my reckoning, put on my hat, and marched to the theatre as calmly as if dining at the Temple, with Fidus Achates pressing my elbow, kicking link-boys aside, and crying, "By George, Mr. Warrington, you are a man of spirit—a Trojan, sir!" So there were men of spirit in Troy, but alas, fate was too strong for them.

No man can say I did not bear my misfortune with calmness; I could no more help the audience's clamor than a captain can help a ship's howling storm. Yet I was determined that the rushing waves and broken masts should impavidum ferient. Sampson told my wife, "Not Regulus, my dear madam, could step into his barrel more coolly." It is unjust to say men of parasitic nature are unfaithful in misfortune; whether prosperous or poor, the wild parson remained equally true and friendly, sharing our crust as eagerly as our better fortune.

Taking my place on the stage, I watched the actors of my poor piece and the portion of the audience condemning me. The performers likely gave me a wide berth out of pity. I felt as little moved as any spectator; no one would judge from my mien that I was the unlucky hero of the night.

But my dearest Theo, when I returned home, looked so pale and white that I knew the knowledge of my disaster had preceded my arrival. Spencer, Sampson, cousin Hagan, and Lady Maria were to come after the play to congratulate the author, God wot! Poor Miss Pritchard was engaged but sent word she was too unwell to sup that night. My friend, the gardener of Bedford House, had given my wife his best flowers to decorate her little table. There they were—the poor little painted standards—and the battle lost! I had borne the defeat well enough, but as I looked at the sweet pale face of my wife across the table and those artless trophies of welcome she had set up for her hero, my courage gave way, and my heart felt a pang almost as keen as any that ever smitten it.

Our meal was dismal, rendered no gayer by our strained conversation. Fortunately, Old Mrs. Hagan was very ill, a blessing in disguise. We discussed his Majesty's approaching marriage, remembering futile incidents of the day, including a tune a carpenter whistled by my side just before the dreary curtain fell. We talked of the death of good Mr. Richardson, author of *Pamela* and *Clarissa*, whose works we all admired. As we spoke of *Clarissa*, my wife wiped her eyes, saying faintly, "You know, my love, mamma and I could never help crying over that dear book. Oh, my dearest, dearest mother, how I wish she could be with me now!" This occasioned open tears, for a young lady may naturally weep for her absent mother. We mixed a gloomy bowl with Jamaica limes and toasted his Excellency the Governor. Then, for a second toast, I filled a bumper, smiling, and drank to "our better fortune!"

This was too much. The two women flung themselves into each other's arms, irrigating each other's neck-handkerchiefs with tears. "Oh, Maria! Is not—is not my George good and kind?" sobbed Theo. "Look at my Hagan—how great, how godlike he was in his part!" gasped Maria. "It was a beastly cabal which threw him over—and I could plunge this knife into Mr. Garrick's black heart—the odious little wretch!" Grasping a weapon at her side, she threw it down and rushed to her lord and master, flinging her arms around him and embracing him in the presence of the little company.

I am not sure if someone else did likewise. We were all in a state of extreme excitement and enthusiasm. In the midst of grief, Love the consoler appeared, soothing us with fond blandishments and tender caresses until one scarcely wished the calamity away. Two or three days later, on our birthday, a letter brought to my study contained these lines:

Returning from the cruel fight
How pale and faint appears my knight!
He sees me anxious at his side

I have already confessed my feelings as an elderly man regarding that rash leap into matrimony, which I persuaded my dear partner to take when we were both barely out of our teens. As a husband and father—with a proper sense of the necessity for mutton chops and the baker's bill, surrounded by a pack of impudent children who might run off to Scotland tomorrow citing our own example—I know I ought to sit in my easy chair, wear a demure air, and offer myself as a warning to imprudent youth.

Yet, truth be told, the married life my relatives prophesied so gloomily has disappointed them. It has had its trials, but I recall them without bitterness; its passionate griefs, which time, by God's ordinance, has soothed; its days of poverty, which we endured to the wonder of our sympathizing kin; and its precious rewards, so great I scarce dare whisper them to this page, save with awful respect to the One Ear to which all men offer their prayers. To marry without a competence is wrong, a crime against social codes; but do not thousands commit this crime yearly trusting only in Heaven, health, and labor? Are young people not to take hope into account, nor begin housekeeping until the cellar is stocked and the strong-box full? The world would stop multiplying if the laws regulating the genteel were made universal. Our gentlefolk tremble in silk stockings waiting for a bridge; the poor do not fear to wet their bare feet in the brook and trust to fate. Who would consign his daughter to poverty? Who would counsel his son to remove the beloved girl from comfort and subject her to debt and misery? I look at my own wife and ask pardon for imposing such a task upon one so gentle. I think of the trials she endured and am thankful for the unfailing love and constancy with which God blessed her. On this question, I am no fair judge: my own marriage was so imprudent and yet so happy that I dare not counsel the young. I have endured poverty, but found it tolerable; had I not, I could never have known the kindness of friends, the delight of gratitude, or the joys accompanying a scanty meal. Much superfluous pity is thrown upon the decent poor. Good-natured fine folks, stepping from sunshine into narrow obscurity, were blinded while we saw cheerfully; they stumbled over obstacles none to us, surprised at our resignation in drinking small beer and saying grace over cold mutton.

My father-in-law, the good General, married his Molly when a subaltern with a purse scarce better than my own. They had their ups and downs. I think, though my wife will never confess it, they married without asking parents' leave. At all events, so pleased were they with their luck that they did not grudge their children's hardships. When I made my pecuniary statements to Mr. Lambert, I was anxious to deceive both of us. Believing me master of two thousand pounds, he went to Jamaica easy in mind regarding his daughter's comfort. After outfitting the family, the worthy man went away not much richer than his son-in-law; a few trinkets, some lace from Aunt Lambert, and twenty new guineas in a purse made by her mother and sisters were Theo's portion. But in valuing my stock, I counted as a good debt a sum my honoured mother never acknowledged until her death. She argued my disbursements were for the estate meant for me, while money she could spare was for my poor brother, who had nothing. The good lady emphasized in many letters that he would have been sole heir but for a half-hour's accident of birth. Now he distinguishes himself in the service of his king. To purchase his promotion was, she supposed, his brother's duty. When I finished my bar-studies and dramatic amusements, Madam Esmond informed me I was welcome to return home to the place my birth entitled me. She communicated this more than once through Mountain, before news of my marriage reached her.

There is no need to recall her expressions of maternal indignation when informed of my step. On the pacification of Canada, my dear Harry asked leave and visited Virginia. He wrote describing his reception and the splendid entertainments my mother made in his honor. Castlewood, uninhabited since our departure for Europe, was thrown open to colonial friends; the friend of Wolfe and soldier of Quebec was received with becoming honor. Some dismal quarrels ensued because Harry persisted in maintaining his friendship with Colonel Washington of Mount Vernon, whose praises Harry never tired of singing. Indeed, I allow the gentleman every virtue; in the struggles terminating fatally for England a few years since, I can admire as well as his warmest friends General Washington's glorious constancy.

If these battles between Harry and our mother were frequent, as his letters described, I wondered why he continued at home. One reason suggested itself, which I scarcely liked to communicate to Mrs. Warrington; for we had both talked over our dear little Hetty's romantic attachment for my brother, wondering he had never discovered it. I need not say my gentleman found some young lady at home more to his taste than our dear Hester, accounting for his prolonged stay.

Presently came a letter from him, not a full confession but an admission of this fact. A person was described, unnamed—a Being all beauty and perfection. My wife asked to see the letter; I showed it with a very sad face. To my surprise, she read it without exhibiting corresponding sorrow.

"I have thought of this before, my love," I said. "I feel with you for your disappointment regarding poor Hetty."

"Ah! poor Hetty," says Theo, looking down at the carpet.

"It would never have done," says I.

"No—they would not have been happy," sighs Theo.

"How strange he never should have found out her secret!" I continued.

She looked me full in the face with an odd expression. "Pray, what does that look mean?" I asked.

"Nothing, my dear—nothing! only I am not surprised!" says Theo, blushing.

"What," I ask, "can there be another?"

"I am sure I never said so, George," says the lady, hurriedly. "But if Hetty has overcome her childish folly, ought we not all to be glad? Do you gentlemen suppose that you only are to fall in love and grow tired, indeed?"

"What!" I say, with a strange commotion of my mind. "Do you mean to tell me, Theo, that you ever cared for any one but me?"

"Oh, George," she whimpers, "when I was at school, there was—one of the boys of Doctor Backhouse's school, who sate in the loft next to us; and I thought he had lovely eyes, and I was so shocked when I recognised him behind the counter at Mr. Grigg's the mercer's, when I went to buy a cloak for baby, and I wanted to tell you, my dear, and I didn't know how!"

I went to see this creature with the lovely eyes, having made my wife describe the fellow's dress. I saw a little bandy-legged wretch in a blue camlet coat, with red hair tied with a dirty ribbon, about whom I forbore generously even to reproach my wife; nor will she ever know that I have looked at the fellow, until she reads the confession in this page. If our wives saw us as we are, I thought, would they love us as they do? Are we as much mistaken in them as they in us? I look into one candid face at least, and think it never has deceived me.

Lest I should encourage my young people to an imitation of my own imprudence, I will not tell them with how small a capital Mrs. Theo and I commenced life. The unfortunate tragedy brought us nothing; though reviewers, since its publication of late, have spoken not unfavourably of its merits, and Mr. Kemble himself has done me the honour to commend it. Our kind friend Lord Wrotham was for having the piece published by subscription, sending me a bank-note requesting a hundred copies for his friends; but I was always averse to that method of levying money, preferring my poverty sine dote, and locked up my manuscript with my poor girl's verses inserted at the first page. I know not why the piece should have given offence at court, except that an actor who had run off with an earl's daughter performed a principal part; but I was told that sentiments I put into the mouths of some Indian characters, declaiming against ambition and British desire of rule, were pronounced dangerous and unconstitutional, taking away my little hope of royal favour.

What was to be done? A few months after the failure of the tragedy, counting up the remains of my fortune, I concluded I must beat a retreat from my pretty apartments in Bloomsbury, giving warning to our good landlady that my wife's health required lodgings in the country. But we went no farther than Lambeth, our faithful Gumbo and Molly following us; and here, though as poor as might be, we were waited on by a maid and a lackey in livery, like folks of condition. Kind relatives cried out against our extravagance; indeed, are they not the people who find our faults out and proclaim them to the world?

Returning home from London, whither I had visited some booksellers, I recognised the family arms and livery on a grand gilt chariot before a public-house near our lodgings. Loitering inhabitants gathered round, looking with awe at the footmen, resplendent in the sun, quaffing blazing pots of beer. I found my Lady Castlewood seated opposite my wife in our little apartment, whence we had a bright prospect of the river covered with barges, and the ancient towers and trees of the Archbishop's palace. Mrs. Theo, with a droll way of describing persons, narrated the particulars of her ladyship's conversation.

"I have been here this ever-so-long," says the Countess, "gossiping with cousin Theo, while you have been away at the coffee-house, I dare say, making merry with your friends. Guess she must find it rather lonely here, with nothing to do but work them little caps and hem them frocks. Never mind, dear; reckon you'll soon have a companion who will amuse you when cousin George is away! What a nice lodging you have got here! Our new house is twenty times as big, covered with gold from top to bottom; but I like this quite as well. Bless you, being rich is no better than being poor. When we lived to Albany, and I did most all the work myself, scoured the rooms, boiled the kettle, helped the wash, and all, I was just as happy as I am now.
