We only had one old negro to keep the store. Why don't you sell Gumbo, cousin George? He ain't no use here idling and dawdling about, and making love to the servant-girl. Fogh! guess they ain't particular, these English people!" So she talked, rattling on with perfect good-humour, until her hour for departure came; when she produced a fine repeating watch and said it was time to pay a call upon her Majesty at Buckingham House. "And mind you come to us, George," says her ladyship, waving a little parting hand out of the gilt coach. "Theo and I have settled all about it."

"Here, at least," said I, when the laced footmen had clambered up behind the carriage and our magnificent little patroness had left us—"here is one who is not afraid of our poverty, nor ashamed to remember her own."

"Ashamed!" said Theo, resuming her lilliputian needlework. "To do her justice, she would make herself at home in any kitchen or palace in the world. She has given me and Molly twenty lessons in housekeeping. She says, when she was at home to Albany, she roasted, baked, swept the house, and milked the cow." (Madam Theo pronounced the word cow archly in our American way, imitating her ladyship's accent very divertingly.)

"And she has no pride," I added. "It was good-natured of her to ask us to dine with her and my lord. When will Uncle Warrington ever think of offering us a crust again, or a glass of his famous beer?"

"Yes, it was not ill-natured to invite us," says Theo, slily. "But, my dear, you don't know all the conditions!" Then my wife, still imitating the Countess's manner, laughingly informed me. "She took out her pocket-book and told me," says Theo, "what days she was engaged abroad and at home. On Monday she received a Duke and a Duchess, with several members of my lord's house. On Tuesday came more earls, two bishops, and an ambassador. 'Of course you won't come on them days?' says the Countess. 'Now you are so poor, you know, that fine company ain't no good for you. Lord bless you! father never dines on our company days! he don't like it; he takes a bit of cold meat anyways.' On which," says Theo, laughing, "I told her that Mr. Warrington did not care for any but the best of company, and proposed that she should ask us on some day when the Archbishop of Canterbury dined with her, and his Grace must give us a lift home in his coach to Lambeth. And she is an economical little person, too," continues Theo. "'I thought of bringing with me some of my baby's caps and things, which his lordship has outgrown, but they may be wanted again, you know, my dear.' And so we lose that addition to our wardrobe," says Theo, smiling, "and Molly and I must do our best without her ladyship's charity. 'When people are poor, they are poor,' the Countess said, with her usual outspokenness, 'and must get on the best they can. What we shall do for that poor Maria, goodness only knows! we can't ask her to see us as we can you, though you are so poor: but an earl's daughter to marry a play-actor! La, my dear, it's dreadful: his Majesty and the Princess have both spoken of it! Every other noble family in this kingdom as has ever heard of it pities us; though I have a plan for helping those poor unhappy people, and have

Little Miles entered this world mere days after the birth of the gracious Prince who now commands the regiment. Great illuminations and thunderous cannonades celebrated the arrival of the Royal George, drawing multitudes to gaze upon him behind the gilt railings of the Palace, tended by noble nurses. In stark contrast, few guards stood watch over the cradle of our own small prince. No courtiers, no faithful retainers offered their salutations, save for our trusty Gumbo and kind Molly, who loved and admired the heir of my poverty with a loyalty that warmed my heart. Why was our boy not named George, like the paragon above and like his father? Instead, I chose the name of a little scapegrace from my own family—a name borne by many generations of Warringtons. Yet, my poor little Miles's love and kindness touched me at a time when affection from my own blood was scarce. Thus, Theo and I agreed that our child should bear the name of that single, bright friend of my paternal race.

We penned letters to inform our royal parents of the auspicious event and boldly announced the birth in the *Daily Advertiser*, specifying our humble abode at Church Street, Lambeth. "My dear," Aunt Bernstein replied in her letter, "how could you point out to all the world that you live in such a trou as that in which you have buried yourself? I kiss the little mamma, and send a remembrance for the child." This remembrance was a fine silk coverlet edged with lace fit for a prince. It was hardly practical; the cost of the lace alone would have served us far better. Yet, Theo and Molly were delighted, and my eldest son's cradle was draped in finery equal to any nobleman's.

Good Dr. Heberden visited my wife several times to ensure all went well, recommending a local surgeon who took charge of her recovery. Luckily, my dear patient required little care beyond what our landlady and her attendant could provide. Soon, our humble precinct was once again adorned with the gilded wheels of Lady Castlewood's chariot. She arrived bearing a pot of jelly, which she believed Theo might enjoy, no doubt having been served at one of her ladyship's banquets the day prior. She regaled us with tales of court ceremonies and the splendor surrounding the birth of the august heir.

Our good Mr. Johnson happened to drop by on one of those days when the Countess's carriage blazed up to our gate. He was struck by her magnificence and offered her bows that were more respectful than graceful. She addressed me as "cousin" with affable warmth and helped transfer her gift of jelly from her silver dish to our crockery pan with benign grace. The Doctor tasted the sweetmeat and pronounced it excellent. "The great, sir," he remarked, "are fortunate in every way. They can engage the most skilful practitioners of the culinary art, as they can assemble the most amiable wits round their table. If, as you suggest, this sweetmeat has already graced his lordship's table, it has done so in good company. It has quivered before celebrated beauties, been tasted by ruby lips, and shared the attention of distinguished company alongside fruits, tarts, and creams, which I make no doubt were equally delicious." As he spoke, the good Doctor consumed a considerable portion of Lady Castlewood's benefaction. Though regarding the epithet "delicious," I must confess that my poor wife, after tasting the jelly, set it aside with distaste, and Molly, throwing up her head, declared it was mouldy.

My boy, however, enjoyed the privilege of having an earl's daughter for his godmother. This honor was performed by his cousin, our poor Lady Maria, whose kindness and attention to both mother and infant were beyond praise. Having lost her own solitary chance for maternal happiness, she yearned over our child in a manner deeply touching to behold. Captain Miles is a mighty fine gentleman, and his uniforms of the Prince's Hussars are as splendid as any that ever bedizened a soldier of fashion; yet he possesses a heart too good, and a nature too truly gentlemanly, to begrudge remembering that his own infant limbs were once dressed in garments prepared for the poor player's child. Sampson christened him in the very chapel in Southwark where our marriage ceremony had taken place. Never were the words of the Prayer-book read more beautifully or impressively than by the celebrant, until the end, when his voice failed him, and he and the small congregation were fain to wipe their eyes. "Mr. Garrick himself, sir," said Hagan, "could not have read those words so nobly. I am sure little innocent never entered the world accompanied by wishes and benedictions more tender and sincere."

Now, I must explain how the Captain came by the name of Miles. A couple of days before the christening, when it was still intended that our firstborn should bear his father's name, a light patter of horse's hoofs galloped up to our gate. Who should pull at the bell but young Miles, our cousin? I fear he had disobeyed his parents on that undutiful journey.

"You know," he said breathlessly, "cousin Harry gave me my little horse; and I can't help liking you, because you are so like Harry, and because they're always saying things of you at home, and it's a shame. I have brought my whistle and coral that my godmamma Lady Suckling gave me for your little boy. And if you're so poor, cousin George, here's my gold moidore. It's worth ever so much, and it's no use to me, because I mayn't spend it, you know."

We lifted the boy up to Theo in her room (he mounted the stairs in his little tramping boots, of which he was very proud). Theo kissed him and thanked him, and that moidore has remained in her purse from that day to this.

My mother, writing through her ambassador as usual, informed me of her royal surprise and displeasure upon learning that my son had been christened Miles—a name unknown, at least in the Esmond family. I did not care to tell the reason at the time. But when, in after years, I recounted to Madam Esmond how my boy came by his name, I saw a tear roll down her wrinkled cheek. I heard afterwards that she had asked Gumbo many questions about the boy who gave his name to our Miles—our Miles Gloriosus of Pall Mall, Valenciennes, Almack's, and Brighton.

In the earliest days of our exile, when Harry and I were so undutiful to our tutor, who would have imagined that Mr. Esmond Warrington of Virginia would one day become a "Bearleader" himself? My mother, when we reunited, could never bring herself to speak directly of this period; she would only allude to it as "that terrible time, my love, which I can't bear to think of," or "those dreadful years when there was difference between us." Though my pupil, a worthy and grateful man, sent me out to Jamestown several barrels of the liquor by which his great fortune was made, Madam Esmond spoke of him merely as "your friend in England" or "your wealthy Lambeth friend," never by his name, nor did she ever taste a drop of his beer. We brewed our own at Warrington Manor, yet our good Mr. Foker never failed to ship to Ipswich annually a couple of butts of his entire. His son was a young sprig of fashion, married to an earl's daughter; the father was a very worthy and kind gentleman, and it was the luck of making his acquaintance that I owed the receipt of some of the most welcome guineas I ever received in my life.

It was not so much the sum, as the occupation and hope given me by the office of Governor—which I took on myself—that were so precious to me. Mr. F.'s Brewery, the site of which has since changed, then stood near Pedlar's Acre in Lambeth. The surgeon who attended my wife in her confinement likewise took care of the wealthy brewer's family. He was a Bavarian, originally named Voelker. Mr. Lance, the surgeon, I suppose, made him acquainted with my name and history. The worthy doctor would smoke many a pipe of Virginia in my garden and had conceived a deep attachment for me and my family. He brought his patron to my house; and when Mr. F. found that I had a smattering of his language and could sing "Prinz Eugen the noble Ritter"—a song my grandfather had brought home from the Marlborough wars—the German conceived a great friendship for me. His lady put her chair and her chariot at Mrs. Warrington's service; his little daughter took a prodigious fancy to our baby (and to do him justice, the Captain, who is as ugly a fellow now as ever wore a queue, was beautiful as an infant, the very image of the Squire at thirty, everybody says so). His son and heir, Master Foker, being much maltreated at Westminster School because of his father's profession of brewer, the parents asked if I would take charge of him, paying me a not insufficient sum for superintending his education.

Mr. F. was a shrewd man of business, and as he and his family really interested themselves in me and mine, I laid all my pecuniary affairs pretty unreservedly before him. My statement, he was pleased to say, augmented the respect and regard which he felt for me. He laughed at our stories of the aid which my noble relatives had given me—my aunt's coverlid, my Lady Castlewood's mouldy jelly, Lady Warrington's contemptuous treatment of us. But he wept many tears over the story of little Miles's moidore; and as for Sampson and Hagan, "I wow," says he, "dey shall have so much beer als ever dey can drink." He sent his wife to call upon Lady Maria and treated her with the utmost respect and obsequiousness whenever she came to visit him. It was with Mr. Foker that Lady Maria stayed when Hagan went to Dublin to complete his college terms; and the good brewer's purse also ministered to our friend's wants and supplied his outfit.

When Mr. Foker came fully to know my own affairs and position, he was pleased to speak of me with terms of enthusiasm, as if my conduct showed some extraordinary virtue. I have said how my mother saved money for Harry, and how the two were in my debt. But when Harry spent money, he spent it fancying it to be his; Madam Esmond never could be made to understand she was dealing hardly with me—the money was paid and gone, and there was an end of it. Now, at the end of '62, I remember Harry sent over a considerable remittance for the purchase of his promotion, begging me at the same time to remember that he was in my debt and to draw on his agents if I had any need. He did not know how great the need was, or how my little capital had been swallowed.

Well, to take my brother's money would delay his promotion, and I naturally did not draw on him, though I own I was tempted; nor, knowing my dear General Lambert's small means, did I care to impoverish him by asking for supplies. These simple acts of forbearance my worthy brewer must choose to consider as instances of exalted virtue. And what does my gentleman do but write privately to my brother in America, lauding me and my wife as the most admirable of human beings, and call upon Madame de Bernstein—who never told me of his visit indeed, but who, I perceived, about this time treated us with singular respect and gentleness, surprising me in one whom I could not but consider as selfish and worldly. In after days I remember asking him how he had gained admission to the Baroness. He laughed: "De Baroness!" says he. "I knew de Baron when he was a walet at Munich, and I was a brewer-apprentice." I think our family had best not be too curious about our uncle the Baron.

Thus, the part of my life which ought to have been most melancholy was in truth made pleasant by many friends, happy circumstances, and strokes of lucky fortune. The bear I led was a docile little cub, and danced to my piping very readily. Better to lead him about than to hang round booksellers' doors or wait the pleasure or caprice of managers! My wife and I, during our exile, as we may call it, spent very many pleasant evenings with these kind friends and benefactors. Nor were we without intellectual enjoyments; Mrs. Foker and Mrs. Warrington sang finely together, and sometimes when I was in the mood, I read my own play of Pocahontas to this friendly audience in a manner better than Hagan's own, Mr. Foker was pleased to say.

After that little escapade of Miles Warrington, junior, I saw nothing of him and heard of my paternal relatives but rarely. Sir Miles was assiduous at court (as I believe he would have been at Nero's), and I laughed one day when Mr. Foker told me that he had heard on 'Change "that they were going to make my uncle a Beer." "A Beer?" says I in wonder. "Can't you understand de vort, ven I say it?" says the testy old gentleman. "Vell, veil, a Lort!" Sir Miles indeed was the obedient humble servant of the Minister, whoever he might be. I am surprised he did not speak English with a Scotch accent during the first favourite's brief reign. I saw him and his wife coming from court when Mrs. Claypool was presented to her Majesty on her marriage. I had my little boy on my shoulder. My uncle and aunt stared resolutely at me from their gilt coach window. The footmen looked blank over their nosegays. Had I worn the Fairy's cap and been invisible, my father's brother could not have passed me with less notice.

We did not avail ourselves much, or often, of that queer invitation of Lady Castlewood to go and drink tea and sup with her ladyship when there was no other company. Old Van den Bosch, however shrewd his intellect and great his skill in making a fortune, was not amusing in conversation except to his daughter, who talked household and City matters, bulling and bearing, raising and selling farming-stock, quite as keenly and shrewdly as her father. Nor was my Lord Castlewood often at home, or much missed by his wife when absent, or very much at ease in the old father's company. The Countess told all this to my wife in her simple way. "Guess," says she, "my lord and father don't pull well together nohow. Guess my lord is always wanting money, and father keeps the key of the box and quite right, too. If he could have the fingering of all our money, my lord would soon make away with it, and then what's to become of our noble family? We pay everything, my dear (except play-debts, and them we won't have nohow). We pay cooks, horses, wine-merchants, tailors, and everybody—and lucky for them too—reckon my lord wouldn't pay 'em! And we always take care that he has a guinea in his pocket and goes out like a real nobleman. What that man do owe to us: what he did before we come—gracious goodness only knows! Me and father does our best to make him respectable: but it's no easy job, my dear. Law! he'd melt the plate, only father keeps the key of the strong-room; and when we go to Castlewood, my father travels with me, and papa is armed too, as well as the people."

"Gracious heavens!" cries my wife, "your ladyship does not mean to say you suspect your own husband of a desire to----"

"To what?—Oh no, nothing, of course! And I would trust our brother Will with untold money, wouldn't I? As much as I'd trust the cat with the cream-pan! I tell you, my dear, it's not all pleasure being a woman of rank and fashion: and if I have bought a countess's coronet, I have paid a good price for it—that I have!"

And so had my Lord Castlewood paid a large price for having his estate freed from incumbrances, his houses and stables furnished, and his debts discharged. He was the slave of the little wife and her father. No wonder the old man's society was not pleasant to the poor victim, and that he gladly slunk away from his own fine house to feast at the club when he had money, or at least to any society save that which he found at home. To lead a bear, as I did, was no very pleasant business, to be sure: to wait in a bookseller's anteroom until it should please his honour to finish his dinner and give me audience was sometimes a hard task for a man of my name and with my pride; but would I have exchanged my poverty against Castlewood's ignominy, or preferred his miserable dependence to my own? At least I earned my wage, such as it was; and no man can say that I ever flattered my patrons, or was servile to them; or indeed, in my dealings with them, was otherwise than sulky, overbearing, and, in a word, intolerable.

Now there was a certain person with whom Fate had thrown me into a life-partnership, who bore her poverty with such a smiling sweetness and easy grace that niggard Fortune relented before her, and, like some savage Ogre in the fairy tales, melted at the constant goodness and cheerfulness of that uncomplaining, artless, innocent creature. However poor she was, all who knew her saw that here was a fine lady; and the little tradesmen and humble folks round about us treated her with as much respect as the richest of our neighbours. "I think, my dear," says good-natured Mrs. Foker, when they rode out in the latter's chariot, "you look like the mistress of the carriage, and I only as your maid." Our landladies adored her; the tradesfolk executed her little orders as eagerly as if a duchess gave them, or they were to make a fortune by waiting on her. I have thought often of the lady in Comus, and how, through all the rout and rabble, she moves, entirely serene and pure.

Several times, as often as we chose indeed, the good-natured parents of my young bear lent us their chariot to drive abroad or to call on the few friends we had. If I must tell the truth, we drove once to the Protestant Hero and had a syllabub in the garden there: and the hostess would insist upon calling my wife her ladyship during the whole afternoon. We also visited Mr. Johnson and took tea with him (the ingenious Mr. Goldsmith was of the company); the Doctor waited upon my wife to her coach. But our most frequent visits were to Aunt Bernstein, and I promise you I was not at all jealous because my aunt presently professed to have a wonderful liking for Theo.

This liking grew so that she would have her most days in the week, or to stay altogether with her, and thought that Theo's child and husband were only plagues to be sure, and hated us in the most amusing way for keeping her favourite from her. Not that my wife was unworthy of anybody's favour; but her many forced absences and the constant difficulty of intercourse with her raised my aunt's liking for a while to a sort of passion. She poured in notes like love-letters; and her people were ever about our kitchen. If my wife did not go to her, she wrote heartrending appeals and scolded me severely when I saw her; and, the child being ill once (it hath pleased Fate to spare our Captain to be a prodigious trouble to us, and a wholesome trial for our tempers), Madame Bernstein came three days running to Lambeth, vowing there was nothing the matter with the baby—nothing at all—and that we only pretended his illness in order to vex her.

The reigning Countess of Castlewood was just as easy and affable with her old aunt as with other folks great and small. "What air you all about, scraping and bowing to that old woman, I can't tell, noways!" her ladyship would say. "She a fine lady! Nonsense! She ain't no more fine than any other lady: and I guess I'm as good as any of 'em with their high heels and their grand airs! She a beauty once! Take away her wig, and her rouge, and her teeth; and what becomes of your beauty, I'd like to know? Guess you'd put it all in a bandbox, and there

The era of my destitution had finally ended. The death of my young charge had irrevocably altered my financial standing, transforming me from a pauper into the presumptive heir to a substantial estate. With my uncle and aunt unlikely to produce further offspring, the path to wealth seemed clear. Yet, the transition was not without its emotional turbulence. My aunt, Lady Warrington, had been shattered by the loss, her grief so profound that her spiritual advisors interpreted it as a divine chastisement for her former worldly ambitions. They reminded her that while her son sought earthly coronets, she was now assured of a heavenly crown. This tragedy rippled through the religious circles of the time, with sermons preached in chapels dedicated to the sudden shift from vanity to piety.

Despite her sorrow, Lady Warrington eventually reached out to me. A year after the accident, during a visit to London, she summoned me for a lesson on my conduct. She viewed my inheritance not merely as a windfall but as a moral imperative to reform my life. She pleaded with me to sever ties with my disreputable associates, abandon the theatre, and embrace the quiet, sacred duties I had neglected. Her speech was a torrent of scripture, a didactic homily that I found exhausting. Upon my departure, she gifted me a packet of sermons for my wife and a hymnal by Miss Dora, a woman who would later become a prominent figure in that fervent society before marrying the celebrated preacher Mr. Juffles.

In the aftermath, the family dynamic shifted. While my aunt struggled to bear the sight of our lost child, my uncle, a man of obsequious loyalty to the government, poured his attention onto our surviving son, Miles. He brought endless toys and sweets, begging the boy to call him "Godpapa." It was a strange tableau: the grieving mother, the doting uncle, and the innocent child who seemed to forget his sorrow in the delight of new clothes and fresh air. His innocent chatter, however, struck a deeper wound in my wife's heart. We returned to our lodgings in Bloomsbury, where Miles was enrolled at the Chartreux School. There, under the care of his friend Charley, he thrived, avoiding the beatings he had suffered elsewhere and excelling under a competent tutor.

With my uncle's influence secured, I was gazetted as one of His Majesty's Commissioners for licensing hackney-coaches. I held this post with honor until a future quarrel with the Minister stripped me of it. I also pursued my education at the Temple, appearing in Westminster Hall in gown and wig. Later, accompanying my friend Mr. Foker to Paris, I was warmly received by Monsieur de Florac, who introduced me to the city's elite. Though I had the spirit to mingle with the nobility, I remained loyal to Foker, whose connections lay firmly with the bourgeoisie, including Monsieur Santerre, a brewer who would later distinguish himself in blood rather than beer. Meanwhile, my wife and I resided at Foker's villa in Wimbledon, amused by the "Parisian letters" I sent home via Mr. Hume, which were eventually published as a volume.

While I discharged these duties in London, the seeds of the great separation between the colonies and the mother country were being sown. When Mr. Grenville proposed the Stamp Duties, I warned my wife of the discontent it would stir, noting our own tendency to extract as much as possible from England. Yet, I never anticipated the fury the scheme ignited. It was a classic case where a pretext for quarrel masked long-standing animosities. The habitual insolence of Englishmen toward colonists, the natural spirit of men outraged by imperial domination, and the blunders of the British system drove the colonies to revolt. Had I been in Virginia rather than London, I might have sided with the provincials, perhaps driven into rebellion by the very resolve of my sister-in-law, Lady Warrington. Was the Stamp Act the true cause? A tax no greater than that cheerfully paid in England. Ten years prior, when the French threatened our borders, would the colonies have rebelled over such a levy? Against the British in America stood thousands of high-spirited men, yet others found profit in the quarrel. I confess I cannot now determine if my own motivations were selfish or patriotic, nor which side held the moral high ground. Having lost the game, I vow that after the initial soreness, the loser felt no lasting rancour.

The true source of my domestic turmoil, however, lay in the correspondence from my brother, Hal. He wrote home with flaming patriotic fervor, a tone that seemed entirely at odds with his usual deference to my wisdom. My wife whispered that he was rebelling against "Madam Esmond," while I suspected some colonial influence. Hal begged me never to allude to the delicate subject in my letters, fearing his mother's scrutiny. Yet, when he learned that I had retained only a hundred pounds from his aunt's legacy despite my own extreme straits, he was moved to mortgage his newly purchased estate to support me, quarrelling with his mother in my defense. Only later did he discover that our mother had cut off my supplies to advance his interests; by then, my financial situation had improved, and his sacrifices were in vain.

Our thrifty parent at Castlewood meticulously archived every scrap of paper, yet we boys were careless with our own correspondence. My wife, however, preserved many of Harry's letters, including one that revealed a shocking development. Reading it, my wife exclaimed, "To think whom he has chosen, and whom he might have had! Oh, 'tis cruel!" I remarked on the beauty of Miss Fanny Mountain, but she countered, "But is she to compare to my Hetty?" We had agreed that Hetty and Harry were not destined for happiness, yet my wife sighed, wishing they had tried, fearing Hetty's superior intellect might have led Harry astray.

Harry's letter detailed his conquest of Miss Fanny Mountain. He wrote with a newfound confidence, aided by a dictionary, declaring that he had given his heart in exchange for hers. He explained that he had not long been home when he realized his fate was accomplished. He praised Fanny's growth since his European travels and noted the rough, haughty treatment she endured from Madam Esmond, who treated her worse than a servant. Harry's love for Fanny was sweet and angelic, enduring her mistreatment with patience. He recounted how Fanny thanked him for rescuing her from prison and paying her debts, expressing her gratitude for his selfless poverty.

Harry revealed that Madam Esmond had seen an opportunity to provide for him through the sale of Tom Diggle's estate, offering six thousand pounds for the farm and stock. With his aunt's legacy arriving opportunely, Harry purchased the property near Richmond, intending to return to his native country and join the House of Burgesses. Madam Esmond had made a condition: he must leave the army and live at home. She had lost one son to literature and England, she claimed, and demanded the other stay.

However, after the purchase was made, Harry's mother attempted to force him to marry Miss Betsy Pitts, a woman scarred by smallpox with crooked eyes and unequal legs. Harry rejected her, comparing her unfavorably to Fanny's graceful ankles. The turning point came when a certain dear girl, Fanny, burst into tears of happiness upon hearing of his departure from the army. She confessed her terror of losing him, her prayers for his safety during Braddock's campaign and Wolfe's expedition. Harry, touched by her sympathy, seized her hand.

Later, finding Fanny crying in her mother's room while sewing a cockade for a hat, Harry asked why her eyes were red. Fanny admitted she was a fool, crying because he was leaving them for a life of honor among gay companions, leaving them in solitude. She began to speak of remembering him, but stopped, hiding her face. Harry, flustered and moved, declared his love, asking if he could think that parting brought her tears. Fanny, realizing the gravity of the situation, cried out for him to consider the difference between them and the potential scandal.

Their mother, Madam Esmond, entered the room, accusing Harry of being an ungrateful, artful, false wretch. She insulted Fanny, calling her the daughter of a housekeeper and suggesting she marry the apothecary's son, Sam Lintot, or even the blacksmith's son. Enraged, Harry swore oaths and blasphemies, defending Fanny's honor against his own mother. He declared that if Lintot offered Fanny any liberty, he would brain him with his own pestle. Madam Esmond, leaning on her tortoiseshell stick, lamented her punishment, claiming she had centered her love on Harry to the neglect of his elder brother, taking unjustly from the eldest to enrich the younger. She accused him of seducing the housekeeper's daughter under her roof.

Harry, furious, insisted he did not intend to seduce anyone and defended Fanny's purity. He knelt before her, offering his heart and hand forever. Fanny accepted, declaring that only Madam Esmond could hold such an opinion of her honor. She refused to stay in the house any longer. Madam Esmond, pale and stunned, ordered her to leave. Harry offered Fanny his own home, nearly ready, inviting her to stay forever as reparation for the insult to her honor.

As Harry spoke to Fanny, he heard his mother outside the room repeatedly muttering, "I am punished for my crime!" He did not immediately grasp the meaning of her words, but later, at a tavern where the ladies had moved with their belongings, Fanny explained. Madam Esmond had announced her intention to return instantly to Castlewood, taking her servants with her. She had decided to leave the country entirely, bargaining for a passage on a ship bound for England. However, the cabin was mercifully engaged by a North Carolina gentleman and his family, who agreed to take the ladies along. Before the next ship sailed, they had arranged to stay with Harry.

Harry's letter concluded with hopes for reconciliation and plans to visit Europe someday. He signed off as "H. E. W." (Henry Esmond Warrington), adding a postscript that revealed the full extent of his mother's manipulation. She had stopped his allowance and charged him nearly a thousand pounds for goods provided for the Virginian property, plus the costs of his release from prison. He drew upon his brother for the sum, instructing him not to acknowledge the account in writing to avoid bothering women with details.

Upon reading the document, we concluded that the ladies had supervised the style and spelling of Hal's letter, but the postscript was added without their knowledge. We feared that the Virginian Squire was under female domination, much like Hercules, Samson, and many strong men before him.

When my mother learned of my decision to remain at home, I suspect she was hardly pleased. It is likely she withdrew her financial support with the intent to starve me into submission, forcing a return to Virginia and a life of dependence beneath her roof. Yet, we never resolved the monetary dispute between us until her dying day. She simply cut off my allowance; I said not a word, but managed to survive without her aid. I never heard her express repentance for this injustice, nor acknowledge her error, except through Harry's private communications to me later. In subsequent meetings, Madam Esmond displayed a profound gentleness and an unusual respect for my wife, perhaps intending for me to interpret this as a tacit admission of her past wrongs. However, she offered no apology, and I asked for none.

With Harry provided for—a matter I could not begrudge—all of my mother's savings and frugal schemes ultimately benefited me, as her heir. Time, once a scarce commodity, had become abundant. A few guineas might have been more useful to me in my youth than the hundreds that eventually fell into my lap when I no longer needed them. By the time we met again, the era of necessity had long passed. I possessed plenty, and she could only add to my store. No doubt she suffered internally, thinking of the hunger my children endured and the strangers who had to relieve the very necessity her proud heart had created. Was she prouder than I? A soft word of explanation between us might have secured a reconciliation years prior, but neither of us spoke. When I commit a wrong and later recognize it, I love to ask pardon; yet, to my own pride, this act is merely an apology for having been wanting to myself. Thus, I rarely debase myself to perform a meanness. How do men feel whose entire lives are constructed of lies, schemes, and subterfuges? What company do they keep when alone? Daily, I observe men whose every smile is an artifice and every wink a hypocrisy. Does such a fellow wear a mask even in his own privacy, before his own conscience? If I choose to overlook an injury, I fear it is not born of a Christian spirit of forgiveness, but because I can afford to remit the debt and disdain to demand a settlement. One or two sweet souls I have known, perhaps tried, to whom forgiveness comes naturally, like a plant growing in its native soil. I know how to remit, I say, not forgive. I wonder if proud men are proud of being proud.

Consequently, I showed no sign of submission toward my parent in Virginia, and we remained estranged for years, exchanging only brief notes—perhaps announcing a birth or similar trivialities—between my wife and her. Following our initial troubles in America regarding the Stamp Act, misfortunes befell me in London as well. Though I stood on the Tory side in that quarrel, believing the Imperial Government had a right to levy taxes in the colonies, I published a sharp letter to a member of the House of Burgesses in Virginia. In it, I freely handled the habitual insolence of the mother country toward the colonies, expressing sentiments so disagreeable to those in power that I was stripped of my position as hackney-coach licenser. This terrified my uncle, who could never bear to love people in disgrace. He had grown to cherish my wife and my little boy deeply, but toward me personally, he held a pitying contempt that always amused me. He possessed a natural scorn for poverty and a corresponding love for success and fortune. Any opinion deviating from the regular track shocked him, and all truth-telling made him turn pale. Yet, he must have retained some warmth of heart and genuine love for kin; despite the dreadful shocks I gave him, he continued to see Theo and the child (and me, offering a mournful recognition when we met). Broken-hearted by my free-spokenness, he did not refuse to speak to me as he had during our first differences, viewing me instead as a melancholy lost creature, past all worldly help or hope. Never mind; I must cast about for a new scheme of life. At this juncture, the repayment of Harry's debt to me enabled me to live, at least for months, perhaps years. O strange fatuity of youth! I often say. How was it that we dared to be so poor and so little cast down?

At this time, His Majesty's royal uncle, the Duke of Cumberland, fell and perished in a fit. Strangely enough, his death occasioned a remarkable change in my fortune. My poor Sir Miles Warrington never missed a court ceremony to which he could introduce himself. He was at every drawing-room, christening, ball, and funeral. If ever a prince or princess was ailing, his coach was at their door. Leicester Fields, Carlton House, Gunnersbury—all were the same to him, and nothing satisfied him now but attending the stout Duke's funeral. He caught a severe cold and inflammation of the throat from standing bareheaded in the rain at this funeral. One morning, before I had even heard of his illness, a lawyer waited upon me at my lodgings in Bloomsbury and saluted me by the name of Sir George Warrington.

Party strife and fear of the future were now over. We laid the poor gentleman beside his little son in the family churchyard, where so many of his race repose. Little Miles and I were the chief mourners. An obsequious tenantry bowed and curtseyed before us, doing their utmost to conciliate my honor and my worship. The dowager and her daughter withdrew to Bath shortly thereafter, and I and my family took possession of the house, of which I have been master for thirty years. Be not too eager, O my son! Have but a little patience, and I too shall sleep under those yew-trees, and the people will be tossing up their caps for Sir Miles.

The records of a prosperous country life are easily and briefly told. The steward's books reveal what rents were paid and forgiven, what crops were raised, and in what rotation. They note what visitors came and how long they stayed; what pensioners my wife had, and how they were doctored, relieved, and died; what year I served as sheriff, and how often the hounds met near us. All these are narrated in our house journals, which any of my heirs may read who choose to take the trouble. We could not afford the fine mansion in Hill Street that my predecessor had occupied, but we took a smaller house in which, however, we spent more money. We made not half the show, with liveries, equipages, and plate, for which my uncle had been famous. Yet our beer was stronger, and my wife's charities were perhaps more costly than those of the Dowager Lady Warrington. No doubt she thought there was no harm in spoiling the Philistines; for she made us pay unconscionably for the goods she left behind in our country-house, and I submitted to most of her extortions with unutterable good humor. What value she imagined the potted plants in her greenhouses bore! What price she set upon that horrible old spinet she left in her drawing-room! And the framed pieces of worsted-work, performed by the accomplished Dora and the lovely Flora—if they had been masterpieces of Titian or Vandyck, to be sure, my lady dowager could hardly have valued them at a higher price. But though we paid so generously, though we were, I may say without boast, far kinder to our poor than ever she had been, for a while we held the very worst reputation in the county, where all sorts of stories had been told to my discredit. I thought I might perhaps succeed to my uncle's seat in Parliament, as well as to his landed property; but I found, I knew not how, that I was voted to be a person of very dangerous opinions. I would not bribe; I would not coerce my own tenants to vote for me in the election of '68. A gentleman came down from Whitehall with a pocket-book full of bank-notes, and I found that I had no chance against my competitor.

Bon Dieu! Now that we were at ease regarding worldly means—now that obedient tenants bowed and curtseyed as we went to church; that we drove to visit our friends or neighboring towns in the great family coach drawn by four fat horses—did we not often regret poverty, and the dear little cottage at Lambeth where Want was ever prowling at the door? Did I not long to be bear-leading again, and vow that translating for booksellers was not such very hard drudgery? When we went to London, we made sentimental pilgrimages to all our old haunts. I dare say my wife embraced all her landladies. You may be sure we asked all the friends of those old times to share the comforts of our new home with us. The Reverend Mr. Hagan and his lady visited us more than once. His appearance in the pulpit at B------(where he preached very finely, as we thought) caused an awful scandal there. Sampson came too, another unlucky Levite, and was welcome as long as he would stay among us. Mr. Johnson talked of coming, but he put us off once or twice. I suppose our house was dull. I know that I myself would be silent for days, and fear that my moodiness must often have tried the sweetest-tempered woman in the world who lived with me. I did not care for field sports. The killing of one partridge was so like killing another that I wondered how men could pass days after days in the pursuit of that kind of slaughter. Their fox-hunting stories would begin at four o'clock, when the tablecloth was removed, and last till supper-time. I sat silent and listened: day after day I fell asleep. No wonder I was not popular with my company.

What admission is this I am making? Here was the storm over, the rocks avoided, the ship in port, and the sailor not overcontented? Was Susan, whom I had sighed for during the voyage, not the beauty I expected to find? In the first place, Susan and all the family can look in William's logbook, and so, madam, I am not going to put my secrets down there. No, Susan, I never had secrets from thee. I never cared for another woman. I have seen more beautiful, but none that suited me as well as your ladyship. I have met Mrs. Carter and Miss Mulso, and Mrs. Thrale and Madam Kaufmann, and the angelical Gunnings, and Her Grace of Devonshire, and a host of beauties who were not angelic, by any means; and I was not dazzled by them. Nay, young folks, I may have led your mother a weary life and been a very Bluebeard over her, but then I had no other heads in the closet. Only, the first pleasure of taking possession of our kingdom over, I own I began to be quickly tired of the crown. When the captain wears it, His Majesty will be a very different Prince. He can ride a-hunting five days in the week and find the sport amusing. I believe he would hear the same sermon at church fifty times and not yawn more than I do at the first delivery. But sweet Joan, beloved Baucis! Being thy faithful husband and true lover always, thy Darby is rather ashamed of having been testy so often! And, being arrived at the consummation of happiness, Philemon asks pardon for falling asleep so frequently after dinner. There came a period of my life, when having reached the summit of felicity, I was quite tired of the prospect I had there: I yawned in Eden and said, "Is this all? What, no lions to bite? no rain to fall? no thorns to prick you in the rose-bush when you sit down?—only Eve, for ever sweet and tender, and figs for breakfast, dinner, supper, from week's end to week's end!" Shall I make my confessions? Hearken! Well, then, if I must make a clean breast of it.

* * * * *

Here three pages are torn out of Sir George Warrington's MS. book, for which the editor is sincerely sorry.

I know the theory and practice of the Roman Church; but, being bred of another persuasion (and skeptical and heterodox regarding that), I can't help doubting the other, too, and wondering whether Catholics, in their confessions, confess all? Do we Protestants ever do so; and has education rendered those other fellow-men so different from us? At least, amongst us, we are not accustomed to suppose Catholic priests or laymen more frank and open than ourselves. Which brings me back to my question—does any man confess all? Does yonder dear creature know all my life, who has been the partner of it for thirty years? Who, whenever I have told her a sorrow, has been ready with the best of her gentle power to soothe it; who has watched when I did not speak, and when I was silent has been silent herself, or with the charming hypocrisy of woman has worn smiles and an easy appearance so as to make me imagine she felt no care, or would not even ask to disturb her lord's secret when he seemed to indicate a desire to keep it private? Oh, the dear hypocrite! Have I not watched her hiding the boys' peccadilloes from papa's anger? Have I not known her cheat out of her housekeeping to pay off their little extravagances; and talk to me with an artless face, as if she did not know that our revered captain had had dealings with the gentlemen of Duke's Place, and our learned collegian, at the end of his terms, had very pressing reasons for sporting his oak (as the phrase is) against some of the University tradesmen? Why, from the very earliest days, thou wise woman, thou wert for ever concealing something from me—this one stealing jam from the cupboard; that one getting into disgrace at school; that naughty rebel (put on the caps, young folks, according to the fit) flinging an inkstand at mamma in a rage, whilst I was told the gown and the carpet were spoiled by accident. We all hide from one another. We have all secrets. We are all alone. We sin by ourselves, and, let us trust, repent too. Yonder dear woman would give her foot to spare mine a twinge of the gout; but, when I have the fit, the pain

The plea of our mother, tender and urgent as it was, possessed a power to soften even the hardest hearts, yet it found us resolute in our refusal to depart immediately. We spoke of a swift journey to Virginia, of securing the entire cabin of the *Young Rachel* for our comfort. Yet, nature intervened with a cruel necessity: our child fell ill, rendering the voyage perilous for her, and from whom a mother could never sever her bond. Thus, the *Young Rachel* sailed that year without us. The following year brought another obstacle, this time in the form of my worship's first onset of the gout—a malady that occupied me significantly, though it later served to clear my wits and enliven my spirits. But now, a far sadder cause for delay presented itself in the tragic tidings from Jamaica.

Some two years after our establishment at the Manor, our dear General returned from his government. He came back a little richer in worldly goods than when he departed, yet he bore a loss for which no wealth could offer solace; indeed, after this blow, he showed little desire to remain in the West Indies. My Theo's poor mother—the most tender and affectionate friend I have ever known, save for one—had died abroad of the fever. Her final regret was that she should not live to witness our children and ourselves in prosperity.

"She sees us, though we do not see her; and she thanks you, George, for having been good to her children," her husband said softly.

We feared he would not long survive to join her. His love for her had been the happiness and the business of his entire life; to be away from her seemed to him a cessation of living. It was pitiable to watch the good man as he sat with us. My wife, through her demeanor and countless gestures, constantly recalled her mother to the bereaved widower's heart. Whatever cheer we could muster for him in his calamity, we offered freely; yet, especially, little Hetty became his chief support and consolation. She had refused more than one advantageous match in the Island, as the General told us, and upon her return to England, the heir of Lord Wrotham had laid himself at her feet. But she loved best to stay with her father, Hetty declared. As long as he was not tired of her, she cared for no husband.

"Nay," we said when this last great match was proposed, "let the General stay six months with us at the Manor here, and you can have him at Oakhurst for the other six."

But Hetty declared her father could never bear Oakhurst again now that her mother was gone; and she would marry no man for his coronet and money—not she! The General, when we discussed this matter gravely, remarked that the child had no desire for marriage, possibly due to some disappointment in early life of which she never spoke. We, respecting her feelings, remained equally silent. By this time, my brother Lambert held a college living near Winchester and a wife to adorn his parsonage. We professed a moderate liking for this lady, welcoming her when she came to us, though our affection was limited. Mrs. Jack was a chatterbox of a woman, prone to speaking her mind freely and priding herself excessively on her skill in inflicting pain upon her friends.

"My dear Sir George," she was pleased to say, "I have often told our dear Theo that I wouldn't have a pretty sister in my house to make tea for Jack when I was upstairs, always at hand when needed in the kitchen or nursery, and always dressed neat and in her best when I was likely making pies or puddings. I have every confidence in Jack, of course. I should like to see him look at another woman, indeed! And so I have in Jemima, but they don't come together in my house when I'm upstairs—that I promise you! And so I told my sister Warrington."

"Am I to understand," the General asked, "that you have done my Lady Warrington the favor to warn her against her sister, my daughter Miss Hester?"

"Yes, pa, of course I have. A duty is a duty, and a woman is a woman, and a man is a man, as I know very well. Don't tell me! He is a man. Every man is a man, with all his sanctified airs!"

"You yourself have a married sister, with whom you were staying when my son Jack first had the happiness of making your acquaintance?" the General remarked.

"Yes, of course I have a married sister; everyone knows that, and I have been as good as a mother to her children!"

"And am I to gather from your conversation that your attractions proved a powerful temptation for your sister's husband?"

"Law, General! I don't know how you can go for to say I ever said any such thing!" cried Mrs. Jack, red and voluble.

"Don't you perceive, my dear madam, that it is you who have insinuated as much, not only regarding yourself, but regarding my own two daughters?"

"Never, never, never, as I'm a Christian woman! And it's most cruel of you to say so, sir. And I do say a sister is best out of the house, that I do! And as Theo's time is coming, I warn her, that's all."

"Have you discovered, my good madam, whether my poor Hetty has stolen any of the spoons? When I came to breakfast this morning, my daughter was alone, and there must have been a score of pieces of silver on the table."

"Law, sir! Who ever said a word about spoons? Did I ever accuse the poor dear? If I did, may I drop down dead at this moment on this hearth-rug! And I ain't used to be spoke to in this way. And me and Jack have both remarked it; and I've done my duty, that I have." With that, Mrs. Jack flounced out of the room, in tears.

"And has the woman had the impudence to tell you this, my child?" the General asked when Theo, who was a little delicate, came to the tea-table.

"She has told me every day since she has been here. She comes into my dressing-room to tell me. She comes to my nursery and says, 'Ah, I wouldn't have a sister prowling about my nursery, that I wouldn't.' Ah, how pleasant it is to have amiable and well-bred relatives, say I."

"Thy poor mother has been spared this woman," groaned the General.

"Our mother would have made her better, papa," said Theo, kissing him.

"Yes, dear." And I saw that both of them were at their prayers.

Yet it must be owned that loving one's relatives is not always an easy task, nor is living with one's neighbors always amusing. From Jack Lambert's demeanor the next day, I could see his wife had given him her version of the conversation. Jack was sulky, though not dignified; he was angry, yet his anger did not diminish his appetite. He preached a sermon for us that was entirely stupid. Little Miles, once more in sables, sat at his grandfather's side, his little hand placed in that of the kind old man.

Should he stay and keep house for us during our Virginian trip? The housekeeper should be placed under the full domination of Hetty. The butler's keys should be handed over to him; for Gumbo, whom I did not think with an overly good grace, was to come with us to Virginia. Having, it must be noted, united himself with Mrs. Molly in the bonds of matrimony, he had peopled a cottage in my park with sundry tawny Gumbos. Under the care of our good General and his daughter, we left our house. We traveled to London, and thence to Bristol, where our obsequious agent declared he would offer up prayers for our prosperity and vowed that children so beautiful as ours—we had an infant by this time to accompany Miles—were never seen on any ship before. We made a voyage without accident.

How strange the feeling was as we landed from our boat at Richmond! A coach and a host of negroes were there in waiting to receive us; and hard by, a gentleman on horseback, with negroes in our livery, sprang from his horse and rushed up to embrace us. Not a little charmed were both of us to see our dearest Hal. He rode with us to our mother's door. Yonder she stood on the steps to welcome us, and Theo knelt down to ask her blessing.

Harry rode in the coach with us as far as our mother's house but would not, as he said, spoil sport by entering with us. "She sees me," he owned, "and we are pretty good friends; but Fanny and she are best apart; and there is no love lost between 'em, I can promise you. Come over to me at the Tavern, George, when thou art free. And tomorrow I shall have the honor to present her sister to Theo. 'Twas only from happening to be in town yesterday that I heard the ship was signalled, and waited to see you. I have sent a negro boy home to my wife, and she'll be here to pay her respects to my Lady Warrington." After this brief greeting, Harry jumped out of the carriage, leaving us to meet our mother alone.

Since I parted from her, I had seen much fine company, and Theo and I had paid our respects to the King and Queen at St. James's; but we had seen no stater person than this who welcomed us. Raising my wife from her knee, he embraced her and led her into the house. 'Twas a plain, wood-built place with a gallery round, as our Virginian houses are; but if it had been a palace with a little empress inside, our reception could not have been more courteous. There was old Nathan, still the major-domo, a score of kind black faces grinning welcome. Some whose names I remembered as children were grown out of remembrance, to be sure, to become buxom lads and lasses; and some I had left with black pates were now grizzling with snowy polls; and some who were born since my time were peering at doorways with their great eyes and little naked feet. It was, "I'm little Sip, Master George!" and "I'm Dinah, Sir George!" and "I'm Master Miles's boy!" said a little chap in a new livery and boots of nature's blacking. Ere the day was over, the whole household found a pretext to pass before us, grinning, bowing, and making us welcome. I don't know how many repasts were served to us. In the evening, my Lady Warrington had to receive all the gentry of the little town, which she did with perfect grace and good humor, while I shook hands with a few old acquaintances—old enemies I was going to say; but I had come into a fortune and was no longer a naughty prodigal. Why, a drove of fatted calves was killed in my honor! My poor Hal was of the entertainment, but gloomy and crestfallen. His mother spoke to him, but it was as a queen to a rebellious prince, her son who was not yet forgiven. We two slipped away from the company and went up to the rooms assigned to me; but there, as we began a free conversation, our mother, taper in hand, appeared with her pale face. Did I want anything? Was everything quite as I wished it? She had peeped in at the dearest children, who were sleeping like cherubs. How she did caress them and delight over them! How she was charmed with Miles's dominating airs and the little Theo's smiles and dimples! "Supper is just coming on the table, Sir George. If you like our cookery better than the tavern, Henry, I beg you to stay." What a different welcome there was in the words and tone addressed to each of us! Hal hung down his head and followed to the lower room.

A clergyman begged a blessing on the meal. He touched with not a little art and eloquence upon our arrival at home, upon our safe passage across the stormy waters, upon the love and forgiveness which awaited us in the mansions of the Heavenly Parent when the storms of life were over.

Here was a new clergyman, quite unlike some whom I remembered about us in earlier days, and I praised him, but Madam Esmond shook her head. She was afraid his principles were very dangerous; she was afraid others had adopted those dangerous principles. Had I not seen the paper signed by the burgesses and merchants at Williamsburg the year before—the Lees, Randolphs, Bassets, Washingtons, and the like, and oh, my dear, that I should have to say it, our name, that is, your brother's (by what influence I do not like to say), and this unhappy Mr. Belman's who begged a blessing last night?

If there had been quarrels in our little colonial society when I left home, what were these to the feuds I found raging on my return? We had sent the Stamp Act to America and been forced to repeal it. Then we must try a new set of duties on glass, paper, and what not, and repeal that Act too, with the exception of a duty on tea. From Boston to Charleston, the tea was confiscated. Even my mother, loyal as she was, gave up her favorite drink; and my poor wife would have had to forgo hers, but we had brought a quantity for our private drinking on board ship, which had paid four times as much duty at home. Not that I for my part would have hesitated about paying duty. The home Government must have some means of revenue, or its pretensions to authority were idle. They say the colonies were tried and tyrannized over; I say the home Government was tried and tyrannized over. 'Tis but an affair of argument and history, now; we tried the question, and were beat; and the matter is settled as completely as the conquest of Britain by the Normans. And all along, from conviction I trust, I own to have taken the British side of the quarrel.

In that brief and unfortunate experience of war which I had had in my early life, the universal cry of the army and well-affected persons was that Mr

What a perverse law of Fate it seems to place me perpetually in the minority. Should a motion be brought forward to surrender this realm to the Pretender of Rome or the Grand Turk, and submit it to the new sovereign's faith, it would surely pass, for I would certainly vote against it. Yet, here in Virginia, I found myself disagreeing with everyone, as was my wont. The Patriots branded me a Tory; the Tories declared me a dangerous Republican. The times were utterly out of joint. Oh, cursed spite! Before a year had passed since I arrived in Virginia, I longed to be back by the banks of the Waveney. But the aspect of affairs was so fraught with peril that I could not abandon my mother, a solitary woman, to face the coming war and disaster, nor would she leave the country at such a critical juncture, nor should a man of spirit forsake it. At His Excellency's table, amidst the plentiful claret, many of the well-affected agreed upon a vow, raising countless brimming bumpers in its honor. "No!" cried the sentiment. "It is *statue signum*, *signifer*! We Cavaliers will all rally round it." And at these moments, our Governor spoke with the courage of the bravest.

Of all my acquaintances in Virginia, Madam Esmond proved the most consistent. Our gentry had flocked to Williamsburg in droves, and many proposed treating Her Excellency, the Governor's lady, to a ball upon the news of the Boston Port Bill. Immediately, the House of Burgesses adopted an indignant protest against Parliament's measure, decreeing a solemn day of fasting and humiliation throughout the country, with prayers to Heaven to avert the calamity of civil war. Meanwhile, the invitation to my Lady Dunmore had already been issued and accepted. The gentlemen resolved that their ball should proceed on the appointed evening, and that sackcloth and ashes should be assumed only several days later.

"A ball!" exclaimed Madam Esmond. "I shall go to a ball given by a set of rebels who intend to publicly insult His Majesty a week hence! I would sooner die!" She wrote to the stewards of the occasion stating that, viewing the dangerous state of the country, she could not conceive of attending.

What was her surprise, then, the next time she rode abroad in her chair, to be cheered by a hundred voices, white and black alike, shouting "Huzzah, Madam!" and "Heaven bless your ladyship!" They evidently mistook her patriotic resolve for a refusal born of principle. To ensure there was no misunderstanding, she leaned from the chair and cried out, "God save the King!" as loudly as she could. The people echoed her cry. Everyone cried "God save the King" in those days. On the night of the entertainment, my poor Harry, as a Burgess and one of the feast's givers, donned his red coat of Wolfe's—which he was soon to exchange for another color—and departed with Madam Fanny to the ball. My Lady Warrington and her humble servant, being strangers in the country and essentially English, were permitted by Madam to attend the assembly from which she, of course, absented herself. I had the honor of dancing a country-dance with the lady of Mount Vernon, whom I found a most lively, pretty, and amiable partner; yet I must confess that my wife's praises of her were received with a very grim acceptance by my mother when Lady Warrington recounted the evening's events. Could not Sir George Warrington have danced with my Lady Dunmore or her daughters, or with anyone but Mrs. Washington? To be sure, the Colonel thought so highly of himself and his wife that he undoubtedly considered her the grandest lady in the room; and she, who remembered him as a road-surveyor earning a guinea a day! Well, indeed! There was no measuring the pride of these provincial upstarts, and as for this gentleman, my Lord Dunmore's partiality for him had evidently turned his head. I do not know about Mr. Washington's pride, but I know that my good mother never could be brought to love him or anything that was his.

She was no better pleased with him for attending the ball than with his conduct three days later, when the day of fasting and humiliation arrived, and he attended the service performed by our new clergyman. She invited Mr. Belman to dinner that day, along with sundry colonial authorities. The clergyman excused himself. Madam Esmond tossed her head and said he might do as he liked. She made a parade of a dinner; she lit her house at night while the rest of the city lay in darkness and gloom; she begged Mr. Hardy, one of His Excellency's aides-de-camp, to sing "God save the King," to which the people in the street outside listened, thinking it part of some religious service Madam was celebrating. But then she called for "Britons, strike home!" which the simple young gentleman, fresh from Europe, began to perform. Instantly, a great yell arose in the street, and a large stone, flung from some rebellious hand, plumped into the punch-bowl before me, scattering it and its contents across our dining-room.

My mother went to the window, nothing daunted. I can see her rigid little figure now, standing with a tossed-up head, outstretched frilled arms, and the twinkling stars for a background, singing in chorus, "Britons, strike home! strike home!" The crowd before the palings shouted and roared, "Silence! for shame! go back!" but she would not go back, not she. "Fling more stones, if you dare!" said the brave little lady. More might have come, but some gentlemen issuing from the Raley Tavern interposed themselves between her and the mob. "You mustn't insult a lady," said a voice I think I knew. "Huzza, Colonel! Hurrah, Captain! God bless your honour!" cried the people in the street. Thus, the enemies were pacified.

My mother, protesting that the whole disturbance was over, would have had Mr. Hardy sing another song, but he gave a sickly grin and said, "he really did not like to sing to such accompaniments," and the concert for that evening was ended; though I am bound to say that some scoundrels returned at night, frightening my poor wife almost out of her wits and breaking every single window in the front of our tenement. "Britons, strike home!" was a little too much; Madam should have contented herself with "God save the King." Militia was drilled, bullets cast, supplies of ammunition gathered, and cunning plans devised to disappoint the royal ordinances; but, to be sure, "God save the King" was the cry everywhere. In reply to my objections to the gentlemen-patriots—"Why, you are scheming for a separation; you are bringing down upon you the inevitable wrath of the greatest power in the world!"—the answer to me was always, "We mean no separation at all; we yield to no men in loyalty; we glory in the name of Britons," and so forth. Powder-barrels were heaped in the cellar, the train laid, but Mr. Fawkes remained persistent in his dutiful petitions to King and Parliament, meaning no harm, not he! 'Tis true that when I spoke of the power of our country, I imagined she would exert it; that she would not expect to overcome three million fellow-Britons on their own soil with a few battalions, a half-dozen generals from Bond Street, and a few thousand mercenaries hired from Germany. As if we wanted to insult the thirteen colonies as well as subdue them, we must set upon them these hordes of Hessians and murderers from the Indian wigwams. Was our great quarrel not to be fought without *tali auxilio* and *istis defensoribus*? Ah! 'Tis easy, now that we are worsted, to look over the map of the great empire wrested from us and show how we ought not to have lost it. Long Island ought to have exterminated Washington's army; he ought never to have emerged from Valley Forge except as a prisoner. The South was ours after the battle of Camden, but for the inconceivable meddling of the Commander-in-Chief at New York, who paralyzed the exertions of the only capable British General who appeared during the war and sent him into that miserable cul-de-sac at York Town, whence he could only issue defeated and a prisoner. Oh, for a week more! A day more, an hour more of darkness or light! In reading over our American campaigns from their unhappy commencement to their inglorious end, now that we can see the enemy's movements and conditions as clearly as our own, I fancy we can see how an advance, a march, might have put enemies into our power who had no means to withstand it, and changed the entire issue of the struggle. But it was ordained by Heaven, and for the good, as we can now have no doubt, of both empires, that the great Western Republic should separate from us: and the gallant soldiers who fought on her side, their indomitable and heroic Chief above all, had the glory of facing and overcoming, not only veteran soldiers amply provided and inured to war, but wretchedness, cold, hunger, dissensions, and treason within their own camp, where all must have gone to rack but for the pure, unquenchable flame of patriotism that burned forever in the bosom of the heroic leader. What constancy, what magnanimity, what surprising persistence against fortune! Washington before the enemy was no better nor braver than hundreds who fought with him or against him (who has not heard the repeated sneers against "Fabius" in which his factious captains indulged?), but Washington the Chief of a nation in arms, doing battle with distracted parties; calm in the midst of conspiracy; serene against the open foe before him and the darker enemies at his back; Washington inspiring order and spirit into troops hungry and in rags; stung by ingratitude but betraying no anger, and ever ready to forgive; in defeat invincible, magnanimous in conquest, and never so sublime as on that day when he laid down his victorious sword and sought his noble retirement:—here indeed is a character to admire and revere; a life without a stain, a fame without a flaw. *Quando invenies parem?* In that more extensive work, which I have planned and partly written on the subject of this great war, I hope I have done justice to the character of its greatest leader. [And I trust that in the opinions I have recorded regarding him, I have shown that I also can be just and magnanimous towards those who view me personally with no favor. For my brother Hal, being at Mount Vernon and always eager to bring me and his beloved Chief on good terms, showed His Excellency some of the early sheets of my History. General Washington (who read but few books and had not the slightest pretensions to literary taste) remarked, "If you will have my opinion, my dear General, I think Sir George's projected work, from the specimen I have of it, is certain to offend both parties."—G. E. W.] And this from the sheer force of respect which his eminent virtues extorted. With the young Mr. Washington of my own early days, I had not the honor to enjoy much sympathy: though my brother, whose character is much more frank and affectionate than mine, was always his fast friend in early times, when they were equals, as in latter days when the General, as I do own and think, was all mankind's superior.

I have mentioned the contrariety in my disposition, and perhaps in my brother's, which somehow placed us on the wrong sides in the quarrel that ensued, raging for five years until the mother country was fain to acknowledge her defeat. Harry should have been the Tory, and I the Whig. Theoretically, my opinions were very much more liberal than those of my brother, who, especially after his marriage, became what our Indian nabobs call a Bahadoor—a person ceremonious, stately, and exacting respect. When my Lord Dunmore talked about liberating the negroes to induce them to join the King's standard, Hal was for hanging the Governor and the Black Guards (as he called them) whom His Excellency had crimped. "If you, gentlemen, are fighting for freedom," said I, "sure the negroes may fight, too." On which Harry roared out, shaking his fist, "Infernal villains, if I meet any of 'em, they shall die by this hand!" And my mother agreed that this idea of a negro insurrection was the most abominable and parricidal notion which had ever sprung up in her unhappy country. She at least was more consistent than brother Hal. She would have black and white obedient to the powers that be; whereas Hal could only admit that freedom was the right of the latter color.

As proof of her argument, Madam Esmond and Harry too would point to an instance in our own family in the person of Mr. Gumbo. Having obtained his freedom from me as a reward for his admirable love and fidelity when times were hard, Gumbo, on his return to Virginia, was scarce a welcome guest in his old quarters among my mother's servants. He was free, and they were not; he was, as it were, a center of insurrection. He gave himself no small airs of protection and consequence among them, bragging of his friends in Europe ("at home," as he called it) and his doings there; and for a while he brought the household around to listen to him and admire him, like a monkey who had seen the world. Now, Sady, Hal's boy, who went to America of his own desire, was not free. Hence jealousies between him and Mr. Gum, and battles in which they both practiced the noble art of boxing and butting, which they had learned at Marybone Gardens and Hockley-in-the-Hole. Nor was Sady the only jealous person: almost all my mother's servants hated Signor Gumbo for the airs he gave himself; and I am sorry to say that our faithful Molly, his wife, was as jealous as his old fellow-servants. The blacks could not pardon her for having demeaned herself so far as to marry one of their kind. She met

In the days when America served as a sanctuary for Britain's outcasts, we exported more than just convicts and indentured servants. We shipped over our "black sheep"—scapegraces, younger sons, and those driven away by debtors' prisons and despair—much like Cook presented English animals to his newly discovered islands. Among these exiles was Hagan, the husband of my kinswoman, whom I had reluctantly helped secure a colonial pulpit in Virginia. Though he served his congregation and his King with the dignity of a true gentleman, I confess a secret relief that he had been sent to the wilderness rather than remaining among us. My cousin, Madam Theo, always defended my conscience, insisting my actions were guided by the highest moral principles, yet I feared I would never have chosen him for our own parish. Still, I acknowledged my error; twice, when I needed support most, this kind Maria offered sympathy and friendship, bearing her own sorrows with courage while soothing others with devoted affection. Yet, shamefully, even I and others looked down upon her, a pride that deserved rebuke.

She was not alone in being banished to the American frontier. The Honourable William Esmond, having exhausted his ability to borrow, steal, and cheat at home, found a place in New York, much to the relief of his noble brother and royal master. When the troubles began, news reached us of William's antics: he was a harbinger of lies and mischief wherever he went. Lord Dunmore informed me that William had publicly declared our estate of Castlewood belonged only to his brother's pleasure, claiming his father had granted it to Madam Esmond for life, while William negotiated to buy the reversion. We possessed the deed of gift in our strongroom and had it registered at Williamsburg, rendering his claims legally void, but the intent behind his words was enough to unsettle us. When Madam Esmond heard these fabrications, her despair was palpable. "What! Is my father, the Marquis of Esmond, a liar, and am I a cheat?" she cried, fearing he would seize her son's property upon her death. She prepared to write to Lord Castlewood in England and even to the King at St. James's, but I calmed her by reminding her that William's lies were notorious among his acquaintances and unlikely to hold weight against our documented rights. Soon, however, we learned he had become a vocal Loyalist in New York, rising to the rank of Major of a volunteer corps eager to die for the mother country.

Unable to endure the scandal in our rented house at Williamsburg, Madam Esmond departed, and my family returned to Richmond, which was likewise deserted by the dissolved Assembly. Captain Hal and his wife returned early to their plantation, while I, troubled by the unfolding events, split my time between my own household and that of our Governor, despite our strong political differences. For now, no personal quarrel existed; even after the Assembly dissolved and its members convened a famous meeting at a tavern—where, I believe, the idea of a continental congress was first born—the leading opposition figures remained friends with His Excellency, sharing his hospitality and joining his pleasure excursions. Once the session ended, the gentry dispersed to their counties, and with Assemblies dissolved across the provinces, it was agreed that a general congress would meet in Philadelphia, the largest city on the continent. These celebrated conferences began, serving as the angry prelude to war. We still sang "God Save the King" and presented humble petitions to the throne, yet fate intervened.

One morning, I rode to visit my brother Harry at Fanny's Mount, his new plantation situated near ours but separated by the Rappahannock and Mattaponey Rivers. Upon arriving, I was told Master Harry had ridden out toward Willis's Ordinary. Thinking no harm, I followed. Not far from the ordinary, emerging from the woods onto a clearing, I encountered Captain Hal on horseback, surrounded by thirty or forty countrymen armed with pikes, scythes, fowling-pieces, and muskets. Under the command of two or three capable young officers, the men were undergoing drill. As I approached, a strange expression crossed Hal's face. "Present arms!" he commanded, and the makeshift army saluted with whatever precision they could muster. "Captain Cade, this is my brother, Sir George Warrington," Hal announced.

"As a relation of yours, Colonel," the man addressed as Captain Cade replied, extending a hand in welcome.

"And—a true friend to Virginia," Hal added, his face flushing slightly.

"Yes, please God, gentlemen," I said, and the regiment erupted in a hearty hurrah for the Colonel and his brother. Once the drill concluded, the officers and men wished to adjourn to Willis's Ordinary for refreshments, but Colonel Hal declined to drink that afternoon. Instead, we rode homeward together.

"So, Hal, the cat's out of the bag!" I remarked.

He shot me a hard look. "I suspect there are wilder cats in it. It must come to this, George. But you must not tell Madam," he added urgently.

"Good God!" I exclaimed. "Do you mean that with fellows like those I saw yonder, you intend to make a stand against the greatest nation and finest army in the world?"

"I guess we shall get an awful whipping," Hal admitted grimly, "and that is the fact. But then, George," he continued, offering his sweet, kind smile, "we are young, and a whipping or two might do us good. Won't it do us good, Dolly, you old slut?" He playfully touched his whip against an old dog of all trades trotting beside him.

I did not press him further, though I had tried many times before to appeal to his British loyalty, the side that seemed to me the stronger. He dismissed my arguments with a shrug: "All mighty well, brother, you speak as an Englishman, and have cast in your lot with your country, as I have with mine." There was no logical answer to such a sentiment; the only resolution lay in fighting until the strongest prevailed. Which side held the right in the wars of the last century? The King or Parliament?
