History showed that whoever stood uppermost was deemed right, and their victories, on the whole, proved more humane than the Cavaliers might have achieved had they won. Yet, imagine if the Tories had triumphed in America! What a frightful, bloody victory it would have been—ropes, scaffolds, and noble heads laid low. This was a strange paradox: I stood on the Loyalist side yet wished for the Whigs to win. Conversely, my brother Hal, who distinguished himself greatly with his regiment, never uttered a word of disrespect against the enemy. "The officers of the British army," he often said, "are gentlemen: at least, I have not heard they have changed much since my time. There may be scoundrels and ruffians among the enemy's troops; I dare say we could find some among our own. Our business is to beat His Majesty's forces, not to call them names—any rascal can do that." Indeed, from a name given to my brother by Mr. Lee, which many of his rough horsemen failed to understand, Harry was often called "Chevaleer Baird" within the Continental army. He was, truly, a knight without fear or reproach.

When I asked Hal what such a ragtag group could possibly achieve against the British army, his answer was confident. "They can beat them," he said firmly. "Mr. George, that is what they can do."

"Great heavens!" I cried. "Do you mean that with your company of Wolfe's, you would hesitate to attack five hundred such?"

"With my company of the 67th, I would go anywhere," Hal replied. "And, agreed with you, at this present moment I know more of soldiering than they. But place me on that open ground where you found us, armed as you please, with half a dozen of my friends and their rifles hidden in the woods around me—who would get the better? You know best, Mr. Braddock's aide-de-camp!"

There was no arguing with such determination. "Thou knowest my way of thinking, Hal," I said. "Having surprised you at your work, I must tell my lord what I have seen."

"Tell him, of course," Hal responded. "You have seen our county militia exercising. You will see as much in every colony from here to the Saint Lawrence or Georgia. As I am an old soldier, they have elected me colonel. What more natural? Come, brother, let us trot on; dinner will be ready, and Mrs. Fan does not like me to keep it waiting." Thus, we made for his house, which stood open like all the homes of our Virginian gentlemen, welcoming every friend, neighbor, stranger, and traveler alike.

"So, Mrs. Fan," I said upon arrival, "I have discovered what game my brother has been playing."

"I trust the Colonel will have plenty of sport ere long," she replied, tossing her head.

My wife believed Harry had been hunting, and I did not care to undeceive her, though what I had witnessed and what he had told me filled me with deep anxiety.

Once my visit to my brother concluded, and my wife and young child had returned to our maternal home at Richmond, I turned my attention to the Governor, who was residing at his country estate near Williamsburg. It was urgent that I confer with him regarding the open preparations for war, which were becoming evident not only within our province but across the colonies. History would later record the names of the gentlemen appointed as Delegates to the General Congress in Philadelphia, but at the time, the political landscape was fractured. In Massachusetts, the populace and royal troops faced one another in near-open hostility; in Maryland and Pennsylvania, we clung to the hope of a loyal spirit; and in the Carolinas and Georgia, the mother country could still count on staunch adherence. We, in Virginia, prided ourselves on our ancient loyalty, despite our scarcity of troops. Our gentry boasted descent from the Cavaliers, and surrounding the Governor were swarms of loud, confident Loyalists, eager to draw their swords and scatter the "rascally rebels."

In these heated councils, I was forced to endure many harsh words directed at my poor Harry. The consensus among the Governor's circle was that his wife had led him to these extreme anti-British views, and that he was infatuated by his attachment to the gentleman of Mount Vernon—George Washington—who was, they claimed, dragging him deeper into a desperate course of resistance. "This is your friend," the men around his Excellency sneered, "the man you favored, who shared your hospitality!" While much of this was true, what the eager Loyalists termed treachery was, in reality, a testament to the desperate desire of Mr. Washington and others to exhaust every chance of reconciliation before risking the terrible alternative of revolt. We, the faithful, would remain loyal; the unconquerable power of England would be exerted, and the misguided provinces punished. With what cheers we toasted His Majesty's health! We vowed to die in defense of his rights and await a Prince of his Royal house to govern our dominions. In the midst of this exaltation, hope, fury, and anxiety, I felt compelled to intercede for my brother.

I wrote to Hal with little hope, reiterating arguments I had used countless times. My mother also employed her authority, assailing him with Scripture texts and threats of divine punishment for disobedience to the powers that be. She hinted, I fear, at his subjection to his wife—the worst possible argument in such a controversy. Though she did not show me her own letter, she displayed his reply. To my surprise, Mr. Hal answered with scores of texts of his own, composing a neat, temperate, and elegant response that I believed his wife could scarcely have penned. Indeed, he had enlisted the services of Mr. Belman, the New Richmond clergyman, who had adopted strong Whig opinions and preached sermons against Hagan, our faction's ally. Belman seemed to have the better of the dispute.

My exhortations, like my mother's, proved futile. Hal ignored my letters. Pressed further by the Government's friends, I wrote imprudently promising to visit him at Fanny's Mount within the week. Upon arrival, I found only my sister, who received me cordially but informed me that Hal had ridden far into the countryside toward the Blue Mountains to inspect horses, with no indication of when he would return. Realizing there was no hope, I remarked to her, "My dear, judging by the signs of the times, the train laid for years must soon be ignited. Harry is riding away. God knows to what end."

"The Lord prosper the righteous cause, Sir George," she replied.

"Amen, with all my heart. You and he speak as Americans; I as an Englishman. Tell him from me that should anything happen to our mother, I have enough in England for myself and mine, and shall resign all our lands here in Virginia to him."

"You don't mean that, George?" she cried, her eyes brightening. "Well, to be sure, it is but right and fair. Why should you, the eldest by an hour, possess everything—a palace and lands in England, the plantation here, the title, and children—while my poor Harry has none? Yet it is generous of you... handsome and proper. And you do not take after your mother in this, Sir George, not at all. Give my love to sister Theo!" She offered me her cheek to kiss before I departed. With a woman like Fanny guiding him, how could I ever hope to convert my brother?

Disappointed, I rode back to the Governor, who agreed it was time to arm earnestly against the impending shock. His Court of Officials was agitated, savage in their abuse of the "wicked Whigs," and loud in their shouts for Old England, yet all were eager for the day when they could ride down their enemies hand-to-hand. I left with the thanks of his Excellency in Council, pledged to raise a body of men to defend the Crown. Thus began the corps known as the Westmoreland Defenders, of which I was appointed Colonel. The announcement in the Government Gazette drew officers readily, but recruits were slow to arrive and quick to vanish. Nevertheless, friend Hagan eagerly offered himself as chaplain, Madam Esmond provided our colors, and my old tutor, little Mr. Dempster, who had fought on the Jacobite side in Scotland, ventured into the Carolinas to recruit among the descendants of his banished comrades, who remained fiercely loyal to the Crown.

Meanwhile, Hal's expedition led him far beyond the Blue Mountains to Annapolis, Baltimore, and finally Philadelphia, where the second General Congress sat. The almanacs recorded the turning point: Lexington had fallen, and the first shots of the war for independence were fired. We still professed loyalty to His Majesty, yet we declared our determination to die or be free. Twenty thousand loyal petitioners assembled around Boston with arms and cannon seized from government stores. Benedict Arnold began his infamous career with the daring capture of two forts. Generals from London marched to aid General Gage, but the British commenced their campaign of conquest with the glorious blunder of Breed's Hill. Fortifying themselves, they watched the rebel armies while Congress deliberated on who should command the confederated forces.

History records the fortunate choice of the nation. Among the Virginian regiments marching to join the new General-in-Chief was one commanded by Henry Esmond Warrington, Esq., formerly a Captain in His Majesty's service, accompanied by his brave little wife. I was glad she had left Virginia; had she remained, our mother would inevitably have joined the fray, sparing our family the terror of civil war.

The rush of farmers and country folk flowed toward the northern army, flattered by the selection of a Virginian gentleman for principal command. The provinces reacted with a thrill of wrath to the blood spilled at Lexington, yelling denunciations against the "bloody British invader." Yet the invader was merely doing his duty, met by men resisting the seizure of their own property. People did not weigh their words when angry; the colonists had chosen their side, determined to test their strength against the domineering mother country. Breed's Hill became a symbol, a mountain where Liberty, Victory, and Glory burned on its summit. Farmers and ploughmen could withstand these dreaded troops; doctors, lawyers, and civilians could outgeneral famous officers! If Britons could conquer the world, surely their children across the Atlantic could match them. Indeed, I cannot decide which deserves the palm for bravery or vainglory.

For the most part, the people around us sided with the revolution. Sir George Warrington found his regiment of Westmoreland Defenders thinly manned at the outset, and woefully diminished thereafter, not only due to news of battles from the north but because of the conduct of our Lord Governor. It had been agreed in countless meetings that he would plant the King's standard and summon loyal gentlemen to rally around it. I could recall the names of many gentlemen, now smug officers of the United States Government, who once prayed to perish under the folds of their country's flag or roared challenges to the "traitors" absent with the rebel army. But let bygones be bygones. Public history records that his lordship, a Scottish peer and the Sovereign's representative, who so loudly invited all lieges to join the King's standard, was the first to pocket it and flee to his ships. He would not leave them unless as a pirate at midnight to burn and destroy.

We loyal gentry remained on shore, committed to our cause, subject only to greater danger due to the weakness and cruelty of our supposed leader. It was early June; our orchards and gardens bloomed with summer plenty. A week prior, I had exchanged compliments with his Excellency in Williamsburg, devising plans to make good head against rebellion, shaking hands heartily, with *vincere aut mori*—to conquer or die—as the last words on our lips. Our family was gathered at Richmond, discussing the prospects in the north and the quarrels between the Assembly and the Governor, when our ghostly Hagan rushed into our parlour. "Have we heard the news of the Governor?" he asked.

"Has he dissolved the Assembly again, and put that scoundrel Patrick Henry in irons?" queried Madam Esmond.

"No such thing! His lordship, with his lady and family, left their palace privately at night. They are aboard a man-of-war off York, whence my lord sent a despatch begging the Assembly to continue sitting, announcing he had only quit his Government House out of fear of the people's fury."

What was to become of the sheep now that the shepherd had fled? No entreaties were more pathetic than those of the gentlemen of the House of Assembly, who guaranteed their Governor security if he would land, imploring him to appear to transact necessary business. No: the man-of-war was his seat of government, and he demanded his House of Commons wait upon him there. This was erecting the King's standard with a vengeance. Our Governor had abandoned us; the Assembly ruled in his stead; a rabble followed the fugitive Viceroy to his ships. A mob of negroes deserted the plantations to join this other deserter. He and his black allies landed here and there in darkness, emulating our opponents in their alacrity to seize and burn. He invited runaway negroes and sent ambassadors to Indians to join his standard. When he came ashore, it was to burn and destroy; when the people resisted, as at Norfolk and Hampton, he retreated to his ships.

Even my mother, after this miserable flight of our chief, was scared by the aspect of affairs, doubting the rebellion's suppression. The arming of negroes, in her opinion, was the most cowardly blow of all. Many loyal gentry were ruined and robbed. A score of our worst hands deserted Richmond and Castlewood to flee to the Governor's fleet; some were slain, and a couple hung by the enemy for plunder. Because her property was wantonly injured and His Majesty's chief officer an imbecile, would Madam Esmond desert the cause of Royalty and Honour? My good mother was never so prodigiously dignified, loudly and enthusiastically loyal, as after hearing of our Governor's lamentable defection. The people around her, though of different minds, listened to her speeches without unkindness. Her oddities were known far and wide, and many young wags smoked her, drawing out her stories of her father the Marquis and her family's splendor. Yet, alongside her oddities, her charities and kindness were remembered, earning her a sneaking regard from many a rebel.

As for the Colonel of the Westmoreland Defenders, though his command dwindled utterly after his chief's outrageous conduct, I escaped serious danger. After the Governor burned the stores at Hampton and issued his proclamation calling negroes to his standard, I boarded his ship to remonstrate with him. I implored him to return to Williamsburg, where hundreds, perhaps thousands, would defend him to the last extremity. My behavior indicated such clear contempt for his conduct that his lordship flew into a rage, declaring me a rebel like all the rest, and ordering me under arrest on his own ship. In my capacity as a militia officer, wearing a red coat to show I wore the King's color, I begged for an immediate court-martial. Turning to two officers present, I requested they remember all that had passed. These gentlemen, undoubtedly sharing my view of the chief's behavior, ensured my interview ended with me going ashore unaccompanied by a guard.

The story spread among the Whig gentry, embellished in the telling. I had spoken my mind manfully; no Whig could have uttered sentiments more liberal. When riots broke out in Richmond and Loyalists sought refuge on the ships, my mother's property and house were never endangered, nor her family insulted. We were still at the stage where reconciliation seemed possible. "Ah! if all the Tories were like you," a distinguished Whig once told me, "we and the people at home should soon come together again." This was before the famous Fourth of July and the Declaration that rendered reconciliation impossible. Afterwards, when parties grew rancorous, motives much less creditable were assigned for my conduct. It was said I chose to be a Liberal Tory because I was a cunning fox wishing to keep my estate regardless of the outcome. And this, I am bound to say, is the opinion regarding my humble self which has obtained in very high quarters at home, where a profound regard for one's own interest is often supposed to dictate conduct during unhappy troubles.

There were two or three persons who knew I had no mercenary motives regarding my resolution to cede my life-interest in our American property to my brother. It was not worth while to undeceive others; what was life worth if a man were forced to feel himself a *la piste* of all calumnies? I do not know exactly why my mother, that notorious Loyalist, was left undisturbed in her house at Castlewood for several years, save for occasional quartering of Continental troops. I can only guess the cause. Madam Fanny, after a campaign before Boston, returned to Fanny's Mount, leaving her Colonel behind. My modest Hal, until the war's conclusion, accepted no higher rank, believing he could be more useful commanding a regiment than a division. Remarkably, after her return, Madam Fanny's old asperity toward my mother seemed removed, replaced by affection for her and all

In Which We Both Fight and Run Away

What utility is there in a Colonel without a regiment? The Governor and Council, who had once paraded such extravagant gratitude for endowing me with my commission, were nowhere to be seen. They had fled to the safety of their ships, leaving behind a trail of piracy and arson on the shore. Lord Dunmore's black allies had scattered his own kin; and beyond these negroes summoned to arms, rumors flew that he had dispatched envoys to the Southern Indians, promising them a descent in numbers to tomahawk our people into submission. "And these are to be our allies!" I told my mother, exchanging a grim look with her, the memory of that savage whose face had glared over mine, and whose knife had been at my throat when Florac struck him down on Braddock's Field, returning with ghastly clarity. We fortified Castlewood as best we could, yet it was the red men and the blacks, not the rebels, that filled us with dread. I had never seen my mother lose her courage until she recounted the particulars of our father's death in an Indian raid more than forty years prior. One night, seeing figures move before our house, the good lady refused all persuasion that they were anything but savages; she sank to her knees, crying, "The Lord have mercy upon us! The Indians—the Indians!"

Lord Dunmore's negro allies vanished aboard his ships or wherever pay and plunder awaited them; the painted heroes from the South never appeared, though I confess I looked upon my mother's grey head, my wife's brown hair, and our child's golden ringlets with a horrible pang of doubt, fearing they might fall victims to this ruffian war. It was we who fought with such weapons and enlisted these allies! Yet, dare I not set myself up as an interpreter of Providence, pointing out the special finger of Heaven as many are wont to do, I would say that our employment of these Indians and German mercenaries brought their own retribution upon us in this war. In the field, where the mercenaries were attacked by the Provincials, they yielded, and it was triumphing over them that so raised the spirit of the Continental army; and the murder of one woman, Miss McCrea, by a half-dozen drunken Indians, did more harm to the Royal cause than the loss of a battle or the destruction of regiments.

Now that the Indian panic had subsided, Madam Esmond's courage returned, and she became seriously uneasy at the danger I ran by remaining in Virginia. "What harm can they do me, a poor woman?" she asked. "If I have one son, a Colonel without a regiment, I have another with a couple of hundred Continentals behind him in Mr. Washington's camp. If the Royalists come, they will let me off for your sake; if the rebels appear, I shall have Harry's passport. I do not wish, sir, I do not like that your delicate wife and this dear little baby should be here, increasing the risk of all of us! We must have them away to Boston or New York. Do not talk of defending me! Who will think of hurting a poor, harmless, old woman? If the rebels come, I shall shelter behind Mrs. Fanny's petticoats, and shall be much safer without you in the house than in it." She said this partly because it was reasonable, but more so because she was determined to remain in the land where her father was buried and where she was born. She was living backwards, so to speak. She had seen the new generation, blessed them, and bade them farewell. She belonged to the past, to old days and memories.

While we debated the Boston scheme, news came that the British had evacuated that luckless city altogether, never having ventured to attack Mr. Washington in his camp at Cambridge, though he lay there for many months without powder at our mercy. They waited until he procured ammunition, seized and fortified Dorchester Heights, which commanded the town, and out of which the whole British army and colony were obliged to beat a retreat. That the King's troops won the battle of Bunker's Hill, there is no more doubt than that they beat the French at Blenheim; but through the war, their chiefs seemed constantly afraid of assaulting entrenched Continentals afterwards. Else, why, from July to March, hesitate to strike an almost defenseless enemy? Why the hesitation at Long Island, when the Continental army was in our hand? Why that astonishing timorousness of Howe before Valley Forge, where the relics of a force starving, sickening, and in rags could scarcely man the lines, which they held before a great, victorious, and perfectly appointed army?

As the hopes and fears of the contending parties rose and fell, it was curious to mark the altered tone of the partisans of either. When the news of the evacuation of Boston reached us in the country, every little Whig in the neighborhood made his bow to Madam and advised her to a speedy submission. She did not carry her loyalty quite so openly as heretofore, flaunting her flag in the faces of the public, but she never swerved. Every night and morning in private, poor Hagan prayed for the Royal Family in our own household, and on Sundays any neighbors were welcome to attend the service, where my mother acted as a very emphatic clerk, and the prayer for the High Court of Parliament under our most religious and gracious King was very stoutly delivered. The brave Hagan was a parson without a living, as I was a Militia Colonel without a regiment. Hagan had continued to pray stoutly for King George in Williamsburg, long after his Excellency our Governor had run away; but on coming to church one Sunday to perform his duty, he found a corporal's guard at the church-door, who told him that the Committee of Safety had put another divine in his place and requested he keep a quiet tongue in his head. He told the men to "lead him before their chiefs"—our honest friend always loved tall words and tragic attitudes—and accordingly was marched through the streets to the Capitol, with a chorus of white and colored blackguards at the skirts of his gown. He had an interview with Messrs. Henry and the new State officers, confronting the robbers, as he said, in their den. Of course, he intended to make an heroic speech before these gentlemen (and was one of many men who perhaps would have no objection to be made martyrs, so that they might be roasted *coram populo*, or tortured in a full house), but Mr. Henry was determined to give him no such chance. After keeping Hagan three or four hours waiting in an anteroom in the company of negroes, when the worthy divine entered the new chief magistrate's room with an undaunted mien and began a prepared speech with—"Sir, by what authority am I, a minister of the----" "Mr. Hagan," says the other, interrupting him, "I am too busy to listen to speeches. And as for King George, he has henceforth no more authority in this country than King Nebuchadnezzar. Mind you that, and hold your tongue, if you please! Stick to King John, sir, and King Macbeth; and if you will send round your benefit-tickets, all the Assembly shall come and hear you. Did you ever see Mr. Hagan on the boards, when you was in London, General?" And, so saying, Henry turned round upon Mr. Washington's second in command, General Lee, who was now come into Virginia upon State affairs, and our shamefaced good Hagan was bustled out of the room, reddening, and almost crying with shame. After this event, we thought that Hagan's ministrations were best confined to us in the country, and removed the worthy pastor from his restive lambs in the city.

The selection of Virginians to the very highest civil and military appointments of the new government bribed and flattered many of our leading people, who, otherwise, and but for the outrageous conduct of our government, might have remained faithful to the Crown and made good head against the rising rebellion. But, although we Loyalists were gagged and muzzled, though the Capitol was in the hands of the Whigs, and our vaunted levies of loyal recruits so many Falstaff's regiments for the most part, the faithful still kept intelligences with one another in the colony and with our neighbors. Although we did not rise, and although we ran away, and although, in examination before committees, justices, and so forth, some of our frightened people gave themselves Republican airs and vowed perdition to kings and nobles, yet we knew each other pretty well. According as the chances were more or less favorable to us, the master more or less hard, we concealed our colors, showed our colors, half showed our colors, or downright apostatised for the nonce, and cried, "Down with King George!" Our negroes bore about, from house to house, all sorts of messages and tokens. Endless underhand plots and schemes were engaged in by those who could not afford the light. The battle over, the neutrals came and joined the winning side, shouting as loudly as the patriots. The runaways were not counted. Will any man tell me that the signers and ardent well-wishers of the Declaration of Independence were not in a minority of the nation, and that the minority did not win? We knew that a part of the defeated army of Massachusetts was about to make an important expedition southward, upon the success of which the very greatest hopes were founded. I, for one, being anxious to make a movement as soon as there was any chance of activity, had put myself in communication with the ex-Governor Martin of North Carolina, whom I proposed to join, with three or four of our Virginian gentlemen, officers of that notable corps of which we only wanted privates. We made no particular mystery about our departure from Castlewood; the affairs of Congress were not going so well yet that the new government could afford to lay any particular stress or tyranny upon persons of a doubtful way of thinking. Gentlemen's houses were still open; and in our southern fashion we would visit our friends for months at a time. My wife and I, with our infant and a fitting suite of servants, took leave of Madam Esmond on a visit to a neighboring plantation. We went thence to another friend's house, and then to another, till finally we reached Wilmington, in North Carolina, which was the point at which we expected to stretch a hand to the succours which were coming to meet us.

Ere our arrival, our brother Carolinian Royalists had shown themselves in some force. Their encounters with the Whigs had been unlucky. The poor Highlanders had been no more fortunate in their present contest in favor of King George than when they had drawn their swords against him in their own country. We did not reach Wilmington until the end of May, by which time we found Admiral Parker's squadron there, with General Clinton and five British regiments on board, whose object was a descent upon Charleston.

The General, to whom I immediately made myself known, seeing that my regiment consisted of Lady Warrington, our infant whom she was nursing, and three negro servants, received us at first with a very grim welcome. But Captain Horner of the *Sphinx* frigate, who had been on the Jamaica station and received, like all the rest of the world, many kindnesses from our dear Governor there when he was stationed there, eagerly received her on board when he heard that my wife was General Lambert's daughter, and gave up his best cabin to our service; and so we were refugees, too, like my Lord Dunmore, having waved our flag, to be sure, and pocketed it, and slipped out at the back door. From Wilmington we bore away quickly to Charleston, and in the course of the voyage and our delay in the river, previous to our assault on the place, I made some acquaintance with Mr. Clinton, which increased to a further intimacy. It was the King's birthday when we appeared in the river; we determined it was a glorious day for the commencement of the expedition.

It did not take place for some days after, and I leave out, purposely, all descriptions of my Penelope parting from her Hector, going forth on this expedition. In the first place, Hector is perfectly well (though a little gouty), nor has any rascal of a Pyrrhus made a prize of his widow: and in times of war and commotion, are not such scenes of woe and terror, and parting, occurring every hour? I can see the gentle face yet over the bulwark, as we descend the ship's side into the boats, and the smile of the infant on her arm. What old stories, to be sure! Captain Miles, having no natural taste for poetry, you have forgot the verses, no doubt, in Mr. Pope's *Homer*, in which you are described as parting with your heroic father; but your mother often read them to you as a boy, and keeps the gorget I wore on that day somewhere amongst her dressing-boxes now.

My second venture at fighting was no more lucky than my first. We came back to our ships that evening thoroughly beaten. The madcap Lee, whom Clinton had faced at Boston, now met him at Charleston. Lee, and the gallant garrison there, made a brilliant and most successful resistance. The fort on Sullivan's Island, which we attacked, was a nut we could not crack. The fire of all our frigates was not strong enough to pound its shell; the passage by which we moved up to the assault of the place was not fordable, as those officers found—Sir Henry at the head of them, who was always the first to charge—who attempted to wade it. Death by shot, by drowning, by catching my death of cold, I had braved before I returned to my wife; and our frigate being aground for a time and got off with difficulty, was agreeably cannonaded by the enemy until she got off her bank.

A small incident in the midst of this unlucky struggle was the occasion of a subsequent intimacy which arose between me and Sir Harry Clinton, and bound me to that most gallant officer during the period in which it was my fortune to follow the war. Of his qualifications as a leader there may be many opinions: I fear to say, regarding a man I heartily respect and admire, there ought only to be one. Of his personal bearing and his courage there can be no doubt; he was always eager to show it; and whether at the final charge on Breed's Hill, when at

To the military mind, the entrenchments of Breed's Hill were the salvation of the Continental Army throughout the entire war. The slaughter inflicted upon us from behind those lines was so severe, and the enemy's behavior so resolute, that the British chiefs thereafter respected the American barricades. If the foe were firing from behind a row of blankets, certain of our generals hesitated to force them. At White Plains, when Washington's army stood at the mercy of the victors, we later learned that our conquering troops were held back before a barricade composed merely of cornstalks and straw. Another opportunity was granted us, lasting through a whole winter, during which the dwindling, dismayed troops of Congress lay starving and unarmed under our grasp. Yet the magnanimous Mr. Howe left the famous camp of Valley Forge untouched, while his great, brave, and perfectly appointed army fiddled and gambled and feasted in Philadelphia. Byng's countrymen erected triumphal arches, held tournaments in pleasant mockery of the Middle Ages, and offered wreaths and garlands to this clement chief, with fantastical mottoes announcing that his laurels should be immortal! Why have my ungrateful countrymen in America never erected statues to this general? They had not in all their army an officer who fought their battles better; who enabled them to retrieve their errors with such adroitness; who took care that their defeats should be so little hurtful to themselves; and who, when the stronger force naturally got the uppermost, showed such untiring tenderness, patience, and complacency in helping the poor disabled opponent onto his legs again. Ah! Think of eighteen years prior, and the fiery young warrior whom England had sent out to fight her adversary on the American continent. Fancy him forever pacing round the defenses behind which the foe lay sheltered; by night and by day alike sleepless and eager; consuming away in his fierce wrath and longing, never closing his eye, so intent was it in watching; winding the track with untiring scent that panted and hungered for blood and battle; prowling through midnight forests, or climbing silent over precipices before dawn; and watching till his great heart was almost worn out, until the foe showed himself at last, when he sprang on him and grappled with him, and, dying, slew him! Think of Wolfe at Quebec, and hearken to Howe's fiddles as he sits smiling amongst the dancers at Philadelphia!

A favorite scheme with our ministers at home and some of our generals in America was to establish a communication between Canada and New York, by which means it was hoped New England might be cut off from the neighboring colonies, overpowered in detail, and forced into submission. Burgoyne was entrusted with the conduct of the plan, and he set forth from Quebec, confidently promising to bring it to a successful issue. His march began in military state: the trumpets of his proclamations blew before him; he bade the colonists to remember the immense power of England; and summoned the misguided rebels to lay down their arms. He brought with him a formidable English force, an army of German veterans not less powerful, a dreadful band of Indian warriors, and a brilliant train of artillery. It was supposed that the people round his march would rally to the Royal cause and standards. The Continental force in front of him was small at first, and Washington's army was weakened by the withdrawal of troops hurried forward to meet this Canadian invasion. A British detachment from New York was to force its way up the Hudson, sweeping away the enemy on the route, and make a junction with Burgoyne at Albany. Then was the time when Washington's weakened army should have been struck too; but a greater Power willed otherwise: nor am I, for one, even going to regret the termination of the war. As we look over the game now, how clear seem the blunders which were made by the losing side! From the beginning to the end we were forever arriving too late. Our supplies and reinforcements from home were too late. Our troops were in difficulty, and our succours reached them too late. Our fleet appeared off York Town just too late, after Cornwallis had surrendered. A way of escape was opened to Burgoyne, but he resolved upon retreat too late. I have heard discomfited officers in after days prove infallibly how a different wind would have saved America to us; how we must have destroyed the French fleet but for a tempest or two; how once, twice, thrice, but for nightfall, Mr. Washington and his army were in our power. Who has not speculated, in the course of his reading of history, upon the "Has been" and the "Might have been" in the world? I take my tattered old map-book from the shelf, and see the board on which the great contest was played; I wonder at the curious chances which lost it: and, putting aside any idle talk about the respective bravery of the two nations, can't but see that we had the best cards, and that we lost the game.

I own the sport had a considerable fascination for me, and stirred up my languid blood. My brother Hal, when settled on his plantation in Virginia, was perfectly satisfied with the sports and occupations he found there. The company of the country neighbors sufficed him; he never tired of looking after his crops and people, taking his fish, shooting his ducks, hunting in his woods, or enjoying his rubber and his supper. Happy Hal, in his great barn of a house, under his roomy porches, his dogs lying round his feet; his friends, the Virginian Will Wimbles, at free quarters in his mansion; his negroes fat, lazy, and ragged: his shrewd little wife ruling over them and her husband, who always obeyed her implicitly when living, and who was pretty speedily consoled when she died! I say happy, though his lot would have been intolerable to me: wife, and friends, and plantation, and town life at Richmond (Richmond succeeded to the honor of being the capital when our Province became a State). How happy he whose foot fits the shoe which fortune gives him! My income was five times as great, my house in England as large, and built of bricks and faced with freestone; my wife—would I have changed her for any other wife in the world? My children—well, I am contented with my Lady Warrington's opinion about them. But with all these plums and peaches and rich fruits out of Plenty's horn poured into my lap, I fear I have been but an ingrate; and Hodge, my gatekeeper, who shares his bread and scrap of bacon with a family as large as his master's, seems to me to enjoy his meal as much as I do, though Mrs. Molly prepares her best dishes and sweetmeats, and Mr. Gumbo uncorks the choicest bottle from the cellar. Ah me! Sweetmeats have lost their savour for me, however they may rejoice my young ones from the nursery, and the perfume of claret palls upon old noses! Our parson has poured out his sermons many and many a time to me, and perhaps I did not care for them much when he first broached them. Dost thou remember, honest friend? (sure he does, for he has repeated the story over the bottle as many times as his sermons almost, and my Lady Warrington pretends as if she had never heard it)—I say, Joe Blake, thou rememberest full well, and with advantages, that October evening when we scrambled up an embrasure at Fort Clinton and a clubbed musket would have dashed these valuable brains out, had not Joe's sword whipped my rebellious countryman through the gizzard. Joe wore a red coat in those days (the uniform of the brave Sixty-third, whose leader, the bold Sill, fell pierced with many wounds beside him). He exchanged his red for black and my pulpit. His doctrines are sound, and his sermons short. We read the papers together over our wine. Not two months ago we read our old friend Howe's glorious deed of the first of June. We were told how the noble Rawdon, who fought with us at Fort Clinton, had joined the Duke of York: and to-day his Royal Highness is in full retreat before Pichegru: and he and my son Miles have taken Valenciennes for nothing! Ah, parson! Would you not like to put on your old Sixty-third coat? (Though I doubt Mrs. Blake could never make the buttons and button-holes meet again over your big body). The boys were acting a play with my militia sword. Oh, that I were young again, Mr. Blake! That I had not the gout in my toe; and I would saddle Rosinante and ride back into the world, and feel the pulses beat again, and play a little of life's glorious game!

The last "hit" which I saw played was gallantly won by our side; though 'tis true that even in this parti the Americans won the rubber—our people gaining only the ground they stood on, and the guns, stores, and ships which they captured and destroyed, whilst our efforts at rescue were too late to prevent the catastrophe impending over Burgoyne's unfortunate army. After one of those delays which always were happening to retard our plans and weaken the blows which our chiefs intended to deliver, an expedition was got under weigh from New York at the close of the month of September, '77; that, could it have but advanced a fortnight earlier, might have saved the doomed force of Burgoyne. *Sed Dis aliter visum*. The delay here was not Sir Henry Clinton's fault, who could not leave his city unprotected; but the winds and weather which delayed the arrival of reinforcements which we had long awaited from England. The fleet which brought them brought us long and fond letters from home, with the very last news of the children under the care of their good Aunt Hetty and their grandfather. The mother's heart yearned towards the absent young ones. She made me no reproaches: but I could read her importunities in her anxious eyes, her terrors for me, and her longing for her children. "Why stay longer?" she seemed to say. "You who have no calling to this war, or to draw the sword against your countrymen—why continue to imperil your life and my happiness?" I understood her appeal. We were to enter upon no immediate service of danger; I told her Sir Henry was only going to accompany the expedition for a part of the way. I would return with him, the reconnaissance over, and Christmas, please Heaven, should see our family once more united in England.

A force of three thousand men, including a couple of slender regiments of American Loyalists and New York Militia (with which latter my distinguished relative, Mr. Will Esmond, went as captain), was embarked at New York, and our armament sailed up the noble Hudson River, that presents finer aspects than the Rhine in Europe to my mind: nor was any fire opened upon us from those beetling cliffs and precipitous "palisades," as they are called, by which we sailed; the enemy, strange to say, being for once unaware of the movement we contemplated. Our first landing was on the Eastern bank, at a place called Verplancks Point, whence the Congress troops withdrew after a slight resistance, their leader, the tough old Putnam (so famous during the war) supposing that our march was to be directed towards the Eastern Highlands, by which we intended to penetrate to Burgoyne. Putnam fell back to occupy these passes, a small detachment of ours being sent forward as if in pursuit, which he imagined was to be followed by the rest of our force. Meanwhile, before daylight, two thousand men without artillery, were carried over to Stoney Point on the Western shore, opposite Verplancks, and under a great hill called the Dunderberg by the old Dutch lords of the stream, and which hangs precipitously over it. A little stream at the northern base of this mountain intersects it from the opposite height on which Fort Clinton stood, named not after our general, but after one of the two gentlemen of the same name, who were amongst the oldest and most respected of the provincial gentry of New York, and who were at this moment actually in command against Sir Henry. On the next height to Clinton is Fort Montgomery; and behind them rises a hill called Bear Hill; whilst at the opposite side of the magnificent stream stands "Saint Antony's Nose," a prodigious peak indeed, which the Dutch had quaintly christened.

The attacks on the two forts were almost simultaneous. Half our men were detached for the assault on Fort Montgomery, under the brave Campbell, who fell before the rampart. Sir Henry, who would never be out of danger where he could find it, personally led the remainder, and hoped, he said, that we should have better luck than before the Sullivan Island. A path led up to the Dunderberg, so narrow as scarcely to admit three men abreast, and in utter silence our whole force scaled it, wondering at every rugged step to meet with no opposition. The enemy had not even kept a watch on it; nor were we descried until we were descending the height, at the base of which we easily dispersed a small force sent hurriedly to oppose us. The firing which here took place rendered all idea of a surprise impossible. The fort was before us. With such arms as the troops had in their hands, they had to assault; and silently and swiftly, in the face of the artillery playing upon them, the troops ascended the hill. The men had orders on no account to fire. Taking the colours of the Sixty-third, and bearing them aloft, Sir Henry mounted with the stormers. The place was so steep that the men pushed each other over the wall and through the embrasures; and it was there that Lieutenant Joseph Blake, the father of a certain Joseph Clinton Blake, who looks with the eyes of affection on a certain young lady, presented himself to the living of Warrington by saving the life of the unworthy patron thereof.

About a fourth part of the garrison, as we were told, escaped out of the fort, the rest being killed or wounded, or remaining our prisoners within the works. Fort Montgomery was, in like manner, stormed and taken by our people; and, at night, as we looked down from the heights where the king's standard had been just planted, we were treated to a splendid illumination in the river below. Under Fort Montgomery, and stretching over to that lofty prominence, called Saint Antony's Nose, a boom

Under the shade of the ancient vine and fig-tree, where the summer air hangs heavy and sweet, I pause to recount the joys of our reunion. The sight of the mother, radiant with the happiness of her brood gathered once more beneath her wings, was written plainly upon her face and acknowledged in the humble posture of her knees. Our home, spacious and welcoming, could easily have housed us all; yet Aunt Hetty refused to remain. With a fairness that belied her sorrow, she declared that to relinquish her motherhood over the elder children—hers for nearly three years—inflicted a pain too great to bear. She could not endure being relegated to the second place among them. Thus, she and her father departed for a house at Bury St. Edmunds, not far from us, where she indulged her eldest nephew and niece in private seclusion.

It was the year following our return that Mr. B, the Jamaican planter, passed away, leaving Aunt Hetty half his fortune. Only then did I learn of the worthy gentleman's profound affection for her in Jamaica; though she had refused him, he had demonstrated his constancy through this legacy. Heaven knows how much of Aunt Hetty's inheritance Monsieur Miles has already consumed—the cost of his commission and attire, his resplendent uniforms, his gambling debts, and his frivolous transactions in the Minories. Do you truly believe, sirrah, that I am unaware of the price of human nature? What is the cost of Pall Mall taverns, *petits soupers*, and even moderate gaming at the Cocoa-Tree? Can a gentleman sustain such pleasures on the five hundred pounds a year I allow him? Aunt Hetty has resolved to remain a spinster. "I vowed never to marry until I found a man as good as my dear father," she told me, "and I never did, Sir George. Nor, my dearest Theo, was there anyone half as good; and Sir George may smoke that thought in his pipe."

Yet, when the good General died—calm, full of years, and glad to depart—I believe it was my wife who wept the most. "I weep because I fear I did not love him enough," the tender creature confessed. In contrast, Hetty barely concealed her composure, outwardly at least, before us. She speaks of him constantly as if he were still alive, recalling his merry sayings and his gentle kindness toward his children, causing her to brighten and look once again like a girl. She sits cheerfully gazing at the slab in the church that records his name and virtues, and for once, she tells no lies.

I had often fancied that my brother Hal, for whom Hetty harbored a youthful passion, retained a hold on her heart. When he visited us ten years prior, I mentioned this childish romance of Hetty's, hoping, I admit, that he might ask her to replace Mrs. Fanny, who had been gathered to her fathers. My wife, with her usual propensity to consider herself a miserable sinner, reproached herself endlessly for not regretting Fanny enough. Hal arrived plunged in grief, vowing that no such woman existed in the world. Our dear old General, still living then, took him in and housed him as he had in his happy early days. The women played him the same tunes he had heard as a boy at Oakhurst. Hearts were softened by old memories, and Harry never tired of pouring out his griefs and recitals of his wife's virtues to Hetty, often speaking fondly of his dear Aunt Lambert, whom he loved with all his heart. The praises of the faithful old husband were always welcome, for his wife's memory seemed never absent from his thoughts for more than three waking minutes.

General Hal went to Paris as an American General Officer in blue and yellow livery—a fashion Mr. Fox and others had introduced here—and was much admired at Versailles. Though presented by Monsieur le Marquis de Lafayette to the Most Christian King and Queen—who did not love the Marquis—a Marquise took a fancy to the Virginian General and would have married him instantly had he not resisted, fleeing back to England, Warrington, and Bury, especially the latter, where the locals listened to his tales of his late wife with endless patience and sympathy. As for us, who had known the poor paragon, we were civil but not entirely enthusiastic regarding her, often puzzled to answer our children's questions about Uncle Hal's angel wife.

The two Generals, myself, Captain Miles, and Parson Blake—who was knocked over at Monmouth the year after I left America to change his coat and take my living—used to fight the battles of the Revolution over our bottle. The parson would cry, "By Jupiter, General" (compounding for Jupiter when he laid down his military habit), "you are the Tory, and Sir George is the Whig! He is always finding fault with our leaders, while you stand forever in their defense. When I prayed for the King last Sunday, I heard you following me quite loudly."

"And so I do, Blake, with all my heart; I can't forget I wore his coat," Hal replied.

"Ah, if Wolfe had been alive for twenty years more!" said Lambert.

"Ah, sir," cried Hal, "you should hear the General talk about him!"

"What General?" I asked, to vex him.

"My General," Hal said, standing up and filling a bumper. "His Excellency General George Washington!"

"With all my heart," I cried, though the parson looked as if he disliked the toast or the claret.

Hal never tired of speaking of his General. It was on such an evening of friendly converse that he told us how he had actually fallen into disgrace with this General whom he loved so fondly. Their difference concerned Monsieur le Marquis de Lafayette, who played such a fine part in recent history and has so suddenly vanished from it. Hal's previous rank in our own service and his acknowledged gallantry during the war ought to have secured his promotion in the Continental army, where a whipper-snapper like M. de Lafayette arrived and was immediately complimented by Congress with the rank of Major-General. Hal, with the freedom of an old soldier, expressed contempt for some appointments made by Congress, where unscrupulous officers greedy for promotion were busy with intrigues and cabals. Mr. Warrington, perhaps imitating his now illustrious friend of Mount Vernon, affected to make the war *en gentilhomme*. He took his pay, certainly, but spent it on comforts and clothing for his men. As for rank, he declared it a matter of no earthly concern, stating he would as soon serve as colonel as in any higher grade. No doubt he added contemptuous remarks regarding certain General Officers of the Congress army, their origins, and the causes of their advancement. He was particularly angry about the sudden promotion of the young French lad, the Marquis, a prodigious favorite of the Chief himself. There were not three officers in the whole Continental force (after poor madcap Lee was taken prisoner and disgraced) who could speak the Marquis's language, allowing Hal to judge the young Major-General more closely and familiarly than other gentlemen, including the Commander-in-Chief. Mr. Washington good-naturedly rated friend Hal for being jealous of the beardless commander of Auvergne; he was himself pleased by the filial regard and profound veneration the enthusiastic young nobleman always showed him, and had the very best politic reasons for treating the Marquis with friendship and favor.

Meanwhile, as it afterwards turned out, the Commander-in-Chief was most urgently pressing Colonel Warrington's promotion upon Congress. As if his difficulties before the enemy were not enough—he was at this hard time of winter entrenched at Valley Forge, commanding five or six thousand men at most, almost without fire, blankets, food, or ammunition, in the face of Sir William Howe's army, which was perfectly appointed and three times as numerous as his own—he had further to encounter the cowardly distrust of Congress and insubordination and conspiracy among the officers in his own camp. During the awful winter of '77, when one blow struck by the sluggard at the head of the British forces might have ended the war, and all was doubt, confusion, and despair in the opposite camp (save in one indomitable breast alone), my brother had an interview with the Chief, which he has subsequently described to me, and of which Hal could never speak without giving way to the deepest emotion. Mr. Washington had won no such triumph as that which the dare-devil courage of Arnold and the elegant imbecility of Burgoyne had procured for Gates and the northern army. Save in one or two minor encounters proving his daring bravery and unceasing watchfulness, General Washington met defeat after defeat from an enemy superior in all points. The Congress mistrusted him. Many an officer in his own camp hated him. Those who had been disappointed in ambition, those detected in peculation, and those whose selfishness or incapacity his honest eyes had spied out were all, more or less, in league against him. Gates was the chief toward whom the malcontents turned. Mr. Gates was the only genius fit to conduct the war; and with a vaingloriousness which he afterwards generously owned, he did not refuse the homage paid him.

To show how dreadful were the troubles and anxieties with which General Washington had to contend, I may mention what was then called the "Conway Cabal." A certain Irishman—a Chevalier of St. Louis and an officer in the French service—arrived in America early in the year '77 in quest of military employment. He was speedily appointed to the rank of brigadier and could not be contented without an immediate promotion to major-general. Mr. C. had friends at Congress who, as the General-in-Chief was informed, had promised him his speedy promotion. General Washington remonstrated, representing the injustice of promoting to the highest rank the youngest brigadier in the service. While the matter was pending, he was put in possession of a letter from Conway to General Gates, whom he complimented, saying, "Heaven had been determined to save America, or a weak general and bad councillors would have ruined it." The General enclosed the note to Mr. Conway without a word of comment; and Conway offered his resignation, which was refused by Congress, who appointed him Inspector-General of the army with the rank of Major-General.

"And it was at this time," says Harry, with many passionate exclamations indicating his rage with himself and his admiration of his leader, "when, by heavens, the glorious Chief was oppressed by troubles enough to drive ten thousand men mad—that I must interfere with my jealousies about the Frenchman! I had not said much, only some nonsense to Greene and Cadwalader about getting some frogs against the Frenchman came to dine with us, and having a bagful of Marquises over from Paris, as we were not able to command ourselves—but I should have known the Chief's troubles, and that he had a better head than mine, and might have had the grace to hold my tongue."

"For a while the General said nothing, but I could remark, by the coldness of his demeanour, that something had occurred to create a schism between him and me. Mrs. Washington, who had come to camp, also saw that something was wrong. Women have artful ways of soothing men and finding their secrets out. I am not sure that I should have ever tried to learn the cause of the General's displeasure, for I am as proud as he is, and besides" (says Hal), "when the Chief is angry, it was not pleasant coming near him, I can promise you." My brother was indeed subjugated by his old friend, obeying him and bowing before him as a boy before a schoolmaster.

"At last," Hal resumed, "Mrs. Washington found out the mystery. 'Speak to me after dinner, Colonel Hal,' says she. 'Come out to the parade-ground, before the dining-house, and I will tell you all.' I left a half-score of general officers and brigadiers drinking round the General's table and found Mrs. Washington waiting for me. She then told me it was the speech I had made about the box of Marquises with which the General was offended. 'I should not have heeded it in another,' he had said, 'but I never thought Harry Warrington would have joined against me.'"

"I had to wait on him for the word that night and found him alone at his table. 'Can your Excellency give me five minutes' time?' I said, with my heart in my mouth. 'Yes, surely, sir,' says he, pointing to the other chair. 'Will you please to be seated?'

"'It used not always to be Sir and Colonel Warrington, between me and your Excellency,' I said.

"He said, calmly, 'The times are altered.'

"'Et nos mutamur in illis,' says I. 'Times and people are both changed.'

"'You had some business with me?' he asked.

"'Am I speaking to the Commander-in-Chief or to my old friend?' I asked.

"He looked at me gravely. 'Well,—to both, sir,' he said. 'Pray sit, Harry.'

"'If to General Washington, I tell his Excellency that I, and many officers of this army, are not well pleased to see a boy of twenty made a major-general over us, because he is a Marquis, and because he can't speak the English language. If I speak to my old friend, I have to say that he has shown me very little of trust or friendship for the last few weeks; and that I have no desire to sit at your table and have impertinent remarks made by others there of the way in which his Excellency turns his back on me.'

"'Which charge shall I take first, Harry?' he asked, turning his chair away from the table and crossing his legs as if ready for a talk. 'You are jealous, as I gather, about the Marquis?'

"'Jealous, sir!' says I. 'An aide-de-camp of Mr. Wolfe is not jealous of a Jack-a-dandy who, five years ago, was being whipped at school!'

"'You yourself declined higher rank than that which you hold,' says the Chief, turning a little red.
